Decimal Encodings Rational #### A.1.1. Decimal Encoding and Compact Format Compact format was designed specifically for use with decimal encoding. The goal was to allow two parties to establish mutual authentication by exchanging a short numeric code — something a person can read aloud, hear, and enter on a keypad without difficulty. To maximize entropy within a small number of digits, Compact format minimizes header overhead, leaving as many bits as possible for IKM. Voice channels (telephone, video call) are a natural fit for this exchange: they are widely accessible, require no special software, and do not leave a long-lived record of the exchanged message. Transmitting an mTOTP message over a persistent unencrypted channel such as email is discouraged (see Section X). - [ ] Figure out which section I was intending to link to and update the above "Section X" note (with link). Decimal encoding is not the highest-entropy encoding available, and Compact format carries fewer negotiation options than Extended. These are accepted tradeoffs in exchange for simplicity and accessibility. #### A.1.2. Decimal Encoding: Message Length Derivation The bit length of a decimal-encoded message is fully determined by the digit count. No out-of-band length field is required. Both Compact (Format bit `0`) and Extended (Format bit `1`) messages are recovered correctly because $B_{message}$ is derived from $N_S$ independently of the integer's magnitude. #### A.1.3. Decimal Encoding: Floating-Point Arithmetic The IKM bit length and message bit length formulas for decimal encoding require floating-point evaluation of $\log_{10}(2)$ and $\log_2(10)$. This has been verified to produce correct results for all values within the scope of this specification using IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic. Implementations SHOULD verify their computed values against the test vectors in [Appendix C.](#appendix-c-test-vectors), which serve as the authoritative reference regardless of floating-point implementation. ### A.2. Key Derivation: Fixed Protocol Salt RFC 9106 recommends a randomly generated 128-bit salt for Argon2id. mTOTP uses a fixed protocol salt instead. This forces an attacker to build a precomputation table specifically for this protocol rather than reusing existing tables. Per-exchange uniqueness is provided by the IKM entropy. ### A.3. TOTP Parameter Compatibility The TOTP parameters defined in Section 6.4 (HMAC-SHA-256, 30-second time step, Unix epoch, 6 output digits) were chosen for compatibility with widely deployed TOTP implementations. Fixing these parameters eliminates the need for per-exchange parameter negotiation and removes them from the message format overhead. ### A.4. Difficulty Scale Rational #### A.4.1. Difficulty Scale Design Goals The KDF difficulty field provides forward-compatible tuning of key-derivation work within a single protocol version, without consuming additional header bits as hardware improves. It is constrained by the following goals: 1. A single integer expresses difficulty for all supported KDFs. 2. The same integer value across algorithms represents approximately equivalent attacker cost, such that capability advertisement does not need to be per-algorithm. 3. The scale spans from parameters implementable on commodity mobile hardware (2018-era smartphones) through parameters intended for hardware at least one decade beyond publication. 4. Parameters for every level are fully specified in this document; no runtime parameter derivation is performed. Both parties MUST produce identical parameters from identical inputs. #### A.4.2. Attacker Cost Model Security is measured in **time-area product (AT)**, the product of the circuit area occupied by a single KDF evaluation and the wall-clock time required for that evaluation on attacker hardware [ARGON2-PAPER]. This is the metric Argon2 was explicitly designed to maximize, and it is the metric used in this document to compare levels across algorithms. The protocol permits a minimum of 64 bits of shared entropy and does not use a salt. The attacker is therefore assumed to perform keyspace precomputation amortized across all users sharing a given entropy length. A difficulty level MUST be chosen such that the AT cost of computing $2^{64}$ KDF evaluations exceeds any economically rational adversary's budget. #### A.4.3. Scale Definition The difficulty field is 3 bits, yielding 8 levels (0 through 7). Each increment of the difficulty field represents approximately a 4x increase in attacker AT cost. The 4x step was chosen for the following reasons: 1. **It matches scrypt's natural granularity.** scrypt's cost parameter N MUST be a power of 2 [RFC7914](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7914). Each doubling of N doubles both memory and the number of sequential operations over that memory, yielding 4x AT cost per step. Finer-grained scrypt scaling requires manipulating the r parameter, which departs from the widely-deployed $r=8$ configuration recommended by [RFC7914](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7914) and degrades performance on common implementations due to cache effects. 2. **It aligns with the hardware improvement rate.** Moore's Law doubles transistor density roughly every 18-24 months. A 4x cost step therefore corresponds to approximately 3-4 years of attacker hardware improvement. An 8-level scale thus covers 24-32 years of projected hardware advancement, which allows additional leeway for unforeseen advancement during that period. 3. **It respects the precision of the underlying threat model.** Estimates of future attacker capability (GPU memory bandwidth, ASIC economics, TMTO advances) are uncertain to well more than a factor of 2. #### A.4.4. I read it carefully. The core construction is sound — symmetric IKM contribution, opposite concatenation orderings to get directional secrets without coordination, decimal encoding for voice exchange. That's a clean idea and the framing around the usability tradeoff is honest. But there are a handful of issues that range from "definitely a bug" to "you should think harder about this," and given your background you'll spot the implications faster than I can spell them out.

**Definitely wrong / contradictions in the spec:**

1. **The Message Format bit table is inverted relative to the rest of the document.** §3.1 says `0` = Extended, `1` = Compact. But §3.2.1 justifies starting Extended versions at `01` "so that any valid Extended message is guaranteed to contain a `1` bit within the first three bits" — which only makes the leading-zero argument work if Extended's format bit is `1`, not `0`. Either the table in §3.1 is backwards or §3.2.1's rationale (and the version numbering scheme) is. Worth a careful pass to figure out which one you meant. Related: §A.1.2 also says "Both Compact (Format bit `0`) and Extended (Format bit `1`)" — which contradicts §3.1 and agrees with §3.2.1.

2. **§5.2 describes negotiation that Compact Format can't actually do.** Step 2 says "select the lower of the two advertised maximum difficulty levels" — but Compact Format has no difficulty field at all (§3.3.1, total overhead 7 bits, no difficulty bits). And step 1's three-way algorithm preference assumes the 3-bit Extended algorithm bitmask, not Compact's 1-bit field. §5.2 needs to branch on format, or you need a separate negotiation section for Compact.

3. **§8.3 references a nonexistent salt.** The text says `"MTOTP-v0"` (uppercase M) "provide domain separation" — both a casing mismatch with the actual `mTOTP-v0` salt used in §3.1.2 and §5.3, and a subject-verb agreement bug. Minor, but it's exactly the kind of thing that ends up copy-pasted into an implementation.

4. **The TOTP parameter table reference is dead.** §A.3 says "The TOTP parameters defined in Section 6.4" — there's no §6.4. They're in §5.4.

**Substantive concerns I'd want you to push on:**

5. **The salt argument in §A.2 is weaker than it reads.** "Forces an attacker to build a precomputation table specifically for this protocol" is true but trivial — the cost of relabeling a precomputation effort to a new protocol is essentially zero once the protocol is public and has any deployed userbase worth attacking. With a 64-bit minimum combined IKM and a *fixed* salt across all users of the protocol, you have exactly the rainbow-table-friendly setup that per-user salts were invented to prevent. The KDF hardness is doing all the work here; the fixed salt is providing domain separation between protocol versions and nothing else of cryptographic substance. The text should say that plainly rather than implying it provides meaningful precomputation resistance. The Critical Review Notice is honest about the entropy floor; §A.2 should match that honesty.

6. **The 5-bit checksum's domain-separation claim is overstated.** §3.1.2 says the HMAC-keyed checksum "makes the checksum distribution distinct from raw SHA-256 output" and reduces the chance of accepting unrelated-system output. With 5 bits of checksum, 1-in-32 random inputs will pass the check regardless of what HMAC key you used. It's a transcription-error detector, not a protocol identifier. I'd cut the domain-separation framing or be much more careful about what it actually buys you (which is: nothing, against a non-pathological adversary).

7. **"Message Format (1 bit)" plus "Message Checksum (5 bits) occupies the five least significant bits" is ambiguous about bit ordering across the byte-boundary padding.** §3.1.2 says B is "zero-padded on the right to the nearest byte boundary" before HMAC, but the checksum field itself is "the five least significant bits of every mTOTP message" — and the message has no natural byte alignment (39 bits for Compact, 14+IKM for Extended). You're treating the message as a big-endian arbitrary-precision integer (per §4.1.1 step 5), which makes "least significant bits" well-defined for the integer — but the HMAC input B is described in terms of bit concatenation with right-padding, which is a different mental model. A reader implementing this needs to know: is the checksum input the bits *as concatenated* (left-justified, right-padded with zeros to byte boundary), or is it derived from the integer representation? These give different answers when the IKM length isn't a multiple of 8. Test vectors will pin this down, but the prose currently lets two reasonable implementations disagree.

8. **The "version starts at `01` to avoid leading-zero ambiguity" reasoning doesn't fully hold up.** The decimal encoding pads to exactly $N_S$ digits with significant leading zeros (§4.1.1 step 6), and the decoder counts digits to recover $B_{message}$ (§4.1.2 step 2). So leading zeros in the *binary* are not ambiguous — they're recovered from the digit count. The first-bit-is-1 rule is doing something else: it's ensuring the integer magnitude is large enough that you can't accidentally type a shorter valid message. That's a useful property but it's not what the rationale says. (And again, it depends on which value of the format bit means Extended — see issue 1.)

9. **§5.3 derives two 256-bit secrets but §5.4 specifies HMAC-SHA-256 TOTP.** That's consistent (HMAC-SHA-256 takes any-length keys, 256 bits is fine) but worth noting that this departs from §6238 deployment reality, where the overwhelmingly common configuration is HMAC-SHA-1 with 160-bit keys and most authenticator apps assume SHA-1 unless the `otpauth://` URI says otherwise. §A.3 claims compatibility with "widely deployed TOTP implementations" which is shaky — Google Authenticator, for example, only added SHA-256/SHA-512 support relatively recently and many third-party apps still don't. If interop with existing TOTP infrastructure is a goal, this is a real friction point. If it isn't, the rationale should say so.

10. **The §A.4.11 math really is wrong, as the TODO suspects.** RFC 9106's anti-tradeoff condition is $t > \log_2(m) - 26$ where $m$ is in *KiB-blocks of 1 KiB* (i.e., memory in KiB). For $m$ = 8192 MiB = 8,388,608 KiB, $\log_2(8{,}388{,}608) = 23$, so the condition is $t > 23 - 26 = -3$. The arithmetic in the draft happens to land on the right answer (trivially satisfied) but the units are sloppy — "memory_in_blocks" with the block size unstated, and 8388608 is the number of KiB, not the number of Argon2 blocks-of-1024-bytes if you read literally. Worth tightening.

**Smaller stuff worth a sweep:**

- §3.2.3 KDF Algorithm field is described as a bitmask ("each bit indicates support") but the table only shows the three single-bit values. What does `011` (PBKDF2 + scrypt) or `111` (all three) mean? The negotiation rule in §5.2 implies these are valid, but §3.2.3 only tabulates singletons. Either say "table shows the bit assignments; any combination is valid" explicitly or list the combinations.
- §A.1.3 hand-waves the floating-point claim ("verified to produce correct results for all values within the scope") without saying what the scope is or showing the calculation. For decimal, $C = \log_2(10) \approx 3.3219$, and $\lfloor N_S \cdot C \rfloor$ can be sensitive to rounding when $N_S \cdot C$ is very close to an integer. A small worked bound (e.g., for $N_S \leq 200$ the error in IEEE 754 double of $N_S \cdot \log_2(10)$ is bounded by X, well below 1) would replace hand-waving with proof. Or just say "use rational arithmetic" if you don't want to do the analysis.
- "Decimal Encodings Rational" / "Difficulty Scale Rational" in the appendix headings — should be "Rationale." Five places.
- §3.3.3's bit table is confusingly framed: "Value 0 = scrypt supported, Argon2id not supported / Value 1 = both supported." That's not really "indicating the highest-security algorithm the device supports" — it's a single bit that means "do I also support Argon2id." Fine, but the prose and table should agree on the framing.

**The big strategic question I'd raise, given your steganography background:** mTOTP's threat model in §8.1 explicitly punts on confidentiality of the exchange ("under user control") — which is fine as a scope boundary, but the protocol then leans heavily on the *KDF* to compensate for low entropy. The implicit security claim is something like: "even if Mallory passively records the 12-digit exchange, brute-forcing 64 bits through Argon2id at level 0 is uneconomical." That's *probably* true today against most adversaries, but the composition you actually want to state and analyze is "$\Pr[\text{adversary forges TOTP after observing exchange}]$ as a function of (entropy, KDF cost, time-since-pairing, attacker AT budget)." The current §8 is, as the TODO admits, a placeholder. When you write the real one, the framing should be: passive eavesdropper on the exchange channel is *the* threat model (active MitM is excluded by assumption), and the security parameter is KDF-AT-cost-times-keyspace-coverage, not "64 bits of entropy" in isolation. Your instinct that security definitions need to compose into something meaningful applies here directly.

The bones of the protocol are fine — symmetric construction, no server, sensible encoding choices. Most of what I've flagged is editorial cleanup, ambiguity tightening, and one genuinely-confusing format-bit inversion. I'd want to see test vectors before signing off on anything though; several of the bit-ordering and encoding details are the kind of thing where two implementers will disagree silently and not interoperate.

chat_messages.text:
The deepfake-defense framing is real and the problem is genuinely worth solving, but I think the premise has a gap your friend should close before going further.

**The use case, charitably reconstructed:** Alice gets a call from "Bob" — her bank, her mother, her CEO, whoever. The voice sounds right. The video looks right. But it might be a real-time deepfake. She wants a way to verify, *during the call*, that the person on the other end is actually Bob. The mTOTP pitch: at some prior trusted moment (in person, or during a call she's confident wasn't deepfaked), Alice and Bob exchange 12-digit codes and each app derives a pair of directional secrets. From then on, when "Bob" calls, Alice's app shows a 6-digit code that Bob's app should be displaying simultaneously, and vice versa. If the codes match in both directions, it's really Bob. A deepfaker who didn't compromise either device can't produce the right code.

That's a coherent threat model and TOTP doesn't solve it as-is, because TOTP is one-directional (server authenticates user) and requires server-mediated provisioning. The bidirectional, peer-to-peer, no-server property is genuinely the thing you need for human-to-human authentication. So far so good.

**Where I think the premise is shakier than she's letting on:**

1. **The "TOTP is too cumbersome" claim is misdirected.** Plain TOTP isn't cumbersome — it's *wrong-shaped* for this problem. You can't just hand someone a TOTP secret and call it mutual auth, because TOTP doesn't authenticate the verifier. The cumbersomeness she's solving isn't TOTP's UX, it's the absence of any peer-to-peer mutual auth primitive in the consumer authenticator-app ecosystem. Framing it as "TOTP but easier" undersells what mTOTP actually is and oversells what TOTP could do if you just streamlined it. She'd be on firmer ground saying "there is no widely-deployed peer-to-peer mutual auth primitive that humans can bootstrap over a voice call, and here's one."

2. **Voice-channel exchange is exactly the channel deepfakes attack.** This is the real conceptual issue. The protocol's security depends on the initial 12-digit exchange happening over a channel where Alice and Bob can authenticate each other — §8.1 says "voice channels where speakers authenticate each other by voice recognition reduce the practical feasibility" of MitM. But the *whole motivation* is that voice recognition is no longer reliable because deepfakes exist. So the bootstrap step assumes the very property the protocol is designed to provide. That's circular. It works if you assume the bootstrap happens *before* deepfakes are good enough or *in person*, and then mTOTP defends all *future* calls — which is a real and useful security gain! But the spec needs to be explicit: this is a trust-on-first-contact protocol, and the first contact has to be authenticated by some means other than mTOTP itself. Deepfakes don't go away; they just get deferred to whenever you couldn't verify in person.

3. **The realistic deployment is in-person bootstrap, not voice.** If you and your mom meet for dinner and exchange 12-digit codes across the table, then forever after you can verify each other on calls — that's a clean story. If you and your bank's fraud department exchange codes when you open the account in branch, ditto. But the spec keeps emphasizing voice/telephone exchange as the natural use case, which is the *one channel where the bootstrap is most vulnerable*. I'd flip the priority: in-person and pre-existing-E2EE-channel are the primary bootstrap modes; voice is a fallback for when those aren't available and the user accepts the residual risk.

4. **The "common scammers" framing in the Critical Review Notice doesn't quite match the deepfake-defense framing.** The notice justifies 64-bit minimum entropy by saying it's for "regular users... quickly and easily protecting themselves from common scammers." The deepfake angle is real and timely, and a peer-to-peer mutual TOTP variant is a legitimately useful primitive. That's worth shipping. The deepfake-eradication framing will get her torn up by reviewers who'll point out — correctly — that the bootstrap problem is the hard part and mTOTP punts on it.

chat_messages.text:
Good topic to dig into. Pyanodons is interesting precisely because it tries harder than most mods to model real industrial chemistry, and coal/kerogen processing is one of the places where the gap between "gestures at reality" and "actually mirrors reality" gets exposed. Let me walk through both pathways.

## Coal distillation in Py

The Py chain (in Py Coal Processing / Py Raw Ores) takes raw coal through a sequence roughly like: coal → coke + coal gas + coal tar (in coke ovens), then coal tar gets fractionated into things like creosote, naphtha, and pitch, with coal gas feeding into early hydrogen and syngas chains.

This actually maps reasonably well onto historical **destructive distillation of coal** (pyrolysis in the absence of oxygen). Real coke oven byproducts in a 19th/early-20th-century gasworks or byproduct coke plant include:

- **Coke** (the solid residue, mostly carbon) — for metallurgy
- **Coal gas** — mostly H₂, CH₄, CO, with some ethylene and benzene vapor
- **Coal tar** — a complex mix of aromatics: benzene, toluene, xylenes (BTX), naphthalene, anthracene, phenols, plus pitch as the heavy residue
- **Ammoniacal liquor** — the source of ammonium sulfate fertilizer historically
- **Light oil** — separately recoverable, source of crude benzene

Where Py gets it right: the *topology* is correct. One feedstock genuinely does fan out into a gas stream, a liquid tar stream, and a solid residue, and the tar genuinely does fractionate further into lighter aromatics and heavier pitch. The fact that early petrochemistry, dye chemistry, and explosives all historically came out of coal tar (Perkin's mauve, picric acid, TNT precursors) before petroleum displaced it is real history.

Where Py simplifies or fudges:

1. **Ammonia and sulfur recovery is usually missing or misattributed.** Real coke ovens are a major historical source of ammonia (→ ammonium sulfate) and elemental sulfur (from H₂S in the gas via Claus process). Py tends to route ammonia through nitrogen fixation instead, which is anachronistic for the early game — Haber-Bosch came *after* coal-tar ammonia was already industrial.
2. **Coal gas composition is collapsed to a single fluid.** Real coal gas is a mixture you'd want to separate (H₂ for hydrogenation, CH₄ for fuel, CO for syngas, ethylene for polymerization). Py mostly treats it as one thing or a small number of things, which loses the interesting separation chemistry.
3. **Naphtha from coal tar is treated as interchangeable with petroleum naphtha.** Coal-tar naphtha is heavily aromatic (BTX-rich); petroleum naphtha is mostly aliphatic. They feed different downstream chains in reality. Py mostly ignores this — a missed opportunity given your design philosophy about physical constraints driving gameplay.
4. **No ash chemistry.** Real coal ash contains recoverable trace elements (germanium, gallium, vanadium, rare earths in some coals). For a geology-grounded sim, this is a natural hook.

## Kerogen from stone mining

This is the more interesting case to interrogate, because Py's framing ("kerogen as a byproduct of stone mining") is doing some violence to geology.

**Kerogen is real and important.** It's the insoluble organic macromolecule in sedimentary rocks — the precursor to petroleum. Type I (lacustrine, algal) gives oil shales like the Green River formation; Type II (marine) gives most conventional petroleum source rocks; Type III (terrestrial, woody) tends to give gas and is associated with coal measures; Type IV is essentially dead carbon.

You extract usable hydrocarbons from kerogen by **retorting** — heating oil shale to ~450–500°C in the absence of oxygen, which thermally cracks the kerogen into shale oil + gas + spent shale. This is genuinely a historical and current industrial process (Estonia runs its power grid on it; the US tried hard in the 1970s/80s; in-situ retorting has been attempted).

**Where Py departs from reality:**

1. **"Stone" is not a kerogen host.** Kerogen lives in **organic-rich sedimentary rocks** — specifically oil shales (which are really kerogen-bearing marlstones or mudstones, not true shales geologically), some coals, and source rocks generally. Generic "stone" in Factorio implicitly suggests something like granite or limestone — neither of which contains meaningful kerogen. A geologically honest version would have kerogen come from a *specific* lithology you have to identify and target.
2. **Conflation of kerogen and bitumen.** Kerogen is *insoluble* in organic solvents — that's the definition. Bitumen (extractable from tar sands) is the soluble fraction. Py sometimes blurs these, treating kerogen as if you could just dissolve it out, which isn't how oil shale processing works.
3. **No retort thermodynamics.** The energy balance of oil shale retorting is famously marginal — you spend a substantial fraction of the recovered energy on the retorting itself, which is *exactly* the kind of constraint that makes for interesting gameplay (and is why oil shale has never displaced conventional petroleum economically). Py treats it as a more-or-less free conversion.
4. **No spent shale problem.** Retorting produces an enormous volume of spent shale (the rock actually *expands* after retorting due to popcorn effects), which is a real disposal headache. Great gameplay hook, ignored.

## Where this points for your project

Given your design philosophy, the Py chains are useful as a *starting topology* but underutilize the constraints that would make them interesting:

- **Lithology specificity.** Coal seams, oil shale beds, tar sands, and conventional petroleum reservoirs should be distinct geological features your mantle/sedimentary simulation can actually produce. Type II marine source rock vs. Type III coal measure isn't flavor text — it determines what the retort outputs.
- **Composition as a vector, not a scalar.** Coal gas, coal tar, shale oil, and crude oil should all be modeled as compositions over a basis of actual compounds (or at least compound classes — paraffins, olefins, aromatics, heteroatoms), and downstream processes should be sensitive to that composition. This is exactly the place your atomic-transformation API (Heat, Mix, Separate) earns its keep — fractional distillation is just `Separate` parameterized by boiling point ranges over a real composition vector.
- **Energy accounting.** Retorting and coking both have real energy balances. If your `Heat` operation tracks enthalpy honestly, the marginal economics of oil shale falls out naturally.
- **Historical sequencing.** Coal tar chemistry → synthetic dyes → explosives → early polymers is a real tech tree that predates petroleum, and matches your bootstrapping arc (stone/charcoal/copper/bronze/iron) well. Petroleum should be a later unlock that *displaces* coal-tar chemistry by being cheaper, not by being unlocked first.

Want me to dig into a specific sub-chain — say, the BTX/aromatics fractionation, or the retort energy balance, or how to represent compositional fluids in the type system?

chat_messages.text:
Good catch on the charcoal question — Py is collapsing two genuinely different processes into one recipe shape, and the chemistry tells you exactly why.

## Wood vs. coal pyrolysis: same operation, different feedstock chemistry

Both processes are **destructive distillation** — heat in the absence of oxygen, drive off volatiles, leave a carbon-rich solid. So at the level of the abstract operation (`Heat` + `Separate` on an organic feedstock with no oxidizer), they really are the same thing. Py's instinct to use one recipe shape isn't crazy.

But the *composition* of what comes out is dramatically different, because the feedstock chemistry is different:

**Wood** is roughly 40–50% cellulose (a glucose polymer), 20–30% hemicellulose (mixed sugar polymers), 20–30% lignin (a cross-linked aromatic polymer), plus extractives. It's heavily oxygenated — the C:H:O ratio is roughly 1 : 1.4 : 0.7, so almost as much oxygen as carbon by mole.

**Bituminous coal** is the diagenetic/metamorphic end product of buried plant matter that has lost most of its oxygen and hydrogen over geological time. C:H:O is more like 1 : 0.8 : 0.1. It's enriched in aromatic carbon and depleted in oxygen.

This compositional difference cascades through the entire output spectrum:

| Output | Wood pyrolysis | Coal pyrolysis |
|---|---|---|
| Solid residue | Charcoal (~80–90% C, porous, reactive) | Coke (~90–95% C, dense, less reactive, fused) |
| Aqueous liquid | **Pyroligneous acid**: ~10% acetic acid, methanol, acetone, water | Ammoniacal liquor: NH₃, phenols, water |
| Tar | Wood tar: phenolics (guaiacol, syringol from lignin), levoglucosan, furans | Coal tar: BTX, naphthalene, anthracene, pitch |
| Gas | CO, CO₂, CH₄, H₂ — heavy on the oxygen-bearing species | H₂, CH₄, CO, ethylene, benzene vapor — much less CO₂ |

Notice the asymmetry: wood pyrolysis produces a *huge* amount of CO₂ and water and acetic acid because wood is full of oxygen that has to go somewhere. Coal pyrolysis can't produce much CO₂ because there isn't much oxygen in the feedstock to begin with — instead the carbon ends up in aromatic rings (the BTX and PAH fraction).

1. **The output should be charcoal, not coal.** These are not interchangeable for metallurgy in subtle ways: charcoal is more reactive (so it ignites and reduces faster), nearly sulfur-free (so it makes better iron and historically *was* the only iron-making fuel until coke was invented in the 1700s), but mechanically weak (so it crushes under blast furnace burden, which is why coke replaced it once iron production scaled up). For your bootstrapping arc this is a meaningful distinction — charcoal-fueled bloomeries should come *before* coke-fueled blast furnaces both technologically and in terms of scale.

2. **"Less fluid" is wrong in volume but right in value.** Wood actually produces *more* condensable liquid per unit dry mass than coal does — wood pyrolysis is famously wet because of all that oxygen. ## A better model

Your atomic-transformation API handles this naturally. The operation is one thing:

```
Pyrolyze : Solid[organic] × Heat → Solid[char] × Liquid[condensables] × Gas[volatiles]
```

```rust

    fixed_carbon: f32,      // becomes char
    volatile_matter: f32,    // becomes tar + gas
    moisture: f32,
    ash: f32,
    // and crucially, the chemistry of the volatile fraction:
    c_h_o_ratio: ElementalRatio,
    aromaticity: f32,        // lignin/coal-rank index
    sulfur: f32,
    nitrogen: f32,
}
```

High-oxygen feedstock → lots of CO₂ and H₂O and carboxylic acids in the condensate. High-aromaticity feedstock → BTX and PAHs in the tar. Sulfur in → H₂S in the gas (Claus-process feedstock). Nitrogen in → NH₃ in the aqueous condensate (fertilizer feedstock).

- **One recipe, infinite variants.** Different wood species, different coal ranks (lignite → sub-bituminous → bituminous → anthracite), peat, even biomass waste streams all use the same machine and the same operation, with outputs that differ in chemically honest ways.

- **Coal rank becomes meaningful gameplay.** Anthracite has high fixed carbon and low volatiles — great as a fuel, terrible for byproduct chemistry. Lignite is the opposite. Bituminous is the sweet spot for coking, which is why historically it's *the* coking coal. Players who survey their geology and find bituminous seams should genuinely have an advantage in the petrochemistry tech tree.

- **Charcoal vs. coke fall out naturally** because the residue inherits the feedstock's ash, sulfur, and structure. Charcoal char + low sulfur + low ash → good for early bloomery iron. Coke char + higher mechanical strength (from the plastic phase that bituminous coal goes through during coking — lignite and anthracite *can't* form coke because they don't soften) → good for blast furnaces.

- **The "plastic phase" is itself interesting.** Real coke-making requires the coal to pass through a softened, plastic state where particles fuse before resolidifying. This is why not all coal cokes well — it's a property of medium-rank bituminous coals specifically. You could model this as a phase-transition requirement on the feedstock composition: only feedstocks within a certain aromaticity/volatile-matter window produce structurally sound coke; outside that window you get a friable char that's fine for fuel but useless for blast furnace burden. That's a real geological constraint creating real gameplay differentiation, exactly in the spirit you're after.

## A historical-tech-tree implication

There's a nice progression that falls out of this:

1. **Charcoal era** (wood pyrolysis in earth pits or beehive kilns): byproducts vented and lost. You get fuel for bloomeries and early blast furnaces. Pyroligneous acid is wasted.
2. **Recovery era** (retort kilns with condensers): same operation, but now you collect the pyroligneous acid → distill it → acetic acid + methanol + acetone. This is real history; it's how acetic acid was made until ~1910 and how acetone was made for cordite production in WWI before Weizmann's bacterial fermentation process.
3. **Coal coking era** (beehive coke ovens): byproducts again vented, you just want coke for blast furnaces. Pollution everywhere.
4. **Byproduct coking era** (Otto-Hoffmann or similar): now you recover coal gas, tar, ammonia, light oil. This unlocks the entire aromatics/dye/explosives chain.

Each stage is the *same operation* with *better recovery infrastructure*, and each unlocks more of the composition vector. That's a clean, honest tech progression where the "tech" is genuinely about engineering capability rather than arbitrary unlock gating.

Good — let's map the real coal tar landscape, because Py's three-path framing actually corresponds to three real industrial choices, but the framing of one of them ("middle oil") is doing some compression that's worth unpacking.

## What coal tar actually is

Coal tar from a byproduct coke oven is a **black, viscous, foul-smelling liquid** that's roughly 10,000+ identified compounds, but practically dominated by:

- **Aromatic hydrocarbons**: benzene, toluene, xylenes (BTX), naphthalene, anthracene, phenanthrene, pyrene, fluoranthene, plus alkylated variants. Naphthalene alone is ~10% of tar by mass — it's the single largest component.
- **Phenolics**: phenol, cresols (o-, m-, p-), xylenols, naphthols. Collectively called "tar acids" because they're weakly acidic and extractable with NaOH.
- **Heterocyclic nitrogen bases**: pyridine, quinoline, isoquinoline, acridine, carbazole. Called "tar bases" because they're extractable with H₂SO₄.
- **Sulfur and oxygen heterocycles**: thiophene, benzothiophene, dibenzofuran.
- **Pitch**: the non-distillable residue, ~50–60% of tar by mass. A complex mixture of high-molecular-weight PAHs and heteroaromatics — essentially "everything that didn't boil off." Solid at room temperature.

The composition varies with coking conditions: high-temperature tar (coke ovens at ~1000°C) is more aromatic and gives less pitch; low-temperature tar (~600°C, semi-coking) is more aliphatic and phenol-rich. Py probably models high-temperature tar.

## The three industrial paths

### 1. Fractional distillation → aromatics

This is the historically dominant path and matches Py's "distillation into aromatics" recipe. Tar goes into a still (or, industrially, a continuous fractionating column) and gets cut into fractions by boiling point:

| Fraction | BP range | Major contents | Real uses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Light oil | <200°C | Benzene, toluene, xylenes, pyridine | Solvents, dye precursors, TNT (toluene → trinitrotoluene) |
| Middle/carbolic oil | 200–250°C | Phenol, cresols, naphthalene | Disinfectants, phenolic resins (Bakelite), naphthalene products |
| Heavy/creosote oil | 250–300°C | Naphthalene, methylnaphthalenes, dibenzofuran | Wood preservative, carbon black feedstock |
| Anthracene oil | 300–350°C | Anthracene, phenanthrene, carbazole | Dye precursors (alizarin from anthracene) |
| Pitch | residue | Heavy PAHs | Roofing, road tar, electrode binder, carbon fiber precursor |

This is one operation (fractional distillation) producing a *spectrum* of products, each of which then becomes a feedstock for a different downstream chain. The fanout you're noticing in Py is real — coal tar fractionation is *the* historical root of the synthetic organic chemicals industry. The first synthetic dye (Perkin's mauve, 1856) came from aniline derived from coal tar benzene. The German dye industry of the late 19th century (BASF, Bayer, Hoechst — the same companies that exist today) was built entirely on coal tar.

After fractionation, each fraction usually undergoes further separation: the light oil gets re-fractionated into pure benzene/toluene/xylenes, the carbolic fraction gets washed with NaOH to extract tar acids, then with H₂SO₄ to extract tar bases, leaving "neutral oil" rich in naphthalene that's recovered by crystallization (naphthalene actually crystallizes out as solid white flakes — this was a major industrial process).

### 2. Hydrogenation/cracking → "middle oil" (fuel)

Py's "refining into middle oil" recipe is, I'd guess, modeling **tar hydrogenation** — the Bergius process and its descendants.

Coal tar is hydrogen-poor (highly aromatic, lots of fused rings, lots of heteroatoms). If you treat it with H₂ at high pressure and temperature over a catalyst, you can:

- Saturate aromatic rings (benzene → cyclohexane, naphthalene → decalin)
- Crack PAHs into smaller fragments
- Hydrodesulfurize, hydrodenitrogenate, hydrodeoxygenate (remove S/N/O as H₂S, NH₃, H₂O)

The output is a mixture of saturated and partially saturated hydrocarbons resembling petroleum middle distillate — essentially **synthetic diesel/jet/heating oil**. This is the path Germany used in WWII to make synthetic fuel from coal (the Bergius-Pier process), and it's the path South Africa's Sasol still uses (though Sasol primarily uses Fischer-Tropsch from syngas, not direct tar hydrogenation).

So "middle oil" in Py is gameplay shorthand for "petroleum-equivalent middle distillate produced by hydrogenating tar instead of fractionating it." It's chemically real but it's a *destructive* path — you're paying a lot of H₂ and pressure to convert all those interesting aromatics into boring saturated fuel. You do it when you want fuel and have plenty of hydrogen, not when you want chemistry.

The interesting tradeoff is: **the same molecule (say, naphthalene) is worth far more as a chemical feedstock than as fuel**. Hydrogenating it to decalin and burning it is throwing away the aromatic ring you spent geological time and pyrolysis energy creating. This is a real economic principle in petrochemistry — "molecules too valuable to burn" — and it's why tar fractionation persisted commercially even after petroleum displaced coal as the primary energy source.

### 3. Quenching → tailings

This one is the most interesting because it's modeling something that's **not really a recipe in the chemistry sense** — it's modeling industrial waste disposal.

Historically, in early coke plants without byproduct recovery, the hot tar coming off the coke oven was quenched with water and either:
- Burned as low-grade fuel under the coke ovens
- Dumped on the ground (creating the "coal tar lagoons" that are now Superfund sites in the US)
- Used as a crude waterproofing agent (roofing tar, ship caulking)

In Py's framing, "quenching into tailings" is the lossy disposal path — you don't have the infrastructure to fractionate or hydrogenate, so you destroy the tar's chemical value to get rid of it. Chemically what's happening is: you're dispersing the tar into water (it doesn't dissolve, it forms an emulsion or sinks as DNAPL — dense non-aqueous phase liquid), letting the volatiles flash off (releasing carcinogenic PAHs into the air, which is why this was an environmental disaster), and the heavy fraction ends up in the solids stream.

If Py's tailings include some recovered material rather than literally everything being lost, that's a reasonable modeling choice — in practice quenched tar still has *some* salvage value (as crude pitch for roofing, etc.), just not the chemical-feedstock value of properly fractionated tar.

## The landscape, conceptually

What you have is one input (coal tar, which is itself a composition vector over ~10,000 compounds dominated by maybe 30 important ones) and three operations that differ in how much of the input's chemical structure they preserve:

1. **Fractionation** preserves molecular identity. You separate the existing molecules by physical property (boiling point), then by acid/base extraction, then by crystallization. No bonds are broken. Maximum information preservation, maximum downstream optionality. Output: a spectrum of pure or near-pure aromatic chemicals.

2. **Hydrogenation** destroys aromatic structure. You're breaking C=C double bonds and C-heteroatom bonds, replacing them with C-H bonds. Information is lost (you can't tell what naphthalene vs. methylnaphthalene became after hydrogenation). Output: a homogenized mixture of saturated hydrocarbons resembling petroleum.

3. **Quenching/disposal** destroys everything. Output: low-value bulk material plus environmental damage.

There's a nice information-theoretic ordering here: fractionation preserves ~all the molecular information in the tar; hydrogenation preserves the carbon skeleton but loses the unsaturation and heteroatom info; quenching loses essentially all of it.

## The fanout from fractionation

Once you've fractionated, the downstream chains are roughly:

- **Benzene** → nitrobenzene → aniline → dyes (mauveine, fuchsin, indigo); → cyclohexane → adipic acid → nylon-6,6; → cumene → phenol + acetone; → styrene → polystyrene; → ethylbenzene; → maleic anhydride
- **Toluene** → TNT; → benzoic acid; → toluene diisocyanate (TDI) → polyurethane; → dealkylation back to benzene
- **Xylenes** → terephthalic acid (from p-xylene) → PET; → phthalic anhydride (from o-xylene) → plasticizers; → isophthalic acid (from m-xylene)
- **Phenol** → phenol-formaldehyde resins (Bakelite); → bisphenol A → epoxy resins, polycarbonates; → salicylic acid → aspirin; → picric acid (early high explosive)
- **Cresols** → cresylic acid (disinfectant, "Lysol" originally); → tricresyl phosphate (plasticizer, hydraulic fluid); → BHT (antioxidant)
- **Naphthalene** → phthalic anhydride (also reachable from o-xylene); → β-naphthol → azo dyes; → naphthalenesulfonic acids → dispersants; → mothballs (the historical bulk use)
- **Anthracene** → anthraquinone → alizarin (the synthetic replacement for madder root, the dye that destroyed the natural dye industry in the 1870s); → vat dyes
- **Pyridine/quinoline** → nicotinic acid (niacin); → quinine analogs; → herbicides (paraquat from pyridine)
- **Pitch** → carbon black (incomplete combustion, used for tires, ink); → graphite electrodes (for steelmaking — full circle!); → carbon fiber precursor (mesophase pitch)

That's a partial list and it's still enormous. The "fanout" you're noticing in Py is faithful to the real industrial reality — coal tar genuinely is the historical wellspring of organic chemistry, and the fanout from a single tar barrel into dyes, plastics, pharmaceuticals, and explosives is one of the more remarkable industrial transformations of the 19th-20th century.

The petrochemical era didn't eliminate this fanout, it just changed the feedstocks. Most of the same end products (benzene, toluene, xylenes, phenol, naphthalene) are now made from petroleum naphtha by catalytic reforming, but the downstream chemistry is unchanged. Coal tar's share of global aromatics dropped from ~100% in 1900 to maybe 5% today, but the chemistry tree it built is still standing.

Want to drill into any particular branch? The aromatics → dyes branch is historically rich, the phenolics branch is where polymers start, and the pitch → carbon materials branch loops back to metallurgy in interesting ways.

If "destructive distillation" is the building that does both raw coal coking *and* the tar-to-aromatics-with-CO₂ recipe, then Py is grouping operations by **operating regime**, not by feedstock. A destructive distillation building is one that runs at high temperature, pyrolytic conditions, with the option of partial combustion — basically a coke oven generalized. That's a sensible equipment class because the same physical hardware (a refractory-lined vessel rated for ~1000°C, with provisions for sub-stoichiometric oxygen and condensable recovery) handles both:

- Coal → coke + tar + gas (the pyrolysis case)
- Tar → BTX + CO₂ + ash residue (the cracking case)

These really are the same operation thermodynamically: high-temperature pyrolytic decomposition of a carbonaceous feed, with partial combustion supplying heat and producing CO₂ as a byproduct. The fact that one starts with solid coal and the other with liquid tar is a feedstock difference, not a process difference. Real industrial coke ovens do in fact recycle heavy tar fractions back through the oven for exactly this reason — it's a natural place to crack the heaviest residues you don't have a market for.

So the "destructive distillation" recipe on tar isn't catalytic cracking in the FCC sense. It's **secondary pyrolysis** — running tar through a coke-oven-equivalent to thermally crack it. The mechanism is purely thermal (no catalyst needed, just heat), and the "rich clay" output is then probably not spent catalyst but rather **mineral residue/coke from the cracking process**, possibly including ash and trace metals concentrated from the tar feedstock. Tar does carry a non-trivial mineral load — vanadium, nickel, sometimes germanium and gallium in significant quantities — and thermal cracking concentrates these into the solid residue. "Rich clay" as a name for that residue is reasonable; it's a mineral-rich carbonaceous solid.

This is actually historically authentic too. Before catalytic cracking was invented in the 1930s-40s, **thermal cracking** was the dominant way to break heavy hydrocarbons into lighter ones — running them through hot tubes or chambers at 450-550°C and letting the high temperature do the work. Aromatics survive thermal cracking better than aliphatics (benzene rings are thermodynamically very stable), so a thermal cracker fed coal tar would preferentially yield BTX in the light fraction with a lot of coke and gas as byproducts. That's exactly the output pattern Py is showing.

## "Tar processing" as a separate building class

Then "tar processing" being a different building doing fractionation makes sense as a *lower-temperature, separation-focused* equipment class. A tar still operates at much milder conditions (200-400°C distillation column), no combustion, no chemical transformation — purely physical separation by boiling point. It's a fundamentally different kind of equipment: a fractionating column with multiple side draws, condensers, reflux. The metallurgy and instrumentation are completely different from a coke oven.

The "tops" and "bottoms" framing in Py is also industrially correct terminology:

- **Tops refining** = light/middle ends of the column. Splits the lighter fractions: light oil → BTX subfractions, middle oil → carbolic oil + naphthalene-rich residual.
- **Bottoms refining** = heavy ends. Splits the heavy fractions: heavy oil → creosote, anthracene oil → anthracene + phenanthrene, pitch as final residue.

Real tar refineries do exactly this — a primary still produces a few coarse cuts, and then dedicated secondary stills handle the tops fraction and the bottoms fraction separately because the temperatures and pressures and crystallization conditions are very different. You don't run benzene recovery on the same column as anthracene recovery.

The **creosote production from various oil grades** is a really nice touch on Py's part if it's modeled the way I think it is. Creosote isn't a pure compound — it's a *blend specification*. Industrial creosote is defined by its application (wood preservation, mostly) and it's produced by blending appropriate fractions from the tar still to hit the right composition: roughly naphthalenes + methylnaphthalenes + phenolics + heavier PAHs in a specified ratio with specified boiling range. So "creosote from various oil grades" reflects the reality that creosote is a *formulation* — you make it by blending heavy oil with anthracene oil and adjusting the phenolic content, not by isolating a single chemical species.

This is actually a more sophisticated modeling choice than treating creosote as a discrete chemical. Outputs are determined by thermodynamics at ~1000°C: stable molecules (benzene rings, CO, CO₂, H₂, CH₄) plus solid residue. Information-destructive: you can't recover the original molecular identity from the outputs.

**Tar processing building** → moderate-temperature separation regime, handles fractional distillation, extraction, and blending. Outputs are determined by physical properties (boiling point, solubility, crystallization). Information-preserving: every molecule that goes in comes out as itself, just sorted into different output streams.

These are genuinely different process classes in real chemistry — pyrolytic vs. separative — and giving them different buildings is a cleaner abstraction than I was crediting Py with. Yes, and I think this is a genuinely good design instinct — it aligns with both how real chemical plants are actually built *and* how your atomic-transformation API wants to factor things. Let me think through what the modular decomposition looks like, because both the pyrolysis column and the tar still are built from a relatively small kit of standard components.

## Real chemical plants are already modular

This is the key insight: a real refinery or coke plant *isn't* a collection of monolithic buildings. It's a collection of standard unit operations connected by piping. Walk into any refinery and you'll see the same kit repeated in different configurations:

- Furnaces (deliver heat at temperature)
- Reactors (vessels where chemistry happens — pyrolytic, catalytic, hydrogenation)
- Distillation columns (separate by boiling point)
- Heat exchangers (recover heat between streams)
- Condensers (phase change vapor → liquid)
- Separators / knockout drums (gravity separation of phases)
- Absorbers / scrubbers (selective extraction with a solvent)
- Pumps and compressors (move fluids, raise pressure)
- Storage tanks (hold inventory between operations)

A "coke oven" in industry is actually: a *furnace* (which is itself a combustion chamber + heat exchanger) feeding heat into a *retort vessel* (pyrolytic reactor), with the offgas going through a *condenser train* (multiple condensers at decreasing temperatures), then a *liquor-tar separator* (gravity separator), then *scrubbers* (for ammonia recovery, light oil recovery), then a *gas holder* (storage). It's seven or eight unit operations. The "building" you see from the outside is just the structural envelope around all of them.

A "tar still" is similarly: a *furnace* feeding a *fractionating column* with multiple side draws, each going to a *condenser*, *receiver tank*, and possibly a *crystallizer* (for naphthalene recovery), with the bottoms going to a *flash drum* and the pitch going to a *cooler*.

So Py's monolithic buildings are concealing a structure that's already there in reality. Decomposing them isn't introducing complexity — it's revealing complexity that the real industry has already abstracted into reusable components.

## The minimal modular kit

Here's what I think the kit looks like for your project, structured around what each component *does* in your atomic-transformation API:

**Furnace** — Heat source. Takes fuel + oxidizer, produces heat at controlled temperature, emits flue gas + ash. The single operation is `Heat`. Variants by temperature range: low (steam generation, ~150-300°C), medium (distillation, ~300-500°C), high (pyrolysis, ~500-1000°C), very high (sintering/smelting, >1000°C). Different fuels (charcoal, coal, coke, gas, oil) and different burner technologies determine achievable temperature and efficiency. The output is an abstract *heat stream* that other components consume.

**Reactor** — Where chemistry happens. A vessel that takes feed + heat (and optionally catalyst, additional reactants like H₂ or steam) and produces transformed products. The atomic operation depends on configuration: a simple thermal reactor does pyrolysis (`Crack`?), a catalyst-bed reactor does selective conversion, a hydrogenation reactor adds H₂ across unsaturated bonds. Variants by pressure rating, temperature rating, residence time, catalyst presence.

**Distillation column** — Separation by boiling point. Takes a multi-component liquid feed, produces multiple product streams with different volatility ranges. The atomic operation is `Separate` parameterized by boiling point cut points. Variants by number of stages (resolution of separation), pressure (atmospheric, vacuum, high pressure), and number of side draws (how many fractions you can pull).

**Condenser** — Vapor → liquid phase change. Takes hot vapor + cold coolant (water, air, refrigerant), produces liquid plus warmed coolant. The atomic operation is the inverse of `Heat` — a heat-removing operation. Variants by coolant type (sets the achievable condensation temperature) and surface area (capacity).

**Heat exchanger** — Heat transfer between two streams. Takes two streams at different temperatures, produces both streams at intermediate temperatures. No phase change in the basic version. This is what makes plants energy-efficient by recovering heat from product streams to preheat feed streams. The atomic operation is `TransferHeat`.

**Phase separator** — Gravity separation of immiscible phases. Takes a multi-phase mixture, produces separated streams (gas / oil / aqueous / solid). The atomic operation is `Separate` parameterized by density and solubility.

**Absorber / scrubber** — Selective extraction with a solvent. Takes a gas/liquid stream + a solvent stream, produces a depleted stream + a loaded solvent stream. The solvent is then regenerated (usually by heating in a separate column) to recover the absorbed component. The atomic operation is `Extract`. Variants by solvent type (NaOH for tar acids, H₂SO₄ for tar bases, water for ammonia, glycol for water removal, amines for CO₂/H₂S).

**Crystallizer** — Solid precipitation from a saturated solution. Takes a hot solution, cools it, produces solid crystals + mother liquor. The atomic operation is a temperature-driven `Separate`. Important for naphthalene recovery, salt production, sugar refining, etc.

**Compressor / pump** — Pressure increase on a fluid. Doesn't transform composition, just moves material against a pressure gradient. The atomic operation is `Pressurize`. Critical for high-pressure processes (hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis).

**Storage / surge tank** — Buffer between batch and continuous operations, or between operations running at different rates. Doesn't transform anything; it's a temporal buffer.

That's roughly ten components. Almost every chemical processing facility you can name is built from this kit plus a handful of specialized pieces (reformers, electrolyzers, polymerization reactors).

## How the kit reconstructs Py's monoliths

**Coke oven** = High-temperature furnace + retort vessel (reactor in pyrolytic mode) + cascade of condensers (high-temp first to drop tar, then lower-temp to drop light oil and aqueous condensate) + phase separator (tar/liquor split) + scrubber train (ammonia absorber, light oil absorber) + gas holder (storage).

**Tar still** = Medium-temperature furnace + fractionating column with side draws + array of condensers (one per side draw) + receiver tanks + optional crystallizer (for naphthalene from the heavy oil cut) + bottoms cooler (for pitch).

**Tops refining unit** = Smaller fractionating column + condenser + acid/base scrubbers (NaOH wash for phenolics, H₂SO₄ wash for pyridines) + neutralizer + crystallizer.

**Bottoms refining unit** = Vacuum fractionating column (vacuum because anthracene oil boils at 300+°C and you don't want to crack it by overheating) + condensers + crystallizer (anthracene crystallizes out) + pitch cooler.

**Catalytic cracker** = High-temperature furnace + reactor with catalyst bed + cyclone separator (catalyst recovery) + condenser train + fractionator + catalyst regenerator (a smaller reactor that burns coke off the spent catalyst).

**Hydrogenator** = High-pressure compressor (for H₂) + heat exchanger (preheat feed) + reactor with hydrogenation catalyst + flash drum (separate H₂ from products) + recycle compressor + product fractionator.

You can see that the same components recur — every one of these has a furnace, a reactor or column, condensers, and separators. The differences are in operating conditions, catalyst presence, and connection topology. *That's exactly the modular structure you want to expose.*

## What players gain from this

A few things that I think would land well for the educational and gameplay goals:

**Insight into industrial chemistry.** The reason real chemical engineers think in unit operations is that it's the right abstraction — it generalizes across feedstocks and products. A student who learns "this is a fractionating column, here's what it does" can then recognize that crude oil refineries, tar refineries, and air separation plants all use fractionating columns, with the differences being feed composition and operating conditions. Py's monoliths conceal this generalization; modular components reveal it.

**Construction as design problem.** Right now in Py you build one monolithic "tar refinery" and feed it tar. With modular components, you have to think about what you actually need: how many fractions do I want? Do I need a vacuum column for the heavy fractions or can I get away with atmospheric? Do I want a crystallizer for naphthalene or am I content to leave it in the heavy oil? This turns plant design into a real engineering exercise rather than a recipe-unlocking exercise.

**Reuse across contexts.** A fractionating column that handles tar can also handle crude oil, can also handle wood pyrolysis liquor, can also handle air separation if cooled enough. A furnace that fires a coke oven can also fire a smelter, a kiln, or a steam boiler. This dramatically reduces the building zoo and replaces it with a smaller component zoo whose members are *meaningful* — each one corresponds to a real engineering capability.

**Failure modes and bottlenecks become visible.** When the column is part of a monolithic building, you don't see that it's the bottleneck. When it's a discrete component with input and output rates, you can see "ah, the column is saturating, I need more stages or a parallel column." This mirrors how real plant engineers think about debottlenecking.

**Tech progression maps onto component improvements.** A primitive furnace might only achieve 600°C with charcoal; a coal-fired furnace reaches 1000°C; a regenerative furnace (with heat exchangers preheating combustion air, the way real Siemens-Martin furnaces work) reaches 1500°C. A primitive distillation column might have 10 theoretical plates; a modern one has 50. A primitive condenser uses ambient air; an advanced one uses refrigerated coolant to reach lower temperatures. The same *logical* operation gets *better parameters* over time. That's a cleaner tech tree than "unlock building X" because it lets the player understand *why* the new tech is better.

## Some design considerations

Two things to think about as you go down this path:

**Granularity tradeoff.** You can decompose further (a furnace is a combustion chamber + a heat exchanger; a column is a stack of trays each of which is a partial condenser/evaporator pair) but at some point the components stop corresponding to engineering decisions and start corresponding to physical-construction details that aren't interesting. The right granularity is "the level at which a real chemical engineer makes design choices." That's roughly the ten components above. Going finer-grained probably hurts more than it helps unless you're specifically trying to teach combustion or transport phenomena.

**Connection topology as content.** Once you have components, the *piping* — what feeds what, where streams split and recombine, where heat is recovered between streams — becomes the interesting design space. This is where chemical engineers spend most of their cognitive effort in real plant design. It's also where Factorio's belt/pipe puzzle becomes genuinely chemistry-relevant rather than just spatial logistics. Heat integration in particular is a beautiful constraint: every stream that needs heating and every stream that needs cooling represents a heat-exchanger opportunity, and a well-integrated plant uses 60-80% less external energy than a naively designed one. That could be a real and rewarding optimization layer.

**Physical-state tracking matters.** For modular components to compose correctly, your fluid system has to track temperature, pressure, and phase explicitly, not just composition. A condenser only works if the input is hot vapor; a column only works if you can boil and condense within it. This is more demanding than Factorio's "fluids are interchangeable colored liquids" model. But it's exactly the kind of physical-honesty constraint your design philosophy embraces — and once you have it, all the modular components compose correctly *because* the physics is being respected.

This is also where your `Heat`, `Mix`, `Separate`, `Flow` decomposition starts to pay off compositionally: each component is a small composition of these atomic operations applied to streams with explicit physical state. The "kit" is really a kit of *configurations* of the underlying atomic operations, parameterized by the operating conditions and equipment specs.

I think the modular approach is strictly better than monoliths for what you're trying to build, both pedagogically and as a simulation architecture. Want to think through one specific decomposition in more detail — maybe the coke oven, since it's the foundational early-game facility and exercises most of the kit?

Great question, and the answer is interesting because the byproduct recovery infrastructure didn't appear all at once — it accreted over about 150 years, with each piece enabled by prior advances in materials, instrumentation, and chemistry. Let me walk through the progression, because the order things became possible tells you a lot about what's *fundamentally hard* versus what's a refinement.

## The progression of coke oven technology

### Beehive ovens (~1620s–1900, dominant ~1800-1880)

The earliest coke ovens were literally domed brick structures shaped like beehives, ~3-4m diameter, holding maybe 5-6 tonnes of coal. You'd load coal through a hole in the top, light it, partially seal the openings, and let it burn slowly for 2-3 days. The combustion of volatiles inside the oven supplied the heat to coke the rest of the charge. After cooking, you'd quench with water and rake out the coke through a side opening.

What's recovered: **only coke**. Everything else — coal gas, tar, ammonia, light oils — burns inside the oven as fuel, or escapes to atmosphere. The pollution was extraordinary: tar fogs settled on surrounding towns, ammonia killed vegetation for miles, the gas flames could be seen at night across entire valleys. Pittsburgh and the Connellsville coke region were famously hellish.

**Why only coke?** Three reasons:

1. The volatiles *had* to burn to supply heat, because there was no external heat source.
2. There was no way to collect the volatiles even if you wanted to — there was no provision for sealing the oven against air ingress, no offgas piping, no condenser, nothing.
3. The economics didn't motivate it: until the 1850s-60s there wasn't much demand for coal tar derivatives. The dye industry hadn't started yet (Perkin's mauve was 1856), and gas lighting gas was made from purpose-built gasworks rather than coke ovens.

The component count in your modular kit: essentially **one component, a primitive reactor**. No furnace separation, no condensers, no separators. The reactor and the furnace are the same vessel because the feedstock is its own fuel.

### Gasworks (~1800s, parallel development)

While beehive coke ovens were burning everything, a parallel industry was developing for *gas lighting*. Gasworks were purpose-built to make coal gas for streetlights and home lighting (London had gas lighting from 1812). These had:

- A retort (sealed cast-iron vessel) heated externally by a coal fire
- Offgas piping to a condenser (just a long pipe to ambient air, or water-cooled)
- A tar/liquor separator (gravity-settled in a tank)
- A scrubber (gas bubbled through water or lime to remove ammonia and CO₂)
- A gas holder (the iconic telescoping water-sealed tank)

Importantly, gasworks were *already separating* what would later become the byproducts of coke production. They had to, because the *gas* was the product and the tar was a nuisance byproduct that had to be removed to keep the gas clean. Tar was a waste stream that gas works basically gave away or burned.

This is where the unit operations were being developed: external furnace + retort reactor + condenser + separator + scrubber + storage. Most of your modular kit existed by ~1820, but it was applied to making lighting gas, not to recovering chemicals.

The materials limit: cast-iron retorts could only hold ~700°C reliably. This made gasworks slower and lower-yield than coke ovens but it kept the equipment alive long enough to recover the byproducts. The high-temperature operation of beehive ovens (~1100°C internally) would have melted cast iron immediately.

### Coppée and semi-byproduct ovens (~1860s-1880s)

The first step toward integration was the **Coppée oven** (Évence Coppée, Belgium, 1860s) — a rectangular slot oven with external heating from gas burners in flues alongside the coking chamber. The coal was no longer its own fuel; the chamber was sealed, and heat came from outside.

This was the conceptual breakthrough: **separating the heat source from the reactor**. Once you do that, the offgas no longer has to burn inside the chamber, and you can pipe it out and do something with it.

But early Coppée ovens still mostly *burned* the offgas — just under the oven instead of inside it. The byproducts went up the stack as combustion products. The advance was thermodynamic (better thermal efficiency, faster coking, more uniform coke quality), not chemical-recovery.

The reason recovery still wasn't happening: the offgas leaving the oven was at 800-1000°C, full of tar fog that would clog any condenser, and there was no good way to clean it. You needed the *gasworks* condenser/scrubber technology applied to the *coke oven* gas stream, which required scaling everything up by ~10x and figuring out how to handle the tar load.

### Otto-Hoffmann byproduct ovens (1880s-1890s, dominant from ~1900)

This is the moment everything comes together. The **Otto-Hoffmann oven** (Carl Otto and Heinrich Hoffmann, Germany, 1880s) integrated three things:

1. **Regenerative heating** (already established in the Siemens-Martin steel furnace from 1865): the hot flue gas from burning the coke gas preheats incoming combustion air through ceramic checker-brick regenerators. Air flow alternates direction every 20-30 minutes — one regenerator absorbs heat from outgoing flue gas while the other releases stored heat into incoming air. This is the heat exchanger of your modular kit, applied to combustion. It dramatically increased fuel efficiency and allowed higher flame temperatures.

2. **Byproduct recovery train**: the offgas from the coking chamber was piped through a condenser cascade (primary cooler → exhauster → tar precipitator → ammonia scrubber → benzol scrubber → gas holder), recovering tar, ammoniacal liquor, light oil, and clean gas as four separate streams.

3. **Self-fueling operation**: the recovered clean gas, after byproduct removal, was returned to the underburners as fuel. Typically only ~40% of the produced gas was needed for heating; the other 60% was net output, sold as town gas or used for other purposes.

The Otto-Hoffmann design also introduced **silica refractories** (replacing fireclay) which could withstand 1400°C+ continuously. Silica brick is critical here — fireclay started softening around 1200°C, and you need higher temperatures than that for the regenerator hot face.

What's recovered in 1900: coke, tar (separated into fractions in a separate tar refinery), ammonia (sold as ammonium sulfate fertilizer), benzol (the light oil, source of benzene and toluene), naphthalene (crystallized from the tar), and clean coal gas. All of your modular kit is now operational and integrated.

### 20th century refinements (1900-present)

The Otto-Hoffmann basic design has remained the template for over a century. What's changed:

- **Larger ovens**: from 6m³ in 1900 to 50-70m³ today, with corresponding scale-up of all auxiliary equipment.
- **Better materials**: silica → silica/alumina composites → modern refractory ceramics, allowing higher temperatures and longer service life (modern coke ovens run 25+ years between rebuilds).
- **Continuous operation**: batch coking → semi-continuous → modern non-recovery and heat-recovery designs.
- **Hydrogen sulfide recovery**: 1930s-onward, the Claus process recovers elemental sulfur from H₂S in the coke gas. Adds another absorber (amine wash) + reactor (Claus reactor) to the kit.
- **Air pollution control**: cyclones, electrostatic precipitators, baghouses for particulate; selective catalytic reduction for NOx; flue gas desulfurization.

The 1880s-1890s were the moment all three stacks aligned: silica refractories matured, gasworks technology was mature and scalable, and the German chemical industry was hungry for aromatic feedstocks. That's why byproduct coke ovens emerged then and not earlier.

## How heat regeneration specifically becomes possible

The regenerative heat exchanger deserves its own section because it's the most *mechanically subtle* component in the kit.

The Siemens regenerator (Friedrich Siemens, 1856; Carl Wilhelm Siemens, applied to steelmaking with Pierre-Émile Martin in 1865) is a beautiful piece of engineering. Two large chambers filled with ceramic checker-brick — bricks stacked in a lattice pattern with gas channels running through. Hot flue gas flows through one chamber, depositing heat in the bricks. Simultaneously, cold combustion air flows through the *other* chamber, absorbing heat from previously-stored bricks. The dimensional stability of the brick matters because the gas channels have to stay open — if bricks spall and fragments fall, the regenerator clogs.

**Why this requires precise valving**: switching the flow direction without losing combustion or letting unburned gas through to the wrong side requires reliable, large-bore, high-temperature valves. The Forter valve and similar designs from the 1880s solved this. Earlier valve technology couldn't have done it.

This was applied science requiring the thermodynamics of Carnot and Clausius.

So regenerative heat exchange becomes possible in the 1860s, but requires:
- Silica or magnesite refractories
- Reliable high-temperature valving
- Theoretical understanding of cyclic heat transfer
- Sufficient capital to build large dual-chamber installations

**Stone/charcoal era**: Charcoal pits and beehive kilns. Wood pyrolysis is happening, but everything except the charcoal vents to atmosphere. The "building" is an earthen mound or a domed clay kiln. No byproduct recovery. No external heat source — the feedstock is its own fuel.

That mirrors the real industrial history almost exactly.

Connellsville-style hellscape was a major political and public-health driver of the transition. Whether you want to model environmental effects is a design choice, but the historical pressure was real.

Good question, and the size progression is interesting because it reveals real physical constraints — there are reasons beehive ovens settled into a particular size range and didn't grow indefinitely.

## Charcoal kilns vs. coke ovens — different traditions

It's worth distinguishing two parallel traditions because they had different size constraints, even though the basic geometry is similar.

**Charcoal kilns** (for wood) developed earlier and stayed smaller, because wood is bulky and low-density, the operation is more delicate (you want to char without burning), and the product is fragile.

**Coke ovens** (for coal) emerged in the early 1700s, used denser feedstock, ran hotter, and could be built larger.

I'll cover both since you asked about wood/charcoal earlier in the conversation.

## Charcoal kilns

**Earth pits / earth mounds (prehistoric–1900s, persisted in poor regions)**: The earliest "kiln" wasn't a structure at all. You'd stack wood in a conical or domed pile (typically 3-5m diameter, 2-3m tall), cover it with leaves/turf/earth to seal it, light it from a central flue, and regulate combustion by opening and closing vents. A typical mound held 20-50 cubic meters of wood and produced 2-5 tonnes of charcoal over 1-2 weeks of careful tending. A skilled collier (charcoal burner) might tend 4-6 mounds at once on a rotation.

This is a very ancient technology — Iron Age sites in Europe show charcoal mound remains, and the technique was essentially unchanged from antiquity until the late 1800s. The "building" is dirt and leaves. The skilled labor is everything.

A charcoal works might have 6-12 such kilns in a battery, allowing continuous production.

## Coke ovens — the size progression

Now the more dramatic story.

**Earliest coke ovens (early 1700s)**: When Abraham Darby first coked coal at Coalbrookdale (~1709), he used what amounted to a charcoal-style mound or a primitive brick oven. Sources are sparse, but the early ovens were ~3-4m diameter, 2-3m tall, holding maybe 2-3 tonnes of coal per charge. Cycle time 2-3 days. Production maybe 1-2 tonnes of coke per cycle.

**Mature beehive ovens (~1800-1880, peak era)**: The classic Connellsville-style beehive oven settled into a fairly standard size: **3.5-4m diameter at the base, 2-2.5m tall at the dome, holding ~5-7 tonnes of coal per charge**. - 1920: ~12m × 0.5m × 3m, ~12 tonnes per charge
- 1960: ~14m × 0.4m × 4m, ~20 tonnes per charge
- 2000s: ~17m × 0.5m × 7m, ~50-70 tonnes per charge (modern "tall" ovens)

Compare with a Connellsville beehive battery from 1900, which might produce ~50,000 tonnes per year from a similar number of ovens.

The size growth in modern slot ovens has been driven by:
- Better refractories (silica → silica/alumina → modern composites)
- Better mechanical handling (the larger the oven, the more mechanized the loading and pushing must be)
- Computer-controlled heating to maintain uniformity across larger volumes
- Process intensification — taller ovens, narrower slots, faster cycles

But the fundamental geometric insight (slot, not beehive) was already there in 1860.

## Some scale comparisons that might be useful

To put numbers on it:

| Technology | Era | Charge mass | Cycle time | Daily output | Footprint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Earth charcoal mound | Prehistoric–1900 | 5-15t wood | 7-14 days | ~0.05-0.1t charcoal | ~25m² |
| Brick charcoal kiln | 1700s-1900s | 10-20t wood | 5-10 days | ~0.3-0.5t charcoal | ~30m² |
| Early beehive coke oven | 1700s | 2-3t coal | 2-3 days | ~0.5t coke | ~12m² |
| Mature beehive coke oven | 1800-1900 | 5-7t coal | 2-3 days | ~1.5-2t coke | ~15m² |
| Coppée slot oven | 1870s-1900 | 6-8t coal | 24-30h | ~5-6t coke | ~5m² (slot itself) |

The footprint numbers exclude the supporting infrastructure (battery walls, flues, byproduct plant, gas holders, etc.). ## What this means for your design

A few things worth noting:

**The size progression isn't continuous — it has phase transitions.** Beehive ovens couldn't grow past ~5m diameter because of geometry; Coppée ovens broke that limit by changing the shape entirely. Modern ovens scale further because of materials and instrumentation. **The "building" gets smaller as the kit gets larger.** A primitive beehive *is* the building. A modern coke battery has a small coking volume embedded in an enormous heat-management and byproduct-recovery infrastructure. If you decompose into modular components, this becomes natural: the reactor (the actual coking chamber) doesn't grow much, but the surrounding kit (regenerators, condensers, separators, scrubbers) grows enormously. This matches reality.

**Footprint and throughput don't scale together.** A modern coke oven occupies similar ground footprint to a beehive but produces 30-50x as much coke per day. This is a really important industrial pattern — capability density grows with technology even when physical footprint doesn't. Your gameplay could reflect this: you don't necessarily need much more land for advanced coking, but you need much more *vertical* infrastructure and supporting plant.

**The gasworks/byproduct kit is independent of the oven kit.** The gasworks technology developed in parallel and could in principle be retrofitted to *any* sealed oven. Players could plausibly build crude beehive coke ovens early, then later build a separate gasworks/byproduct facility, then *connect* the two by piping the offgas from beehive ovens to the byproduct plant. This is an architectural intermediate stage that historically existed (some late-19th-century beehive operations did capture offgas through specially designed "byproduct beehive" hybrids) and would map nicely onto a modular component system.
