chat_messages.text:
Good question, and you're right to suspect that hardwood/softwood is too coarse. The problem with that binary split is that it doesn't actually predict use cases reliably — many "hardwoods" are actually quite soft (balsa, basswood) and the working properties that matter for end uses (strength, durability, workability, dimensional stability, rot resistance) aren't tightly correlated with the botanical hardwood/softwood classification.

Let me work through what variation actually matters for end uses, and then propose a minimum set that captures the meaningful gameplay differentiation.

## What properties actually drive use cases

Before listing wood types, it's worth being clear about which wood properties drive different applications, because the categories should fall out of the property combinations that matter:

**Strength and stiffness** matter for structural uses — building frames, ship hulls, mill components. Higher density generally means higher strength, but the relationship varies by species and grain.

**Durability and rot resistance** matter for any wood in contact with ground, weather, or water. Some species naturally resist decay (oak, cedar, teak); others rot rapidly without preservative treatment (most softwoods, pale hardwoods).

**Workability** — how easily the wood can be worked with hand tools — varies enormously. Some wood splits cleanly along the grain (oak, ash); some refuses to split (elm, sycamore); some carves cleanly (lime, basswood); some chips out under tools (interlocked tropical hardwoods).

**Dimensional stability** — how much the wood expands and contracts with moisture changes — matters for fine joinery, instruments, and any application where tight fits must hold. Some woods are notoriously unstable (American beech, sweet chestnut); others are remarkably stable (mahogany, teak, white oak).

**Hardness and wear resistance** matter for surfaces subject to wear: floors, tool handles, gear teeth, bearings. Hard, fine-grained woods (boxwood, hornbeam, lignum vitae) excel here.

**Bending and shaping** matters for curved components: ship frames, barrel staves, wheel rims, furniture. Some species bend well with steam (oak, ash, beech); others crack rather than bend.

**Acoustic properties** matter for musical instruments. Specific species (spruce for soundboards, maple for backs, ebony for fingerboards) are functionally irreplaceable for high-quality instruments.

**Tannin and chemistry** matter for some applications. High-tannin woods (oak especially) suit barrels for wine and spirits because the tannin contributes to flavor; they're poor for vegetable barrels because the tannin contaminates the contents.

**Rot resistance underwater specifically** is different from above-ground rot resistance. Some woods (oak, especially European white oak) are remarkable underwater — Venice is built on millions of submerged oak piles that have been structurally sound for 1500 years. Other woods rot quickly in water.

**Density and buoyancy** matter for marine applications and for transport. Lighter woods float and are cheaper to ship; denser woods sink and are harder to handle.

These properties cluster in specific combinations that have driven specific use cases throughout history. The minimum interesting set should capture the most economically and historically important property clusters.

## A minimum interesting set

Here's a proposed minimum that I think captures essentially all the gameplay-relevant variation. Five categories, each representing a real cluster of properties and use cases:

### 1. Construction softwood (pine, fir, spruce)

The workhorse structural and general-purpose wood. Properties:
- Light to medium density, easy to work with hand tools
- Reasonable strength-to-weight ratio for structural use
- Grows fast and straight, producing long clear timbers
- Modest rot resistance (poor without preservative treatment)
- Modest durability (decades, not centuries, in normal use)
- Cheap and abundant in temperate climates

Uses: framing for buildings, general construction, roofing, flooring, packaging, fuelwood, charcoal feedstock, paper pulp (in industrial era), boat planking for inland and coastal use, masts and spars for sailing vessels (specific species like white pine for masts).

In gameplay terms, this is the "default lumber" — abundant, versatile, suitable for most bulk uses, but lacking the specific properties needed for demanding applications. Spruce specifically has notable acoustic properties (musical instrument soundboards) that might warrant a sub-distinction at higher tech levels.

### 2. Strong durable hardwood (oak, chestnut)

The premium structural wood, especially for any application requiring durability or contact with moisture. Properties:
- High density, high strength, high stiffness
- Excellent rot resistance, especially in white oak and chestnut
- High tannin content (relevant for cooperage and chemistry)
- Splits well along grain (good for splitting into planks and shingles)
- Bends well with steam (good for ship frames and furniture)
- Slow-growing and expensive
- Heavy and difficult to work with hand tools

Uses: shipbuilding (frames and planking for serious vessels), heavy structural carpentry (cathedrals, mills, bridges), cooperage (especially for wine, spirits, and brining), wheelwright work (spokes, hubs, felloes), tool handles, fence posts, charcoal (oak charcoal is preferred for some metallurgical applications because of its density), tannin extraction for leather working.

Oak specifically is the most strategically important wood in pre-modern European history — it's the wood for naval construction, for high-quality cooperage, for cathedrals, for mills. Sweet chestnut is similar in property profile and was used as an oak substitute in regions where chestnut was more abundant. They're the same gameplay category.

### 3. Tough resilient hardwood (ash, hickory, elm)

A distinct category for wood that needs to absorb shock and flex without breaking. Properties:
- Medium-to-high density
- High shock resistance and toughness (resists splitting under impact)
- Good elasticity (springs back from deformation)
- Hard but workable with metal tools
- Modest rot resistance (similar to most temperate hardwoods)
- Specific species (elm) have interlocked grain that resists splitting entirely

Uses: tool handles (axes, hammers, picks — anything that gets impact loads), wheel hubs (elm specifically, for the shock resistance), bows and weapon handles, sports equipment (later periods), wagon and cart construction, bentwood furniture, ship oars and paddles.

The historical importance of this category is sometimes overlooked — without good ash or hickory, you can't make decent tool handles or wagon parts, and your tools and vehicles will fail under load. Elm specifically was important in pre-modern Europe for hub work because its resistance to splitting let you drive multiple radial spokes into a single hub without the hub splitting apart. Different species cover the same gameplay role — Europe had ash and elm; North America had ash, hickory, and oak; Asia had various analogs.

### 4. Fine workable hardwood (beech, maple, birch, lime/basswood)

Wood for fine work and carving. Properties:
- Medium density (lighter than oak, heavier than pine)
- Fine, even texture suitable for carving and turning
- Takes paint, stain, and finish well
- Stable in dry conditions (less stable than the premium furniture woods, but adequate for indoor use)
- Modest rot resistance (poor in outdoor use)
- Easier to work than the dense structural hardwoods

Uses: furniture frames and panels (before the era of fine cabinet woods), turned components (chair legs, balusters, tool handles for finer tools), wooden tableware (plates, bowls, spoons), carving and sculpture, tool components (plane bodies, mallet heads — beech especially), interior joinery and paneling, gunstocks (walnut and maple specifically), printing blocks (boxwood and lemonwood for fine work, maple for coarser work).

This category fills the niche between coarse construction lumber and the specialty woods. It's the wood for everyday objects that need quality but don't need extraordinary performance. Lime/basswood specifically is the carver's wood — used for everything from medieval altarpieces to modern decoy carving — because it's soft, even-grained, and holds detail well.

### 5. Specialty rot-resistant wood (cedar, cypress, larch)

The natural-preservative woods, where the heartwood contains chemicals that inhibit decay. Properties:
- Medium-low density (cedar is lightweight; larch is denser)
- Outstanding natural rot resistance (decades to centuries in damp conditions)
- Often aromatic (cedar especially)
- Easy to work
- Modest strength (not for heavy structural use)
- Resistant to insect attack

Uses: shingles and exterior cladding, fence posts, water tanks and cisterns, boat planking for small craft, exterior trim, lining for chests and closets (the aroma deters moths — the original cedar chest), specialty cooperage for some applications, foundation piles in damp ground.

This is a smaller category by volume than the others, but it fills a niche that nothing else does well. Without rot-resistant wood, you have problems with anything that gets wet or sits in damp ground, and the alternatives (chemical preservatives) are a much later technology.

## What this minimum captures

These five categories cover essentially all the major historical use distinctions:

- General construction → softwood
- Heavy structural and shipbuilding → strong durable hardwood
- Tools and vehicles → tough resilient hardwood
- Furniture, fine work, household goods → fine workable hardwood
- Outdoor/wet applications → rot-resistant specialty wood

If a player wants to build a sailing ship, they need oak (category 2) for the frames and planking, fir or pine (category 1) for the masts and decking, ash (category 3) for the oars, and possibly cedar (category 5) for some interior elements. Each category does something the others can't, and the player has to source and manage them separately.

## Possible additions for richer gameplay

If you want to extend beyond five, here are the natural next additions:

**Premium cabinet/furniture wood (walnut, cherry, mahogany if tropical trade is in scope)**: Distinct from category 4 in being significantly more dimensionally stable, taking finer finishes, and being specifically prized for high-end furniture. This becomes economically important in the 17th-19th centuries with the rise of fine cabinetmaking. Could be an unlock at higher tech tiers or with trade access to specific regions.

**Tropical hardwood (teak, ironwood, lignum vitae, ebony)**: Specifically valuable for marine use (teak), high-wear applications (lignum vitae was the standard for ship propeller bearings before bronze became economical for that use; it's literally self-lubricating), and decorative work (ebony, rosewood). These require trade with tropical regions or colonial expansion to access. Lignum vitae specifically is interesting because it's used as bearing material for some applications where bronze is overkill — it's a niche specialty material.

**Bow wood (yew, osage orange)**: Specific species with the right combination of compression strength and elastic recovery for bow construction. Yew was strategically important in medieval Europe for the same reason oak was — England's longbow tradition depended on yew imports from continental Europe because English yew was inferior. If your game has weapons differentiation, bow wood might be worth a category.

**Specialty acoustic wood (spruce, maple, ebony, rosewood)**: Various species used for specific musical instrument components. Probably not a separate primary category but a sub-distinction at higher tech tiers if instrument-making is a meaningful gameplay feature.

**Pulp/fiber wood (poplar, willow, fast-growing softwoods)**: A specifically modern category for paper and pulp production. Becomes relevant only in late industrial development.

**Bamboo (in regions where applicable)**: Technically a grass, not wood, but functions as a structural fiber in many Asian and tropical contexts and has unique properties. If your game has regional variation, bamboo is an important alternative material in the right climates.

## A note on how this fits geological/biome systems

Here's where your game's design philosophy becomes relevant: **wood types should fall out of biome/climate, not be a separate flavor layer**. Different climates produce different forest compositions, and the wood available to a player should be a function of their geographic location.

A rough mapping:

- **Boreal/cold temperate** (high latitude or high altitude): conifers dominate. Pine, fir, spruce, larch. Limited hardwood diversity. Birch in transition zones. This region is rich in construction softwood and some rot-resistant softwood (larch), but poor in premium hardwoods.
- **Cool temperate** (much of Europe, eastern North America, parts of East Asia): mixed hardwood-conifer forests. Oak, beech, ash, elm, maple, birch dominate hardwoods; pine, fir, spruce in conifer zones. The richest region for diverse temperate woods, with all categories represented.
- **Warm temperate to subtropical**: chestnut, walnut, cherry hardwoods; cypress and bald cypress for rot resistance; mixed pine forests. Mediterranean region historically had oak, chestnut, cypress, but suffered severe deforestation from antiquity onward.
- **Tropical**: enormous diversity but the *useful* species are scattered through the forest at low density, making harvest difficult. Teak, mahogany, ebony, ironwood, rosewood — but each species is a small fraction of the forest, requiring selective harvest and substantial labor. This is one reason tropical hardwoods historically required colonial-scale logistics to extract economically.
- **Arid regions**: limited tree growth generally; juniper, mesquite, olive, and other drought-adapted species. Wood is locally precious; large construction projects historically had to import wood from afar (Egypt's Lebanese cedar trade is a famous example).

For your game design, the wood available in any given region should be determined by climate, with the player's wood economy shaped by their geographic position. A player in the boreal zone can build extensively with softwood but lacks oak for shipbuilding without trade. A player in the tropical zone has access to specialty woods but at low density, requiring extensive forest area. A player in the temperate zone has the richest wood resources but may face competition for high-value species.

This embeds wood variation in the geological/biome system rather than treating it as flavor, and it creates real geographic specialization and trade dynamics. A medieval Hanseatic trader shipping Baltic oak to England isn't doing it for flavor — they're doing it because England's domestic oak supplies were strained by shipbuilding demand, and Baltic oak filled a real shortage. Modeling this honestly creates real gameplay.

## A practical suggestion

If you want to start with a minimum and add complexity later, I'd suggest starting with **the five primary categories** above (softwood, durable hardwood, resilient hardwood, fine hardwood, rot-resistant specialty) and adding tropical hardwood and premium cabinet wood as later unlocks tied to trade and tech progression. That gives you immediate meaningful differentiation without overwhelming the player with species, while preserving the option to expand to more granular distinctions as the tech tree advances.

The five categories also map cleanly onto biome distribution, making the wood economy a natural part of the regional/geographic gameplay rather than a separate system. Players in different starting regions face genuinely different wood economies — boreal players have softwood and limited hardwood; temperate players have the full range; arid-region players have wood scarcity as a constant pressure. This is honest historical reality and creates real strategic differentiation between starting locations.

One final thought: the categories I've described are about *use properties*, not botanical taxonomy. This is the right framing for game design because the player cares about what they can build, not about what taxonomic family the tree belongs to. A player who finds "durable hardwood forest" knows what they can do with it; whether it's specifically oak or chestnut or some equivalent species matters less than the property profile.

- Modest durability (decades, not centuries, in normal use)
- Cheap and abundant in temperate climates

Uses: framing for buildings, general construction, roofing, flooring, packaging, fuelwood, charcoal feedstock, paper pulp (in industrial era), boat planking for inland and coastal use, masts and spars for sailing vessels (specific species like white pine for masts).

In gameplay terms, this is the "default lumber" — abundant, versatile, suitable for most bulk uses, but lacking the specific properties needed for demanding applications. Spruce specifically has notable acoustic properties (musical instrument soundboards) that might warrant a sub-distinction at higher tech levels.

### 2. Strong durable hardwood (oak, chestnut)

The premium structural wood, especially for any application requiring durability or contact with moisture. Properties:
- High density, high strength, high stiffness
- Excellent rot resistance, especially in white oak and chestnut
- High tannin content (relevant for cooperage and chemistry)
- Splits well along grain (good for splitting into planks and shingles)
- Bends well with steam (good for ship frames and furniture)
- Slow-growing and expensive
- Heavy and difficult to work with hand tools

Uses: shipbuilding (frames and planking for serious vessels), heavy structural carpentry (cathedrals, mills, bridges), cooperage (especially for wine, spirits, and brining), wheelwright work (spokes, hubs, felloes), tool handles, fence posts, charcoal (oak charcoal is preferred for some metallurgical applications because of its density), tannin extraction for leather working.

Oak specifically is the most strategically important wood in pre-modern European history — it's the wood for naval construction, for high-quality cooperage, for cathedrals, for mills. Sweet chestnut is similar in property profile and was used as an oak substitute in regions where chestnut was more abundant. They're the same gameplay category.

### 3. Tough resilient hardwood (ash, hickory, elm)

A distinct category for wood that needs to absorb shock and flex without breaking. Properties:
- Medium-to-high density
- High shock resistance and toughness (resists splitting under impact)
- Good elasticity (springs back from deformation)
- Hard but workable with metal tools
- Modest rot resistance (similar to most temperate hardwoods)
- Specific species (elm) have interlocked grain that resists splitting entirely

Uses: tool handles (axes, hammers, picks — anything that gets impact loads), wheel hubs (elm specifically, for the shock resistance), bows and weapon handles, sports equipment (later periods), wagon and cart construction, bentwood furniture, ship oars and paddles.

The historical importance of this category is sometimes overlooked — without good ash or hickory, you can't make decent tool handles or wagon parts, and your tools and vehicles will fail under load. Elm specifically was important in pre-modern Europe for hub work because its resistance to splitting let you drive multiple radial spokes into a single hub without the hub splitting apart. Different species cover the same gameplay role — Europe had ash and elm; North America had ash, hickory, and oak; Asia had various analogs.

### 4. Fine workable hardwood (beech, maple, birch, lime/basswood)

Wood for fine work and carving. Properties:
- Medium density (lighter than oak, heavier than pine)
- Fine, even texture suitable for carving and turning
- Takes paint, stain, and finish well
- Stable in dry conditions (less stable than the premium furniture woods, but adequate for indoor use)
- Modest rot resistance (poor in outdoor use)
- Easier to work than the dense structural hardwoods

Uses: furniture frames and panels (before the era of fine cabinet woods), turned components (chair legs, balusters, tool handles for finer tools), wooden tableware (plates, bowls, spoons), carving and sculpture, tool components (plane bodies, mallet heads — beech especially), interior joinery and paneling, gunstocks (walnut and maple specifically), printing blocks (boxwood and lemonwood for fine work, maple for coarser work).

This category fills the niche between coarse construction lumber and the specialty woods. It's the wood for everyday objects that need quality but don't need extraordinary performance. Lime/basswood specifically is the carver's wood — used for everything from medieval altarpieces to modern decoy carving — because it's soft, even-grained, and holds detail well.

### 5. Specialty rot-resistant wood (cedar, cypress, larch)

The natural-preservative woods, where the heartwood contains chemicals that inhibit decay. Properties:
- Medium-low density (cedar is lightweight; larch is denser)
- Outstanding natural rot resistance (decades to centuries in damp conditions)
- Often aromatic (cedar especially)
- Easy to work
- Modest strength (not for heavy structural use)
- Resistant to insect attack

Uses: shingles and exterior cladding, fence posts, water tanks and cisterns, boat planking for small craft, exterior trim, lining for chests and closets (the aroma deters moths — the original cedar chest), specialty cooperage for some applications, foundation piles in damp ground.

This is a smaller category by volume than the others, but it fills a niche that nothing else does well. Without rot-resistant wood, you have problems with anything that gets wet or sits in damp ground, and the alternatives (chemical preservatives) are a much later technology.

## What this minimum captures

These five categories cover essentially all the major historical use distinctions:

- General construction → softwood
- Heavy structural and shipbuilding → strong durable hardwood
- Tools and vehicles → tough resilient hardwood
- Furniture, fine work, household goods → fine workable hardwood
- Outdoor/wet applications → rot-resistant specialty wood

If a player wants to build a sailing ship, they need oak (category 2) for the frames and planking, fir or pine (category 1) for the masts and decking, ash (category 3) for the oars, and possibly cedar (category 5) for some interior elements. Each category does something the others can't, and the player has to source and manage them separately.

## Possible additions for richer gameplay

If you want to extend beyond five, here are the natural next additions:

**Premium cabinet/furniture wood (walnut, cherry, mahogany if tropical trade is in scope)**: Distinct from category 4 in being significantly more dimensionally stable, taking finer finishes, and being specifically prized for high-end furniture. This becomes economically important in the 17th-19th centuries with the rise of fine cabinetmaking. Could be an unlock at higher tech tiers or with trade access to specific regions.

**Tropical hardwood (teak, ironwood, lignum vitae, ebony)**: Specifically valuable for marine use (teak), high-wear applications (lignum vitae was the standard for ship propeller bearings before bronze became economical for that use; it's literally self-lubricating), and decorative work (ebony, rosewood). These require trade with tropical regions or colonial expansion to access. Lignum vitae specifically is interesting because it's used as bearing material for some applications where bronze is overkill — it's a niche specialty material.

**Bow wood (yew, osage orange)**: Specific species with the right combination of compression strength and elastic recovery for bow construction. Yew was strategically important in medieval Europe for the same reason oak was — England's longbow tradition depended on yew imports from continental Europe because English yew was inferior. If your game has weapons differentiation, bow wood might be worth a category.

**Specialty acoustic wood (spruce, maple, ebony, rosewood)**: Various species used for specific musical instrument components. Probably not a separate primary category but a sub-distinction at higher tech tiers if instrument-making is a meaningful gameplay feature.

**Pulp/fiber wood (poplar, willow, fast-growing softwoods)**: A specifically modern category for paper and pulp production. Becomes relevant only in late industrial development.

**Bamboo (in regions where applicable)**: Technically a grass, not wood, but functions as a structural fiber in many Asian and tropical contexts and has unique properties. If your game has regional variation, bamboo is an important alternative material in the right climates.

## A note on how this fits geological/biome systems

Here's where your game's design philosophy becomes relevant: **wood types should fall out of biome/climate, not be a separate flavor layer**. Different climates produce different forest compositions, and the wood available to a player should be a function of their geographic location.

A rough mapping:

- **Boreal/cold temperate** (high latitude or high altitude): conifers dominate. Pine, fir, spruce, larch. Limited hardwood diversity. Birch in transition zones. This region is rich in construction softwood and some rot-resistant softwood (larch), but poor in premium hardwoods.
- **Cool temperate** (much of Europe, eastern North America, parts of East Asia): mixed hardwood-conifer forests. Oak, beech, ash, elm, maple, birch dominate hardwoods; pine, fir, spruce in conifer zones. The richest region for diverse temperate woods, with all categories represented.
- **Warm temperate to subtropical**: chestnut, walnut, cherry hardwoods; cypress and bald cypress for rot resistance; mixed pine forests. Mediterranean region historically had oak, chestnut, cypress, but suffered severe deforestation from antiquity onward.
- **Tropical**: enormous diversity but the *useful* species are scattered through the forest at low density, making harvest difficult. Teak, mahogany, ebony, ironwood, rosewood — but each species is a small fraction of the forest, requiring selective harvest and substantial labor. This is one reason tropical hardwoods historically required colonial-scale logistics to extract economically.
- **Arid regions**: limited tree growth generally; juniper, mesquite, olive, and other drought-adapted species. Wood is locally precious; large construction projects historically had to import wood from afar (Egypt's Lebanese cedar trade is a famous example).

For your game design, the wood available in any given region should be determined by climate, with the player's wood economy shaped by their geographic position. A player in the boreal zone can build extensively with softwood but lacks oak for shipbuilding without trade. A player in the tropical zone has access to specialty woods but at low density, requiring extensive forest area. A player in the temperate zone has the richest wood resources but may face competition for high-value species.

This embeds wood variation in the geological/biome system rather than treating it as flavor, and it creates real geographic specialization and trade dynamics. A medieval Hanseatic trader shipping Baltic oak to England isn't doing it for flavor — they're doing it because England's domestic oak supplies were strained by shipbuilding demand, and Baltic oak filled a real shortage. Modeling this honestly creates real gameplay.

## A practical suggestion

If you want to start with a minimum and add complexity later, I'd suggest starting with **the five primary categories** above (softwood, durable hardwood, resilient hardwood, fine hardwood, rot-resistant specialty) and adding tropical hardwood and premium cabinet wood as later unlocks tied to trade and tech progression. That gives you immediate meaningful differentiation without overwhelming the player with species, while preserving the option to expand to more granular distinctions as the tech tree advances.

The five categories also map cleanly onto biome distribution, making the wood economy a natural part of the regional/geographic gameplay rather than a separate system. Players in different starting regions face genuinely different wood economies — boreal players have softwood and limited hardwood; temperate players have the full range; arid-region players have wood scarcity as a constant pressure. This is honest historical reality and creates real strategic differentiation between starting locations.

One final thought: the categories I've described are about *use properties*, not botanical taxonomy. This is the right framing for game design because the player cares about what they can build, not about what taxonomic family the tree belongs to. A player who finds "durable hardwood forest" knows what they can do with it; whether it's specifically oak or chestnut or some equivalent species matters less than the property profile.

chat_messages.text:
Great idea using spoilage for seasoning — it's actually a really apt mechanic for that, because seasoning is genuinely a time-passes-and-the-material-transforms process, not an active operation. Let me work through the full wood processing chain because there's quite a lot of structure here, and seasoning is one of several processes that fit nicely into your game's mechanics.

## The processing chain from standing tree to finished lumber

The full chain has more stages than people typically appreciate. Each one serves a distinct purpose and requires distinct tools and infrastructure.

### 1. Felling

Cutting down the standing tree. This is the entry point of the chain. Tools needed: axes (stone/bronze/iron/steel) for cutting, possibly wedges for directing the fall on large trees, and rope or cable for guiding the fall in difficult terrain.

The output is a felled tree with branches and crown still attached. Felling is fast for small trees but substantial work for large ones — a single skilled axeman could fell maybe 5-10 medium trees per day, fewer for very large ones.

In game terms, felling produces a "felled tree" or raw log object. The tool quality affects productivity (steel axes are much faster than stone) but doesn't fundamentally change capability — even stone-age people felled large trees successfully, just slowly.

### 2. Limbing and bucking

Removing branches (limbing) and cutting the trunk into transportable lengths (bucking). Tools: axes for limbing, axes or saws for bucking depending on log size and tool tier.

This stage is where the tree becomes a set of logs. The branches are typically left in the forest or burned (in some forest management systems they're collected for firewood). The clean trunk sections are the primary product.

Bucking length is determined by intended use: short bucks (1-2m) for firewood and small-section work, medium bucks (3-4m) for general lumber, long bucks (6-12m+) for shipbuilding and large structural timbers. The longest sections require specific transportation infrastructure because they're awkward to handle.

### 3. Hauling / transport from forest

Getting logs from where they fell to where they'll be processed. This is often the most labor-intensive part of the entire chain, especially for large logs.

Methods used historically:
- **Manhandling**: with poles, cant hooks, peavies. Effective for small logs, very labor-intensive for large ones.
- **Animal traction**: oxen or horses dragging logs along trails. Standard for medieval and early-modern forestry. A team of oxen can drag substantially larger logs than humans can handle.
- **Skidding and sledding**: dragging logs over the ground or on simple sleds, sometimes using prepared skid roads with slick surfaces. Winter operations using snow or ice were particularly efficient because of low friction.
- **Water transport**: floating logs down rivers (river drives), or rafting them tied together. The dominant method for long-distance log transport throughout history. Many regions were chosen for forestry specifically because they had drivable rivers.
- **Log flumes**: artificial channels of water to transport logs from upland forests to mills or rivers. Used in mountainous terrain where roads weren't practical.

For your game design, log transport is a real bottleneck and probably worth modeling. Forest siting near transportation corridors (rivers, established roads) is much more economically valuable than equivalent forest in remote terrain. This creates real geographic differentiation in forest value.

### 4. Initial conversion (the most variable stage)

This is where logs become usable timber. The processing technique varies dramatically based on intended use and tool availability, and the output forms are quite different.

**Splitting**: cleaving logs along the grain with wedges and froe. Produces split timbers with naturally rough surfaces but excellent strength because the grain runs continuously through the piece. Used for shingles, fence rails, riven planks, barrel staves, structural timbers in some traditions. Splitting is achievable with stone-age tools and remained important throughout pre-industrial woodworking because split wood is structurally superior to sawn wood for many applications.

**Hewing**: shaping a log into a rectangular timber by chopping away the rounded surfaces with a broad axe and adze. Produces a "hewn" timber with characteristic flat-but-not-perfectly-smooth surfaces showing axe marks. The dominant method for producing structural timbers throughout most of history. A skilled hewer could convert a log into a square timber with surfaces flat enough for building work in a few hours of skilled work.

**Pit sawing**: two workers using a long saw with one above the log on a frame and one below in a pit, sawing the log into planks. Slow and labor-intensive — a pit-sawing pair could produce maybe 10-15 board-feet per hour, depending on wood. The pitman below got the worse job (sawdust falling on him). This was the standard method for producing sawn lumber from antiquity until water-powered sawmills became widespread.

**Water-powered sawing**: a sawmill driven by a waterwheel, with one or more sawblades reciprocating to cut planks from logs. Dramatically more productive than pit sawing — a single water-powered saw could produce maybe 100+ board-feet per hour depending on the design. The first water-powered sawmills appear in late antiquity (the Hierapolis sawmill in Roman Asia Minor, ~3rd century CE) but become widespread only in the medieval period in Europe.

**Steam and circular sawing**: industrial-era developments with much higher productivity.

For your game, the conversion stage probably wants to differentiate at least:
- Hand tools (splitting and hewing): achievable with stone, bronze, or iron tools, productivity scales with tool quality
- Pit sawing: requires iron saw blades (bronze saws are technically possible but inefficient)
- Water-powered sawmill: requires water power infrastructure, iron blades, and bronze bearings

The output forms are different: split timbers and hewn timbers are produced as discrete shaped pieces; sawn lumber is produced as standardized planks and boards. Sawn lumber is much more versatile for downstream uses but requires more sophisticated infrastructure to produce.

### 5. Seasoning

This is where the spoilage mechanic comes in. Freshly cut wood ("green" wood) contains substantial water — typically 30-200% moisture content by dry weight, depending on species and time of year. This moisture must be removed before the wood can be used for most purposes.

What seasoning actually does:

- **Reduces moisture content** to equilibrium with ambient humidity (typically 12-18% in temperate climates, lower in arid environments)
- **Stabilizes dimensions** — green wood shrinks substantially as it dries, and shrinks unevenly along different axes (radial vs. tangential vs. longitudinal). Seasoning lets this shrinkage happen before the wood is used in critical applications.
- **Reduces weight** — dramatically. A green oak log can weigh 2x or more what the same log weighs after seasoning, simply from water loss.
- **Allows checking and cracking to occur** while the wood is in stockpile rather than in use. Wood that dries too fast checks badly; properly seasoned wood develops minor surface checks but maintains structural integrity.
- **Reduces weight-cost of further transport** because dry wood is much lighter than green.

The seasoning process is **slow**. The traditional rule of thumb is one year per inch (2.5cm) of thickness for air seasoning of typical hardwoods. So a 2-inch oak plank needs 2 years of seasoning; a 4-inch beam needs 4 years. Softwoods are somewhat faster but still measured in months to years for substantial pieces.

This is genuinely time-scale-of-game stuff, and modeling it as spoilage with a long timer is exactly right. A few specific aspects worth modeling:

- **Stack and stickering**: seasoned wood is stacked with spacer sticks ("stickers") between layers to allow air circulation. Without proper stacking, wood develops mold, stains, and uneven drying. This is a real practice that distinguishes proper seasoning from just leaving wood in a pile.
- **Covered or weather-protected storage**: seasoning sheds protect the stack from rain (which would re-wet the wood) but allow air flow. Covered seasoning is significantly slower than air seasoning but produces better quality wood.
- **End sealing**: the end grain of timber dries much faster than the side grain, which causes end checking (cracks). Sealing the ends with paint, wax, or animal fat slows end-grain drying and reduces checking. This is a small but real practice in good lumber production.

The specific spoilage-mechanic implementation might be:
- Green lumber has a "seasoning timer" that decrements over game time
- During seasoning, the lumber occupies stockpile space but cannot be used for high-quality applications
- After seasoning completes, the lumber transforms into seasoned lumber and is available for downstream uses
- Stack quality affects timer rate and possibly final quality (a well-stickered stack seasons faster and with less defect; a sloppy pile seasons slower or produces lower-quality output)

**Kiln drying** is the industrial alternative to air seasoning, developed in the 19th century but with antecedents going back to drying wood near hearths. A heated drying chamber forces moisture out of the wood much faster than air drying — days to weeks rather than months to years. The cost is energy input (heating fuel) and the risk of damaging the wood with too-rapid drying. For your game, kiln drying might be a tier-3 unlock that converts seasoning from a slow background process into an active, fuel-consuming process — a real economic tradeoff.

**Different uses tolerate different seasoning levels**:
- Firewood and charcoal feedstock can be used green (though dry wood burns better and produces more heat per unit mass)
- Construction-grade structural timber can use moderately seasoned wood (it will shrink in place, but mostly safely)
- Joinery and furniture wood needs thoroughly seasoned wood (or it will move and crack after assembly)
- Musical instruments, tool handles, and precision applications need very thoroughly seasoned wood, sometimes years beyond standard seasoning

This creates a natural quality gradient in the seasoning process: shorter seasoning gives lower-quality wood suitable for less demanding uses; longer seasoning gives higher-quality wood for premium applications. The player can choose where on this gradient to operate based on their needs and time horizon.

### 6. Secondary processing — surfacing and milling

After seasoning, lumber typically requires surface finishing before final use. The seasoned plank from the sawmill has rough surfaces, possibly some checking, and isn't dimensionally accurate enough for fine work.

**Hand planing**: smoothing rough lumber to a finished surface using hand planes. Achievable with bronze plane irons but works much better with iron and steel. A good cabinetmaker could surface a plank in minutes with sharp tools; the same work with dull or soft tools takes much longer.

**Power planing**: industrial-era machines that surface lumber automatically. Much later technology, requires steam or electric power.

**Resawing**: cutting seasoned lumber into thinner pieces. A 4-inch plank might be resawed into two 2-inch pieces, or four 1-inch pieces. Pit sawing or water-powered sawing handles this; the seasoned wood is much easier to cut than green wood because it's lighter and the cuts are cleaner.

**Joinery preparation**: cutting tenons, mortises, dovetails, and other joinery details. Hand tools (chisels, saws, planes) handle this throughout pre-industrial history; the quality of work is determined by tool sharpness and craftsman skill.

For game purposes, surfacing might be folded into the final product recipes (i.e., making a "finished plank" or "joinery stock" includes the surfacing work) rather than being a separate step. But it's worth knowing that it exists, because the tool and skill requirements are real.

### 7. End-product fabrication

This is where wood becomes specific objects: furniture, building components, ships, tools, vessels. Each end product has its own production chain with specific tool and skill requirements.

For game purposes, this is the recipe-output stage where seasoned, surfaced wood becomes finished goods. The fabrication itself is typically done in dedicated workshops (cabinetmaker's shop, shipyard, cooperage, wheelwright shop, joinery) with specific tooling.

## Variations and special processes

A few specific processes deserve mention because they're real and either historically important or gameplay-interesting:

### Steam bending

Bending wood to permanent curves by steaming it (heating in steam at ~100°C) and then clamping it to a form while it cools. Used for ship frames, furniture (Thonet's bentwood chairs are the classic example), barrel staves, wheel rims, musical instruments.

Not all wood bends well — oak, ash, beech, hickory, and elm are good benders; many other species crack rather than bend. Steam bending is a real specialized process requiring a steam box (a sealed wooden box with steam piped in) and bending forms. For your game, it might be a specialty process available with appropriate equipment.

### Riving (controlled splitting)

Splitting wood along the grain with a froe and mallet to produce thin, strong pieces with continuous grain. Used for shingles, basket splints, chair backs, and specialty applications where grain continuity matters more than dimensional accuracy. The output has rougher surfaces than sawn material but is structurally superior because no grain is cut.

Rived wood was a major product category throughout pre-industrial woodworking and remained important even after sawmills became common, because it's better than sawn material for some uses.

### Charring and pyrolysis

Wood charcoal production we've already discussed extensively, but related processes include:

- **Charring of fence posts and pile butts** — burning the surface of buried wood to a shallow charcoal layer, which significantly extends the wood's life in ground contact. A primitive but effective preservation technique.
- **Bog wood / preserved underwater storage** — submerging timber in oxygen-poor environments preserves it indefinitely. Was used historically to store ship timbers and other valuable wood. Connects to the rot-resistance properties of certain woods underwater.
- **Wood tar and pitch production** — a byproduct of charcoal making (especially from pine and other resinous woods), used as a wood preservative, ship caulking, and various other purposes. We touched on this briefly when discussing pyrolysis.

### Veneering and laminating

Cutting very thin sheets of premium wood (veneer) and gluing them to substrates of cheaper wood. Allows expensive woods to cover large areas at a fraction of the cost of solid wood, and was an important technique in fine cabinetmaking from the medieval period onward.

Veneer was originally cut by hand with very fine saws — a slow, expensive process that produced thick veneers (3-5mm). Modern thin veneers (less than 1mm) require specialized equipment and are an industrial-era development.

For your game, veneer might be a high-tier process producing premium decorative goods at lower wood cost than solid premium lumber. It requires very fine saws (steel) and skilled labor.

### Plywood and engineered wood

Modern composite materials made from wood. Plywood (cross-laminated thin sheets of wood) is a 20th-century product that revolutionized construction and packaging. Particle board, OSB, MDF, and laminated veneer lumber are all later industrial products.

These probably belong in a late-tier industrial section of your tech tree rather than the pre-industrial woodworking core. They require specific adhesives (glues that themselves are advanced products) and pressing equipment.

## Byproducts and waste streams

Wood processing produces substantial byproducts that have their own uses and economic significance:

**Sawdust**: a major byproduct of sawmilling. Uses include packing material, fuel (briquettes or direct burning), animal bedding, smoking meat, ice insulation (a major historical use — sawdust packed around blocks of ice in icehouses extended ice lifespan dramatically), and as feedstock for various industrial processes (eventually including pulp and particle board in industrial periods).

**Bark**: removed during processing for some uses, retained for others. Tan-bark (especially oak bark) was a major industrial product for leather tanning throughout the pre-industrial era — tannin extracted from bark was the dominant leather preservation chemistry until synthetic tannins emerged in the 19th-20th centuries. Cork (from cork oak) is bark used directly. Birch bark was used for canoes, containers, and as a writing surface in some traditions. Other barks have specific uses (cinchona bark for quinine, willow bark for salicylic acid, various medicinal barks).

**Wood chips and offcuts**: smaller pieces left from processing. Used as fuel, charcoal feedstock, and sometimes in specific products (offcut lumber for fence pickets, chips for smoking meat).

**Branches and tops**: the parts of the tree above the main bole, removed during limbing. Historically used as firewood (the largest single use), charcoal feedstock, and small constructional material (wattle for wattle-and-daub construction, small poles for tool handles and minor framing).

**Stumps and roots**: typically left in place when trees are felled; sometimes excavated for specific uses (root burls have decorative value; oak roots and stump wood produces particularly dense charcoal). Usually a labor-intensive proposition for limited additional yield.

**Resin and pitch**: from coniferous species, harvested either by tapping living trees (for turpentine and rosin from pine) or by pyrolysis (for pitch and tar). Major industrial products throughout pre-industrial history.

**Specialty chemical extracts**: tannin from oak and chestnut bark, dye chemicals from various tropical hardwoods (logwood for purple, brazilwood for red), medicinal compounds from specific species. The chemical economy of pre-modern wood is richer than people often appreciate.

## How this might map into your game

For a workable wood processing chain in your game, I'd suggest something like the following structure, with the spoilage mechanic for seasoning as you proposed:

**Forestry stage**:
- Felling produces raw logs (different species based on biome)
- Limbing produces logs + branch byproduct (firewood/charcoal feedstock)
- Hauling moves logs from forest to processing site (transport-distance dependent on terrain and available infrastructure)

**Conversion stage**:
- Splitting (low-tech, suitable for some products like shingles and rails)
- Hewing (low-tech, produces structural timbers)
- Pit sawing (mid-tech, produces sawn planks, requires iron saws)
- Water-powered sawing (high-tech, produces sawn planks at industrial rates, requires water mill + bronze bearings + iron blades)

**Seasoning stage** (your spoilage mechanic):
- Green lumber → seasoning stack with timer (months to years depending on thickness and species)
- Stacking quality affects timer and final quality
- Optionally: kiln drying as later-tier alternative converting time to energy

**Surfacing stage** (probably folded into product recipes):
- Hand planing for fine surfaces
- Joinery preparation for assembled products

**Product stage**:
- Specific recipes for end products (furniture, ship components, tool handles, building lumber, etc.)
- Different products require different wood types (your category system) and different seasoning levels

**Byproduct streams**:
- Branches/limbs → firewood, charcoal feedstock
- Sawdust → minor uses (packing, fuel, animal bedding)
- Bark → tannin (for leather), specific specialty uses
- Resin (from conifers) → turpentine, pitch, tar

The seasoning spoilage mechanic specifically is interesting because it creates real time-pressure on wood inventory management. A player with a productive forestry operation has a lot of green wood and a small amount of immediately usable seasoned wood. They have to plan ahead — wood seasoned today is for projects starting in a year. This creates real long-term planning gameplay around wood supply, which is actually historically accurate. Pre-modern shipbuilders maintained large stocks of seasoning oak for years before it would be used.

## A note on regional and cultural variation

Different woodworking traditions emphasized different parts of this chain. Some examples:

- **Japanese carpentry** developed extreme precision in joinery using primarily hand tools, with sawn lumber as the input. Japanese saws cut on the pull stroke (rather than push stroke as in European tradition), allowing thinner blades and more precise cuts. Japanese woodworking culture is associated with specific species (hinoki cypress, Japanese cedar) and specific construction methods (post-and-beam frames with no metal fasteners, joinery executed to extraordinary precision).

- **Scandinavian timber framing** emphasizes hewing and splitting techniques for log construction, with characteristic notched corner joinery (saddle notches, dovetail notches). Construction is essentially log-on-log with axe-cut joinery, no sawn lumber required.

- **English oak framing** developed elaborate joinery for great houses, cathedrals, and ships, with mortise-and-tenon connections pegged with treenails, scarf joints for joining long timbers, and complex bracing systems. The carpentry tradition supported building roof spans and ship structures of remarkable size.

- **Chinese carpentry** developed dougong bracket systems for supporting heavy roofs, with elaborate stacked joinery requiring no metal fasteners. The system is structurally interesting because it's earthquake-resistant — the joints can flex and absorb seismic loads.

For your game, these regional variations might be flavor (different aesthetic styles for the same functional outputs) or might be meaningful gameplay differentiation (different production techniques with different efficiencies and resource requirements). Either way, it's worth knowing that "woodworking" isn't a single universal tradition but a diverse set of regional approaches, each adapted to local conditions and materials.

## A final thought on the spoilage mechanic

Using spoilage for seasoning is a really nice match because it captures something true about the material: **wood is a living material that transforms over time without active intervention**. This is unusual in industrial production — most materials sit inert in inventory until acted on. Wood is different. It's actively drying, possibly developing defects, possibly improving in quality (some woods like wine, actually improving with age — old oak from a 200-year-old beam is more stable than freshly seasoned oak).

The spoilage mechanic captures the time-passes dimension of wood economy. A player who plans ahead and starts seasoning stocks years before they're needed has a strategic advantage; a player who tries to use green wood for fine work produces inferior products that fail in service. This is honest material physics translated into gameplay, which is what your design philosophy is aiming for.

If you want to go further, you could even model **green wood having distinct properties from seasoned wood** — heavier, more flexible, easier to work with hand tools (because it's softer when wet), but unsuitable for joinery because it will shrink. Some traditional crafts actually use green wood deliberately — Welsh chairmakers (the bodgers) traditionally turned chair legs from green wood and assembled them while green, with the dried legs gripping their tenons more tightly as they shrank. This is a real technique with specific properties, and modeling it would give a small but interesting gameplay differentiation.

But that's perhaps more granularity than you want. The basic spoilage-as-seasoning mechanic captures the essential dynamic, and it integrates naturally with the rest of the wood processing chain you'll be modeling.

content.text:
Great idea using spoilage for seasoning — it's actually a really apt mechanic for that, because seasoning is genuinely a time-passes-and-the-material-transforms process, not an active operation. Let me work through the full wood processing chain because there's quite a lot of structure here, and seasoning is one of several processes that fit nicely into your game's mechanics.

## The processing chain from standing tree to finished lumber

The full chain has more stages than people typically appreciate. Each one serves a distinct purpose and requires distinct tools and infrastructure.

### 1. Felling

Cutting down the standing tree. This is the entry point of the chain. Tools needed: axes (stone/bronze/iron/steel) for cutting, possibly wedges for directing the fall on large trees, and rope or cable for guiding the fall in difficult terrain.

The output is a felled tree with branches and crown still attached. Felling is fast for small trees but substantial work for large ones — a single skilled axeman could fell maybe 5-10 medium trees per day, fewer for very large ones.

In game terms, felling produces a "felled tree" or raw log object. The tool quality affects productivity (steel axes are much faster than stone) but doesn't fundamentally change capability — even stone-age people felled large trees successfully, just slowly.

### 2. Limbing and bucking

Removing branches (limbing) and cutting the trunk into transportable lengths (bucking). Tools: axes for limbing, axes or saws for bucking depending on log size and tool tier.

This stage is where the tree becomes a set of logs. The branches are typically left in the forest or burned (in some forest management systems they're collected for firewood). The clean trunk sections are the primary product.

Bucking length is determined by intended use: short bucks (1-2m) for firewood and small-section work, medium bucks (3-4m) for general lumber, long bucks (6-12m+) for shipbuilding and large structural timbers. The longest sections require specific transportation infrastructure because they're awkward to handle.

### 3. Hauling / transport from forest

Getting logs from where they fell to where they'll be processed. This is often the most labor-intensive part of the entire chain, especially for large logs.

Methods used historically:
- **Manhandling**: with poles, cant hooks, peavies. Effective for small logs, very labor-intensive for large ones.
- **Animal traction**: oxen or horses dragging logs along trails. Standard for medieval and early-modern forestry. A team of oxen can drag substantially larger logs than humans can handle.
- **Skidding and sledding**: dragging logs over the ground or on simple sleds, sometimes using prepared skid roads with slick surfaces. Winter operations using snow or ice were particularly efficient because of low friction.
- **Water transport**: floating logs down rivers (river drives), or rafting them tied together. The dominant method for long-distance log transport throughout history. Many regions were chosen for forestry specifically because they had drivable rivers.
- **Log flumes**: artificial channels of water to transport logs from upland forests to mills or rivers. Used in mountainous terrain where roads weren't practical.

For your game design, log transport is a real bottleneck and probably worth modeling. Forest siting near transportation corridors (rivers, established roads) is much more economically valuable than equivalent forest in remote terrain. This creates real geographic differentiation in forest value.

### 4. Initial conversion (the most variable stage)

This is where logs become usable timber. The processing technique varies dramatically based on intended use and tool availability, and the output forms are quite different.

**Splitting**: cleaving logs along the grain with wedges and froe. Produces split timbers with naturally rough surfaces but excellent strength because the grain runs continuously through the piece. Used for shingles, fence rails, riven planks, barrel staves, structural timbers in some traditions. Splitting is achievable with stone-age tools and remained important throughout pre-industrial woodworking because split wood is structurally superior to sawn wood for many applications.

**Hewing**: shaping a log into a rectangular timber by chopping away the rounded surfaces with a broad axe and adze. Produces a "hewn" timber with characteristic flat-but-not-perfectly-smooth surfaces showing axe marks. The dominant method for producing structural timbers throughout most of history. A skilled hewer could convert a log into a square timber with surfaces flat enough for building work in a few hours of skilled work.

**Pit sawing**: two workers using a long saw with one above the log on a frame and one below in a pit, sawing the log into planks. Slow and labor-intensive — a pit-sawing pair could produce maybe 10-15 board-feet per hour, depending on wood. The pitman below got the worse job (sawdust falling on him). This was the standard method for producing sawn lumber from antiquity until water-powered sawmills became widespread.

**Water-powered sawing**: a sawmill driven by a waterwheel, with one or more sawblades reciprocating to cut planks from logs. Dramatically more productive than pit sawing — a single water-powered saw could produce maybe 100+ board-feet per hour depending on the design. The first water-powered sawmills appear in late antiquity (the Hierapolis sawmill in Roman Asia Minor, ~3rd century CE) but become widespread only in the medieval period in Europe.

**Steam and circular sawing**: industrial-era developments with much higher productivity.

For your game, the conversion stage probably wants to differentiate at least:
- Hand tools (splitting and hewing): achievable with stone, bronze, or iron tools, productivity scales with tool quality
- Pit sawing: requires iron saw blades (bronze saws are technically possible but inefficient)
- Water-powered sawmill: requires water power infrastructure, iron blades, and bronze bearings

The output forms are different: split timbers and hewn timbers are produced as discrete shaped pieces; sawn lumber is produced as standardized planks and boards. Sawn lumber is much more versatile for downstream uses but requires more sophisticated infrastructure to produce.

### 5. Seasoning

This is where the spoilage mechanic comes in. Freshly cut wood ("green" wood) contains substantial water — typically 30-200% moisture content by dry weight, depending on species and time of year. This moisture must be removed before the wood can be used for most purposes.

What seasoning actually does:

- **Reduces moisture content** to equilibrium with ambient humidity (typically 12-18% in temperate climates, lower in arid environments)
- **Stabilizes dimensions** — green wood shrinks substantially as it dries, and shrinks unevenly along different axes (radial vs. tangential vs. longitudinal). Seasoning lets this shrinkage happen before the wood is used in critical applications.
- **Reduces weight** — dramatically. A green oak log can weigh 2x or more what the same log weighs after seasoning, simply from water loss.
- **Allows checking and cracking to occur** while the wood is in stockpile rather than in use. Wood that dries too fast checks badly; properly seasoned wood develops minor surface checks but maintains structural integrity.
- **Reduces weight-cost of further transport** because dry wood is much lighter than green.

The seasoning process is **slow**. The traditional rule of thumb is one year per inch (2.5cm) of thickness for air seasoning of typical hardwoods. So a 2-inch oak plank needs 2 years of seasoning; a 4-inch beam needs 4 years. Softwoods are somewhat faster but still measured in months to years for substantial pieces.

This is genuinely time-scale-of-game stuff, and modeling it as spoilage with a long timer is exactly right. A few specific aspects worth modeling:

- **Stack and stickering**: seasoned wood is stacked with spacer sticks ("stickers") between layers to allow air circulation. Without proper stacking, wood develops mold, stains, and uneven drying. This is a real practice that distinguishes proper seasoning from just leaving wood in a pile.
- **Covered or weather-protected storage**: seasoning sheds protect the stack from rain (which would re-wet the wood) but allow air flow. Covered seasoning is significantly slower than air seasoning but produces better quality wood.
- **End sealing**: the end grain of timber dries much faster than the side grain, which causes end checking (cracks). Sealing the ends with paint, wax, or animal fat slows end-grain drying and reduces checking. This is a small but real practice in good lumber production.

The specific spoilage-mechanic implementation might be:
- Green lumber has a "seasoning timer" that decrements over game time
- During seasoning, the lumber occupies stockpile space but cannot be used for high-quality applications
- After seasoning completes, the lumber transforms into seasoned lumber and is available for downstream uses
- Stack quality affects timer rate and possibly final quality (a well-stickered stack seasons faster and with less defect; a sloppy pile seasons slower or produces lower-quality output)

**Kiln drying** is the industrial alternative to air seasoning, developed in the 19th century but with antecedents going back to drying wood near hearths. A heated drying chamber forces moisture out of the wood much faster than air drying — days to weeks rather than months to years. The cost is energy input (heating fuel) and the risk of damaging the wood with too-rapid drying. For your game, kiln drying might be a tier-3 unlock that converts seasoning from a slow background process into an active, fuel-consuming process — a real economic tradeoff.

**Different uses tolerate different seasoning levels**:
- Firewood and charcoal feedstock can be used green (though dry wood burns better and produces more heat per unit mass)
- Construction-grade structural timber can use moderately seasoned wood (it will shrink in place, but mostly safely)
- Joinery and furniture wood needs thoroughly seasoned wood (or it will move and crack after assembly)
- Musical instruments, tool handles, and precision applications need very thoroughly seasoned wood, sometimes years beyond standard seasoning

This creates a natural quality gradient in the seasoning process: shorter seasoning gives lower-quality wood suitable for less demanding uses; longer seasoning gives higher-quality wood for premium applications. The player can choose where on this gradient to operate based on their needs and time horizon.

### 6. Secondary processing — surfacing and milling

After seasoning, lumber typically requires surface finishing before final use. The seasoned plank from the sawmill has rough surfaces, possibly some checking, and isn't dimensionally accurate enough for fine work.

**Hand planing**: smoothing rough lumber to a finished surface using hand planes. Achievable with bronze plane irons but works much better with iron and steel. A good cabinetmaker could surface a plank in minutes with sharp tools; the same work with dull or soft tools takes much longer.

**Power planing**: industrial-era machines that surface lumber automatically. Much later technology, requires steam or electric power.

**Resawing**: cutting seasoned lumber into thinner pieces. A 4-inch plank might be resawed into two 2-inch pieces, or four 1-inch pieces. Pit sawing or water-powered sawing handles this; the seasoned wood is much easier to cut than green wood because it's lighter and the cuts are cleaner.

**Joinery preparation**: cutting tenons, mortises, dovetails, and other joinery details. Hand tools (chisels, saws, planes) handle this throughout pre-industrial history; the quality of work is determined by tool sharpness and craftsman skill.

For game purposes, surfacing might be folded into the final product recipes (i.e., making a "finished plank" or "joinery stock" includes the surfacing work) rather than being a separate step. But it's worth knowing that it exists, because the tool and skill requirements are real.

### 7. End-product fabrication

This is where wood becomes specific objects: furniture, building components, ships, tools, vessels. Each end product has its own production chain with specific tool and skill requirements.

For game purposes, this is the recipe-output stage where seasoned, surfaced wood becomes finished goods. The fabrication itself is typically done in dedicated workshops (cabinetmaker's shop, shipyard, cooperage, wheelwright shop, joinery) with specific tooling.

## Variations and special processes

A few specific processes deserve mention because they're real and either historically important or gameplay-interesting:

### Steam bending

Bending wood to permanent curves by steaming it (heating in steam at ~100°C) and then clamping it to a form while it cools. Used for ship frames, furniture (Thonet's bentwood chairs are the classic example), barrel staves, wheel rims, musical instruments.

Not all wood bends well — oak, ash, beech, hickory, and elm are good benders; many other species crack rather than bend. Steam bending is a real specialized process requiring a steam box (a sealed wooden box with steam piped in) and bending forms. For your game, it might be a specialty process available with appropriate equipment.

### Riving (controlled splitting)

Splitting wood along the grain with a froe and mallet to produce thin, strong pieces with continuous grain. Used for shingles, basket splints, chair backs, and specialty applications where grain continuity matters more than dimensional accuracy. The output has rougher surfaces than sawn material but is structurally superior because no grain is cut.

Rived wood was a major product category throughout pre-industrial woodworking and remained important even after sawmills became common, because it's better than sawn material for some uses.

### Charring and pyrolysis

Wood charcoal production we've already discussed extensively, but related processes include:

- **Charring of fence posts and pile butts** — burning the surface of buried wood to a shallow charcoal layer, which significantly extends the wood's life in ground contact. A primitive but effective preservation technique.
- **Bog wood / preserved underwater storage** — submerging timber in oxygen-poor environments preserves it indefinitely. Was used historically to store ship timbers and other valuable wood. Connects to the rot-resistance properties of certain woods underwater.
- **Wood tar and pitch production** — a byproduct of charcoal making (especially from pine and other resinous woods), used as a wood preservative, ship caulking, and various other purposes. We touched on this briefly when discussing pyrolysis.

### Veneering and laminating

Cutting very thin sheets of premium wood (veneer) and gluing them to substrates of cheaper wood. Allows expensive woods to cover large areas at a fraction of the cost of solid wood, and was an important technique in fine cabinetmaking from the medieval period onward.

Veneer was originally cut by hand with very fine saws — a slow, expensive process that produced thick veneers (3-5mm). Modern thin veneers (less than 1mm) require specialized equipment and are an industrial-era development.

For your game, veneer might be a high-tier process producing premium decorative goods at lower wood cost than solid premium lumber. It requires very fine saws (steel) and skilled labor.

### Plywood and engineered wood

Modern composite materials made from wood. Plywood (cross-laminated thin sheets of wood) is a 20th-century product that revolutionized construction and packaging. Particle board, OSB, MDF, and laminated veneer lumber are all later industrial products.

These probably belong in a late-tier industrial section of your tech tree rather than the pre-industrial woodworking core. They require specific adhesives (glues that themselves are advanced products) and pressing equipment.

## Byproducts and waste streams

Wood processing produces substantial byproducts that have their own uses and economic significance:

**Sawdust**: a major byproduct of sawmilling. Uses include packing material, fuel (briquettes or direct burning), animal bedding, smoking meat, ice insulation (a major historical use — sawdust packed around blocks of ice in icehouses extended ice lifespan dramatically), and as feedstock for various industrial processes (eventually including pulp and particle board in industrial periods).

**Bark**: removed during processing for some uses, retained for others. Tan-bark (especially oak bark) was a major industrial product for leather tanning throughout the pre-industrial era — tannin extracted from bark was the dominant leather preservation chemistry until synthetic tannins emerged in the 19th-20th centuries. Cork (from cork oak) is bark used directly. Birch bark was used for canoes, containers, and as a writing surface in some traditions. Other barks have specific uses (cinchona bark for quinine, willow bark for salicylic acid, various medicinal barks).

**Wood chips and offcuts**: smaller pieces left from processing. Used as fuel, charcoal feedstock, and sometimes in specific products (offcut lumber for fence pickets, chips for smoking meat).

**Branches and tops**: the parts of the tree above the main bole, removed during limbing. Historically used as firewood (the largest single use), charcoal feedstock, and small constructional material (wattle for wattle-and-daub construction, small poles for tool handles and minor framing).

**Stumps and roots**: typically left in place when trees are felled; sometimes excavated for specific uses (root burls have decorative value; oak roots and stump wood produces particularly dense charcoal). Usually a labor-intensive proposition for limited additional yield.

**Resin and pitch**: from coniferous species, harvested either by tapping living trees (for turpentine and rosin from pine) or by pyrolysis (for pitch and tar). Major industrial products throughout pre-industrial history.

**Specialty chemical extracts**: tannin from oak and chestnut bark, dye chemicals from various tropical hardwoods (logwood for purple, brazilwood for red), medicinal compounds from specific species. The chemical economy of pre-modern wood is richer than people often appreciate.

## How this might map into your game

For a workable wood processing chain in your game, I'd suggest something like the following structure, with the spoilage mechanic for seasoning as you proposed:

**Forestry stage**:
- Felling produces raw logs (different species based on biome)
- Limbing produces logs + branch byproduct (firewood/charcoal feedstock)
- Hauling moves logs from forest to processing site (transport-distance dependent on terrain and available infrastructure)

**Conversion stage**:
- Splitting (low-tech, suitable for some products like shingles and rails)
- Hewing (low-tech, produces structural timbers)
- Pit sawing (mid-tech, produces sawn planks, requires iron saws)
- Water-powered sawing (high-tech, produces sawn planks at industrial rates, requires water mill + bronze bearings + iron blades)

**Seasoning stage** (your spoilage mechanic):
- Green lumber → seasoning stack with timer (months to years depending on thickness and species)
- Stacking quality affects timer and final quality
- Optionally: kiln drying as later-tier alternative converting time to energy

**Surfacing stage** (probably folded into product recipes):
- Hand planing for fine surfaces
- Joinery preparation for assembled products

**Product stage**:
- Specific recipes for end products (furniture, ship components, tool handles, building lumber, etc.)
- Different products require different wood types (your category system) and different seasoning levels

**Byproduct streams**:
- Branches/limbs → firewood, charcoal feedstock
- Sawdust → minor uses (packing, fuel, animal bedding)
- Bark → tannin (for leather), specific specialty uses
- Resin (from conifers) → turpentine, pitch, tar

The seasoning spoilage mechanic specifically is interesting because it creates real time-pressure on wood inventory management. A player with a productive forestry operation has a lot of green wood and a small amount of immediately usable seasoned wood. They have to plan ahead — wood seasoned today is for projects starting in a year. This creates real long-term planning gameplay around wood supply, which is actually historically accurate. Pre-modern shipbuilders maintained large stocks of seasoning oak for years before it would be used.

## A note on regional and cultural variation

Different woodworking traditions emphasized different parts of this chain. Some examples:

- **Japanese carpentry** developed extreme precision in joinery using primarily hand tools, with sawn lumber as the input. Japanese saws cut on the pull stroke (rather than push stroke as in European tradition), allowing thinner blades and more precise cuts. Japanese woodworking culture is associated with specific species (hinoki cypress, Japanese cedar) and specific construction methods (post-and-beam frames with no metal fasteners, joinery executed to extraordinary precision).

- **Scandinavian timber framing** emphasizes hewing and splitting techniques for log construction, with characteristic notched corner joinery (saddle notches, dovetail notches). Construction is essentially log-on-log with axe-cut joinery, no sawn lumber required.

- **English oak framing** developed elaborate joinery for great houses, cathedrals, and ships, with mortise-and-tenon connections pegged with treenails, scarf joints for joining long timbers, and complex bracing systems. The carpentry tradition supported building roof spans and ship structures of remarkable size.

- **Chinese carpentry** developed dougong bracket systems for supporting heavy roofs, with elaborate stacked joinery requiring no metal fasteners. The system is structurally interesting because it's earthquake-resistant — the joints can flex and absorb seismic loads.

For your game, these regional variations might be flavor (different aesthetic styles for the same functional outputs) or might be meaningful gameplay differentiation (different production techniques with different efficiencies and resource requirements). Either way, it's worth knowing that "woodworking" isn't a single universal tradition but a diverse set of regional approaches, each adapted to local conditions and materials.

## A final thought on the spoilage mechanic

Using spoilage for seasoning is a really nice match because it captures something true about the material: **wood is a living material that transforms over time without active intervention**. This is unusual in industrial production — most materials sit inert in inventory until acted on. Wood is different. It's actively drying, possibly developing defects, possibly improving in quality (some woods like wine, actually improving with age — old oak from a 200-year-old beam is more stable than freshly seasoned oak).

The spoilage mechanic captures the time-passes dimension of wood economy. A player who plans ahead and starts seasoning stocks years before they're needed has a strategic advantage; a player who tries to use green wood for fine work produces inferior products that fail in service. This is honest material physics translated into gameplay, which is what your design philosophy is aiming for.

If you want to go further, you could even model **green wood having distinct properties from seasoned wood** — heavier, more flexible, easier to work with hand tools (because it's softer when wet), but unsuitable for joinery because it will shrink. Some traditional crafts actually use green wood deliberately — Welsh chairmakers (the bodgers) traditionally turned chair legs from green wood and assembled them while green, with the dried legs gripping their tenons more tightly as they shrank. This is a real technique with specific properties, and modeling it would give a small but interesting gameplay differentiation.

But that's perhaps more granularity than you want. The basic spoilage-as-seasoning mechanic captures the essential dynamic, and it integrates naturally with the rest of the wood processing chain you'll be modeling.

I have a clear picture now. The creator is Ray Hidayat (raysplaceinspace), a solo dev in New Zealand.
