That's a meaningful prior, not a vibe-coded debut.

Easel is a multi-year solo project (his first post calls out "two years" in 2024, and the beta announcement says "3 years"), written in Rust compiled to WebAssembly. The post you read makes that pretty clear in retrospect — building a custom 2D physics engine with incremental snapshotting/rollback so it composes cleanly with their netcode layer, and benchmarking specific behaviors against Rapier, Box2D 2.4/3.0, and Photon Quantum, is not vibe-coded territory. You have to know exactly why position correction is solved separately from velocity to write that section, and you have to have actually read those engines' source to make those comparisons.

The website copy reading as AI-flavored is, I think, partly genuine LLM assistance for marketing prose and partly the cheerful didactic register he's leaning into deliberately — Easel is positioned as a teaching tool (Pico-8-adjacent, "great first language"), so the homepage is written for parents and teachers, not for HN. The blog voice is noticeably tighter and more technical than the homepage, which is consistent with a developer who hand-writes the engineering content and was looser with marketing copy.

The actually-interesting design claim, from your angle: the *language itself* is the synchronization boundary. Reactive + hierarchical + concurrent semantics, with lifetimes implied by lexical nesting, and the multiplayer-determinism invariants enforced by the compiler rather than by programmer discipline. It's the same instinct you keep coming back to — push correctness into the type system / language semantics so opaque scripting can't violate it — applied to netcode instead of resource flow. The rollback physics post is the same philosophy one layer down: incremental snapshotting at the engine level mirrors incremental computation at the language level. The whole stack is built around "only re-do what changed," which is why he could justify writing a bespoke physics engine instead of bolting Rapier on.

# A Physics Engine with Incremental Rollback

May 1, 2026 · 9 min read

[![raysplaceinspace](https://easel.games/img/authors/raysplaceinspace.jpg)](https://twitter.com/raysplacenspace)

[raysplaceinspace](https://twitter.com/raysplacenspace)

Creator of Easel

We want Easel to be powerful enough to make the kinds of games you would play for hours.
Popular multiplayer games like **Among Us** let you walk around an entire spaceship, completing tasks and evading impostors.
Unfortunately, up to this point, games of that scale were out of reach for Easel,
because the off-the-shelf physics engine would have to snapshot and roll back the entire world
to support Easel's predictive multiplayer architecture.
It's too much to do every frame.

Until this point, you were required to keep your world **small**. But **not anymore**!

Easel's new **custom-built physics engine** only snapshots and rolls back the parts of the world that **change**.
That big spaceship might have thousands of objects forming the walls, the control panels, the vents, and so on.
However, each frame, a surprisingly few number of objects actually change - perhaps less than 30 per frame
as the players walk around and interact with the world.
A smart implementation keeps objects sleeping while they are offscreen.

With only 30 objects out of thousands needing to be snapshotted each frame,
a factor of 30-50x fewer than before, multiplayer Easel games with large worlds suddenly becomes feasible.
Release the feral hogs!

## Under the Hood[​](#under-the-hood "Direct link to Under the Hood")

Easel's new physics engine is custom-built for Easel, which is why it supports everything Easel supports, but better!
Here is a tour of some of the features that make it special.

### Sleep[​](#sleep "Direct link to Sleep")

The fastest way to do something is to not do it at all.
When a body is asleep, it does not require any snapshotting, rollback,
or any physics calculations until it wakes up again.
Unlike other engines which wait for a few seconds of inactivity,
Easel puts bodies to sleep immediately when their velocity reaches zero (within a small epsilon threshold, of course, we're not *slow*).

One tricky case here is **gravity**, which has the potential to keep your entire world awake with its constant nagging force.
Easel tracks the forces and reaction forces on every object and can see whether they are balanced or unbalanced.
Regardless of whether it is at zero velocity, as long as one body in a stack has unbalanced forces,
the stack has not settled into equilibrium and so the whole stack stays awake.

### Spatial Indexing[​](#spatial-indexing "Direct link to Spatial Indexing")

Like many other physics engines, Easel's **broad phase** uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to quickly find potential collisions.
Easel's BVH algorithms are optimized to minimize unnecessary snapshotting and rollback,
only performing incremental rebalancing when the tree is already undergoing change.
Do you only do the vacuuming just before your friends come over? Easel's BVH is ~~lazy~~ efficient just like you.

One additional trick is Easel's BVH also tracks the [Categories](https://easel.games/docs/learn/physics/categories) of each collider,
which speeds up common game queries dramatically.
It is very common, for example, for a bot to target the nearest player, and if the player is on the other side of the map,
it would have to traverse through every single collider in the world to find the nearest player.
Finding the nearest `Category:Needle` amongst a sea of `Category:Haystack` colliders is a lot faster with a metal detector!

### Stepping[​](#stepping "Direct link to Stepping")

Making a character take a step is something so common but surprisingly complex in physics engines.
A common method is to add velocity for the step, then subtract it after the physics simulation is complete,
but a problem arises when the character collides with an obstacle mid-step.

Even if the physics engine does its job correctly and zeroes out the velocity,
later on when the previously-added step velocity gets subtracted, it reintroduces the bounce back that the physics engine just zeroed out.
It makes your character feel really bouncy.

* Some games fix this by **damping** out all velocity, which removes bounce back but also removes knockback too,
  removing some of the fun and feel of the game. Walk into a wall? No bounce, good. Get hit by a fireball? No knockback. Seems wrong.
* Other games fix this by creating a **kinematic character controller** based on raycasting.
  In physics engine terms, **kinematic** (as opposed to static or dynamic) means that the character is not affected by forces and collisions.
  In other words, the physics engine has failed to produce the desired results, and so it is now being bypassed entirely.
  *You had one job physics engine. Physics. Do it. Please. Not not like that. Okay fine I'll do it myself.*

Non-bouncy stepping has been built directly into the solver of the Easel physics engine.
Simply use [ForcefulStep](https://easel.games/docs/reference/physics#forcefulstep) with the new `restitution=0` parameter,
and Easel's new physics engine will make sure the step does not bounce back.

#### How does it work?[​](#how-does-it-work "Direct link to How does it work?")

The trick is, Easel treats stepping in a similar way to how it corrects for position overlap.

Have you ever played a game where your character gets stuck in a wall,
and the physics engine tries to **eject** you, sending you flying across the map?
It is a common physics engine glitch.
Super Mario 64 speedrunners famously love to make him slide backwards up the stairs on his backside using a glitch like this.
Ow.

Modern physics engines try to avoid this problem by solving for **position correction** separately.
The force that would eject your character out of the wall is applied immediately to the position without changing your velocity,
which means the **ejection velocity does not last** beyond the current frame.

`ForcefulStep` in Easel is implemented as part of position correction,
which is why it does not cause bounce back, unless you want it to.
We're killing two (angry) birds with one stone!

info

In reality, it is a bit more complicated for numerous reasons.
Easel first solves for both ejection+stepping and velocity at the same time,
then we store that ejection velocity, then we remove the ejection+stepping constraints and solve again, storing the stabilized velocity.
At this point, nothing has moved yet, which is why we are now free to sweep for the next time-of-impact using the correct velocities.
When it comes time to take a step, we use the ejection velocity, but at the end of the frame we only commit the stabilized velocity
and so the bounce disappears.

In other words, Easel collects all the data it needs up front without making changes, so that when it does make a move, it can make the correct one.

### Continuous Collision Detection[​](#continuous-collision-detection "Direct link to Continuous Collision Detection")

We love it when two fireballs collide with each other in mid-air.

Finding the collision between two fast-moving objects like this requires continous collision detection,
because if we just checked for collisions once every frame,
we might miss the precise moment when the two fireballs overlap.

Continuous collision detection is Easel is performed by sweeping and then shape casting like other physics engines,
but in doing this we noticed a few differences between Easel other physics engines
which may be interesting to some ~~nerds~~ game developers:

* The **Rapier** physics engine can produce an incorrect result when the fireball begins the frame touching a mirror.
  In Easel, collisions are resolved first, causing the fireball to bounce and change direction,
  and **only then** does it search for the time-of-impact of those two fireballs.
  In Rapier, the time-of-impact is searched for first using the original velocities,
  meaning that in this case, it starts by sweeping that fireball in the wrong direction.
  This difference happens because Rapier does the position integration early,
  committing to a substep length before it knows what the time of impact is going to be.
  Easel stores enough information up front that it can do the position integration after it knows the time of impact, avoiding this problem.
* **Box2D 2.4** does sweep using the correct velocities but takes a different approach of doing the full normal physics simulation,
  then backtracking, which is why all collisions are already resolved before continuous collision detection.
  Interestingly, the new **Box2D 3.0** does not support dynamic-to-dynamic continuous collision detection at all,
  meaning those two fireballs would have no choice but to miss each other like ships in the night.
  Perhaps this is a future direction for Box2D as, besides this, it seems they have achieved the holy grail of avoiding substepping at all
  by using speculative contacts.
* **Photon Quantum**, a professional multiplayer rollback netcode engine, does not support continuous collision detection at all,
  citing that their physics engine is stateless and so it would be too expensive.
  It seems incremental snapshotting and rollback of our physics state has enabled Easel to support this feature performantly.

### Bodies can move themselves[​](#bodies-can-move-themselves "Direct link to Bodies can move themselves")

One inconvenient edge case with the previous physics engine is that a body with a `velocity` or `turnRate` and no colliders
would not move at all.

It could be argued that this is correct. If there is no mass to hold momentum, there's no movement,
but we are not just making a *physics* engine, we are making a *game* engine.
Sometimes bodies are just a way to group sprites together, and the physics is not important.

Now if you give a body a `velocity` or `turnRate`, it will move itself even if it has no colliders.
Attach a `TextSprite` and you could have a simple billboard floating up the screen,
scrolling away to a galaxy far, far away.

*Sidenote: Photons don't have mass but they still have velocity,
in fact there are `10^17` of them hitting your eyes right now every second,
so maybe some physics engines need a reality check.*

## Thanks to[​](#thanks-to "Direct link to Thanks to")

Easel's physics engine is built upon the collision detection algorithms of [Parry](https://parry.rs),
an excellent open source library created by Dimforge that powers the [Rapier](https://rapier.rs) physics engine.

Making a physics engine has been a huge endeavor.
Many little decisions have been made to make implement it in a way
that is neat, efficient and works well with Easel's multiplayer architecture.
Now everything, not just the physics engine, but all parts of Easel only snapshot and rollback
the parts that change, meaning you can make much bigger worlds.

It's time think bigger!

# Make games with EaselEasel

Make **games**. Play **together**. So **easy**.

[Tutorial](https://easel.games/docs/learn/quickstart)[Try it now](https://easel.games/Editor/Sample/quickstart)

**Easel** is a **beginner-friendly** game engine, programming language, and online platform for 2D **browser** games

### Specialized for Games

The Easel programming language is designed specifically for games. That's why it is so **fast**, so **easy** and so **fun** to make games with Easel.

### Share Easily, Play Instantly

With just a link, Easel games can be **played instantly** right here in your **browser**, no download required. Easy to **share**, recommend, and talk about.

### Effortless Multiplayer

Code as if all your players are inside one shared game world, like a **singleplayer** game, and Easel makes your game **[multiplayer](https://easel.games/docs/learn/multiplayer)** automatically.

### Beginner-Friendly

**Simple** yet **powerful**. Lots of features built-in. All documentation in one place. A great choice for your first programming language.

### Try It Now

Explore the [**Sample Project**](https://easel.games/Editor/Sample/quickstart) in the **online editor** right now. Do the [**tutorial**](https://easel.games/docs/learn/quickstart) this afternoon! No signup required.

# Make games with ease

Easel is what happens when a programming language is **fundamentally reshaped** for making games and only games. Common game concepts like state, ownership, behaviors, user interfaces and multiplayer are sculpted into shape of the language, not just the library. That's why it's so **fast**, so **easy** and so **fun** to make games with Easel.

```
pub game fn World.Main(maxHumanPlayers=10) {  
    SpawnEachPlayer owner {  
        Subspawn ship {  
            use body=ship, radius=1, shape=Equilateral(numPoints=3)  
            Body(pos=20*RandomVector)  
            PolygonSprite(color=#00ffbb, layer=1)  
              
            on Pointer {  
                Heading = Angle(Pointer - Pos)  
            }  
            on ButtonDown(Click) {  
                behavior<thrust> on BeforePhysics {  
                    Velocity += Heading.Direction * 0.5  
                    Spark(color=#ff8800, bloom=5, shine=1, splatter=1, velocity=-25*Heading.Direction)  
                }  
            }  
            on ButtonUp(Click) {  
                delete behavior<thrust>  
            }  
        }  
    }  
}
```

[Try this code in the online editor](https://easel.games/Editor/Sample/example/main.easel)

Tap on a line of code to learn more about it.

Hover over a line of code to learn more about it.

# Code multiplayer games without coding the multiplayer

**Effortless multiplayer:** Code as if all your players are inside one shared game world, **like a singleplayer game**, and Easel will make your game multiplayer. **Automatically**.

**Automatic multiplayer? How is that possible?**Multiplayer is baked into the fabric of the Easel programming language itself. That is why anything you code in Easel is multiplayer without any special effort on your part. It's like **magic**!

**Beginner-friendly:** Multiplayer normally takes years of programming experience to master, but not with Easel. No need to learn a thing about networking or synchronization. No pitfalls or traps to avoid. With Easel, it's **impossible to make mistakes** when it comes to multiplayer, even if you're a complete beginner. **It just works**.

**Share instantly:** With just a click you can publish your game online and share the link with your friends. No download required, they can play in their browser. Immediately.

# Learn to code, the fun way!

**Make games you can play together:** Learning to code is so much more engaging when you can actually play your game with your friends, family, teachers and classmates. Even on your first day of coding, Easel lets you make games you can instantly share and play together!

**A great choice for your first programming language:** Powerful yet accessible. Lots of built-in features. All the documentation in one place. Easy to get started but lots of room to grow. Perfect for your first programming language.

**Get started right away:** Code games in your web browser using our online editor, no download required. Even works on a Chromebook or iPad (with a keyboard), which makes it perfect for school students.

**A safe, ad-free zone:** Worried what your teenagers are being shown online? There are no ads on the Easel platform, so that is one less thing for you to worry about.

**Intrigued?** Try our [quickstart tutorial](https://easel.games/docs/learn/quickstart) and see for yourself how easy it is to learn to code with Easel!

What is Easel?

Easel is a beginner-friendly game engine, programming language and online platform for 2D browser games. There are two things that make it really stand out:

* Easel can make your game **multiplayer** automatically.
* Easel has a unique programming model that is designed to match how **humans**, not computers, think about game logic.
Why is it so easy to make multiplayer games with Easel?

Even for experienced programmers, **multiplayer is hard**. When coding a multiplayer game, your entire codebase must be written in a "multiplayer safe" way. If even a single line of your entire codebase is not multiplayer safe, the entire game will desynchronize. It is **easy to get wrong**, especially for a beginner.

In Easel, **multiplayer is baked in** to the programming language itself. That is why, any code you write in Easel can be made multiplayer **automatically**, without any special effort on your part. Code as if all your players are in one shared world, like a singleplayer game, and Easel takes makes it multiplayer for you, taking care of all the networking and synchronization. It is completely automatic, and you can never get it wrong, even if it is literally your first day of coding. It **just works**.

Additionally, Easel is also the online platform that hosts all Easel games. Because all Easel games are made with the Easel programming language, they can efficiently share the same servers, making it cost-efficient enough that we can empower everyone of all ages to develop multiplayer games. Easel is **democratizing** multiplayer game development.

What does it mean, that Easel is designed to match how humans, not computers, think about game logic?

Most game engines require you to think in a frame-by-frame model to match how the **computer** is executing your code. Sometimes this requires converting your code into state machines, where the code flows in a non-linear fashion and so can be more difficult to follow.

Easel is a high level programming language/game engine. With its **hierarchical**, **reactive**, and **asynchronous** programming style, it goes even further than most to match how **humans** think about game logic. This makes Easel refreshingly productive for experienced programmers, and approachable and fun for beginners. Easel takes the barriers away so you can unleash your creativity.

What is reactive programming and why is it useful?

The way you code Easel is quite different to how you would code a game in another programming language because Easel is [reactive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reactive_programming). Below is a very short example which attempts to capture the essence of this idea. Imagine you want a health bar that transitions from green to red as the the hero loses health:

```
with Health {  
  PolygonSprite(color = (Health / MaxHealth).Mix(#ff0000, #00ff00))  
}
```

Reactive programming is about declaring **state** (using a [property](https://easel.games/docs/learn/entities/props) like `Health`), then using a construct like a [with block](https://easel.games/docs/learn/language/behaviors#with) to declare how your game should use that state, not just initially, but also every time the state changes. In this case we displaying it by creating/replacing a [PolygonSprite](https://easel.games/docs/reference/graphics#polygonsprite) component. From that point on, we can forget about how the `Health` is displayed, we only need worry about changing the state (`Health`) and the game will respond accordingly by itself. This is how Easel lets you think at a higher level.

Easel does a lot behind the scenes to make those 3 lines work efficiently, only re-executing them when change occurs, and automatically removing the hook when it is no longer needed. See [Why Easel?](https://easel.games/docs/learn/why#reactive) for a deeper dive into the details.

What is an asynchronous and concurrent programming language, and why is that useful?

Easel is an **asynchronous** programming language, which means you can simply use the [await](https://easel.games/docs/learn/language/await) keyword to wait for something to happen, even if it takes a long time and crosses multiple frames. This allows your code to be written as a straightforward sequence of step-by-step instructions. The top-to-bottom layout matches the order they are executed. This makes your code more natural, intuitive and easier to understand.

```
loop {  
    await SpawnMonsters(99)  
    await AllMonstersDestroyed  
}
```

Other game engines use a frame-by-frame model. That means if any actions take more than one frame, you need to split your code into a state machine so you can pickup the task again later. This means the flow of your code jumps around, which is not as intuitive.

For all of this to be possible, Easel is also a **concurrent** programming language. Easel games often consist of thousands of concurrently-executing [behaviors](https://easel.games/docs/learn/language/behaviors). When a behavior is [waiting](https://easel.games/docs/learn/language/await) for something to happen, it goes to sleep and does not take any resources, while other behaviors continue executing like normal.

In what way is Easel a hierarchical programming language, and how is that useful?

In Easel, you nest blocks inside of blocks inside of blocks:

```
Subspawn ship {  
    on ButtonDown(Click) {  
        Spawn projectile {  
            // ...  
        }  
    }  
}
```

This is useful in two ways:

* **Automatic cleanup:** In Easel, lifespan is *implied* by the hierarchy. When a `ship` despawns, everything declared inside of it (like the `on ButtonDown(Click)` behavior), will automatically stop. This avoids an entire category of bugs with things outliving their intended lifespan and wreaking havoc. Structurally removing this worry is what enables **concurrent** programming in Easel, where games are often made of thousands of concurrently-executing behaviors. While that might be a nightmare to manage in another programming language, in Easel, nothing ever lives longer than it should. It's so worry-free beginners are constantly doing concurrent programming in Easel without realising it.
* **Reduce indirection:** Some programming languages/game engines require you to declare a new function whenever you want to spawn an entity, attach an event handler, or create a particle system. When the effect is small and short-lived, the overhead of splitting off that code into another place, sometimes in another file altogether, makes your code hard to follow. Easel's hierarchical style lets you write the code within the context that it is relevant.
What is a game engine?

Imagine if, whenever an author wanted to write a novel, they first had to code their word processor (e.g. Google Docs or Microsoft Word). Only people who possessed both programming skills and creative writing skills would ever write books, and the world would miss out on many masterpieces. Your favorite book might never have been written.

When it comes to games, not everyone has the time or interest to program all the graphics pipelines, audio systems, physics, etc needed for a game. A game engine to games is like Microsoft Word is to books. It is a tool full of features that let you skip ahead and start actually making your game. Easel is one example of a game engine, but there are many.

What is the benefit of an integrated game engine/programming language?

A game engine needs to have a lot of features to be useful - graphics, audio, user interface systems, physics, multiplayer and more. Most game engines include a programming language of some form to coordinate everything, but because both making and learning a programming language are such a great challenge, most use an existing programming language like C# or Lua, and are unable to reshape the programming language to fit their needs.

Easel is unique in that it is both a game engine and a programming language, in one. Being able to reshape the programming language for the game engine enables certain features to be achieved that could not be achieved any other way:

* Most notably, the only reason [multiplayer](https://easel.games/docs/learn/multiplayer) can be automatic in Easel is because it is baked into the programming language itself.
* The [user interface](https://easel.games/docs/learn/ui) system can only be so simple because some parts have been built into the Easel compiler.
* [Behaviors](https://easel.games/docs/learn/language/behaviors) are a key Easel feature that reshape how you do everything in Easel. Their reliable order-of-execution and controlled lifespans that make them worry-free are only possible because they have been built into the programming language itself.
I'm new to programming. Is Easel for me?

Yes! Easel is designed to be a great first programming language. Learning to code is like learning to swim or riding a bike - you cannot just read books about it or watch video tutorials. You have to actually do it. Easel makes this easy in a number of ways:

1. **No installation required**, which is often the first hurdle. Get started instantly with the online editor and all game-making functionality built-in.
2. Because Easel is designed for making games, it enables a **quick iteration cycle** between writing code and seeing its effects visually, allowing you to learn by doing.
3. Easel has intentionally been designed to be **intuitive** with its hierarchical and event-driven programming style, which makes it easier to learn while **having fun** way and without getting discouraged.
4. **Learn by example.** Lets say you want want to add a leaderboard to your game. The source code to every Easel game is available, which means you can find another Easel game with a leaderboard and learn how they did it!
5. **Play together!** Easel games can be published online with just a few clicks and instantly shared with your friends, family, teachers, classmates or other people online. Sharing your learning-to-code journey with other people will make it more meaningful and help you stay motivated.
I've been programming for a long time. Is Easel for me?

If you've programmed before, you'll have a lot of **fun** making games with Easel. Its hierarchical approach and its event-driven concurrency model let you be refreshingly **productive**. Easel is both familiar but different from other programming languages and it will inspire you to think in **new ways**.

At the same time, Easel is first and foremost designed to be approachable to beginners, and there are numerous instances where we have intentionally chosen simplicity over power. Be warned - Easel is not Unity, Unreal or Godot and ambitious programmers may become frustrated by its limitations. We hope people love Easel in a similar way to [Pico-8](https://www.lexaloffle.com/pico-8.php), another [fantasy console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantasy_video_game_console) engine that has been kept simple intentionally. The constraints breed creativity, and allow you to actually **finish** games instead of letting your dreams spiral out of reach.

Is Easel free?

Easel's generous free tier is enough to make a complete games and share them with your friends and classmates, so you can get started right now!

If you intend to make your game for the world (we are talking hundreds of players a month), you may need to subscribe to [Easel+](https://easel.games/pricing) to cover the bandwidth costs, and/or encourage your players to subscribe. By subscribing to Easel+, you'll be helping in our mission to bring the joy of coding to the next generation.

Ready to make your first game with **Easel**?

[Tutorial](https://easel.games/docs/learn/quickstart)[Try it now](https://easel.games/Editor/Sample/quickstart)

raysplaceinspaceCreator of Easel · We want Easel to be powerful enough to make the kinds of games you would play for hours. Popular multiplayer games like Among Us let you walk around an entire spaceship, completing tasks and evading impostors. Unfortunately, up to this point, games of that scale were out of reach for Easel, because the off-the-shelf physics engine would have to snapshot and roll back the entire world to support Easel's predictive multiplayer architecture. It's too much to do every frame. Until this point, you were required to keep your world small. But not anymore! Easel's new custom-built physics engine only snapshots and rolls back the parts of the world that change. That big spaceship might have thousands of objects forming the walls, the control panels, the vents, and so on. However, each frame, a surprisingly few number of objects actually change - perhaps less than 30 per frame as the players walk around and interact with the world.

raysplaceinspaceCreator of Easel · We want Easel to be powerful enough to make the kinds of games you would play for hours. Popular multiplayer games like Among Us let you walk around an entire spaceship, completing tasks and evading impostors. Unfortunately, up to this point, games of that scale were out of reach for Easel, because the off-the-shelf physics engine would have to snapshot and roll back the entire world to support Easel's predictive multiplayer architecture. It's too much to do every frame. Until this point, you were required to keep your world small. But not anymore! Easel's new custom-built physics engine only snapshots and rolls back the parts of the world that change. That big spaceship might have thousands of objects forming the walls, the control panels, the vents, and so on. However, each frame, a surprisingly few number of objects actually change - perhaps less than 30 per frame as the players walk around and interact with the world.

With only 30 objects out of thousands needing to be snapshotted each frame, a factor of 30-50x fewer than before, multiplayer Easel games with large worlds suddenly becomes feasible. Release the feral hogs! Easel's new physics engine is custom-built for Easel, which is why it supports everything Easel supports, but better! Here is a tour of some of the features that make it special. The fastest way to do something is to not do it at all. When a body is asleep, it does not require any snapshotting, rollback, or any physics calculations until it wakes up again. Unlike other engines which wait for a few seconds of inactivity, Easel puts bodies to sleep immediately when their velocity reaches zero (within a small epsilon threshold, of course, we're not slow). One tricky case here is gravity, which has the potential to keep your entire world awake with its constant nagging force.

One additional trick is Easel's BVH also tracks the Categories of each collider, which speeds up common game queries dramatically. It is very common, for example, for a bot to target the nearest player, and if the player is on the other side of the map, it would have to traverse through every single collider in the world to find the nearest player. Finding the nearest Category:Needle amongst a sea of Category:Haystack colliders is a lot faster with a metal detector! Making a character take a step is something so common but surprisingly complex in physics engines. A common method is to add velocity for the step, then subtract it after the physics simulation is complete, but a problem arises when the character collides with an obstacle mid-step. Even if the physics engine does its job correctly and zeroes out the velocity, later on when the previously-added step velocity gets subtracted, it reintroduces the bounce back that the physics engine just zeroed out.

Some games fix this by damping out all velocity, which removes bounce back but also removes knockback too, removing some of the fun and feel of the game. Walk into a wall? No bounce, good. Get hit by a fireball? No knockback. Seems wrong. Other games fix this by creating a kinematic character controller based on raycasting. In physics engine terms, kinematic (as opposed to static or dynamic) means that the character is not affected by forces and collisions. In other words, the physics engine has failed to produce the desired results, and so it is now being bypassed entirely. You had one job physics engine. Physics. Do it. Please. Not not like that. Okay fine I'll do it myself. Non-bouncy stepping has been built directly into the solver of the Easel physics engine. Simply use ForcefulStep with the new restitution=0 parameter, and Easel's new physics engine will make sure the step does not bounce back.

content.title: Introducing Easel | Easel
content.text:
Learn to code the fun way: by making games you can play with your friends! Easel is an entirely solo project that I have been working on for two years, and I am excited to finally share it with you all.

raysplaceinspaceCreator of Easel · Welcome to Easel, a 2D game programming language that lets you code multiplayer like singleplayer. Learn to code the fun way: by making games you can play with your friends! Easel is an entirely solo project that I have been working on for two years, and I am excited to finally share it with you all. When I made my previous game, Acolyte Fight, I found that a large proportion of the players were more interested in modding the game than playing it. The easy-to-use tools that I had created for myself turned out to be a hit with people who were new to coding. Unfortunately, the tools were limited to the design the existing game and so there was a limit not just to what could be made, but what could be learned. Ever since then, I wondered, what would happen if someone would make a new game engine with the same declarative style of editing, but with substantially more power and flexibility?

Learning to code can be a long journey. You've got to find a way to do it that is engaging enough that you can stick with it for the long haul. When I was a child, I learned to code by making the tools I needed to mod StarCraft, one of the most popular games at the time. That kept me interested. I hope Easel can do the same for a new generation of coders. Easel is a specifically online multiplayer engine because I believe that one of the most engaging ways to learn to code is to do it with other people. I hope that Easel can be a place where people can come together to learn and create. I imagine a community of people of all skill levels coming together, helping each other out, sharing their latest creations, and creating amazing things together. One thing that I really loved about Acolyte Fight was that it introduced coding to people who had never coded before.

I hope that the same happens for Easel. The people I hope to reach are not specifically the ones who already want to make games, but instead its the people who want to play games, but gradually become curious about how their favourite game is made. That is why I hope to see some truly fun and engaging games made with Easel that will reach a wide audience and somewhat accidently inspire people to look behind the curtain. Coding can be a life-changing skill, it was for me, and I hope that Easel can be a part of that journey for you or someone you love. If you are interested in learning more about Easel, a good place to start is the Quickstart tutorial.

content.title: Show HN: Easel – Code multiplayer games like singleplayer | Hacker News
content.text: Normally when coding multiplayer you have to worry about following "the rules of multiplayer" like avoiding non-determinism, or not modifying entities your client has no authority over, but all that is just way too hard for someone who just wants to get straight into making games. So my idea was that if we put multiplayer into the fabric of the programming language, below all of your code, we can make the entire language multiplayer-safe. In Easel the entire world is hermetically sealed - there is nothing you can do to break multiplayer, which means it suits someone who just wants to make games and not learn all about networking. I've had people make multiplayer games on their first day of coding with Easel because you basically cannot go wrong · There were so many other interesting things that went into this project. It's written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly because I think ...

I have a clear picture now. The creator is Ray Hidayat (raysplaceinspace), a solo dev in New Zealand. He previously made Acolyte Fight! — a browser multiplayer wizard-dueling game with a built-in spell modding system that built a real community around tinkering with code. That's a meaningful prior, not a vibe-coded debut.

Easel is a multi-year solo project (his first post calls out "two years" in 2024, and the beta announcement says "3 years"), written in Rust compiled to WebAssembly. The post you read makes that pretty clear in retrospect — building a custom 2D physics engine with incremental snapshotting/rollback so it composes cleanly with their netcode layer, and benchmarking specific behaviors against Rapier, Box2D 2.4/3.0, and Photon Quantum, is not vibe-coded territory. You have to know exactly why position correction is solved separately from velocity to write that section, and you have to have actually read those engines' source to make those comparisons.

The website copy reading as AI-flavored is, I think, partly genuine LLM assistance for marketing prose and partly the cheerful didactic register he's leaning into deliberately — Easel is positioned as a teaching tool (Pico-8-adjacent, "great first language"), so the homepage is written for parents and teachers, not for HN. The blog voice is noticeably tighter and more technical than the homepage, which is consistent with a developer who hand-writes the engineering content and was looser with marketing copy.

The actually-interesting design claim, from your angle: the *language itself* is the synchronization boundary. Reactive + hierarchical + concurrent semantics, with lifetimes implied by lexical nesting, and the multiplayer-determinism invariants enforced by the compiler rather than by programmer discipline. It's the same instinct you keep coming back to — push correctness into the type system / language semantics so opaque scripting can't violate it — applied to netcode instead of resource flow. The rollback physics post is the same philosophy one layer down: incremental snapshotting at the engine level mirrors incremental computation at the language level. The whole stack is built around "only re-do what changed," which is why he could justify writing a bespoke physics engine instead of bolting Rapier on.

chat_messages.text:
Yes — and the more I look at how he's framed Easel, the more it lines up with the architectural intuitions you've been working through, just applied at a different layer of the stack.

The kernel-concepts read is, I think, exactly right. Reading between the lines of his "what makes Easel different" sections, the irreducible concepts seem to be:

- **Entities with hierarchical lifetimes** (Spawn/Subspawn) — lifetime is *implied by lexical nesting*, not tracked separately
- **Reactive properties** (`with` blocks that re-fire on change) — state is the primary thing, derivations are declarative
- **Behaviors** as first-class concurrent units with controlled order-of-execution and bounded lifespans
- **Awaitable events** crossing frame boundaries (so logic flows top-to-bottom even when it spans seconds of wall time)
- **Categories** as a typed dimension for spatial/relational queries (the BVH-tracks-categories trick)
- **Ownership** baked into the language — which is what makes the multiplayer-safety invariant hold

That's a small kernel, and the claim is that *everything else falls out of it* — the physics integration, the netcode, the UI system, sprite hierarchies, particle effects. He's explicit that some of these features only work because they're built into the compiler rather than the library. That's the same move you've been circling on: declarative structure in the language → optimizations and guarantees that escape into intractability when behavior lives in opaque scripts.

The reactive piece is where it gets genuinely interesting and worth digging into. What he's describing — declare state, declare a derivation, and the runtime figures out when to re-run — is the same shape as Jane Street Incremental, Frere's reactivity post, Krouse's DCTP work. But he's also tied it to *rollback*: the rollback physics post is essentially saying "incremental dependency tracking applies to physics state too, not just UI state." Snapshot the changed nodes in the dependency DAG, not the whole world. That's the same algorithm Incremental uses to avoid recomputing untouched cells, lifted into a netcode setting where the "recomputation" is rollback-and-resimulate. The lazy BVH rebalancing comment is the same idea again — rebalance only on the path that's already dirty.

There's a deeper structural point underneath: **rollback netcode and reactive evaluation are the same problem**. Both need to know, given a change to some input, the minimal set of downstream state that must be invalidated and recomputed. Most rollback engines re-simulate the whole world from a snapshot N frames back; Easel is treating the world as a reactive computation graph and only rolling back the dirty subgraph. If that's actually what he's doing, it's a genuinely novel synthesis — and it's the kind of thing that's only tractable because he controls the language semantics, so the compiler can track dependencies precisely instead of guessing.

The thing that should resonate with your DSL thesis specifically: he's made the same bet you're making, that *a sufficiently well-typed declarative substrate makes possible optimizations that are unreachable when behavior lives in scripts*. He's just cashing it out for netcode determinism rather than credit assignment for AI. The compositional structure carries the guarantee — multiplayer-safety in his case, differentiability or learnability in yours.

If you want to go deeper, the two most worthwhile things to actually read are probably his [language reference docs](https://easel.games/docs/reference/) (to see the kernel concepts laid out concretely) and the [Why Easel?](https://easel.games/docs/learn/why) page he linked, which from the homepage hint goes into the reactive evaluation model in more detail. The "behaviors" page is also probably where the meat of his concurrency model lives. Want me to pull any of those?

chat_messages.text: It’s really fascinating that he’s positioned this as a “next step after Scratch” because the engine and compiler are probably extraordinarily sophisticated. Makes me feel like his heart is in the right place… or that he has given up on convincing existing game devs to switch to an entirely new language and runtime and instead is hoping to hook the next generation of game devs 😏

content.text: It’s really fascinating that he’s positioned this as a “next step after Scratch” because the engine and compiler are probably extraordinarily sophisticated. Makes me feel like his heart is in the right place… or that he has given up on convincing existing game devs to switch to an entirely new language and runtime and instead is hoping to hook the next generation of game devs 😏

chat_messages.text:
Both, probably, and they're not really in tension — they're the only viable strategy for a solo dev shipping a new language.

The "post-Scratch" positioning is genuinely smart from a pure adoption standpoint. The brutal reality of new programming languages is that experienced developers have enormous switching costs and very little to gain — they already know how to write multiplayer netcode, or they've already picked their abstraction and tooling stack and built muscle memory around it. Pitching Rust-to-C++ veterans on a new browser-only 2D engine is a losing battle no matter how clever the semantics. But kids and classroom learners have *zero* switching cost, and the thing Easel is selling them — "make a game your friends can play in 20 minutes, from a Chromebook, with no install" — is genuinely best-in-class for that audience. Scratch can't do real multiplayer, Roblox requires Lua and a heavier mental model, Unity is a cliff. There's a real gap and he's aimed precisely at it.

But here's where I think the "heart in the right place" reading is also genuine, and it connects to something you've thought about a lot in your own teaching context: **the pedagogical bet is that the simple kernel is also the correct kernel**. He's not dumbing down a "real" language for kids — he's claiming that hierarchical lifetimes, reactive properties, behaviors, and awaitable events are the *right* primitives for game programming, and that the reason existing engines feel hard is that they expose the wrong abstractions (frame-by-frame loops, manual state machines, manual netcode). If that bet is right, the post-Scratch beginner and the experienced dev frustrated with Unity's lifecycle gotchas converge on the same thing, just from opposite directions. The beginner never has to unlearn anything; the expert finds that the things they used to do by hand are just gone.

That's a pretty pure expression of the "games are fun because reality is fun" instinct, transplanted to language design: the constraints aren't artificial scaffolding for beginners, they're the actual structure of the domain, and once you've got the structure right, sophistication compounds rather than fights you. Rich Hickey made a version of this argument for Clojure — "simple made easy" — and it's the same energy. The reason Easel's compiler can be doing what it's doing is precisely *because* the surface language is constrained enough that the semantics are tractable.

There's also a less charitable but probably also-true version: he tried the "convince adults" path with Acolyte Fight!'s modding community and watched what actually happened, which was that the modders were beginners discovering coding for the first time, not pros looking for a better tool. So he updated. The Easel story he tells in the introductory post is essentially "the beginners taught me what they actually wanted, and I built that." That's not really giving up on game devs so much as noticing that the beginners were the ones who were most underserved and most receptive to a fundamentally new model.

The cynical-but-also-strategic version of your reading is that *if* the next generation of game devs grows up natively fluent in Easel's reactive concurrent model, then in ten years the conversation about "real" engines will have shifted under Unity's feet, the way it shifted under MFC's feet when a generation grew up on web frameworks. You don't convert the establishment, you outlive them. Which, frankly, has worked before.

The thing I find most telling is the rollback physics post itself — *that's not a post for beginners*. No 12-year-old learning to code cares about Box2D 3.0's lack of dynamic-to-dynamic CCD or how Rapier orders position integration. That post is aimed squarely at exactly the experienced devs he's allegedly given up on. So I'd read the strategy as: market to beginners (because that's where adoption lives), but build the engine to a standard that earns respect from experts (because that's where credibility lives, and credibility is what convinces parents and teachers and CS departments to take it seriously). It's a two-audience play, and the HN post you found is the credibility leg of it doing its job.

chat_messages.text: Someone made an interesting game on Easel and posted it on social media with the comment that it was “like Processing, but for games” which is an interesting insight. What do you think he meant by that, specifically?

content.text: Someone made an interesting game on Easel and posted it on social media with the comment that it was “like Processing, but for games” which is an interesting insight. What do you think he meant by that, specifically?

chat_messages.text:
That's a sharp comparison, and worth unpacking because Processing is a very specific kind of thing and the analogy only works if you pick up on exactly which dimensions are being mapped across.

Processing's defining move, going back to Reas and Fry at the MIT Media Lab around 2001, was to take a general-purpose language (Java, originally) and wrap it in an environment where the *medium itself* — pixels, shapes, color, motion — was the primary abstraction the programmer thinks in. You don't open a Processing sketch and reason about windowing toolkits or event loops; you write `ellipse(x, y, 50, 50)` and you get a circle. The `setup()` / `draw()` loop is given to you for free, the canvas is given to you for free, the input handling is given to you for free. The language hasn't really changed — it's still Java semantics underneath — but the *cognitive surface* has been reshaped so that the friction between "I have an idea about a visual thing" and "I have running code that does the visual thing" is as close to zero as the authors could make it.

The cultural consequence of that was significant: Processing became the lingua franca of creative coding, generative art, data visualization sketches, and intro-to-programming-via-visuals courses. It wasn't trying to compete with "real" graphics programming, and it wasn't trying to be a production tool — it was trying to make the *act of expressing a visual idea in code* feel direct and playful. The constraint of "you're going to make a thing on a canvas" wasn't a limitation, it was the whole point. Everything else got out of the way.

So when someone says Easel is "like Processing, but for games," I think they're picking up on three specific things, in roughly increasing order of depth:

The shallowest layer is just the friction profile. Processing made graphics programming feel immediate; Easel makes game programming feel immediate. No project setup, no engine configuration, no separate "now I need to add networking" phase — you open the editor, you write a few lines, you have a thing. The directness of the loop between idea and running artifact is the same.

The middle layer is the deliberate-constraint-as-creative-substrate move. Processing chose 2D canvas + simple I/O and committed to it; the constraint is what made the medium legible. Easel has chosen 2D + browser + multiplayer + reactive semantics and committed to that. Both projects share the conviction that *a well-chosen constraint is generative*, not limiting — that you make a better tool for a creative domain by aggressively narrowing scope rather than by trying to be everything. The Pico-8 comparison Ray himself draws on the homepage is reaching for this same idea, but Processing is actually a stronger reference point because Processing is about a *programming model* for a medium, where Pico-8 is more about hardware-style constraints (memory, palette, resolution).

The deepest layer, and the one I think is the most interesting, is that both are taking a shot at *reshaping the cognitive primitives of a domain* rather than just providing a library for it. Processing didn't just give you drawing functions; it gave you a way to think about coding visually that has shaped how a generation of designers and artists relate to programming. Easel is making the analogous bet for games: that "spawn this entity," "react to this state," "wait for this event," and "share this world with other players" should be primitive verbs of the language, not patterns you assemble out of lower-level pieces. In both cases the language is the curriculum — learning the tool teaches you the domain's actual structure, not the incidental complexity of whatever general-purpose stack the tool happens to sit on.

There's one place the analogy is imperfect, and it's worth naming because it's the part of Easel that goes *beyond* what Processing does. Processing's semantic model is still essentially imperative Java with a nice façade — `draw()` runs sixty times a second and you mutate state. Easel's semantic model is genuinely novel: reactive, hierarchical, concurrent, with multiplayer-safety enforced at the language level. So in a sense Easel is what Processing would be if the underlying language had also been redesigned for the medium, not just the API surface. The friend's comparison is undershooting on that dimension — but it's undershooting in a way that's probably appropriate for a casual social-media comment, and it captures the *spirit* of what Easel is trying to be culturally even if it doesn't fully capture what it is technically.

If you wanted to repay the compliment with a sharper version, you could say something like: Easel is what Processing would have been if Reas and Fry had also gotten to redesign Java. Same spirit, deeper commitment.

Some interesting discussion on the Easel discord:

One thing i dont understand; why do i handle collideWith inside of colliders instead of through categories
lets say after making my game i want to change it so all projectiles cant collide with projectiles, no i've gotta find every projectile in my game's pollygon collider and change the collideWith
it would be way easier and way more intuitive if i could do it inside of the Category, make the projectile's category collideWith Tangibles but not Projectiles
is there any reason why this isnt a thing?

One thing you could do there is have a property of World that is something like Category:ProjectileCollidesWIth, and for each projectile's collider, make a little with block to update it.
And I had never thought about that as an option, but that does make a lot of sense. I think its not like that so the system is more flexible.
And, I'm not sure what the syntax would be. would it be something like:
`pub tangible category Category:Projectile collides Category:All`?

you could make a default collidesWith rules for each category but still override it in the Collider
thanks for the tip, its a good solution to store it in a const and reuse it, if it is **the** solution i'd add it to https://easel.games/docs/learn/physics/best-practices

agreed on adding it there. Also, you'll want a `prop` not a `const` if you want to be able to change it mid-game

(This last series of comments is Ray)

So yes like NotAHat said, if you want to dynamically change the categories on your projectiles you would need a property and have every projectile hook itself to it.

```easel
pub prop World.NoInterProjectileCollision
```

```easel
with NoInterProjectileCollision {
    PolygonCollider(
        category = Category:Projectile,
        collideWith = NoInterProjectileCollision ? Category:Tangible ^ Category:Projectile : Category:Tangible,
        // ... other stuff goes here
    )
}
```

Now you just set `NoInterProjectileCollision = true`, and all projectiles update themselves. Set it back to `false` and they will collide again.

This is a cool pattern that I use everywhere in Easel! You can keep extending this. Maybe at some point you'll give you player a powerup that gives your projectiles extra knockback. You could implement this using a `DensityBonus` property. Your `with` block would now have two properties:

```easel
with NoInterProjectileCollision, DensityBonus {
    PolygonCollider(
        category = Category:Projectile,
        collideWith = NoInterProjectileCollision ? Category:Tangible ^ Category:Projectile : Category:Tangible,
        density = DensityBonus * density,
        // ... other stuff goes here
    )
}
```

I think that the best practice in Easel is to use the `with` block for things like this. It's really common to use `with` blocks and if you're not using them too much yet, you're going to be using them everywhere. I sometimes call Easel a "reactive" programming language and this is what I mean - reactive meaning you tell Easel how something should use state (i.e. `prop`) not just to start with, but every time it changes in the future too. The `with` block lets you react to state not just now but forever.

One thing which makes category defaults difficult is that Categories are bitflags, maybe in a simple game you just have `Category:Projectile` on everything, but in a more sophisticated game you have combinations. Like in Acolyte Fight, the Meteorite is `category = Category:Projectile | Category:Grabbable | Category:Aoe | Category:Disintegrator` and the Forcefield is  `category = Category:Shield | Category:Obstacle | Category:Aoe`.

chat_messages.text:
This exchange is great, and it's actually a nice window into both his design philosophy and the kind of subtle tension that any "kernel concepts" language eventually has to navigate. Worth pulling apart what's going on here, because it touches on something you've been thinking about quite a bit.

The user's instinct is the natural one and frankly the one I'd expect from someone who's spent any time with type systems or scene graphs: *the category is the natural locus of the collision-rule decision*, so let me write the rule there and have all members of the category inherit it. That's the data-modeling instinct talking — pull the invariant up to where it's most concisely expressible, and let the instances be derived. It's also the inheritance-flavored solution, where Category becomes a kind of class with associated behavior, and it's exactly what most type-oriented programmers reach for first.

Ray's response is interesting because he doesn't dismiss it — he actually says "I had never thought about that as an option, but that does make a lot of sense" — but then he gently routes around it, and the routing reveals the deeper architectural commitment. The reason he gives at the end is the technically substantive one: **categories in Easel are bitflags, not classes**. A meteorite isn't *a* Projectile, it's `Projectile | Grabbable | Aoe | Disintegrator`. Once you accept that an entity can belong to multiple categories simultaneously, "default collision rules per category" becomes ambiguous in exactly the way multiple inheritance is ambiguous — which category's defaults win when they conflict? You're back to MRO problems, or to some ad-hoc precedence rule that the user has to memorize. The bitflag design choice forecloses the inheritance-style solution at the level of the type system.

So instead of pushing the rule up into the category, he pushes the *variability* up into a reactive property on `World`, and lets each collider hook itself to that property via a `with` block. The collision rule still lives at the collider, but now it's a *function* of a piece of shared state, and changing that state propagates everywhere automatically. The data flow is still bottom-up (each collider is responsible for its own rule), but the *parameter* of that rule lives top-down, in a single place the user can mutate.

This is actually a really elegant move and it's worth seeing what it accomplishes:

It preserves the principle that **each entity declares its own behavior**, which is what makes the lifetime semantics work cleanly — when the entity despawns, its `with` block goes with it, no orphan rules sitting on a Category waiting to be cleaned up. ---

...inheritance has a hidden cost that doesn't show up until your game gets bigger: it makes the *category* the thing that owns the rule, and now your collision behavior lives in a place that's separate from the entities it affects. That's fine when there's one rule per category, but games rarely stay that simple. The Meteorite in Acolyte Fight is `Projectile | Grabbable | Aoe | Disintegrator` — four categories at once. If each category came with its own default collision rules, what happens when they conflict? You'd need precedence rules, or override mechanisms, or some way to say "this category wins over that one." Anyone who's worked in a language with multiple inheritance knows where this road ends.

Ray's pattern sidesteps the whole problem by keeping the rule *at the collider* (where the entity already knows about all its own categories and can make a coherent decision) but letting the *parameter* of the rule live on `World` as a reactive property. Each collider hooks itself to that property via a `with` block, and the runtime takes care of fanning the change out to everyone who cares.

Here's the part I think is genuinely beautiful about it: the user's original complaint — "I don't want to edit every projectile when I change the rule" — is solved, but not in the way they expected. They were asking for a way to write the rule *once* and have it apply everywhere. The `with`-block solution writes the rule once *per entity type*, but the rule references shared state, so changing the state changes the behavior everywhere automatically. The cost the user was worried about (O(n) edits to source code) doesn't exist; what looks like O(n) declarations in the source is really just each entity declaring its participation in a shared reactive computation that costs O(1) to update at runtime.

And it composes. Ray's `DensityBonus` extension is the giveaway — once you've got the pattern, you can keep stacking axes of global modulation by adding properties and extending the `with` block, and none of the entities need to know about each other or about a central rule registry. New global behaviors are just new props. The reactive substrate is doing the work that inheritance would have done in an OOP language, but without the rigidity.

There's a more general principle here that I think is the actual reason Easel feels different: **state is the primary thing, and behavior is a local declaration of how to use that state**. Once you internalize that, a lot of features that *look* like they'd need dedicated language machinery (default values per type, override hierarchies, global modifiers) turn out to just be props with `with` blocks. The kernel of the language stays small because the reactive primitive is general enough to absorb them.

The one fair point in mytoasterdied's complaint, though, is that this idiom isn't immediately obvious if you're new — you see `collideWith` on a Collider and naturally look for a global place to set it, not a reactive prop to wrap it in. Here's a postscript that picks up the bitflag/performance angle. I tried to keep it framed as "and one more thing worth noticing" rather than starting a new essay:

---

**P.S.** — Worth noting one more thing about the bitflag detail Ray mentioned, because I think it actually reinforces the whole argument rather than being a side technicality.

Collision detection runs on potentially every pair of nearby objects, every frame. For a physics engine to be fast — and Easel's needs to be *very* fast, because it's also doing snapshot-and-rollback on top of regular physics work — the inner loop has to be tight. Bitflags are basically the gold standard for this: a category set fits in a single 32-bit (or even smaller) word, and "do these two things collide?" reduces to a single `AND` operation between two integers. No dictionary lookups, no class hierarchy traversal, no virtual dispatch. CPUs love it, cache lines love it, and you can check millions of pairs per frame without breaking a sweat.

But that performance comes with a constraint: bitflags are a *flat, finite* namespace. Every category is just one bit in a fixed-width word. There's no inheritance relationship between bits, no "this bit is a sub-type of that bit," because bits don't have structure — they're just on or off. If you wanted category-level default rules with precedence, you'd be sneaking a richer data model in alongside the bitflag, and now your inner loop is doing two things instead of one.

So when you start from "collision detection has to be a single bitwise AND in the hot path," a lot of design choices upstream of that get *forced*. You can't have rich category semantics, because that would require a rich category representation, which would blow up the hot path. Categories have to stay flat and structureless. And once categories are flat and structureless, the place to put rules and behavior *can't* be the category — there's nowhere to put it. It has to live somewhere else, and Ray's choice of "at the collider, parameterized by reactive props" is what falls out naturally once you accept the constraint.

This is one of those cases where the performance floor of the engine and the right design choice for the language are actually pointing in the same direction. The bitflag isn't a grubby implementation detail that the language has to work around — it's a *commitment* to keeping the hot path fast, and the reactive-prop pattern is the elegant high-level idiom that respects that commitment. You get the clean composable model at the language level *and* the tight inner loop at the runtime level, and they're not in tension because they were designed together.

It's a nice example of something I think Easel does better than most engines I've looked at: when the language semantics and the runtime constraints agree on the answer, you know the underlying model is well-chosen. When they disagree, you get the kind of leaky-abstraction friction that plagues bolted-together stacks. Ray controlling both layers is what makes the agreement possible.

---

A few notes:

I framed it as performance forcing the upstream design choice, which is the actual causal story and also the framing most likely to land with a technical audience — engineers respect "the hot path constrains everything else" reasoning. It also positions the bitflag not as an unfortunate limitation but as a *deliberate commitment* that the rest of the design lives up to, which is more interesting and more accurate.

The closing point about "language semantics and runtime constraints agreeing" is your kind of observation and I think it's worth landing because it generalizes — it's the same principle that's behind why ASPECT can do what it does (FEM with adaptive mesh refinement is the right answer for both numerical accuracy *and* the physical structure of mantle dynamics), and it's the principle that makes you trust Easel as a serious project. If the abstractions and the implementation are pulling in opposite directions, the abstractions are wrong; if they're pulling together, you've found something real. That's also a nice thing for Ray to read because it names the thing he's actually doing well.

Tone-wise this is a touch more technical than the main post, which feels right for a P.S. — anyone who skipped to "P.S." is signaling they want the engineering details, so you can dial up the engine-internals talk a notch. The teenagers who got bored will have stopped reading, and the people still with you are exactly the audience that the bitflag argument is for. Ray included.

If you want to trim, the paragraph I'd cut is the third one (the "so when you start from..." one), since it's mostly restating the constraint argument in a more abstract form. The concrete "bitwise AND in the hot path" framing in paragraph two does most of the work, and the closing two paragraphs land the meta-point. content.text:
Alright, next set of questions for early-game processing chains: stonemasonry.

Unlike Factorio, I need to model multiple types of stone since (just like with timber) there are multiple end uses that have very different requirements. So let's run through the design space and settle on a small set of actual stone types that we surface in the game.

chat_messages.text:
Good problem. Let me think through this carefully before proposing a taxonomy, because "types of stone" can be sliced along several orthogonal axes and I want to get the axes right before picking the categories.

## The axes that actually matter for gameplay

The geological classification (igneous/sedimentary/metamorphic) is the wrong primary axis for player-facing categories — it's a *cause* taxonomy, not a *use* taxonomy. Two stones with very different origins can have nearly identical end-use properties (a fine-grained basalt and a fine-grained hornfels both make excellent tool stone), and two stones from the same origin class can be wildly different in use (granite vs. pumice are both igneous). The geological classification should drive *availability and distribution* in the world (which is huge — it determines where players find what), but the player-facing material categories should be organized by **what the stone does under load and tool**.

The properties that drive end use, roughly:

- **Hardness / toughness ratio** — hardness resists abrasion, toughness resists fracture. These trade off. Tool edges want both high; mortars and crushing surfaces want hardness; impact-bearing structural elements want toughness.
- **Workability** — can it be split along predictable planes (slate, sandstone bedding), carved (limestone, soapstone), knapped to a sharp edge (flint, obsidian), or only dressed with great effort (granite)?
- **Grain / texture** — fine-grained stones take a sharp edge and a fine carved detail; coarse-grained stones don't, but often have better thermal shock resistance.
- **Thermal behavior** — refractoriness (does it survive in a hearth, kiln, or furnace lining?), thermal shock resistance, thermal mass, decomposition temperature (limestone calcines, that's a feature for lime-burning and a bug for hearth-stones).
- **Chemical behavior** — does it dissolve, react with acid, weather quickly? Limestone is soluble; this matters for both flux and for "this wall won't last a thousand years in your climate."
- **Density** — for fortification, ballast, counterweights, millstones.
- **Aesthetic / cultural value** — separate from utility; marble's mechanical properties are mediocre but its cultural role is enormous.

## The natural functional clusters

If I cluster real-world stone uses by which properties they demand, I get something like:

1. **Knappable tool stone** — needs conchoidal fracture, very fine grain, high hardness. Real examples: flint, chert, obsidian, fine basalt, novaculite. Pre-metal tool edges live here.
2. **Carving / dimensional stone** — needs uniform texture, workable with chisels, holds detail. Soft end: soapstone, alabaster, tuff. Medium: limestone, sandstone, marble. Hard: granite (very late tech).
3. **Refractory stone** — survives furnace temperatures without spalling or decomposing. Real examples: fireclay-bearing rocks, soapstone (excellent), dunite, quartzite (with caveats), specific sandstones. Critically, common limestones and granites *fail* here, so this is a real gameplay constraint.
4. **Structural building stone** — bulk masonry, doesn't need to be pretty or sharp, just needs to stack and bear load and not weather away. Most stones qualify; cost is mostly extraction effort.
5. **Hydraulic / chemical stone** — limestone (→ lime, mortar, flux), gypsum (→ plaster), specific clays. These are *consumed by transformation*, not used as durable material.
6. **Abrasive stone** — millstones, grindstones, whetstones. Needs hard grains in a matrix that wears uniformly. Sandstone (millstone grit), novaculite, specific quartzites.

These six clusters are not all the same kind of category — note that #5 is really "stones that are feedstock for chemical transformation" and overlaps with your resource-flow taxonomy more than your material-properties taxonomy. That's worth flagging.

## Proposed surfaced types

Given your design principle that *players who understand geology gain genuine advantage*, I'd lean toward **a small set of named material categories that map to clear functional roles, with property variation within each category coming from the geological generator**. Something like:

- **Flintstone** (knappable cryptocrystalline silica) — tool edges, strike-a-light, eventually gunflints. Found in chalk/limestone nodules and in specific volcanic deposits (covers chert, flint, obsidian as a single player-facing category with property variants).
- **Freestone** (workable fine-grained stone that can be carved in any direction) — covers fine sandstones, fine limestones, tuff, soapstone. The "good carving stone" category. Player-facing distinction within this: *soft freestone* (soapstone, tuff — also refractory!) vs. *medium freestone* (limestone, sandstone).
- **Hardstone** (granite, gneiss, hard basalt) — structural, durable, hard to work without metal tools. Late-game dimensional stone, early-game rubble masonry only.
- **Limestone** specifically as its own category, because its chemical role (lime burning, flux, mortar) is so distinctive and gameplay-critical that folding it into "freestone" would hide its most important use. Same argument for **gypsum**.
- **Sandstone** likely also as its own category for the same reason — millstone grit and whetstones are a distinctive role, and sandstone's bedded structure makes it behave differently from limestone even when both are "freestone."
- **Slate** — splits into thin sheets. Roofing, flagstones, writing surfaces. Distinctive enough in behavior to deserve its own category.

That gives roughly: **flintstone, freestone (soft), limestone, sandstone, slate, hardstone, gypsum**. Seven categories, each with a clear functional identity, each with internal property variation driven by your geological generator (so two granite deposits in the same world play differently).

I'm deliberately *not* surfacing marble as separate from limestone at the category level — its mechanical properties are limestone-ish, and the "this is beautiful" axis is better handled as a per-deposit quality property than a category. Same logic argues against splitting obsidian from flint at the category level (same functional role, same tools work on it, just different distribution and slightly different stats).

A few questions before we lock this in:

1. **Do you want refractoriness to be a per-deposit property or a category-level guarantee?** Soapstone is reliably refractory; sandstone *sometimes* is. If you want players to learn-by-deposit, push it down to per-deposit. If you want clean tech gates, lift it to category.
2. **Where does clay sit?** It's not stone but it's adjacent (refractories, ceramics, mortar). Separate taxonomy or folded in?
3. **Is gypsum actually distinct enough early-game to warrant its own category, or does it ride along with limestone as "calcinable stones" until plaster matters?**
