In part thanks to Bevy’s modular architecture and the ECS, Avian is also highly composable, as it consists of several independent plugins and provides lots of options for configuration and extensions, from custom schedules and plugins to custom joints and constraints. One disadvantage of Avian is that it is still relatively young, so it can have more bugs, some missing features, and fewer community resources and third party crates. However, it is growing quite rapidly, and it is already pretty close to feature-parity with Rapier. At the end of the day, both engines are solid options. If you are looking for a more mature and tested physics integration, bevy_rapier is the better choice, but if you prefer an engine with less overhead and a more native Bevy integration, consider using Avian. Their core APIs are also quite similar, so switching between them shouldn’t be too difficult.

Avian is an ECS-driven 2D and 3D physics engine for the Bevy game engine. Check out the GitHub repository for more information about the design, read the Getting Started guide below to get up to speed, and take a look at the Table of Contents for an overview of the engine’s features and their documentation. You can also check out the FAQ, and if you encounter any further problems, consider saying hello on the Bevy Discord! This short guide should help you get started with Avian.

There are also some third party character controllers such as bevy_ahoy (kinematic) and bevy_tnua (dynamic) that work with Avian. For custom character controllers, you can take a look at the dynamic_character_2d and kinematic_character_2d examples to get started. While Transform can be used for the vast majority of things, Avian internally uses separate Position and Rotation components. These are automatically kept in sync by the PhysicsTransformPlugin. There are several reasons why the separate components are currently used. Position and rotation should be global from the physics engine’s point of view. Transform scale and shearing can cause issues and rounding errors in physics. Transform hierarchies can be problematic. There is no f64 version of Transform. There is no 2D version of Transform (yet), and having a 2D version can optimize several computations.

In external projects however, using Position and Rotation is only necessary when you need to manage positions within PhysicsSystems::StepSimulation. Elsewhere, you should be able to use Transform. There is also a possibility that we will revisit this if/when Bevy has a Transform2d component. Using Transform feels more idiomatic and simple, so it would be nice if it could be used directly as long as we can get around the drawbacks. Yes! Networking often requires running the simulation in a specific schedule, and in Avian it is straightforward to set the schedule that runs physics and configure the timestep if needed. By default, physics runs at a fixed timestep in FixedPostUpdate. Physics engines are very large and Avian is still young, so stability issues and bugs are to be expected. If you encounter issues, please consider first taking a look at the issues on GitHub and open a new issue if there already isn’t one regarding your problem.

You can also come and say hello on the Bevy Discord server. There, you can find an Avian Physics topic on the #ecosystem-crates channel where you can ask questions. Avian is free and open source. All code in the Avian repository is dual-licensed under either: MIT License (LICENSE-MIT or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) Apache License, Version 2.0 (LICENSE-APACHE or http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) ... Utilities for implementing character controllers. ... Tree acceleration structures for spatial queries on colliders. ... Collision detection for Colliders. ... Specialized data structures used by Avian. ... Renders physics objects and properties for debugging purposes. ... Diagnostics support for tracking physics timers and counters. Useful for profiling and debugging. ... Rigid body dynamics, handling the motion and physical interactions of non-deformable objects.

content.text:
Avian is an ECS-based 2D and 3D physics engine for Bevy, a refreshingly simple data-driven game engine built in Rust. Avian prioritizes ergonomics and modularity, with a focus on providing a native ECS-driven user experience.

Related to physics or motion in some way (avian: relates to birds and flight). Not tied to a specific physics implementation like Bevy XPBD was. Unique and has its own brand identity. Like Bepu, Jolt, Havok, and so on! Relatively short, ideally 4-6 characters. Easy to pronounce and spell. SEO-friendly and googleable. Ideally has some kind of connection to Bevy, and relates to birds or flight 🐦 · …but not strictly tied to it. Maybe one day we find a way to use the engine without the Bevy core and the ECS? I just personally like the name and how it looks. I had dozens (or even hundreds!) of name ideas, most of which were already taken or only satisfied a few of these criteria. A bunch of community members also helped with great suggestions, thanks for all of them <3 · After a long time trying to come up with a name, I landed on Avian, because it fits all of these criteria perfectly.

A name like bevy_avian would sort of imply that it is a Bevy integration for an avian crate, not the core crate itself. Things could get confusing if someone else made an avian crate. 3rd party crate names don’t have to be as long, and we could even have official sub-crates like avian_collision, avian_spatial, and avian_math (although in practice, these could just have their own names) Several people stated they prefer names without the prefix. This is also not uncommon in the ecosystem: big-brain, big_space, lightyear, leafwing-input-manager (and other Leafwing crates) are all popular Bevy plugins with no bevy_ prefix. After lots of iteration, design help from community members, and some finishing touches, we ended up with the following logo: The logo went through several iterations. Click this open to see a few! Here’s the initial mock-up design I made for the logo: Looks too much like a quill!

On a more personal note: I have officially graduated from high school, and will start university in late August. There’s still a decent amount of time until then, but once it does start, I will most likely have less time for development. I will try my best though, and I am very invested in trying to improve the state of physics and collision detection in the Bevy ecosystem. With that being said, I am going to take at least a few days off to recharge my batteries before starting work on new features again. Going through the rebrand and various rewrites has been quite a stressful undertaking, but I am glad that we did it and that everything turned out so well in the end. As always, huge thanks to everyone for all of the incredible support! Without you, this project would not be where it is today. While Avian will always be free and permissively licensed, developing and maintaining it takes a lot of time and effort.

As Bevy XPBD had already gained a lot of popularity in the ecosystem, Bevy’s maintainers reached out to share their concerns about the XPBD patent situation. This discussion convinced me to finally commit to the idea of rebranding the project and transitioning away from XPBD entirely. I announced the rebrand in the form of a rather long GitHub issue in early March this year. It is important to note that soon after the announcement, we actually got a response from Miles Macklin, one of the inventors of XPBD, about whether there are issues with creating an open source game physics engine with XPBD: … I don’t believe there is any restriction here - you can already find many open source and commercial examples of XPBD implementations online. … · This suggests that using XPBD should actually be fine. However, the wording is still slightly too vague to my liking, and of course we cannot be entirely certain, as NVIDIA still holds the patent.

content.title: Avian Physics 0.6 - Joona Aalto
content.text:
Avian is an ECS-based 2D and 3D physics engine for Bevy, a refreshingly simple data-driven game engine built in Rust. Avian prioritizes ergonomics and modularity, with a focus on providing a native ECS-driven user experience.

Avian is an ECS-based 2D and 3D physics engine for Bevy, a refreshingly simple data-driven game engine built in Rust. Avian prioritizes ergonomics and modularity, with a focus on providing a native ECS-driven user experience. Check out the GitHub repository and the introductory post for more details. Avian 0.6 brings several major optimizations and features: Move-and-slide: Avian now supports move-and-slide, the fundamental movement and collision algorithm used by Kinematic Character Controllers (KCC). Joint motors: Revolute joints and prismatic joints now support motors with both velocity and position control. BVH broad phase: Broad phase collision detection now uses OBVHS, massively improving performance for large scenes and static geometry. Spatial query optimizations: Spatial queries now reuse the BVH used by the broad phase, significantly reducing overhead.

Avian has slowly but surely been reaching closer parity with other big physics engines in terms of features and performance. While there’s still a lot more to be done there, I think it’s time to shift gears towards refining both the internals and the public API for a moment. Low-hanging fruit includes reorganizing modules and concerns, adding more tests and documentation, reducing dependencies between plugins, and making minimal configurations easier. I would also like to try depending on sub-crates like bevy_ecs instead of bevy directly, in order to improve compile times and be more mindful of our dependencies. Why depend on sub-crates instead of bevy with default-features = false? This is a somewhat controversial topic in the ecosystem. On one hand, depending on sub-crates like bevy_ecs has the following caveats: Unless end users also use subcrates (most don’t), they need to manually specify all bevy features required by third party crates, or otherwise DefaultPlugins and the prelude

If a third party crate exposes a macro that uses a subcrate like bevy_ecs, but downstream users use bevy, the macro will return an error. Note that this also applies the other way if users were using subcrates and third party crates were using bevy. However, (1) and (3) are not actually meaningful problems for Avian, and (2) is only a problem for advanced users. Users are also likely to run into (2) regardless of what Avian does, as a large portion of other third party crates in the ecosystem already depend on sub-crates. The biggest benefit of depending on sub-crates is faster cold compile times. If Avian depends on bevy, it needs to wait for all of bevy to compile first (including rendering, UI, audio…), but if it only depends on crates like bevy_ecs, bevy_app, and bevy_math, it can start compiling much sooner. It also lets us be more intentional about our dependencies and features, and make sure we only depend on what we actually need.

For years(!) now, a very common pain point for users of Avian has been the lack of a Kinematic Character Controller (KCC). There have been some dynamic character controllers (bevy_tnua), and numerous scattered KCC experiments from different people, but no concentrated effort on a built-in solution. Avian 0.6 takes the first steps towards official character controller support by implementing move-and-slide or collide-and-slide, the movement and collision algorithm at the heart of most KCCs. In short, move-and-slide attempts to move a shape along a desired velocity vector, sliding along any obstacles that are encountered along the way. You can see it in action here for a simple 3D test scene: The kinematic_character_2d and kinematic_character_3d examples have also been updated to use move-and-slide: ... Novel GJK-like algorithm for projecting velocity against an arbitrary number of planes using project_velocity ·

Yes, your read is essentially correct, and the architectural distinction the Avian docs draw is exactly the one we've been circling around. Let me unpack what this case study actually demonstrates.

## What Rapier-vs-Avian crystallizes

The crucial line is the one from the Tainted Coders guide: "Avian is using components and doing the calculations on them directly within Bevy's ECS. Rapier keeps a separate representation of the game's physics that are projected back on to Bevy's ECS."

That's the two-tier-vs-one-tier distinction made concrete. Rapier maintains its own internal data structures (its own broadphase, its own narrowphase, its own constraint solver state), and the Bevy integration is a bridge layer that synchronizes ECS components into Rapier's world before each step and copies results back after. Avian, by contrast, makes Bevy's ECS *itself* the storage for physics state — rigid bodies, colliders, velocities, constraints all live as components in the world, and Avian's systems iterate over them directly using ordinary Bevy queries.

The Avian project's stated design principles spell this out as a deliberate philosophy: "No wrappers around existing engines... Utilize the ECS as much as possible. The engine should feel like a part of Bevy, and it shouldn't need to maintain a separate physics world."

## What this actually proves (and doesn't)

Here's where I want to push back gently on the obvious conclusion. The popularity of Avian and the community's frustration with Rapier's glue layer is *real evidence*, but it's evidence about ergonomics and integration friction, not about whether single-tier is architecturally superior in general. The reasons people prefer Avian are mostly:

The synchronization layer is genuinely awkward — every frame you have to copy ECS state into Rapier's representation and back, with all the failure modes that round-tripping introduces (lossy conversions, ordering bugs, frames where the two views disagree). Avian eliminates the synchronization because there's only one representation.

Rapier's API doesn't compose with Bevy's idioms — you can't write a single Bevy system that reads physics state and game state in the same query, you can't use Bevy's change detection on physics components, you can't easily write extension plugins that interleave with Rapier's internals. Avian's components are first-class Bevy components, so all the ECS machinery just works on them.

Debugging and inspection — Bevy's editor, gizmos, and inspector tools work on components. Rapier's state is opaque to those tools without custom integration.

Notice what these reasons have in common: they're all about Rapier's data being *outside* the ECS world, which forces glue and forecloses idiomatic Bevy patterns. They're not about whether the underlying simulation algorithms could benefit from specialized non-ECS storage. They're about whether the *interface* is ECS-native.

## The deeper lesson for your architecture

This is actually the most useful thing the case study teaches you, because it sharpens what "two-tier" should and shouldn't mean.

The mistake to avoid is what Rapier does: making the kernel tier a black box with its own opaque world that the coordination tier has to mirror and synchronize against. That's where the glue-code pain comes from, and it's the pattern that makes Bevy users grumble.

The version you want is different: the kernel tier has *specialized storage* (wgpu buffers, FEM meshes, whatever the physics of the situation demands) but its *interface* is algebraic and first-class. The coordination tier doesn't mirror the kernel state into ECS components and synchronize back; it accesses kernel state through the algebraic write/event interface we've been discussing, and that interface is designed to feel as native to the coordination layer as ordinary component access. The kernel state never round-trips into ECS storage because it doesn't need to — the optic-based access path lets coordination focus into kernel state directly without copying.

Concretely, for your project: the mantle simulation lives in wgpu buffers. A coordination-level system that needs to know "what's the surface elevation at point P?" doesn't get that by reading a Bevy component; it gets it by going through an optic into the geological kernel that resolves to a buffer read. The optic is the interface, not a synchronized ECS component. Similarly, a write — "deposit material here" — goes through the algebraic write layer into the kernel, not through an ECS component that gets mirrored back.

This is *architecturally* closer to Rapier (specialized non-ECS storage for the heavy stuff) but *ergonomically* closer to Avian (the interface feels native, no synchronization layer, queries compose). The third option you want is the one neither Rapier nor Avian fully demonstrates: **specialized kernel storage with an ECS-idiomatic algebraic interface on top**.

## Why Avian's choice is reasonable for *physics specifically*

It's worth noting that for a rigid-body physics engine, the case for non-ECS storage is actually weaker than for the systems you care about. Rigid body physics has maybe thousands of bodies in a serious game, each with O(10) floats of state. The constraint solver does benefit from specialized layouts (contiguous islands, sorted constraints, etc.), but it's not GPU-resident in most game engines, and the per-body state genuinely is the kind of thing ECS components handle well. Avian achieving close-to-feature-parity with Rapier while staying ECS-native suggests that for this workload the ECS layout is fine.

Your kernel populations are different in kind. Mantle convection at meaningful resolution is millions to billions of cells, GPU-resident, with FEM connectivity that doesn't map to entity/component storage at all. Hydrology fields are similar. These aren't "physics-shaped" workloads where Avian's choice would generalize — they're closer to the workloads that *no* current Bevy plugin handles well, because the community's work has focused on the rigid-body case where ECS storage is adequate.

So the lesson isn't "follow Avian's lead and put everything in ECS." It's "follow Avian's lead on *interface design* — make the kernel feel native to the coordination layer — but recognize that the storage layer underneath has to be chosen for the workload, and for your workloads that means going outside ECS entirely and bridging through an algebraic interface that hides the specialized storage from coordination-tier code."

## A small validation

The Avian author's own stated principle — "Use a highly modular plugin architecture. Users should be able to replace parts of the engine with their own implementations" — is itself a vote of confidence in algebraic interface design, even within the ECS-native approach. He's saying that even within Avian's all-ECS world, the *contracts* between subsystems should be explicit and replaceable. That's the same instinct that motivates the algebraic write/event layer; he's just applying it within a single tier instead of across tiers. Your generalization is consistent with where the best Bevy ecosystem thinking is already pointing.

Good, this confirms what I suspected. Let me give you the careful answer.

## What Bevy actually offers

Bevy has *exactly two* component storage strategies, and the choice is per-component-type at compile time via the derive macro: "pub enum StorageType { Table, SparseSet }". "Each component type uses either Table storage or SparseSet storage" — period. There is no third option, no extension point, no trait you can implement to plug in your own storage backend. The `StorageType` enum is closed.

Both options are still fundamentally CPU-side, ECS-shaped storage. Table storage is "components stored in dense Vec-like structures" with "excellent cache locality for iteration", and SparseSet is the same kind of CPU structure with a different access pattern optimized for frequent insert/remove. Neither is a wgpu buffer, neither is a FEM mesh, neither is a hierarchical octree, neither lives on the GPU.

And it's worth noting that the Bevy community is currently *debating whether to remove* SparseSet entirely as not pulling its weight: "It takes a lot of effort to maintain, test, and bench the ecs when there are two fundamentally different storages interacting. In my opinion, the benefits of sparse set storage are not worth this effort, not by a long shot." So the trajectory is toward *fewer* storage backends, not a pluggable system that could accommodate yours.

So the literal answer to "does Bevy already support this?" is: **no, not even close**. Bevy supports two flavors of CPU-resident, archetype-organized storage, and the choice between them is essentially "how often do you add/remove this component." That's a much narrower notion of storage flexibility than what your architecture would need.

## Why "just add more storage backends to Bevy" isn't quite the right framing

Here's where I want to push back on your formulation, because I think it slightly misdiagnoses what's needed.

Your phrasing — "Bevy just needs to support multiple component storage backends" — implies that the kernel-tier data should still be *components*, just stored differently. That a mantle convection field could be modeled as N million entities each with a `MantleCell` component, where `MantleCell` happens to use a custom GPU-resident storage backend instead of Table storage.

This doesn't really work, and the reasons are instructive. The ECS data model assumes that storage is *organized by entity*: each piece of data belongs to some entity, queries iterate over entities filtered by component composition, the unit of identity is the entity. But the kernel populations you care about aren't naturally entity-shaped:

A FEM mesh is organized by *connectivity*, not by entity-as-bag-of-components. Cell *i* is meaningful in terms of its neighbors, its faces, the basis functions defined over it. There's no useful sense in which each cell is an "entity" with a "MantleCell component" — the connectivity structure is the storage structure. Forcing it into entity-component shape would either be a lie (one entity holds the whole mesh as an opaque blob, which is the Resource pattern, which is what Bevy already does and which is exactly the Rapier-style "opaque world" trap) or absurd (millions of entities, each pointing into a shared mesh, with components that are basically just indices).

GPU buffers don't have entity semantics at all. A wgpu storage buffer is a flat array indexed by thread ID in a compute dispatch. The whole point of putting data on the GPU is that it's *not* accessed by per-entity queries from the CPU — it's accessed by compute shaders that process the whole buffer in parallel. If you tried to expose it as ECS components, you'd be either constantly round-tripping data to CPU (which destroys the performance you went to the GPU to get) or having components that you can't actually read without a stall.

Spatial indices, octrees, BVHs are organized by spatial hierarchy, not by entity. They're updated as a whole (rebuilt or refit), queried as a whole, and individual nodes don't correspond to game entities.

So the issue isn't that ECS storage *implementations* are too rigid — it's that the ECS *data model* itself (entity → set of components, queryable by component composition) is the wrong abstraction for these workloads. You don't want a pluggable storage backend that happens to be GPU-resident; you want a storage layer that isn't pretending to be ECS-shaped at all.

## The sharper version of your insight

What I think you're actually correctly identifying is this: **Bevy's architecture has the right shape at the *interface* level — composable plugins, scheduled systems, declared dependencies, deferred mutations — but it commits prematurely to a single storage paradigm at the *implementation* level.**

The fix isn't "add more storage backends to ECS." The fix is "let non-ECS storage participate in the same scheduling, dependency, and deferred-mutation infrastructure that ECS storage uses." That's a different and more interesting design problem.

Concretely, what you'd want is something like:

A way to register a *kernel population* with the Bevy scheduler — declaring what it reads and writes, what its event outputs are, what its synchronization points are — *without* its data living in the ECS world. The scheduler treats it as a participant in the dependency graph, schedules it parallel to compatible systems, and respects its sync requirements, but the data itself lives wherever makes sense for the workload (wgpu buffer, custom mesh structure, whatever).

A way for ECS systems to *declare access* to kernel-population state through the same declared-data-dependency mechanism that Bevy uses for ECS queries — so the scheduler knows that "this system reads geological state in region R" and can sequence it correctly relative to "this system writes geological state in region R" — *without* the kernel state being mirrored as components.

A unified deferred-mutation interface where commands targeting kernel populations are queued and applied at sync points, just like ECS commands, but with the algebraic-fusion properties we discussed earlier.

This is genuinely not what Bevy offers. Bevy's scheduling assumes the data lives in the World as components or resources. If your kernel state is a `Resource` containing a wgpu handle, the scheduler treats the whole resource as a single read/write unit — it can't see *into* the resource to know that two systems are touching disjoint regions and can run in parallel. That granularity loss is significant for the kernel populations you're talking about.

So to give you the cleanest version of the answer:

**Your instinct is right that Bevy's architectural shape is closer than I might have implied — the scheduling, dependency-tracking, and command-deferral patterns are exactly the ones a multi-tier engine needs.** What's missing isn't storage flexibility per se; it's the ability to *extend the participation in those patterns* to data that doesn't live in ECS storage. Bevy is structured as "ECS world + scheduling around it," and what you need is "scheduling + dependency tracking as the primary abstraction, with ECS as one participant among several."

In practice, what people building this sort of thing on Bevy do is: put kernel state in a `Resource` (which makes the scheduler treat it as one big read/write unit), implement the algebraic interface and fine-grained dependency tracking *inside* that resource, and accept some parallelism loss at the Bevy-scheduler level in exchange for keeping the rest of the integration smooth. It works, but it's a workaround, and you can feel the abstraction not quite fitting. That's the honest situation.

Whether that workaround is good enough for your project is an empirical question that depends on how often the geological kernel actually needs to run in parallel with other Bevy systems versus being a phase that runs to completion at known sync points. My guess is that for a colony sim, the geological kernel runs at a much slower tick rate than the gameplay layer (geology updates in seconds-to-minutes of wall clock; agent decisions in milliseconds), so the coarse-grained Resource treatment might not actually cost you much. But that's worth measuring before committing.

content.title: Consider Removing Sparse Set Component Storage · bevyengine/bevy · Discussion #19164
content.text:
For each entity, we need to store a table id and row. SparseSet has slow(er) iteration speed, sparse storage, and needs it's own Entity to "sparse set row" map. For each sparse set component, for each entity, we need to store its sparse set row.

Right now, Bevy has two kinds of storage: Table and SparseSet. Table has fast iteration speed, dense storage, and can have its exact location found per entity with just a TableId and TableRow. For each entity, we need to store a table id and row. SparseSet has slow(er) iteration speed, sparse storage, and needs it's own Entity to "sparse set row" map. For each sparse set component, for each entity, we need to store its sparse set row. So why use sparse set? It has one small advantage: it's much faster than tables at insertion and removal. But, the insert and remove cost is not zero! In fact, there have already been times when even sparse set was too slow, and the best solution was to have a table component that was just an Option<MyActualComponent>. So if you don't need insert/remove speed, Table is way better, and if you are inserting/removing enough that Table isn't worth the iteration speed, even SparseSet is also too slow.

This isn't an exhaustive list, but it's enough to get my point across. It takes a lot of effort to maintain, test, and bench the ecs when there are two fundamentally different storages interacting. In my opinion, the benefits of sparse set storage are not worth this effort, not by a long shot. When is the last time you needed a sparse set component? Probably never. If you did, it was because you were inserting and removing it a lot, but a Option<MyActualComponent> table component would be faster for that anyway. The only reason you might need sparse set today is if you needed an observer/hook for when an insertion/removal happened, and you were inserting/removing very frequently. The only reason not to use a Option<MyActualComponent> table component when you need fast insertion/removal is because it currently has horrible UX, like not having hooks, etc.

When inserting a MaybeTable component, we would set the row to Some if its table already has a column for it, otherwise we do a table move. When removing it, we just set it to None. When removing a normal table component, we also change its table to one that has no columns for any of the MaybeTable columns for which the row has None on that column. This is cheaper (since there's less to move) and it prevents the ecs from retaining memory that is no longer needed if the component will not be inserted on that entity again. In general, this idea benefits from the apparent pattern that entities generally have a "kind" associated with them. For example, a 3d physics entity is unlikely to have a 2d ui widget component. There are times when an entity of the same kind has component removed/inserted without changing its kind. For example, an enemy entity may have an OnFire component inserted when the player hits it with a flame arrow, removed after 5 seconds, and inserted again with another arr

I know this is a hot take, but I do think this could improve performance and vastly simplify complexity in the ecs. I'm definitely curious if others share this opinion. Bevy ECS is an Entity Component System custom-built for the Bevy game engine. It aims to be simple to use, ergonomic, fast, massively parallel, opinionated, and featureful. It was created specifically for Bevy’s needs, but it can easily be used as a standalone crate in other projects. All app logic in Bevy uses the Entity Component System paradigm, which is often shortened to ECS. ECS is a software pattern that involves breaking your program up into Entities, Components, and Systems. Entities are unique “things” that are assigned groups of Components, which are then processed using Systems. For example, one entity might have a Position and Velocity component, whereas another entity might have a Position and UI component. You might have a movement system that runs on all entities with a Position and Velocity component. The ECS pattern encourages clean, decoupled designs by forcing you to break up your app data and logic into its core components.

Bevy ECS makes this pattern a first class citizen. Resource is a special kind of component that does not belong to any entity.

Bevy ECS is Bevy’s implementation of the ECS pattern. Unlike other Rust ECS implementations, which often require complex lifetimes, traits, builder patterns, or macros, Bevy ECS uses normal Rust data types for all of these concepts: Components are normal Rust structs. They are data stored in a World and specific instances of Components correlate to Entities. use bevy_ecs::prelude::*; #[derive(Component)] struct Position { x: f32, y: f32 } Entities, Components, and Resources are stored in a World. Worlds, much like std::collections’s HashSet and Vec, expose operations to insert, read, write, and remove the data they store. use bevy_ecs::world::World; let world = World::default(); Entities are unique identifiers that correlate to zero or more Components.

Good, this confirms what I suspected. Let me give you the careful answer.

## What Bevy actually offers

Bevy has *exactly two* component storage strategies, and the choice is per-component-type at compile time via the derive macro: "pub enum StorageType { Table, SparseSet }". "Each component type uses either Table storage or SparseSet storage" — period. There is no third option, no extension point, no trait you can implement to plug in your own storage backend. The `StorageType` enum is closed.

Both options are still fundamentally CPU-side, ECS-shaped storage. Table storage is "components stored in dense Vec-like structures" with "excellent cache locality for iteration", and SparseSet is the same kind of CPU structure with a different access pattern optimized for frequent insert/remove. Neither is a wgpu buffer, neither is a FEM mesh, neither is a hierarchical octree, neither lives on the GPU.

And it's worth noting that the Bevy community is currently *debating whether to remove* SparseSet entirely as not pulling its weight: "It takes a lot of effort to maintain, test, and bench the ecs when there are two fundamentally different storages interacting. In my opinion, the benefits of sparse set storage are not worth this effort, not by a long shot." So the trajectory is toward *fewer* storage backends, not a pluggable system that could accommodate yours.

So the literal answer to "does Bevy already support this?" is: **no, not even close**. Bevy supports two flavors of CPU-resident, archetype-organized storage, and the choice between them is essentially "how often do you add/remove this component." That's a much narrower notion of storage flexibility than what your architecture would need.

## Why "just add more storage backends to Bevy" isn't quite the right framing

Here's where I want to push back on your formulation, because I think it slightly misdiagnoses what's needed.

Your phrasing — "Bevy just needs to support multiple component storage backends" — implies that the kernel-tier data should still be *components*, just stored differently. That a mantle convection field could be modeled as N million entities each with a `MantleCell` component, where `MantleCell` happens to use a custom GPU-resident storage backend instead of Table storage.

This doesn't really work, and the reasons are instructive. The ECS data model assumes that storage is *organized by entity*: each piece of data belongs to some entity, queries iterate over entities filtered by component composition, the unit of identity is the entity. But the kernel populations you care about aren't naturally entity-shaped:

A FEM mesh is organized by *connectivity*, not by entity-as-bag-of-components. Cell *i* is meaningful in terms of its neighbors, its faces, the basis functions defined over it. There's no useful sense in which each cell is an "entity" with a "MantleCell component" — the connectivity structure is the storage structure. Forcing it into entity-component shape would either be a lie (one entity holds the whole mesh as an opaque blob, which is the Resource pattern, which is what Bevy already does and which is exactly the Rapier-style "opaque world" trap) or absurd (millions of entities, each pointing into a shared mesh, with components that are basically just indices).

GPU buffers don't have entity semantics at all. A wgpu storage buffer is a flat array indexed by thread ID in a compute dispatch. The whole point of putting data on the GPU is that it's *not* accessed by per-entity queries from the CPU — it's accessed by compute shaders that process the whole buffer in parallel. If you tried to expose it as ECS components, you'd be either constantly round-tripping data to CPU (which destroys the performance you went to the GPU to get) or having components that you can't actually read without a stall.

Spatial indices, octrees, BVHs are organized by spatial hierarchy, not by entity. They're updated as a whole (rebuilt or refit), queried as a whole, and individual nodes don't correspond to game entities.

So the issue isn't that ECS storage *implementations* are too rigid — it's that the ECS *data model* itself (entity → set of components, queryable by component composition) is the wrong abstraction for these workloads. You don't want a pluggable storage backend that happens to be GPU-resident; you want a storage layer that isn't pretending to be ECS-shaped at all.

## The sharper version of your insight

What I think you're actually correctly identifying is this: **Bevy's architecture has the right shape at the *interface* level — composable plugins, scheduled systems, declared dependencies, deferred mutations — but it commits prematurely to a single storage paradigm at the *implementation* level.**

The fix isn't "add more storage backends to ECS." The fix is "let non-ECS storage participate in the same scheduling, dependency, and deferred-mutation infrastructure that ECS storage uses." That's a different and more interesting design problem.

Concretely, what you'd want is something like:

A way to register a *kernel population* with the Bevy scheduler — declaring what it reads and writes, what its event outputs are, what its synchronization points are — *without* its data living in the ECS world. The scheduler treats it as a participant in the dependency graph, schedules it parallel to compatible systems, and respects its sync requirements, but the data itself lives wherever makes sense for the workload (wgpu buffer, custom mesh structure, whatever).

A way for ECS systems to *declare access* to kernel-population state through the same declared-data-dependency mechanism that Bevy uses for ECS queries — so the scheduler knows that "this system reads geological state in region R" and can sequence it correctly relative to "this system writes geological state in region R" — *without* the kernel state being mirrored as components.

A unified deferred-mutation interface where commands targeting kernel populations are queued and applied at sync points, just like ECS commands, but with the algebraic-fusion properties we discussed earlier.

This is genuinely not what Bevy offers. Bevy's scheduling assumes the data lives in the World as components or resources. If your kernel state is a `Resource` containing a wgpu handle, the scheduler treats the whole resource as a single read/write unit — it can't see *into* the resource to know that two systems are touching disjoint regions and can run in parallel. That granularity loss is significant for the kernel populations you're talking about.

So to give you the cleanest version of the answer:

**Your instinct is right that Bevy's architectural shape is closer than I might have implied — the scheduling, dependency-tracking, and command-deferral patterns are exactly the ones a multi-tier engine needs.** What's missing isn't storage flexibility per se; it's the ability to *extend the participation in those patterns* to data that doesn't live in ECS storage. Bevy is structured as "ECS world + scheduling around it," and what you need is "scheduling + dependency tracking as the primary abstraction, with ECS as one participant among several."

In practice, what people building this sort of thing on Bevy do is: put kernel state in a `Resource` (which makes the scheduler treat it as one big read/write unit), implement the algebraic interface and fine-grained dependency tracking *inside* that resource, and accept some parallelism loss at the Bevy-scheduler level in exchange for keeping the rest of the integration smooth. It works, but it's a workaround, and you can feel the abstraction not quite fitting. That's the honest situation.

Whether that workaround is good enough for your project is an empirical question that depends on how often the geological kernel actually needs to run in parallel with other Bevy systems versus being a phase that runs to completion at known sync points. My guess is that for a colony sim, the geological kernel runs at a much slower tick rate than the gameplay layer (geology updates in seconds-to-minutes of wall clock; agent decisions in milliseconds), so the coarse-grained Resource treatment might not actually cost you much. But that's worth measuring before committing.

## Yes, you've got the architectural picture right

Rigid-body physics in conventional games is genuinely small enough that ECS-with-Avian works fine. A hundred to a few thousand bodies, each with order-of-magnitude-ten floats of state, constraint solver running once per frame at 60Hz — that's a workload where the ECS storage is a non-issue and the algorithmic cost dominates. Avian gets to be ECS-native because the workload doesn't strain the abstraction.

What you'd do for heavy-duty physics in Bevy is exactly what you described: put the simulation state in a `Resource` (or a non-ECS data structure that an entity holds a handle to), expose a coarse interface to the ECS world, accept the synchronization friction at the boundary. That's the Rapier pattern, and it's the pattern any sufficiently demanding kernel ends up in. The friction is real, the glue code is annoying, but it's the architecturally honest choice when the workload doesn't fit the ECS data model.

Your geological simulation is way past that line. Teardown's voxel physics is way past that line. Any FEM mantle code is way past that line. The question isn't whether to take the Resource-with-glue hit — that's forced — it's how to make the glue principled rather than ad hoc, which is exactly the algebraic-interface conversation we've been having.

## What Gustafsson's talk actually shows

The deeper point Gustafsson is making is one I want to dwell on, because it complicates the picture in a useful way. The naive parallelization story is: "find independent work, dispatch to threads, collect results." Physics happens to expose obvious parallelism — "if we have a bunch of objects over there and a bunch of objects here, and they don't touch, those can be solved as separate simulation islands, uh, on multiple threads". So you'd think it's a slam dunk.

But it isn't, because of the latency floor on coordination. Spinning up a thread, queuing a job, signaling completion, waking a sleeping thread — these operations have costs measured in microseconds. If your physics step takes 2ms total and you're trying to split it across 16 threads, you've got 125µs per thread of actual work, and your job-system overhead can easily eat half of that. The parallelism *exists*, but you can't *exploit* it without a coordination layer that's faster than the work itself. That's why Gustafsson's talk turned into a talk about "low-latency thread pools and job system that I had to write to make it all run efficiently on modern hardware" rather than a talk about constraint solvers.

This generalizes beyond physics in a way that's directly relevant to your architecture. **Every time you add a coordination boundary, you pay a latency tax.** ECS systems running on Bevy's scheduler pay it. Commands deferred to the next sync point pay it. Events crossing tier boundaries pay it. The algebraic write/event interface we've been discussing pays it. None of these costs are huge in absolute terms, but they accumulate, and they put a floor on how fast your hot loops can actually run when they need to coordinate with anything else.

## The implication for your architecture

This is where I want to refine something we said earlier. We talked about the kernel/coordination split as if the kernel tier were fundamentally one thing — a population of state with bulk updates. Gustafsson's talk reveals that the kernel tier itself has internal coordination structure that's part of the design, not an implementation detail. The mantle simulation isn't *one* tight loop; it's a *system* of tight loops with their own scheduling, their own sync points, their own work-stealing job system. The "kernel tier" isn't a single layer — it's its own multi-layered subsystem with its own internal coordination algebra.

Concretely, this means:

The kernel tier has its own *internal* sync points that are much faster than the kernel↔coordination sync points. A FEM solver might run dozens of internal iterations per outer tick, each with its own work distribution, before publishing any state to the coordination tier. The job system that runs those internal iterations can't go through Bevy's scheduler — it has to be a low-latency thread pool inside the kernel itself, exactly like Gustafsson's.

This in turn means your "algebraic write/event interface" sits at the *outer* boundary of the kernel, not at every level. The transcript snippet confirms exactly the framing you described: "this talk isn't going to be that much about the constraint solver or how to parallelize it. It actually is going to be more about the low-latency thread pools and job system that I had to write to make it all run efficiently on modern hardware". Coordination overhead, not the math, is the bottleneck. Let me work with this.

## Yes, you've got the architectural picture right

Rigid-body physics in conventional games is genuinely small enough that ECS-with-Avian works fine. A hundred to a few thousand bodies, each with order-of-magnitude-ten floats of state, constraint solver running once per frame at 60Hz — that's a workload where the ECS storage is a non-issue and the algorithmic cost dominates. Avian gets to be ECS-native because the workload doesn't strain the abstraction.

What you'd do for heavy-duty physics in Bevy is exactly what you described: put the simulation state in a `Resource` (or a non-ECS data structure that an entity holds a handle to), expose a coarse interface to the ECS world, accept the synchronization friction at the boundary. That's the Rapier pattern, and it's the pattern any sufficiently demanding kernel ends up in. The friction is real, the glue code is annoying, but it's the architecturally honest choice when the workload doesn't fit the ECS data model.

Your geological simulation is way past that line. Teardown's voxel physics is way past that line. Any FEM mantle code is way past that line. The question isn't whether to take the Resource-with-glue hit — that's forced — it's how to make the glue principled rather than ad hoc, which is exactly the algebraic-interface conversation we've been having.

## What Gustafsson's talk actually shows

The deeper point Gustafsson is making is one I want to dwell on, because it complicates the picture in a useful way. The naive parallelization story is: "find independent work, dispatch to threads, collect results." Physics happens to expose obvious parallelism — "if we have a bunch of objects over there and a bunch of objects here, and they don't touch, those can be solved as separate simulation islands, uh, on multiple threads". So you'd think it's a slam dunk.

But it isn't, because of the latency floor on coordination. Spinning up a thread, queuing a job, signaling completion, waking a sleeping thread — these operations have costs measured in microseconds. If your physics step takes 2ms total and you're trying to split it across 16 threads, you've got 125µs per thread of actual work, and your job-system overhead can easily eat half of that. The parallelism *exists*, but you can't *exploit* it without a coordination layer that's faster than the work itself. That's why Gustafsson's talk turned into a talk about "low-latency thread pools and job system that I had to write to make it all run efficiently on modern hardware" rather than a talk about constraint solvers.

This generalizes beyond physics in a way that's directly relevant to your architecture. **Every time you add a coordination boundary, you pay a latency tax.** ECS systems running on Bevy's scheduler pay it. Commands deferred to the next sync point pay it. Events crossing tier boundaries pay it. The algebraic write/event interface we've been discussing pays it. None of these costs are huge in absolute terms, but they accumulate, and they put a floor on how fast your hot loops can actually run when they need to coordinate with anything else.

## The implication for your architecture

This is where I want to refine something we said earlier. We talked about the kernel/coordination split as if the kernel tier were fundamentally one thing — a population of state with bulk updates. Gustafsson's talk reveals that the kernel tier itself has internal coordination structure that's part of the design, not an implementation detail. The mantle simulation isn't *one* tight loop; it's a *system* of tight loops with their own scheduling, their own sync points, their own work-stealing job system. The "kernel tier" isn't a single layer — it's its own multi-layered subsystem with its own internal coordination algebra.

Concretely, this means:

The kernel tier has its own *internal* sync points that are much faster than the kernel↔coordination sync points. A FEM solver might run dozens of internal iterations per outer tick, each with its own work distribution, before publishing any state to the coordination tier. The job system that runs those internal iterations can't go through Bevy's scheduler — it has to be a low-latency thread pool inside the kernel itself, exactly like Gustafsson's.

This in turn means your "algebraic write/event interface" sits at the *outer* boundary of the kernel, not at every level. Inside the kernel, the work is dispatched through whatever low-latency mechanism the workload demands; the algebraic interface is what the *coordination tier* sees, not what the kernel's internal subroutines see. The two need to be co-designed but they're not the same thing.

And — this is the subtle part — the rate at which the algebraic interface can be exercised is bounded by the kernel's outer tick rate, which is much slower than its internal work. If the mantle kernel publishes state every 10ms but its internal solver iterates every 100µs, the coordination tier sees a 10ms-granular event stream and can issue commands at a 10ms cadence. That's totally fine for geology — geological time is slow — but it means the *expressive granularity* of the algebraic interface and the *temporal granularity* of the simulation are decoupled in a way that you should design intentionally rather than discover by accident.

The juxtaposition with Muratori's "Big OOPs" talk at the same conference is significant. Muratori's talk is "a 35-year retrospective on object-oriented programming—its origins, why inheritance hierarchies hurt, and how modern approaches like entity-component systems can produce more maintainable, efficient architectures". You also have to get the *coordination model* right, and the coordination model is harder than the data model because its costs are dominated by latency rather than throughput, which means standard parallelization patterns don't help you. You need *latency-optimized* coordination, which is a different design problem than throughput-optimized parallel computation.

This is, I think, where your categorical/algebraic framing genuinely pays off, and not just at the level of "expressive interfaces." Algebraic structure on writes is the thing that lets the engine *batch* and *fuse* operations to amortize coordination overhead — if 100 small writes can be fused into one large write at the kernel boundary, you've paid the coordination cost once instead of 100 times. The free-applicative whole-program-as-value approach lets you *defer* dispatch decisions until you know what work is actually pending, so you can schedule batches of comparable size rather than dispatching small jobs that drown in overhead. These are coordination-optimization techniques that *require* the algebraic structure to be available; they can't be retrofitted onto opaque commands.

So Gustafsson's talk validates one part of the picture (the kernel tier is its own coordination problem with its own latency floor) and motivates another part (the coordination *between* tiers needs to amortize overhead through algebraic structure, because per-write coordination is too expensive). chat_messages.text:
Yes, in principle, and that's actually the architecturally clean answer — but I want to draw the line carefully because "in principle" is doing some work in that sentence.

## What plugins genuinely can do

Bevy's plugin system is not just a packaging convention; it's a real extension mechanism with significant reach. A plugin gets full access to the `App` builder, which means it can register systems into any schedule, add new schedules, install custom resources, register components, hook into the startup and shutdown lifecycle, and add its own runner if it wants to replace the main loop entirely. It can also add types to the type registry, install custom asset loaders, and inject middleware between Bevy's stages. That's a lot of surface area, and most of what we've been discussing fits inside it:

The algebraic write/event interface is just code — types, traits, functions. Nothing about it requires engine-level support. A plugin can expose a `KernelCommands<MantlePopulation>` resource that systems write into, and add a system at the end of each frame that drains the buffer, fuses operations, and dispatches them to the kernel. The fact that this is "just a Bevy plugin" doesn't diminish its architectural significance; it's exactly how Avian and Rapier integrate.

A custom kernel population (the mantle, hydrology, whatever) lives as a `Resource` containing whatever non-ECS data structures the workload demands. The plugin owns the resource, owns the update systems, owns the synchronization with whatever thread pool or GPU pipeline runs the heavy work. Nothing about this fights Bevy.

A low-latency internal job system, à la Gustafsson, lives entirely inside the kernel resource. Bevy's scheduler dispatches the *outer* "step the mantle simulation" system once per tick; what happens inside that system is whatever the kernel wants — including spawning OS threads with whatever coordination primitives the workload demands, monopolizing cores during the critical-path window, and returning when done. Bevy's scheduler doesn't see or care.

The free-applicative coordination DSL is again just code. Programs are values, the interpreter is a function, the dispatch logic is a system. None of this requires engine support.

So the architectural picture is genuinely buildable as a Bevy plugin (or a stack of them), and that's the right approach: don't fork Bevy, don't rewrite Bevy, build on top of it. The Bevy ecosystem has lots of evidence that this works — Avian, Rapier integration, bevy_xpbd, bevy_egui, the entire rendering stack is technically a plugin (`DefaultPlugins`).

## Where the qualifier matters

The places where plugins-on-Bevy is *almost* but not quite frictionless are worth being explicit about, because they tell you what to expect when you actually build it.

**Scheduler granularity around your kernel.** Bevy's scheduler operates at the granularity of systems, and a system's read/write set is declared through its query and resource access types. When your kernel state is a single `Resource`, the scheduler treats *any* access to it as a read-or-write of the whole resource. This means you can't have two systems running in parallel where one writes region A of the geological state and the other writes region B, even though they're physically independent. The scheduler will serialize them because it can't see *into* the resource.

For a heavy kernel that runs once per outer tick, this is fine — there's only one system touching it anyway. For a kernel that has multiple coordinated sub-systems running interleaved with regular gameplay, this is where you'd feel the abstraction not quite fitting. You'd end up doing your *own* dependency tracking inside the kernel and exposing a single coarse system to Bevy. Workable, but not ideal.

**Thread pool conflict with Bevy's own.** Bevy uses `bevy_tasks` (which sits on top of a custom thread pool) for its parallel system execution. If your kernel spins up its own OS threads that monopolize cores during a critical-path window — which is what Gustafsson's design implies — those threads are competing with Bevy's task pool for CPU time. The two pools don't know about each other. In practice this is usually managed by running the kernel during a phase when no other parallel work is happening (e.g., as an exclusive system), but it does mean you give up some of Bevy's parallel scheduling during that window. Again, fine for many designs, but a real consideration.

**Inspection and tooling.** When kernel state lives in a `Resource` rather than as components, Bevy's editor, gizmos, and inspector tools don't see into it. You'd need to build your own debug visualization for the geological state, the hydrology fields, etc. This is genuinely just work — not architectural friction — but it's work that ECS-native plugins like Avian get for free.

**The `Resource` size and access pattern.** Bevy's `Resource` was designed for things like configuration, asset handles, and small global state — not for multi-gigabyte simulation buffers. It works fine for that case (a `Resource` is just a typed slot in the World), but you're somewhat off the beaten path. You'll occasionally hit places where the ergonomics assume small resources — e.g., reflection, serialization defaults, hot-reload patterns — and you'll have to opt out or work around them. None of this is a blocker, but it's the kind of thing that adds friction.

## The honest summary

Plugins-on-Bevy is the right approach and is genuinely sufficient for what you're building. You don't need to fork the engine or do anything heroic. What you'll find is that the *first* layer of integration is smooth — you can get a kernel resource with an algebraic write interface and a working event stream up and running quickly — and the *second* layer of integration is where you'll feel some friction, because Bevy's idioms don't extend cleanly into the territory you're operating in. You'll end up writing some glue, accepting some coarseness in the scheduler's view of your kernel, and building some of your own tooling. That's the cost of being off the well-trodden path, and it's a reasonable cost.

The Avian-style alternative — putting kernel state into components and getting full ECS-native integration for free — is structurally not available to you because your data model isn't entity-component-shaped. So you take the Resource-with-glue path, but you do it *principled* (algebraic interfaces, well-defined sync points, declarative composition) rather than ad hoc (opaque commands, hand-rolled synchronization, tangled interactions).

One small recommendation: design the algebraic interface and the kernel tier as a *separate crate* that doesn't depend on Bevy at all, and then have a small `bevy_yourkernel` crate that provides the Bevy plugin wrapping it. This pays off in three ways: it forces you to keep the kernel architecturally clean (it can't reach into ECS state because it doesn't know ECS exists); it makes the kernel testable and benchmarkable in isolation; and it leaves you the option to swap engines later if you ever need to. The Bevy plugin becomes a thin adapter rather than a load-bearing piece of the architecture, which is the right place for it to be.

A plugin can expose a `KernelCommands<MantlePopulation>` resource that systems write into, and add a system at the end of each frame that drains the buffer, fuses operations, and dispatches them to the kernel. The fact that this is "just a Bevy plugin" doesn't diminish its architectural significance; it's exactly how Avian and Rapier integrate.

A custom kernel population (the mantle, hydrology, whatever) lives as a `Resource` containing whatever non-ECS data structures the workload demands. The plugin owns the resource, owns the update systems, owns the synchronization with whatever thread pool or GPU pipeline runs the heavy work. Nothing about this fights Bevy.

A low-latency internal job system, à la Gustafsson, lives entirely inside the kernel resource. Bevy's scheduler dispatches the *outer* "step the mantle simulation" system once per tick; what happens inside that system is whatever the kernel wants — including spawning OS threads with whatever coordination primitives the workload demands, monopolizing cores during the critical-path window, and returning when done. Bevy's scheduler doesn't see or care.

The free-applicative coordination DSL is again just code. Programs are values, the interpreter is a function, the dispatch logic is a system. None of this requires engine support.

So the architectural picture is genuinely buildable as a Bevy plugin (or a stack of them), and that's the right approach: don't fork Bevy, don't rewrite Bevy, build on top of it. The Bevy ecosystem has lots of evidence that this works — Avian, Rapier integration, bevy_xpbd, bevy_egui, the entire rendering stack is technically a plugin (`DefaultPlugins`).

## Where the qualifier matters

The places where plugins-on-Bevy is *almost* but not quite frictionless are worth being explicit about, because they tell you what to expect when you actually build it.

**Scheduler granularity around your kernel.** Bevy's scheduler operates at the granularity of systems, and a system's read/write set is declared through its query and resource access types. When your kernel state is a single `Resource`, the scheduler treats *any* access to it as a read-or-write of the whole resource. This means you can't have two systems running in parallel where one writes region A of the geological state and the other writes region B, even though they're physically independent. The scheduler will serialize them because it can't see *into* the resource.

For a heavy kernel that runs once per outer tick, this is fine — there's only one system touching it anyway. For a kernel that has multiple coordinated sub-systems running interleaved with regular gameplay, this is where you'd feel the abstraction not quite fitting. You'd end up doing your *own* dependency tracking inside the kernel and exposing a single coarse system to Bevy. Workable, but not ideal.

**Thread pool conflict with Bevy's own.** Bevy uses `bevy_tasks` (which sits on top of a custom thread pool) for its parallel system execution. If your kernel spins up its own OS threads that monopolize cores during a critical-path window — which is what Gustafsson's design implies — those threads are competing with Bevy's task pool for CPU time. The two pools don't know about each other. In practice this is usually managed by running the kernel during a phase when no other parallel work is happening (e.g., as an exclusive system), but it does mean you give up some of Bevy's parallel scheduling during that window. Again, fine for many designs, but a real consideration.

**Inspection and tooling.** When kernel state lives in a `Resource` rather than as components, Bevy's editor, gizmos, and inspector tools don't see into it. You'd need to build your own debug visualization for the geological state, the hydrology fields, etc. This is genuinely just work — not architectural friction — but it's work that ECS-native plugins like Avian get for free.

**The `Resource` size and access pattern.** Bevy's `Resource` was designed for things like configuration, asset handles, and small global state — not for multi-gigabyte simulation buffers. It works fine for that case (a `Resource` is just a typed slot in the World), but you're somewhat off the beaten path. You'll occasionally hit places where the ergonomics assume small resources — e.g., reflection, serialization defaults, hot-reload patterns — and you'll have to opt out or work around them. None of this is a blocker, but it's the kind of thing that adds friction.

## The honest summary

Plugins-on-Bevy is the right approach and is genuinely sufficient for what you're building. You don't need to fork the engine or do anything heroic. What you'll find is that the *first* layer of integration is smooth — you can get a kernel resource with an algebraic write interface and a working event stream up and running quickly — and the *second* layer of integration is where you'll feel some friction, because Bevy's idioms don't extend cleanly into the territory you're operating in. You'll end up writing some glue, accepting some coarseness in the scheduler's view of your kernel, and building some of your own tooling. That's the cost of being off the well-trodden path, and it's a reasonable cost.

The Avian-style alternative — putting kernel state into components and getting full ECS-native integration for free — is structurally not available to you because your data model isn't entity-component-shaped. So you take the Resource-with-glue path, but you do it *principled* (algebraic interfaces, well-defined sync points, declarative composition) rather than ad hoc (opaque commands, hand-rolled synchronization, tangled interactions).

One small recommendation: design the algebraic interface and the kernel tier as a *separate crate* that doesn't depend on Bevy at all, and then have a small `bevy_yourkernel` crate that provides the Bevy plugin wrapping it. This pays off in three ways: it forces you to keep the kernel architecturally clean (it can't reach into ECS state because it doesn't know ECS exists); it makes the kernel testable and benchmarkable in isolation; and it leaves you the option to swap engines later if you ever need to. The Bevy plugin becomes a thin adapter rather than a load-bearing piece of the architecture, which is the right place for it to be.

chat_messages.text:
This is a fun question to think about, and I want to engage with it seriously — but I also want to be honest with you about the scope, because I think this is a substantially bigger lift than "a nice bounded project" suggests, even setting aside the social/political work of getting it merged. Let me walk through what's involved.

## What you'd actually be proposing

Restated precisely: you want Bevy's scheduler to understand that a resource has *internal structure* such that two systems both claiming "write access" to that resource can be safely parallelized when they target disjoint regions of the resource's internal structure. The scheduler currently treats `ResMut<T>` as an opaque exclusive lock on the whole `T`; you want it to treat `ResMut<T>` (with some opt-in declaration) as parameterized by an algebraic *region descriptor* such that two systems with non-overlapping region descriptors can run concurrently.

Generalizing further: this is the same problem as fine-grained parallelism within any aggregate. The current ECS already does a version of this for components — two systems that both write to entities-with-Position can run concurrently if their *queries* don't overlap (different archetype filters, disjoint entity sets), because the scheduler analyzes query specifications. What you're proposing is to extend the same conceptual move to resources: let resources publish a region algebra, let systems declare which region they touch, let the scheduler use the region algebra's commutativity laws to determine compatibility.

This is a clean and genuinely valuable generalization. It's also a deep change to Bevy's scheduling model, and I think it's worth being precise about why.

## The technical surface area

The places this proposal touches in Bevy's codebase:

**The `SystemParam` trait and its derivations.** Currently every `SystemParam` declares its access through `Access<ComponentId>` (for components) and a separate access set for resources, where resource access is essentially "this system reads/writes resource R." You'd need to extend this so a resource access can be parameterized — something like `Access<ResourceId, RegionDescriptor>`. The `SystemParam` derivation logic, which is used by every parameter type in the engine, would need to flow region information through.

**The access conflict detection.** Bevy's scheduler builds a graph where edges represent access conflicts between systems and uses this for parallel scheduling. The conflict detection currently does set-intersection on component IDs and resource IDs. You'd need it to call into a region-algebra-defined "do these regions conflict?" check for resources that opt into structured access. This is per-resource-type custom logic that the scheduler has to dispatch to, which means trait objects or generic dispatch in the scheduler hot path.

**The borrow checker for system parameters.** When a system runs, Bevy gives it `&mut T` access to resources, which Rust's borrow checker enforces is exclusive. With region-based access, you'd need to give two systems *partial* mutable access to the same `T` simultaneously, which Rust's type system does not natively support. You'd need either (a) interior mutability with runtime region checks (e.g., a `RegionalCell<T>` wrapper that hands out region-scoped guards), (b) a custom system-parameter type that provides region-scoped access through unsafe code with runtime invariants, or (c) some kind of compile-time region typing that's well beyond what Bevy currently does.

Option (a) is the most practical but means region access goes through a runtime check, which has overhead and means region violations are runtime panics rather than compile errors. Option (b) is what most production engines do but requires careful unsafe code to be sound. Option (c) would be lovely but is research-level.

**The schedule build process.** Bevy's schedule build computes a dependency graph from system access declarations and uses it to determine parallelizable batches. Region-based conflict checking changes the asymptotic shape of this analysis: instead of "do these access sets share a resource ID?" (O(1) per pair) it becomes "do these region descriptors overlap?" (O(region-algebra-complexity) per pair). For a region algebra as simple as "interval over a 1D index space" this is fine; for a region algebra as complex as "spatial bounding boxes in 3D mesh space" it could be expensive. The scheduler's build cost matters because schedules are rebuilt when systems are added/removed.

**The exclusive-system fallback.** Currently when a system needs full mutable access to the world, it's an "exclusive system" and the scheduler runs it serially with everything. With region-based access, you'd want a richer story: "this system has full access to region R of resource T, parallel with systems touching only disjoint regions." This affects the executor logic.

**The reflection and inspection tooling.** `bevy-inspector-egui` and the planned editor introspect resources. They'd need to either understand region algebras or treat region-structured resources opaquely.

**The change detection layer.** Bevy tracks per-component change ticks and per-resource change ticks. Region-structured resources would presumably want per-region change tracking, which is another extension.

## The design questions that need to be answered before any of this is implementable

Before code, there are real design questions, and I'd guess the discussion around these is where the proposal would spend most of its time:

**What's the type of the region descriptor?** Is it a single trait `RegionDescriptor` with associated overlap check? Is it generic over a region algebra type per resource? How does it compose across multiple resources? Is the descriptor owned by the resource type, or by the access declaration? What happens when a system needs to dynamically compute its region from data it reads at runtime (which would force a synchronization point — you can't determine the region until you've read the data, but you need the region to schedule)?

**How is the region declared at the system parameter site?** It can't be a value-level argument because the scheduler needs it before the system runs. It could be a type-level annotation (phantom types parameterizing the access), but then dynamic regions are out. It could be a function from system metadata that the scheduler calls during build (which works for static regions). The community will want to see this addressed before any code is written.

**What's the soundness story?** If two systems are running concurrently with overlapping regions due to a bug in a region descriptor's overlap check, you have a data race. The trust model around region descriptors needs to be articulated — are they `unsafe` to implement? Is there a verified subset? Can the engine fall back to serialization if a check is wrong?

**How does this compose with components?** Components already have query-based fine-grained access. Are component queries one specific instance of region-based access, or is there a separate region-of-resources mechanism that lives alongside the existing component access? Unifying them is conceptually attractive but architecturally invasive; keeping them separate is simpler but adds another concept to learn.

**What's the migration story?** Existing resources that don't opt in continue to work as opaque locks. Easy. But what about resources in third-party plugins that *should* be region-structured but aren't yet? Is there a graceful incremental path, or does the ecosystem fragment between region-aware and region-opaque resources?

These are the questions a thoughtful reviewer is going to ask, and you need to have crisp answers to all of them before any code lands.

## What "fork and PR" actually looks like for a change of this size

I want to recalibrate the social side of this honestly. Bevy is a fast-moving project with an active maintainer team and a deliberate design process. Changes of this scope don't go in as PRs; they go in as RFCs. Looking at how comparable structural changes have happened — relations, the recent observer system, required components — the pattern is roughly:

1. **An issue or discussion thread** where you propose the problem and gather initial feedback. This is where you find out whether the maintainers think the problem is worth solving and whether your framing of it makes sense to them.

2. **An RFC document** in the bevy-rfcs repository, which is a substantial design document — typically several thousand words — covering motivation, detailed design, alternatives considered, drawbacks, unresolved questions, and prior art. RFCs go through extensive review and revision, often over months.

3. **A prototype implementation**, sometimes done in parallel with the RFC, sometimes after, demonstrating that the design works and quantifying its costs and benefits. For a scheduler-touching change, you'd want microbenchmarks of build cost and runtime overhead, plus a real-world demo showing the parallelism gain.

4. **A series of merged PRs** that land the change incrementally. Big changes don't go in as one PR; they go in as a sequence — the trait extensions first, then the scheduler integration, then opt-in usage, then migration of internal types, then deprecation of old APIs. Each of these is a real review cycle.

The total time investment for a change of this scope is honestly more like a year of part-time work than "a nice bounded project," and a meaningful fraction of that time is on documents, discussion, and iteration rather than code. The maintainers are friendly and the process is well-organized, but it's not fast, and it's not solo work — you'll be incorporating feedback that significantly shapes the design.

## The smaller version that's actually a reasonable starting point

Here's what I'd suggest as the actually-bounded project, which I think is more likely to land somewhere useful:

**Build it as a third-party plugin first.** Implement region-structured resource access entirely outside Bevy, using interior mutability and runtime region checks. Provide a `RegionalResource<T, R>` wrapper, a `RegionalRes<T, R>`/`RegionalResMut<T, R>` system parameter, and a side-band scheduler that consults region overlaps before letting systems run concurrently against the same resource. This gives up some of the integration cleanliness — your systems will need to use your custom params rather than Bevy's — but it lets you actually build the thing, deploy it, and see whether the design holds up under real use.

**Use it for your own kernel populations.** Build the geological kernel, the hydrology kernel, the production process kernel against this interface. Find the friction. Discover what region algebras you actually need. Find out whether the runtime overhead of region checks is acceptable, whether the ergonomics work, whether the dynamic-region case actually matters in practice or whether static regions are sufficient.

**Then, with that experience, write the RFC.** You'll have real data, real motivating examples, real benchmarks, and a worked-out design. The RFC becomes "here's a thing I built, here's why it works, here's what would be needed to integrate it cleanly into Bevy's core, here's the migration story." That's an enormously stronger position than proposing the design from scratch, and it dramatically improves your odds of getting the maintainers' attention and goodwill.

**The PR series, if it happens, is the third year of the project.** Possibly. And by that point you may have decided that the third-party-plugin version is good enough for your needs and the upstreaming work isn't worth the cost. That's a fine outcome too.

## The honest meta-point

I'd push back gently on the framing of "nice bounded project" because I think it understates what you'd be taking on, and I want to be straight with you about that rather than cheerleading. Scheduler-level changes to a major game engine are not bounded; they ripple through everything. *But* — and this is the part worth saying — the underlying design work, building region-structured resource access and proving it out in your own engine, is genuinely valuable regardless of whether it ever lands in upstream Bevy. You'd be solving a real problem for your own project, demonstrating something useful for the broader Rust gamedev community, and producing the kind of artifact that *might* eventually become a Bevy upstream contribution if the timing and design alignment work out.

The upstream contribution is a possible eventual outcome of doing the design work for your own engine. It's not the project itself. The project is "build the right kernel architecture for my game"; if it happens to also be the right architecture for Bevy upstream, that's a bonus.
