Yes — and this is the harder pedagogical problem, because loose coupling is fundamentally about *costs that don't exist yet*. Encapsulation-as-portability has visible payoff: the code compiles on a different platform. Encapsulation-as-loose-coupling has *invisible* payoff: the bug that didn't happen, the refactor that took an hour instead of three days, the team conflict that didn't occur because two modules didn't accidentally entangle. Students who've never maintained code can't see what isn't there.

The teaching challenge is to make the invisible cost *visible*, in a setting compressed enough to fit in a classroom. A few approaches that might work, varying in how much classroom time they take:

**The "now change it" exercise.** Give students working code that uses a class with exposed fields, ask them to do something with it, then say: "now the underlying representation has to change — the field that was an `int` is now stored as a `String` that needs parsing, because we moved to a database backend." Watch them propagate the change. Then show them the same exercise with a properly encapsulated version — only the class itself changes, no client code touches the diff. The cost difference is *felt*, not lectured. The whole exercise takes maybe 20 minutes and is worth more than an hour of explanation about why coupling is bad.

This is essentially making them experience the cost of tight coupling in fast-forward. The "future pain" is no longer hypothetical; it's pain they just experienced 30 seconds ago, traceable to a specific design decision.

**The "two teams" framing.** Even when students write both the class and its client code, you can structurally separate the roles. "For this assignment, you write the class first and submit it. Then I'll give you back *someone else's* implementation of the same interface, and you have to make your client code work with it." This forces them to encounter the discipline from both sides: as an author, they have to write something a stranger can use; as a client, they have to use something a stranger wrote. Suddenly the interface is *the only thing they share* with the other party, and they can feel the value of having that interface be clean.

This is logistically harder — it requires assignment infrastructure that swaps implementations between students — but it's pedagogically dramatic. PrairieLearn might actually make this tractable if you can set up the autograder to test student code against a reference implementation they didn't write.

**The "your past self is the stranger" framing.** A more accessible version: code you wrote six months ago is, for practical purposes, written by someone else. Anyone who's tried to modify a non-trivial project after a long break has felt this. You don't remember which fields were supposed to be read-only by convention. You don't remember which methods called which. You reach into a field directly because it's "your own code, you can do that" — and then discover you broke an invariant your past self was relying on. The discipline of encapsulation is *a gift to your future self*, who will be a stranger to your current intentions. This framing has the advantage of being usable in a single lecture sentence, repeated as a refrain.

Students who don't yet have the experience to *believe* this will at least remember the framing when they later encounter it. And they will encounter it — every working programmer does. You're planting a flag they'll find later.

**The OpenJDK observation, turned around.** Your point that students can just go read the JDK source is actually a teaching opportunity if you frame it right. Yes, they *can* look. But what happens when they *do* and then *write client code that depends on what they saw*? This is exactly how `sun.misc.Unsafe` became a catastrophe for the JDK developers — third-party libraries reached into "private" implementation details that were never meant to be public, and now the JDK can't refactor those internals without breaking the ecosystem. The encapsulation was *technically* enforced (the classes were in `sun.*` packages that were "internal"), but *socially* defeated because too many people peeked.

The lesson: *just because you can see the implementation doesn't mean you should depend on it*. The discipline of treating "private" as private — even when it's only socially enforced, even when the source is right there — is what keeps systems maintainable. The JDK's Project Jigsaw (modules) and the eventual restriction of `sun.misc.Unsafe` are the cleanup costs from a generation of programmers who treated visibility as "what I can technically reach" rather than "what I'm contractually allowed to depend on." That's not a hypothetical — it's a billion-dollar industry-wide refactor that's still ongoing.

For students who like the deep cut, this is a great example. The JDK itself has been *paying the cost* of insufficient encapsulation for twenty years, and the cleanup is one of the most expensive language evolutions in software history. Encapsulation isn't busy work; it's the discipline that *prevents that situation*. Java the language is now, finally, mechanizing what should have been a social discipline from the start — because the social discipline turned out not to scale.

**The "what changed?" diff exercise.** Show students two versions of a class: v1 has public fields, v2 has private fields with proper methods. Both pass the same tests. Then show them the *changelog* of what happens when the class needs to evolve: "we added a derived field that has to stay consistent with the others." In v1, every client that touched those fields is now broken — and you have to find them all. In v2, only the class itself changes. The git blame is short in v2 and long in v1. The cost of v1's "convenience" was paid by someone six months later, who happens to be the same person who wrote v1, but who has no memory of the assumptions they baked in.

This exercise can be done with prepared materials in 10 minutes. It doesn't require live coding, doesn't require platform infrastructure, doesn't require students to have any maintenance experience. It just shows them, concretely, what the cost looks like.

**The structural argument from your design principles.** Stepping back: I think the deepest version of the loose-coupling argument, which lands once students have some of the above experiences, is actually *information-theoretic*. Every public field, every public method, every visible implementation detail is a *commitment* — a promise the class makes to its clients about what it provides. Each commitment is a *liability*. The more you commit to, the less you can change. The discipline of minimizing the interface is the discipline of *minimizing future liability*. This is why your "all public methods come from interfaces" rule is doing real work: it forces you to commit to *only* the vocabulary you've deliberately chosen, never to incidental implementation details.

Phrased this way, loose coupling is *the same idea as keeping options open*. A class with a small, deliberate public surface has retained more freedom to change than a class with a sprawling one. The cost of tight coupling is *paid in lost flexibility* — which is precisely the cost that's invisible to students because it's the cost of options they never knew they had.

There's a sentence I'd suggest using somewhere in the week, possibly as a refrain: *"every public name is a promise, and promises are easier to make than to keep."* It's compact, memorable, and inverts the usual default of "make things public unless there's a reason not to" into "make things private unless there's a reason to commit to them." That inversion is the design discipline in seed form.

**On making them feel it.** Honestly, I think the most powerful single move is the "now change it" exercise, done early in the week and referenced repeatedly. Once students have *felt* the cost of cascade-edits through client code that touched fields it shouldn't have, every later mention of encapsulation calls back to that specific feeling. They have a concrete memory of the pain, not a hypothetical. The rest of the discipline can then be motivated as "remember when you had to change six files to add one feature? That's what we're preventing."

The deeper truth — which you might want to share with them explicitly at some point — is that *senior engineers feel this pain so acutely that they preemptively design to avoid it*. The reason your design principles look the way they do isn't that someone derived them from first principles; it's that people who've maintained large codebases for decades have all converged on similar disciplines because the alternatives keep producing the same pain. You're not handing them a religion; you're handing them shortcuts that experienced engineers earned the hard way.

**Synthesizing into the week.** I'd suggest this rough placement:

The `FILE` example opens the encapsulation discussion in the way we developed earlier — *here's why encapsulation was load-bearing for C portability, and here's how Java mechanized it*. Then the pivot: *but in Java, the portability story isn't the whole motivation, because the JVM handles platform variance. So why do we still encapsulate?* This is where the "now change it" exercise lands — to make the loose-coupling cost concrete. Then the refrain — *every public name is a promise* — and the framing of your design principles as the accumulated wisdom of people who've made too many promises they couldn't keep.

The student is now equipped with two motivations for encapsulation — the hard one (portability/portability-analogues) and the soft one (loose coupling/future flexibility) — and they've felt the cost of getting it wrong at least once in a controlled setting. That foundation should hold up through the rest of the course as you keep invoking it.

Want to design the "now change it" exercise concretely, or push on to one of the other threads?

Phrased this way, loose coupling is *the same idea as keeping options open*. A class with a small, deliberate public surface has retained more freedom to change than a class with a sprawling one. The cost of tight coupling is *paid in lost flexibility* — which is precisely the cost that's invisible to students because it's the cost of options they never knew they had.

There's a sentence I'd suggest using somewhere in the week, possibly as a refrain: *"every public name is a promise, and promises are easier to make than to keep."* It's compact, memorable, and inverts the usual default of "make things public unless there's a reason not to" into "make things private unless there's a reason to commit to them." That inversion is the design discipline in seed form.

**On making them feel it.** Honestly, I think the most powerful single move is the "now change it" exercise, done early in the week and referenced repeatedly. Once students have *felt* the cost of cascade-edits through client code that touched fields it shouldn't have, every later mention of encapsulation calls back to that specific feeling. They have a concrete memory of the pain, not a hypothetical. The rest of the discipline can then be motivated as "remember when you had to change six files to add one feature? That's what we're preventing."

The deeper truth — which you might want to share with them explicitly at some point — is that *senior engineers feel this pain so acutely that they preemptively design to avoid it*. The reason your design principles look the way they do isn't that someone derived them from first principles; it's that people who've maintained large codebases for decades have all converged on similar disciplines because the alternatives keep producing the same pain. You're not handing them a religion; you're handing them shortcuts that experienced engineers earned the hard way.

**Synthesizing into the week.** I'd suggest this rough placement:

The `FILE` example opens the encapsulation discussion in the way we developed earlier — *here's why encapsulation was load-bearing for C portability, and here's how Java mechanized it*. Then the pivot: *but in Java, the portability story isn't the whole motivation, because the JVM handles platform variance. So why do we still encapsulate?* This is where the "now change it" exercise lands — to make the loose-coupling cost concrete. Then the refrain — *every public name is a promise* — and the framing of your design principles as the accumulated wisdom of people who've made too many promises they couldn't keep.

The student is now equipped with two motivations for encapsulation — the hard one (portability/portability-analogues) and the soft one (loose coupling/future flexibility) — and they've felt the cost of getting it wrong at least once in a controlled setting. That foundation should hold up through the rest of the course as you keep invoking it.

Want to design the "now change it" exercise concretely, or push on to one of the other threads?

Agreed — and I think it's worth being deliberate about what we're designing *for*, because "feel the pain" can mean several different things, and the exercise that produces each kind of pain looks different.

Let me lay out the design space first, then we can pick which corner to start exploring concretely.

**Axes worth varying:**

1. **Which pain?** Different design disciplines have different pains they prevent. Some candidates:
   - *Cascading edits when implementation changes* — the classic encapsulation pain.
   - *Invariant violation through unmediated state access* — what happens when clients can reach in and break consistency.
   - *Interface bloat when concrete types leak into client code* — variable declared as `ArrayList`, now you can't swap to a different `List`.
   - *Inheritance fragility* — superclass changes break subclass behavior, or subclass invariants get violated by inherited methods the subclass didn't think about.
   - *The boilerplate-vs-flexibility tradeoff* — composition's "boilerplate" delegation methods, which feel pointless until they aren't.
   - *Coupling through shared mutable state* — two clients touching the same object, no contract about ordering.

2. **Who pays the cost?** The exercise can be structured so the same student feels the cost, or so a different student feels it. Each has merits — self-inflicted pain is more visceral, but pain inflicted by others is more realistic.

3. **When is the cost paid?** Immediately (within the same class session), after a delay (next assignment), or in the long arc (referenced back to weeks later).

4. **What's the artifact?** A diff to apply, a failing test to fix, a feature to add, a bug to track down, code review of someone else's submission.

5. **How much scaffolding?** Pre-built code with a small change required, vs. students writing the whole thing and then being surprised.

**A few concrete starting points to react to:**

*The Mutable Point.* You give students a working `Rectangle` class that takes two `Point` objects (top-left and bottom-right). The `Rectangle` exposes `area()`, `width()`, `height()`. Now they add a feature — say, "rectangles should never have negative width or height." They add a check in the constructor. Tests pass. Then you reveal: someone else's code does `rect.getTopLeft().setX(999)` after construction. The invariant is dead. The pain is the realization that *the constructor check did nothing* because the rectangle never owned its points — it just held references to objects the caller could still mutate. The fix is either defensive copying (encapsulation by value) or immutable points (encapsulation by design). The general lesson: *you don't own state you don't control access to.*

This one targets invariant-violation pain and has the nice property that the "fix" naturally leads into a discussion of immutability and value semantics — both of which become important later.

*The Inheritance Time Bomb.* Give them a `CountingArrayList<T> extends ArrayList<T>` that overrides `add` to increment a counter. They write tests; everything passes. Then you change the assignment: "now we need to also count `addAll`." They override `addAll`. But — and here's the catch — depending on the JDK version, the parent's `addAll` may or may not call `add` internally. If it does, every element gets counted twice. If it doesn't, it works fine. The behavior is *correct under one JDK and wrong under another*, and the student can't tell from reading their own code which case they're in. This is Bloch's famous example, and it lands hard because the bug *isn't in the student's code*; it's in their *assumption about the parent class*.

The lesson is sharp: *inheritance commits you to depending on implementation details that aren't part of the documented interface.* The fix is composition — and now the "boilerplate" of delegating each method explicitly looks like an *advantage*, because every counted operation is *visible in the source*.

*The Leaky Interface.* Students declare a variable as `ArrayList<Customer>` and pass it around. Three classes deep, someone does `customers.ensureCapacity(1000)`. Works fine. Then you change the requirement: "Customers should now be stored in a `LinkedHashSet` for deduplication." They change one declaration; the compile errors cascade because `LinkedHashSet` doesn't have `ensureCapacity`. The fix is to declare *all* variables as `Collection<Customer>` or `List<Customer>` from the start — and the lesson is that *the type you declare is a contract about what you'll depend on*. Concrete types in declarations are promises you didn't mean to make.

This one is fast — maybe 15 minutes — and produces the cascade-edit pain cleanly.

*The Cross-Student Implementation Swap.* The most ambitious: students implement a `Stack<T>` interface that you provide. Their implementations all conform to the interface but differ internally (array-backed, linked-node-backed, dynamically-resizing, fixed-capacity-with-error, etc.). Then they write client code that uses `Stack<T>`. Then you have them run their client code against *another student's* implementation. The client code works *if and only if* it depended only on the interface, not on the specific implementation. Anyone who, say, cast to `ArrayStack` to access an internal method finds their code suddenly broken when paired with a `LinkedStack`.

This is logistically harder but pedagogically the most direct version of "the interface is the contract, the implementation is private." It also previews real-world engineering — your code has to work against implementations written by people you've never met, who chose differently than you would have.

**My instinct on priorities.** If you're going to invest serious time on one of these, I'd start with the Mutable Point or the Inheritance Time Bomb, because they're both *small enough to do in a single session* and produce *immediate, visceral* surprise. The Leaky Interface is a good supplement that takes less time. The Cross-Student Swap is the ambitious one — it might be a great culminating exercise for the week, but it requires PrairieLearn infrastructure to be smooth, and it might be better as a v2 target after you've seen what the simpler ones do.

The Mutable Point in particular has a quality I like: the *surprise* is structural. Students think they understood references from the week-one Q1-Q3 polling, but they didn't *apply* that understanding to design. The exercise reveals that knowing the notional machine isn't enough — you have to use it as a *design tool*. That bridge — from "I can predict what code does" to "I can design code that does what I want, robustly" — is the bridge the week is fundamentally trying to build.

Which of these resonates as the starting point worth developing in detail? Or is there a *different* pain you're more interested in targeting first that I haven't named?

Climbing Above C-Level
Bill Venners: In an interview, you said, "The C++ community has yet to internalize the facilities offered by standard C++. By reconsidering the style of C++ use, major improvements in ease of writing, correctness, maintainability, and efficiency can be obtained." How should C++ programmers reconsider their style of C++ use?

Bjarne Stroustrup: It's always easier to say what not to do, rather than what to do, so I'll start that way. A lot of people see C++ as C with a few bits and pieces added. They write code with a lot of arrays and pointers. They tend to use new the way they used malloc. Basically, the abstraction level is low. Writing C-style code is one way to get into C++, but it's not using C++ really well.

I think a better way of approaching C++ is to use some of the standard library facilities. For example, use a vector rather than an array. A vector knows its size. An array does not. You can extend a vector's size implicitly or explicitly. To get an array of a different size, you must explicity deal with memory using realloc, malloc, memcpy, etc. Also, use inline functions rather than macros, so you don't get into the macro problems. Use a C++ string class rather than manipulating C strings directly. And if you've got a lot of casts in the code, there's something wrong. You have dropped from the level of types, a high level of abstraction, down to a level of bits and bytes. You shouldn't do that very often.

To get out of writing low level code, you needn't start writing a lot of classes. Instead, start using facilities provided in libraries. The standard library is the first and most obvious source, but there are also good libraries for things like math or systems programming. You don't have to do threading at the C level. You can use a C++ threading library, for example, Boost.Threads. There are quite a few threading libraries. If you want callbacks, don't use just plain C functions. Get libsigc++, and you'll have a proper library that deals with callbacks—callback classes, slots and signals, that kind of stuff. It's available. It's conceptually closer to what you're thinking about anyway. And you don't have to mess with error prone details.

Most of these techniques are criticized unfairly for being inefficient. The assumption is that if it is elegant, if it is higher level, it must be slow. It could be slow in a few cases, so deal with those few cases at the lower level, but start at a higher level. In some cases, you simply don't have the overhead. For example, vectors really are as fast as arrays.

Object-Orientaphilia
The other way people get into trouble is exactly the opposite. They believe that C++ should be an extremely high level language, and everything should be object-oriented. They believe that you should do everything by creating a class as part of a class hierarchy with lots of virtual functions. This is the kind of thinking that's reflected in a language like Java for instance, but a lot of things don't fit into class hierarchies. An integer shouldn't be part of a class hierarchy. It doesn't need to. It costs you to put it there. And it's very hard to do elegantly.

You can program with a lot of free-standing classes. If I want a complex number, I write a complex number. It doesn't have any virtual functions. It's not meant for derivation. You should use inheritance only when a class hierarchy makes sense from the point of view of your application, from your requirements. For a lot of graphics classes it makes perfect sense. The oldest example in the book is the shape example, which I borrowed from Simula. It makes sense to have a hierarchy of shapes or a hierarchy of windows, things like that. But for many other things you shouldn't plan for a hierarchy, because you're not going to need one.

So you can start with much simpler abstractions. Again the standard library can provide some examples: vector, string, complex number. Don't go to hierarchies until you need them. Again, one indication that you've gone too far with class hierarchies is you have to write casts all the time, casting from base classes to derived classes. In really old C++, you would do it with a C style cast, which is unsafe. In more modern C++, you use a dynamic cast, which at least is safe. But still better design usually leads you to use casting only when you get objects in from outside your program. If you get an object through input, you may not know what it is until a bit later, and then you have to cast it to the right type.

Bill Venners: What is the cost of going down either of those two paths, being too low-level or too enamored with object-orientation? What's the problem?

Bjarne Stroustrup: The problem with the C way is that if you write code C-style, you get C-style problems. You will get buffer overflows. You will get pointer problems. And you will get hard to maintain code, because you're working at a very low level. So the cost is in development time and maintenance time.

Going to the big class hierarchy is again, you write more code than you need to, and you get too much connection between different parts. I particularly dislike classes with a lot of get and set functions. That is often an indication that it shouldn't have been a class in the first place. It's just a data structure. And if it really is a data structure, make it a data structure.

Classes Should Enforce Invariants
Bjarne Stroustrup: My rule of thumb is that you should have a real class with an interface and a hidden representation if and only if you can consider an invariant for the class.

Bill Venners: What do you mean by invariant?

Bjarne Stroustrup: What is it that makes the object a valid object? An invariant allows you to say when the object's representation is good and when it isn't. Take a vector as a very simple example. A vector knows that it has n elements. It has a pointer to n elements. The invariant is exactly that: the pointer points to something, and that something can hold n elements. If it holds n+1 or n-1 elements, that's a bug. If that pointer is zero, it's a bug, because it doesn't point to anything. That means it's a violation of an invariant. So you have to be able to state which objects make sense. Which are good and which are bad. And you can write the interfaces so that they maintain that invariant. That's one way of keeping track that your member functions are reasonable. It's also a way of keeping track of which operations need to be member functions. Operations that don't need to mess with the representation are better done outside the class. So that you get a clean, small interface that you can understand and maintain.

Bill Venners: So the invariant justifies the existence of a class, because the class takes the responsibility for maintaining the invariant.

Bjarne Stroustrup: That's right.

Bill Venners: The invariant is a relationship between different pieces of data in the class.

Bjarne Stroustrup: Yes. If every data can have any value, then it doesn't make much sense to have a class. Take a single data structure that has a name and an address. Any string is a good name, and any string is a good address. If that's what it is, it's a structure. Just call it a struct. Don't have anything private. Don't do anything silly like having a hidden name and address field with get_name and set_address and get_name and set_name functions. Or even worse, make a virtual base class with virtual get_name and set_name functions and so on, and override it with the one and only representation. That's just elaboration. It's not necessary.

Bill Venners: It's not necessary because there's one and only representation. The justification is usually that if you make it a function, then you can change the representation.

Bjarne Stroustrup: Exactly, but some representations you don't change. You don't change the representation of an integer very often, or a point, of a complex number. You have to make design decisions somewhere.

And the next stage, where you go from the plain data structure to a real class with real class objects, could be that name and address again. You probably wouldn't call it name_and_address. You'll maybe call it personnel_record or mailing_address. At that stage you believe name and address are not just strings. Maybe you break the name down into first, middle, and last name strings. Or you decide the semantics should be that the one string you store really has first, middle, and last name as parts of it. You can also decide that the address really has to be a valid address. Either you validate the string, or you break the string up into first address field, second address field, city, state, country, zip code, that kind of stuff.

When you start breaking it down like that, you get into the possibilities of different representations. You can start deciding, does it really add to have private data, to have a hierarchy? Do you want a plain class with one representation to deal with, or do you want to provide an abstract interface so you can represent things in different ways? But you have to make those design decisions. You don't just randomly spew classes and functions around. And you have to have some semantics that you are defending before you start having private data.

The way the whole thing is conceived is that the constructor establishes the environment for the member functions to operate in, in other words, the constructor establishes the invariant. And since to establish the invariant you often have to acquire resources, you have the destructor to pull down the operating environment and release any resources required. Those resources can be memory, files, locks, sockets, you name it—anything that you have to get and put back afterwards.

Designing Simple Interfaces
Bill Venners: You said that the invariant helps you decide what goes into the interface. Could you elaborate on how? Let me attempt to restate what you said, and see if I understand it. The functions that are taking any responsibility for maintaining the invariant should be in the class.

Bjarne Stroustrup: Yes.

Bill Venners: Anything that's just using the data, but not defending the invariant, doesn't need to be in the class.

Bjarne Stroustrup: Let me give an example. There are some operations you really can't do without having direct access to the representation. If you have an operation that changes the size of a vector, then you'd better be able to make changes to the number of elements stored. You move the elements and change the size variable. If you've just got to read the size variable, well, there must be a member function for that. But there are other functions that can be built on top of existing functions. For example, given efficient element access, a find function for searching in a vector is best provided as a non-member.

Another example would be a Date class, where the operations that actually change the day, month, and year have to be members. But the function that finds the next weekday, or the next Sunday, can be put on top of it. I have seen Date classes with 60 or 70 operations, because they built everything in. Things like find_next_Sunday. Functions like that don't logically belong in the class. If you build them in, they can touch the data. That means if you want to change the data layout, you have to review 60 functions, and make changes in 60 places.

Instead, if you build a relatively simple interface to a Date class, you might have five or ten member functions that are there because they are logically necessary, or for performance reasons. It's hard for me to imagine a performance reason for a Date, but in general that's an important concern. Then you get these five or ten operations, and you can build the other 50 in a supporting library. That way of thinking is fairly well accepted these days. Even in Java, you have the containers and then the supporting library of static methods.

I've been preaching this song for the better part of 20 years. But people got very keen on putting everything in classes and hierarchies. I've seen the Date problem solved by having a base class Date with some operations on it and the data protected, with utility functions provided by deriving a new class and adding the utility functions. You get really messy systems like that, and there's no reason for having the utility functions in derived classes. You want the utility functions to the side so you can combine them freely. How else do I get your utility functions and my utility functions also? The utility functions you wrote are independent from the ones I wrote, and so they should be independent in the code. If I derive from class Date, and you derive from class Date, a third person won't be able to easily use both of our utility functions, because we have built dependencies in that didn't need to be there. So you can overdo this class hierarchy stuff.

Excellent source — and what's striking is how much of your week-one framing is already *there*, articulated by someone with no particular axe to grind against OOP (he invented C++). The convergence is itself a teaching point: when the inventor of the language and the maintainers of every large codebase end up saying the same thing, students should notice.

Three threads in this interview worth pulling on, with pointers to where each leads:

**1. "Classes should enforce invariants" is the load-bearing claim.** This is *exactly* your point about anemic classes, but with a sharper formulation. Stroustrup's rule — *you should have a real class with an interface and a hidden representation if and only if you can consider an invariant for the class* — is more precise than "encapsulate stateful behavior." It tells you the *test*: can you state, in one sentence, what makes an object of this class valid? If yes, you have a class. If no, you have a struct or a record.

Worth chasing further:

- **Bertrand Meyer's *Object-Oriented Software Construction* (1988/1997)** introduced *Design by Contract* — preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants as *formal* properties. Eiffel had language-level support for them. Meyer's chapter on class invariants is the most rigorous treatment in the literature; it's where Stroustrup's informal rule has its theoretical roots. The book is long but the invariant material is concentrated.
- **Liskov & Guttag's *Program Development in Java* (2000)** has an excellent chapter on rep invariants and abstraction functions — the formal machinery for thinking about what makes a representation valid. Liskov's earlier CLU papers are the deeper source if you want them.
- **Joshua Bloch's *Effective Java* Item 17 ("Minimize mutability") and Item 50 ("Make defensive copies when needed")** — Bloch translates the invariant discipline into Java idioms. The defensive copy example (Period class with mutable Date) is *exactly* the Mutable Point exercise we sketched. Bloch credits the example to a 2004 conference talk; the underlying point goes back to Meyer.

**2. The "get/set anti-pattern" critique has a name in the wider literature.** Stroustrup's observation — *I particularly dislike classes with a lot of get and set functions. That is often an indication that it shouldn't have been a class in the first place* — is the *anemic domain model* anti-pattern, named by Martin Fowler in 2003.

Worth chasing further:

- **Fowler's "AnemicDomainModel" article (martinfowler.com, 2003)** is short and quotable. Fowler attributes the original observation to Eric Evans's *Domain-Driven Design* (also 2003) — which is the canonical book-length treatment of "what should a class actually encapsulate?" Evans's distinction between *entities*, *value objects*, and *services* is essentially a taxonomy of what wants to be a class and what doesn't.
- **Allen Holub's *"Why getter and setter methods are evil"* (JavaWorld, 2003)** is a more polemical treatment of the same point. Worth reading as a counterpoint — Holub is more extreme than Stroustrup, but the core argument is the same.
- **William Cook's *"On Understanding Data Abstraction, Revisited"* (OOPSLA 2009)** is the deep theoretical treatment. Cook distinguishes *abstract data types* (records of behavior, where the representation is hidden behind operations) from *objects* (procedural abstractions). It's a paper that will *change how you think* about the data-vs-behavior distinction. Probably too dense for students, but extraordinary for your own framing.

**3. The "functions that don't need access shouldn't be members" point connects to a deeper design tradition.** Stroustrup's example — *Date class with `find_next_Sunday` as a free function, not a member* — is making a case that classes should be *minimal*, with the broader vocabulary built on top *externally*. This is the "non-member non-friend interface" principle, and it has its own substantial literature.

Worth chasing further:

- **Scott Meyers, "How Non-Member Functions Improve Encapsulation" (C/C++ Users Journal, 2000)** — the canonical short article. Meyers argues, with Stroustrup's blessing, that *non-member functions actually increase encapsulation* because they can only use the public interface. This is counterintuitive and worth exploring — it inverts the usual student intuition that "more methods inside the class = more encapsulated."
- **Herb Sutter's "Monoliths Unstrung" / *Exceptional C++ Style* Item 1** develops the same point with the `std::string` interface as a case study — `std::string` has too many member functions, many of which should have been free functions. Sutter's analysis is forensic and quotable.
- **In the Java world, this point shows up as "prefer static utility methods to instance methods" when the operation doesn't need internal state.** It's also implicit in Java's standard library design — `Collections.sort` is a static method that takes a `List`, not a method on `List` itself. The reason is exactly Stroustrup's reason.

**A few cross-cutting suggestions for assembling your reading library:**

The interview itself is a good week-one assigned reading — it's short, it's by someone whose authority students will accept, and it pre-states most of the points you're going to make. Having students read it *before* the week starts and then noticing how often the lectures echo it builds the sense that you're teaching them established wisdom, not personal preference.

Bloch's *Effective Java* is the single most quotable source for Java-specific design discipline. The items most directly relevant to your week-one themes:

- **Item 15** (Minimize accessibility) — the encapsulation argument.
- **Item 18** (Favor composition over inheritance) — Bloch's famous treatment, with the `HashSet`-with-counter example that's even sharper than the `ArrayList` version.
- **Item 19** (Design and document for inheritance, or else prohibit it) — the case for `final` classes.
- **Item 20** (Prefer interfaces to abstract classes) — the case for interface-first design.
- **Item 64** (Refer to objects by their interfaces) — the case against concrete types in declarations.

Almost every design discipline you're advocating has a corresponding Bloch item, often with a real-world cautionary tale attached. The book is also short-chapter format, which makes individual items assignable as outside reading.

For the inheritance critique specifically, the *canonical* historical references are:

- **The GoF book's introduction** (Gamma et al., *Design Patterns*, 1994) where "favor composition over inheritance" first appears in print as a principle. The introduction is freely excerpted in many places.
- **The "fragile base class problem"** — coined by various people in the 1990s but rigorously analyzed by Mikhajlov & Sekerinski in *"A Study of the Fragile Base Class Problem"* (ECOOP 1998). The paper is a formal treatment of why inheritance breaks across version boundaries — it's the deep version of Bloch's `ArrayList`/`addAll` time bomb.

For the broader "what is OOP actually for" discussion:

- **Alan Kay's various retrospectives** — Kay coined the term "object-oriented programming" and has spent forty years saying that *nobody got it right*. His "I made up the term object-oriented and I can tell you I did not have C++ in mind" line is famous and quotable. Kay's emphasis was on *messaging* and *late binding*, not class hierarchies — which is a useful counterpoint to show students that even the foundational terms are contested.
- **Cook's paper above** is the rigorous version of this debate.

**One thing the Stroustrup interview suggests that might be worth incorporating directly:** his framing of "starting from C-style code" versus "starting from object-oriented code" as the *two opposite failure modes*. This is a nice rhetorical structure for your unit — you can position the discipline as the *middle path*, avoiding both the under-abstraction of "structs and free functions everywhere" and the over-abstraction of "everything is a deep hierarchy with virtual methods." Students who feel pulled toward either extreme can be redirected toward the middle by name. *"You're falling into the C trap"* / *"You're falling into the OOP trap"* are useful diagnostic phrases.

Want me to keep going on any of these threads — Bloch's items in detail, Cook's paper, the fragile base class literature, the Kay/Cook debate about what OOP even is? Or do you want to bring in more source material yourself first and we can react to it together as you assemble the library?

Oh, this is a *gift*. Oracle's own tutorial is a near-perfect specimen of every pedagogical anti-pattern we've been diagnosing — and it's the document students have likely already encountered. Putting it next to Stroustrup's interview is one of the most powerful teaching moves available to you: *the language's official tutorial and the language designer's principles disagree, and here's why the designer is right*.

Let me catalog what's wrong with it, because I think the catalog itself is teaching material.

**The "bicycle" example violates Stroustrup's invariant rule by design.** Look at the `Bicycle` class. It has three fields — `cadence`, `speed`, `gear` — all package-private (not even `private`!), with public mutators (`changeCadence`, `changeGear`, `speedUp`, `applyBrakes`) that *do nothing but assign to the field*. There is no invariant. The tutorial *itself acknowledges* that an invariant could exist — "if the bicycle only has 6 gears, a method to change gears could reject any value that is less than 1 or greater than 6" — but then provides an implementation where `changeGear` does no such check. The conditional is hypothetical; the code is anemic. This is Stroustrup's "structure in a tuxedo" exactly.

Worse, this is presented as the *canonical* example of "how to design a class." Students who internalize this pattern have learned: *a class is a struct with mutator methods that don't actually do anything different from direct field assignment*. They've learned the form without the function. When they later write `class Student { ...getters and setters... }`, they're not making a mistake — they're correctly applying the pattern they were taught.

**The "real-world objects" framing is the noun/verb fallacy in its purest form.** "Look around right now and you'll find many examples of real-world objects: your dog, your desk, your television set, your bicycle." This is the *exact* failure mode you identified — students are being told that the structure of their program should mirror the structure of the world. Worse, the examples are *passive nouns with no interesting computational behavior*. A desk has no state transitions worth modeling in software. A television does, but the tutorial doesn't model it; it just gestures at the noun.

The deep problem with this framing is that it teaches students the *wrong abstraction operation*. The right operation is: "given a computational problem, what stateful behaviors need encapsulating?" The tutorial's operation is: "given a real-world object, transcribe its parts into fields and its actions into methods." These produce dramatically different software. The first produces `ArrayList` and `HashMap` and `BufferedReader`. The second produces `Dog` and `Desk` and `Bicycle` — which is to say, it produces almost nothing that exists in any real Java codebase.

**The "data encapsulation" claim is performed but not delivered.** The tutorial explicitly invokes the term: *"Hiding internal state and requiring all interaction to be performed through an object's methods is known as data encapsulation — a fundamental principle of object-oriented programming."* But the `Bicycle` class then *doesn't hide its state* — the fields aren't `private`. And the methods it provides aren't *enforcing* anything that direct field access wouldn't permit. The "encapsulation" is purely syntactic — the field is accessed through a method-shaped hole — without any of the *semantic* properties that make encapsulation valuable. This is encapsulation-as-ritual, divorced from encapsulation-as-discipline.

**The benefits list is correct in the abstract but unsupported by the example.** "Modularity, Information-hiding, Code re-use, Pluggability and debugging ease" — all real benefits, none demonstrated by the `Bicycle` class. The `Bicycle` class can't be plugged-in-and-replaced because there's no interface to plug into. Its "information hiding" hides nothing. Its "modularity" amounts to "lives in its own file." The list reads as a sales pitch for a product the example doesn't deliver.

**The two diagrams are pedagogically meaningful.** The first diagram shows an object as "a circle with an inner circle filled with items, surrounded by gray wedges representing methods." This *picture* embodies the encapsulation discipline correctly — state at the center, methods as the boundary. The code below it then *doesn't implement* the picture. The wedges in the diagram are doing real work; the methods in the code aren't. A student who looks at the picture and then reads the code is being shown two different things and told they're the same.

**The class definition demonstrates anemic encapsulation as the default.** Notice that the tutorial doesn't even use `private`. The fields are package-private by accident of omission. Every Java codebase I've ever seen treats `private` as the default for fields and is explicit about widening it. The tutorial teaches the *opposite* default. This may be unintentional — the author may have just been keeping the example short — but the effect on students is to teach them that field protection is optional decoration.

---

**The pedagogical opportunity this presents.** Putting Stroustrup's interview and this tutorial side-by-side is a *forensic exercise* that students can do themselves. You can frame it as: *"Here is what Oracle teaches. Here is what the inventor of C++ says. Identify the disagreements. Whose position is better defended?"* This kind of exercise — analyzing two authoritative sources that contradict each other — is genuinely intellectually demanding in a way that lectures rarely are. Students have to *exercise judgment* rather than absorb conclusions.

Specific contradictions worth surfacing:

- Stroustrup: *"I particularly dislike classes with a lot of get and set functions. That is often an indication that it shouldn't have been a class in the first place."* Oracle: presents a class whose methods are literally `changeCadence`, `changeGear`, `speedUp` — setters with cosmetic naming.

- Stroustrup: *"You should have a real class with an interface and a hidden representation if and only if you can consider an invariant for the class."* Oracle: presents a class with no invariant, no validation, no internal consistency to maintain.

- Stroustrup: *"You should use inheritance only when a class hierarchy makes sense from the point of view of your application, from your requirements."* Oracle: introduces inheritance immediately after classes, as if every domain naturally has hierarchical structure.

- Stroustrup: *"If every data can have any value, then it doesn't make much sense to have a class... Just call it a struct."* Oracle: presents a Bicycle whose `cadence` can be anything, `speed` can be anything, `gear` can be anything — and calls it a class.

The exercise of having students identify these contradictions is genuinely educational, because it teaches them *that authoritative sources can be wrong*, and that the way to evaluate them is to ask whether the principles they teach actually produce the outcomes they promise. This is a meta-skill that extends far beyond the OOP unit.

**What to do with this in lecture.** A few options:

The most direct: open the unit by showing the Oracle bicycle. Ask students if anything seems off. They probably won't see it — the example is the canonical form they've been trained to accept. Then, *after* developing the invariant principle and the anemic-class critique, return to the bicycle and dissect it together. The "oh, *that's* what was wrong" moment is the payoff. Students who initially saw nothing wrong now see it everywhere — including in their own past code.

A more confrontational version: assign both readings as outside material before the relevant lecture, and ask students to identify points of disagreement. Some will notice; some won't. The classroom discussion of *who noticed what* surfaces the misconceptions in the room directly. This is essentially the PI methodology applied to readings instead of code.

A subtler version: never explicitly criticize the Oracle tutorial, but constantly invoke its examples as counterexamples. "Remember the Bicycle from the Oracle tutorial? Let's fix it." Each session does one piece of the fix — add the invariant, add `private`, extract the interface, defensive-copy the inputs. By the end of the week, the Bicycle is a properly-designed class, and students have *transformed* the tutorial's example into something defensible. This is the gentlest approach but the most experientially powerful, because students do the corrective work themselves.

**One deeper observation about why the tutorial is the way it is.** The Java Tutorials were originally written in the late 1990s, in the era when OOP was *being sold* to programmers raised on C. The tutorial's rhetoric — "real-world objects," "blueprint," "modularity" — is *marketing copy* from that era, designed to make OOP feel intuitive and approachable. It succeeded as marketing: a generation of programmers learned to think this way. But it failed as pedagogy: the same generation produced enormous amounts of badly designed code, because the tutorial taught them the *shape* of OOP without the *discipline*. The fact that Oracle has never substantially revised these pages — they still target JDK 8 in 2024 — is itself a story about how educational materials calcify around the wrong defaults.

This is worth saying to students at some point. Not to undermine Oracle's authority gratuitously, but to give them a framework for understanding *why* so much OOP teaching is bad. It isn't that the teachers were stupid or careless. It's that the materials they inherited were optimized for *acceptance* of a new paradigm, not for *competence* in it. Your job — and theirs — is to move past the acceptance phase into the competence phase. Which requires unlearning some of what the acceptance phase taught.

**The "Bicycle" as a recurring teaching artifact for the course.** Given how perfectly it embodies what *not* to do, you might consider making `Bicycle` a running example through the unit and beyond. Each design principle gets applied to the Bicycle: invariants, encapsulation, interface extraction, immutability, composition. By the time the class has finished week one, the Bicycle has been transformed from Oracle's version into a class that would pass Stroustrup's tests. This gives students a *single concrete artifact* to track across all the abstract principles — and a vivid before/after they can refer to whenever they need to remember what good design looks like.

Want to develop the Bicycle-redesign sequence concretely — what does each step add, in what order, with what motivation? Or to keep pulling on the Oracle tutorial threads (the inheritance and interface pages are likely just as instructive)?

# Lesson: Object-Oriented Programming Concepts

If you've never used an object-oriented programming language before, you'll need to learn a few basic concepts before you can begin writing any code. This lesson will introduce you to objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, and packages. Each discussion focuses on how these concepts relate to the real world, while simultaneously providing an introduction to the syntax of the Java programming language.

## [What Is an Object?](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/object.html)

An object is a software bundle of related state and behavior. Software objects are often used to model the real-world objects that you find in everyday life. This lesson explains how state and behavior are represented within an object, introduces the concept of data encapsulation, and explains the benefits of designing your software in this manner.

## [What Is a Class?](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/class.html)

A class is a blueprint or prototype from which objects are created. This section defines a class that models the state and behavior of a real-world object. It intentionally focuses on the basics, showing how even a simple class can cleanly model state and behavior.

## [What Is Inheritance?](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/inheritance.html)

Inheritance provides a powerful and natural mechanism for organizing and structuring your software. This section explains how classes inherit state and behavior from their superclasses, and explains how to derive one class from another using the simple syntax provided by the Java programming language.

## [What Is an Interface?](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/interface.html)

An interface is a contract between a class and the outside world. When a class implements an interface, it promises to provide the behavior published by that interface. This section defines a simple interface and explains the necessary changes for any class that implements it.

## [What Is a Package?](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/package.html)

A package is a namespace for organizing classes and interfaces in a logical manner. Placing your code into packages makes large software projects easier to manage. This section explains why this is useful, and introduces you to the Application Programming Interface (API) provided by the Java platform.

## [Questions and Exercises: Object-Oriented Programming Concepts](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/concepts/QandE/questions.html)

Use the questions and exercises presented in this section to test your understanding of objects, classes, inheritance, interfaces, and packages.

# What Is an Object?

Objects are key to understanding *object-oriented* technology. Look around right now and you'll find many examples of real-world objects: your dog, your desk, your television set, your bicycle.

Real-world objects share two characteristics: They all have *state* and *behavior*. Dogs have state (name, color, breed, hungry) and behavior (barking, fetching, wagging tail). Bicycles also have state (current gear, current pedal cadence, current speed) and behavior (changing gear, changing pedal cadence, applying brakes). Identifying the state and behavior for real-world objects is a great way to begin thinking in terms of object-oriented programming.

Take a minute right now to observe the real-world objects that are in your immediate area. For each object that you see, ask yourself two questions: "What possible states can this object be in?" and "What possible behavior can this object perform?". Make sure to write down your observations. As you do, you'll notice that real-world objects vary in complexity; your desktop lamp may have only two possible states (on and off) and two possible behaviors (turn on, turn off), but your desktop radio might have additional states (on, off, current volume, current station) and behavior (turn on, turn off, increase volume, decrease volume, seek, scan, and tune). You may also notice that some objects, in turn, will also contain other objects. These real-world observations all translate into the world of object-oriented programming.

![A circle with an inner circle filled with items, surrounded by gray wedges representing methods that allow access to the inner circle.](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/figures/java/concepts-object.gif)

A software object.

  

Software objects are conceptually similar to real-world objects: they too consist of state and related behavior. An object stores its state in *fields* (variables in some programming languages) and exposes its behavior through *methods* (functions in some programming languages). Methods operate on an object's internal state and serve as the primary mechanism for object-to-object communication. Hiding internal state and requiring all interaction to be performed through an object's methods is known as *data encapsulation* — a fundamental principle of object-oriented programming.

Consider a bicycle, for example:

![A picture of an object, with bicycle methods and instance variables.](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/figures/java/concepts-bicycleObject.gif)

A bicycle modeled as a software object.

  

By attributing state (current speed, current pedal cadence, and current gear) and providing methods for changing that state, the object remains in control of how the outside world is allowed to use it. For example, if the bicycle only has 6 gears, a method to change gears could reject any value that is less than 1 or greater than 6.

Bundling code into individual software objects provides a number of benefits, including:

1. Modularity: The source code for an object can be written and maintained independently of the source code for other objects. Once created, an object can be easily passed around inside the system.
2. Information-hiding: By interacting only with an object's methods, the details of its internal implementation remain hidden from the outside world.
3. Code re-use: If an object already exists (perhaps written by another software developer), you can use that object in your program. This allows specialists to implement/test/debug complex, task-specific objects, which you can then trust to run in your own code.
4. Pluggability and debugging ease: If a particular object turns out to be problematic, you can simply remove it from your application and plug in a different object as its replacement. This is analogous to fixing mechanical problems in the real world. If a bolt breaks, you replace *it*, not the entire machine.

content.text:
Oh, this is a *gift*. Oracle's own tutorial is a near-perfect specimen of every pedagogical anti-pattern we've been diagnosing — and it's the document students have likely already encountered. Putting it next to Stroustrup's interview is one of the most powerful teaching moves available to you: *the language's official tutorial and the language designer's principles disagree, and here's why the designer is right*.

Let me catalog what's wrong with it, because I think the catalog itself is teaching material.

**The "bicycle" example violates Stroustrup's invariant rule by design.** Look at the `Bicycle` class. It has three fields — `cadence`, `speed`, `gear` — all package-private (not even `private`!), with public mutators (`changeCadence`, `changeGear`, `speedUp`, `applyBrakes`) that *do nothing but assign to the field*. There is no invariant. The tutorial *itself acknowledges* that an invariant could exist — "if the bicycle only has 6 gears, a method to change gears could reject any value that is less than 1 or greater than 6" — but then provides an implementation where `changeGear` does no such check. The conditional is hypothetical; the code is anemic. This is Stroustrup's "structure in a tuxedo" exactly.

Worse, this is presented as the *canonical* example of "how to design a class." Students who internalize this pattern have learned: *a class is a struct with mutator methods that don't actually do anything different from direct field assignment*. They've learned the form without the function. When they later write `class Student { ...getters and setters... }`, they're not making a mistake — they're correctly applying the pattern they were taught.

**The "real-world objects" framing is the noun/verb fallacy in its purest form.** "Look around right now and you'll find many examples of real-world objects: your dog, your desk, your television set, your bicycle." This is the *exact* failure mode you identified — students are being told that the structure of their program should mirror the structure of the world. Worse, the examples are *passive nouns with no interesting computational behavior*. A desk has no state transitions worth modeling in software. A television does, but the tutorial doesn't model it; it just gestures at the noun.

The deep problem with this framing is that it teaches students the *wrong abstraction operation*. The right operation is: "given a computational problem, what stateful behaviors need encapsulating?" The tutorial's operation is: "given a real-world object, transcribe its parts into fields and its actions into methods." These produce dramatically different software. The first produces `ArrayList` and `HashMap` and `BufferedReader`. The second produces `Dog` and `Desk` and `Bicycle` — which is to say, it produces almost nothing that exists in any real Java codebase.

**The "data encapsulation" claim is performed but not delivered.** The tutorial explicitly invokes the term: *"Hiding internal state and requiring all interaction to be performed through an object's methods is known as data encapsulation — a fundamental principle of object-oriented programming."* But the `Bicycle` class then *doesn't hide its state* — the fields aren't `private`. And the methods it provides aren't *enforcing* anything that direct field access wouldn't permit. The "encapsulation" is purely syntactic — the field is accessed through a method-shaped hole — without any of the *semantic* properties that make encapsulation valuable. This is encapsulation-as-ritual, divorced from encapsulation-as-discipline.

**The benefits list is correct in the abstract but unsupported by the example.** "Modularity, Information-hiding, Code re-use, Pluggability and debugging ease" — all real benefits, none demonstrated by the `Bicycle` class. The `Bicycle` class can't be plugged-in-and-replaced because there's no interface to plug into. Its "information hiding" hides nothing. Its "modularity" amounts to "lives in its own file." The list reads as a sales pitch for a product the example doesn't deliver.

**The two diagrams are pedagogically meaningful.** The first diagram shows an object as "a circle with an inner circle filled with items, surrounded by gray wedges representing methods." This *picture* embodies the encapsulation discipline correctly — state at the center, methods as the boundary. The code below it then *doesn't implement* the picture. The wedges in the diagram are doing real work; the methods in the code aren't. A student who looks at the picture and then reads the code is being shown two different things and told they're the same.

**The class definition demonstrates anemic encapsulation as the default.** Notice that the tutorial doesn't even use `private`. The fields are package-private by accident of omission. Every Java codebase I've ever seen treats `private` as the default for fields and is explicit about widening it. The tutorial teaches the *opposite* default. This may be unintentional — the author may have just been keeping the example short — but the effect on students is to teach them that field protection is optional decoration.

---

**The pedagogical opportunity this presents.** Putting Stroustrup's interview and this tutorial side-by-side is a *forensic exercise* that students can do themselves. You can frame it as: *"Here is what Oracle teaches. Here is what the inventor of C++ says. Identify the disagreements. Whose position is better defended?"* This kind of exercise — analyzing two authoritative sources that contradict each other — is genuinely intellectually demanding in a way that lectures rarely are. Students have to *exercise judgment* rather than absorb conclusions.

Specific contradictions worth surfacing:

- Stroustrup: *"I particularly dislike classes with a lot of get and set functions. That is often an indication that it shouldn't have been a class in the first place."* Oracle: presents a class whose methods are literally `changeCadence`, `changeGear`, `speedUp` — setters with cosmetic naming.

- Stroustrup: *"You should have a real class with an interface and a hidden representation if and only if you can consider an invariant for the class."* Oracle: presents a class with no invariant, no validation, no internal consistency to maintain.

- Stroustrup: *"You should use inheritance only when a class hierarchy makes sense from the point of view of your application, from your requirements."* Oracle: introduces inheritance immediately after classes, as if every domain naturally has hierarchical structure.

- Stroustrup: *"If every data can have any value, then it doesn't make much sense to have a class... Just call it a struct."* Oracle: presents a Bicycle whose `cadence` can be anything, `speed` can be anything, `gear` can be anything — and calls it a class.

The exercise of having students identify these contradictions is genuinely educational, because it teaches them *that authoritative sources can be wrong*, and that the way to evaluate them is to ask whether the principles they teach actually produce the outcomes they promise. This is a meta-skill that extends far beyond the OOP unit.

**What to do with this in lecture.** A few options:

The most direct: open the unit by showing the Oracle bicycle. Ask students if anything seems off. They probably won't see it — the example is the canonical form they've been trained to accept. Then, *after* developing the invariant principle and the anemic-class critique, return to the bicycle and dissect it together. The "oh, *that's* what was wrong" moment is the payoff. Students who initially saw nothing wrong now see it everywhere — including in their own past code.

A more confrontational version: assign both readings as outside material before the relevant lecture, and ask students to identify points of disagreement. Some will notice; some won't. The classroom discussion of *who noticed what* surfaces the misconceptions in the room directly. This is essentially the PI methodology applied to readings instead of code.

A subtler version: never explicitly criticize the Oracle tutorial, but constantly invoke its examples as counterexamples. "Remember the Bicycle from the Oracle tutorial? Let's fix it." Each session does one piece of the fix — add the invariant, add `private`, extract the interface, defensive-copy the inputs. By the end of the week, the Bicycle is a properly-designed class, and students have *transformed* the tutorial's example into something defensible. This is the gentlest approach but the most experientially powerful, because students do the corrective work themselves.

**One deeper observation about why the tutorial is the way it is.** The Java Tutorials were originally written in the late 1990s, in the era when OOP was *being sold* to programmers raised on C. The tutorial's rhetoric — "real-world objects," "blueprint," "modularity" — is *marketing copy* from that era, designed to make OOP feel intuitive and approachable. It succeeded as marketing: a generation of programmers learned to think this way. But it failed as pedagogy: the same generation produced enormous amounts of badly designed code, because the tutorial taught them the *shape* of OOP without the *discipline*. The fact that Oracle has never substantially revised these pages — they still target JDK 8 in 2024 — is itself a story about how educational materials calcify around the wrong defaults.

This is worth saying to students at some point. Not to undermine Oracle's authority gratuitously, but to give them a framework for understanding *why* so much OOP teaching is bad. It isn't that the teachers were stupid or careless. It's that the materials they inherited were optimized for *acceptance* of a new paradigm, not for *competence* in it. Your job — and theirs — is to move past the acceptance phase into the competence phase. Which requires unlearning some of what the acceptance phase taught.

**The "Bicycle" as a recurring teaching artifact for the course.** Given how perfectly it embodies what *not* to do, you might consider making `Bicycle` a running example through the unit and beyond. Each design principle gets applied to the Bicycle: invariants, encapsulation, interface extraction, immutability, composition. By the time the class has finished week one, the Bicycle has been transformed from Oracle's version into a class that would pass Stroustrup's tests. This gives students a *single concrete artifact* to track across all the abstract principles — and a vivid before/after they can refer to whenever they need to remember what good design looks like.

Want to develop the Bicycle-redesign sequence concretely — what does each step add, in what order, with what motivation? Or to keep pulling on the Oracle tutorial threads (the inheritance and interface pages are likely just as instructive)?
