*Eagerness* — the axis between data and codata. A fully materialized list is data. A generator that produces elements on demand is codata. A list that materializes lazily (memoized) is intermediate — it's *becoming* data through observation, starting as codata. This is exactly the territory of streams, generators, lazy sequences, and the like.

*Finite-vs-infinite* — also along the data/codata axis. Data is necessarily finite (you have to be able to enumerate it). Codata can be infinite (the protocol may never terminate). Streams of natural numbers, server loops, event loops — all codata, all potentially infinite.

So the manifold has, roughly, the two duality axes as its primary dimensions, with secondary axes (mutability, sharing, storage, eagerness, finiteness) refining the position. Most design decisions are *not* "which corner am I in" but rather "how do I slide along these axes to balance the competing concerns of my actual problem."

**What this reveals about Java's design choices.**

Now your earlier complaint comes into focus with new precision. Java's *defaults* push everything toward one specific point on the manifold: *identity-typed, heap-allocated, GC-managed, mutable, shared by reference, eagerly materialized*. Every class instance, by default, sits at this point. The language *permits* moving along other axes — `final` fields move toward immutability, `record` types move toward value semantics, `Iterator` moves toward codata, generics move toward parametric reuse — but every move requires explicit effort against the default.

They don't see it as a *position* on a *manifold of choices*; they see it as just "how things are." And then when they encounter a language with different defaults — Rust's value semantics, Haskell's laziness, C's manual layout — they experience it as alien rather than as a different point in the same design space.

You’ve elaborated much of my reasoning, but I think the biggest value in this conceptual framework is in showing how storage strategy fits into the rest of it, since that’s what is most often buried inside of implementation details that students never learn about.

The first observation is exactly what you said, that values don’t care about storage strategy. Thus, it is only pertinent to entities (things with unique identity). And this is where Java causes students to conflate identity with storage: Java objects are implicitly identified by their address. This is of course a consequence of how computer memory is implemented, and honestly it is mostly inherited from C, but it means that there’s an unnecessarily tight coupling between storage and identity which also leaks through the equality operator.

The other place where the default coupling creates problems, as you mentioned, is in aliasing. When identity is tightly coupled to storage, to the extent that knowledge of an object’s identity provides *de facto* access to its interface (and possibly its actual structure) then you can no longer reason about correctness in the presence of concurrency.

My working theory is that concurrent programming has been considered an advanced or even graduate-level topic in CS for so long because the prevailing programming paradigms, especially as manifested in teaching languages like Java and Python, conflate storage and identity to the point that concurrent programming is only possible by bolting on an extra layer of access control that requires its own course sequence to fully explore.

Yes — and the working theory is genuinely correct, I think, though it can be made even sharper. Let me try to lay out why.

**The identity/storage conflation is doing more damage than just complicating concurrency.** It's the root cause of an entire family of phenomena that get treated as separate problems, when they're all symptoms of the same underlying confusion. Let me list a few:

*Aliasing bugs.* Two references to the same object; mutation through one is visible through the other. The student's intuition is "I have two `Point`s," but the reality is "I have two pointers to one `Point`." The bug arises because the student's identity model (*these are two things*) and the storage model (*these are one allocation*) disagree, and the language enforces the storage model silently.

*Reference equality leakage.* The `==` operator tests storage identity. If your "identity" was meant to be something else — say, "two `Customer`s with the same customer-id are the same customer" — then `==` lies to you, and you have to override `equals` to tell the truth. But even when you do, you can't make `==` go away, so the storage-identity remains observable. Students who never explicitly choose an identity model end up with whatever the language defaults to, which is *storage*.

*Defensive copying.* When you want value semantics over identity-typed storage (the `Date` field in your `Period` class), you have to copy on the way in and on the way out. The copying isn't a feature; it's *paying down the conflation*. In a language that didn't conflate, you'd just declare the field to be a value type and the compiler would handle it. Java doesn't have that option, so you copy manually.

*The need for immutability as a discipline.* The reason "prefer immutable types" is good advice in Java isn't that mutability is inherently bad — it's that *Java has no way to express "this object has identity but its observable state never changes."* Immutability is the workaround: if the state never changes, then aliasing is harmless, reference equality almost works, defensive copying is unnecessary, concurrency is automatic. All these properties fall out of the same workaround, because all the problems came from the same conflation.

*Hash-consing, interning, flyweight patterns.* These are all *manual* attempts to reverse the conflation in the other direction: instead of values pretending to be identities, make identities behave like values by ensuring only one of each. The pattern only exists because the language can't natively say "I want values here." Note that interning *exploits* the conflation in a clever way — it makes storage identity coincide with value identity by construction — which is why `String` literal interning happens to work but `Integer` cache only works for small values.

*Object pooling, weak references, the entire menagerie of GC dances.* All of these exist because storage identity *carries weight* (lifecycle, reachability, finalization) that value semantics wouldn't impose. If your objects were *values*, the GC wouldn't be tracking them at all; they'd live wherever was convenient, including being duplicated freely.

When you see this list together, the conflation isn't a "leaks through the equality operator" — it's the *founding assumption of the language*, with consequences that ripple into every part of the system. Java is *built on* the equation of storage with identity, and almost every "best practice" in the Java world is, on some level, a workaround for the consequences.

**Now your concurrency observation.** This is the deepest version of the conflation problem, and you're right that it's been *misclassified* as an advanced topic when it's actually a *consequence* of the elementary mistake. Let me lay it out.

In a *value-based* world, concurrency is nearly trivial. Two threads can both *have* the same value at the same time, because values can be freely shared. Reads from one don't conflict with reads from the other, because reads are observation of content, and the content can be copied to wherever the reader is. Writes don't exist — values can't be mutated. The whole apparatus of locks, mutexes, atomic operations, memory barriers, and happens-before relations *doesn't apply* to pure values. They're not a concurrency primitive; they're a *concurrency non-issue*.

In an *identity-based* world, concurrency is hard, but it's also *coherent*. An identity has a definite location; mutations happen at that location; the question of "what does this identity look like *now*" is well-defined relative to a moment in time. The challenge of concurrency is then about *coordinating observations and mutations across threads*, which requires explicit synchronization. The conceptual model is intricate but principled — you can reason about it.

In the *Java world*, concurrency is bewildering because *the identity model is implicit and the consequences ripple unpredictably*. A `String` is a value (immutable, structurally compared via `equals`) — except `==` exposes its underlying identity. A `Date` is identity — except many APIs return defensive copies, so the identity isn't stable. An `ArrayList` is identity, but if you don't realize that and pass it across thread boundaries, you get torn reads and silent corruption. The language doesn't help you know which is which. Every type in your program might be playing a different game, and the type system doesn't tell you.

This is what makes Java concurrency a graduate topic: it's not that *concurrency* is graduate-level; it's that *concurrency in a language that conflates identity and storage and won't tell you which is which* is graduate-level. The conceptual baggage you have to carry to do concurrent Java correctly is enormous, and most of it is bookkeeping about which of your variables are aliasing which heap-allocated mutable thing, and which mutations might race with which reads.

By contrast, in languages that *separate* identity from storage cleanly — Erlang, Clojure, Rust, Haskell — concurrency is teachable to undergraduates, and often to *beginners*. Erlang's processes can't share state at all; communication is by message-passing of values. Clojure makes the immutable/mutable distinction explicit in the type system. Rust uses the borrow checker to enforce that aliasing and mutation can't happen together. Haskell's purity means most code is value-based by default and concurrent execution is free. In none of these languages is concurrency "advanced." It's *foundational*, because the underlying type system makes it tractable.

The implication: the reason concurrency is considered advanced *in CS curricula* is because the curricula were designed around languages (originally C, then C++, then Java, then Python) that all share the storage/identity conflation. The conflation makes concurrency hard. The hardness gets misattributed to concurrency itself. Then it gets deferred to a later course. The later course teaches concurrency *in the conflated language*, which requires additional machinery (locks, atomics, memory models) to manage. Students learn to associate "concurrency" with "this giant pile of mechanisms," when actually most of the mechanism is *paying down the conflation*, not doing concurrency.

You're describing what's known in some circles as the *"shared mutable state"* critique, but you've stated it more precisely than that critique usually does. The standard version says "shared mutable state is bad," which is true but unmotivated. Your version says "*the conflation of identity and storage makes shared mutable state the default*, and the consequences ripple outward into concurrency, aliasing, equality, and lifecycle management." That's the structural explanation, and it makes the bad-vs-good framing fall out as a *consequence* rather than as a moralistic prescription.

1. *Values don't care about storage.* This is the easy half. A `5` is a `5` no matter where it lives. Two `5`s in different memory locations are still "the same `5`." The storage question is *moot* for values, and this is *why* values are easy to reason about — there's nothing extra to track.

2. *Identity does care about storage, but doesn't have to be conflated with it.* This is the harder half, and it's the conceptual leap most students never make. You can have an identity-typed thing whose identity is *not* its address. A `Customer` identified by customer-id, a `File` identified by path, an `Account` identified by account number — all of these have identity that is *defined* by some property, not by where the object happens to live. The language can still allocate them anywhere, garbage-collect them when convenient, deduplicate them if useful, *as long as* the identity-defining property remains stable.

It works terribly for objects whose identity should have been defined by something else, and worse, it makes the distinction *invisible to the type system*. The programmer has to choose carefully *outside the language* whether each class plays the storage-is-identity game or some other game, and then the language can't help them maintain that choice.

4. *Concurrency is impossible to reason about correctly until you've separated identity from storage.* Because: concurrency is fundamentally about *coordinating observations of changes over time*. To coordinate observations, you have to know *what is being observed* (the identity), and *what counts as a change* (the value transitions). If the identity is "wherever this happens to be in memory," then observation and change are mediated by *the storage*, and synchronization requires protecting *the storage*. If the identity is a logical thing distinct from the storage, then synchronization can happen at the *logical* level (e.g., "only one thread updates customer-id 42's balance at a time"), independent of what storage strategy is in use.

C didn't conflate identity with storage; it *defined* identity *as* storage, and the conflation was inherited by C's descendants without anyone noticing that *the higher-level languages didn't have to do that*. Java could have defined object identity as a separate concept from address — and indeed, the JVM internally is free to move objects around during GC, so the address isn't even stable — but the language *surface* preserves the C-style equation of identity with reference. This is, in some sense, a *historical accident*: Java was designed to be familiar to C programmers, so it kept the conflation as a syntactic feature even though the runtime didn't need it.

The same is true of Python, of Ruby, of every dynamic OO language. They all inherit the conflation from C through their implementation choices, even though the user-facing language could have made a different decision. The languages that *did* make a different decision — Erlang, Haskell, Clojure, Rust — are exactly the ones with first-class concurrency stories.

This historical observation is worth making to students because it shows that the design space *was* and *is* genuinely open. The conflation isn't necessary; it's contingent. Languages can be designed without it. And the languages that are designed without it have systematically different properties, particularly in the concurrency dimension. The students leave the course not just knowing about the conflation, but knowing that *the conflation could have been otherwise, and that the choice has consequences*. That's the kind of intellectual independence you want them to have.

*Aliasing bugs.* Two references to the same object; mutation through one is visible through the other. The student's intuition is "I have two `Point`s," but the reality is "I have two pointers to one `Point`." The bug arises because the student's identity model (*these are two things*) and the storage model (*these are one allocation*) disagree, and the language enforces the storage model silently.

*Reference equality leakage.* The `==` operator tests storage identity. If your "identity" was meant to be something else — say, "two `Customer`s with the same customer-id are the same customer" — then `==` lies to you, and you have to override `equals` to tell the truth. But even when you do, you can't make `==` go away, so the storage-identity remains observable. Students who never explicitly choose an identity model end up with whatever the language defaults to, which is *storage*.

*Defensive copying.* When you want value semantics over identity-typed storage (the `Date` field in your `Period` class), you have to copy on the way in and on the way out. The copying isn't a feature; it's *paying down the conflation*. In a language that didn't conflate, you'd just declare the field to be a value type and the compiler would handle it. Java doesn't have that option, so you copy manually.

*The need for immutability as a discipline.* The reason "prefer immutable types" is good advice in Java isn't that mutability is inherently bad — it's that *Java has no way to express "this object has identity but its observable state never changes."* Immutability is the workaround: if the state never changes, then aliasing is harmless, reference equality almost works, defensive copying is unnecessary, concurrency is automatic. All these properties fall out of the same workaround, because all the problems came from the same conflation.

*Hash-consing, interning, flyweight patterns.* These are all *manual* attempts to reverse the conflation in the other direction: instead of values pretending to be identities, make identities behave like values by ensuring only one of each. The pattern only exists because the language can't natively say "I want values here." Note that interning *exploits* the conflation in a clever way — it makes storage identity coincide with value identity by construction — which is why `String` literal interning happens to work but `Integer` cache only works for small values.

*Object pooling, weak references, the entire menagerie of GC dances.* All of these exist because storage identity *carries weight* (lifecycle, reachability, finalization) that value semantics wouldn't impose. If your objects were *values*, the GC wouldn't be tracking them at all; they'd live wherever was convenient, including being duplicated freely.

When you see this list together, the conflation isn't a "leaks through the equality operator" — it's the *founding assumption of the language*, with consequences that ripple into every part of the system. Java is *built on* the equation of storage with identity, and almost every "best practice" in the Java world is, on some level, a workaround for the consequences.

**Now your concurrency observation.** This is the deepest version of the conflation problem, and you're right that it's been *misclassified* as an advanced topic when it's actually a *consequence* of the elementary mistake. Let me lay it out.

In a *value-based* world, concurrency is nearly trivial. Two threads can both *have* the same value at the same time, because values can be freely shared. Reads from one don't conflict with reads from the other, because reads are observation of content, and the content can be copied to wherever the reader is. Writes don't exist — values can't be mutated. The whole apparatus of locks, mutexes, atomic operations, memory barriers, and happens-before relations *doesn't apply* to pure values. They're not a concurrency primitive; they're a *concurrency non-issue*.

In an *identity-based* world, concurrency is hard, but it's also *coherent*. An identity has a definite location; mutations happen at that location; the question of "what does this identity look like *now*" is well-defined relative to a moment in time. The challenge of concurrency is then about *coordinating observations and mutations across threads*, which requires explicit synchronization. The conceptual model is intricate but principled — you can reason about it.

In the *Java world*, concurrency is bewildering because *the identity model is implicit and the consequences ripple unpredictably*. A `String` is a value (immutable, structurally compared via `equals`) — except `==` exposes its underlying identity. A `Date` is identity — except many APIs return defensive copies, so the identity isn't stable. An `ArrayList` is identity, but if you don't realize that and pass it across thread boundaries, you get torn reads and silent corruption. The language doesn't help you know which is which. Every type in your program might be playing a different game, and the type system doesn't tell you.

This is what makes Java concurrency a graduate topic: it's not that *concurrency* is graduate-level; it's that *concurrency in a language that conflates identity and storage and won't tell you which is which* is graduate-level. The conceptual baggage you have to carry to do concurrent Java correctly is enormous, and most of it is bookkeeping about which of your variables are aliasing which heap-allocated mutable thing, and which mutations might race with which reads.

By contrast, in languages that *separate* identity from storage cleanly — Erlang, Clojure, Rust, Haskell — concurrency is teachable to undergraduates, and often to *beginners*. Rust uses the borrow checker to enforce that aliasing and mutation can't happen together. Haskell's purity means most code is value-based by default and concurrent execution is free. Students learn to associate "concurrency" with "this giant pile of mechanisms," when actually most of the mechanism is *paying down the conflation*, not doing concurrency.

The standard version says "shared mutable state is bad," which is true but unmotivated. Your version says "*the conflation of identity and storage makes shared mutable state the default*, and the consequences ripple outward into concurrency, aliasing, equality, and lifecycle management." That's the structural explanation, and it makes the bad-vs-good framing fall out as a *consequence* rather than as a moralistic prescription.

You can have an identity-typed thing whose identity is *not* its address. A `Customer` identified by customer-id, a `File` identified by path, an `Account` identified by account number — all of these have identity that is *defined* by some property, not by where the object happens to live. Exactly — and this is the cleanest example you could ask for, because the leak is *visible in the language's own contract*. Java *requires* you to make a choice between identity-equality and value-equality the moment you put your class into a hash-based collection, and the requirement is enforced not by the type system but by the *behavioral contract* of `Object`. It's an admission, encoded into the standard library, that the conflation breaks down here and the programmer has to step in.

Let me work through why this is so revealing.

**The `equals`/`hashCode` contract is a value-semantics requirement smuggled into an identity-default language.** The contract says: if `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must be true. There's no other way to phrase this contract that makes sense. It's literally saying: *if you decide that two objects represent the same value, their value-derived hash must agree.* The contract is fundamentally about value semantics. The word "value" isn't used, but the structure is unmistakable.

And the contract is *enforced socially*, not by the language. `HashMap` *trusts* you to maintain it. If you violate it — say, you override `equals` to compare names but leave `hashCode` returning the default address-derived value — your code will *silently malfunction*. Objects that compare equal will land in different buckets, lookups will fail, the map will lose entries it nominally contains. The bug is invisible until it isn't. The compiler can't help you. The runtime won't tell you. You have to know the contract and obey it.

This is *exactly* the kind of contract that a value-aware type system would enforce automatically. In Haskell, the `Eq` and `Hashable` typeclasses are derived from the structural definition of the type; you can't get the contract wrong because you don't write the implementations by hand for normal cases. In Rust, `PartialEq` and `Hash` are derivable, and the compiler enforces the contract automatically when you derive both. In Java, you write both methods manually, and the language doesn't even know they're supposed to be related. The fact that they must agree is a *fact about your program's semantics that the language has no way to express*.

**The hash function's purity requirement is a value-semantics requirement.** A hash function maps values to bucket indices. For the map to work, the same value must map to the same bucket every time. If the hash changes — *for the same object* — between when it was inserted and when it's looked up, the lookup will fail. This is exactly what happens when you put a *mutable* object into a `HashMap` and then mutate it: the map effectively *loses* the object, because its hash position no longer matches its content.

The standard textbook advice is: *don't mutate keys in a hash map*. But the deeper observation is: *keys must behave as values*. The map's contract demands it. The language permits you to violate it — keys can be any reference, and references can point to mutable objects — but the violation is silent and catastrophic. Java's mutable-by-default model is *fundamentally incompatible* with hash-based lookup, and the language provides no mechanism to enforce the compatibility. The programmer has to manually inhabit value-semantics for any object that's going to be a hash key, even though nothing in the type system says they have to.

**The escape hatch of `Object`'s defaults reveals the conflation directly.** `Object.equals` defaults to `==`, which is reference equality. `Object.hashCode` defaults to some address-derived value (technically, an identity hash that the JVM is free to compute however it likes, but functionally tied to the object's identity-as-allocation). The contract is *satisfied by these defaults*, because two references that are `==` will have the same address-derived hash. This works! For identity-based hashing, the defaults are correct.

But notice what's happened: the *default* `equals`/`hashCode` behavior treats every object as an *identity*, with identity defined as storage location. The moment you want value semantics — the moment you want two `Customer` instances with the same customer-id to count as equal — you have to *override both methods together*. You have to pull the object out of the identity regime and put it into the value regime by hand. The language doesn't make this easy or safe; it just makes it possible. And if you do it wrong, the bug is silent.

This is what the conflation actually *looks like* in practice. The defaults assume storage-is-identity. The contract is a *value-semantics contract* that you can opt into. The opt-in requires manually overriding two methods that must agree, with no compiler enforcement. The result is a system where doing the right thing requires sustained, error-prone discipline, and doing the wrong thing is silent.

**The contract reveals what `Object` would have looked like in a value-aware language.** Imagine a Java where every class had to declare itself as `value class` or `identity class`. Value classes get structural `equals` and `hashCode` automatically, derived from their fields. Identity classes get the reference-equality defaults. The compiler refuses to put an identity-class instance into a `HashMap` as a key, because identity classes don't have a stable value-hash. You can override the defaults for either kind, but you have to declare what you're doing.

This isn't a fantasy — it's roughly what Java's `record` keyword does, several decades late. A `record` is a class whose `equals` and `hashCode` are auto-derived from its fields, whose fields are final, and whose semantics are explicitly value-flavored. The fact that Java *added* records in 2020 (Java 14) is the language *admitting* that the original design conflated two things that should have been separable, and that programmers need an explicit way to say "I want a value here." Records are the *retroactive separation* of value from identity, built atop a language that originally fused them.

But records are still bolted on. They live alongside the rest of the language, which still defaults to identity. A `HashMap<Customer, Account>` will still happily accept a non-record `Customer` whose `equals` and `hashCode` are inconsistent. The language doesn't enforce the value discipline; it just provides a *convention* (records) that makes opting in cheaper. The fundamental conflation is still there, in every non-record class.

**The pedagogical payoff of this example.** I think `equals`/`hashCode` is the single example that most cleanly *exposes* the conflation to students. It has several properties that make it ideal:

It's a contract students will encounter in their first weeks of using `HashMap`, so it's not hypothetical. They will need to override these methods. They will need to understand why. The motivation is concrete.

The contract is *visible* — `Object`'s Javadoc states it explicitly. Students can read the contract themselves. The tension between the contract (value-semantics) and the language defaults (identity-semantics) is *right there in the documentation*, if you know how to read it.

The bug mode is *catastrophic and silent*. You can show students a working program that breaks the moment you mutate a key. The pain is immediate and dramatic. This is the kind of demonstration that lodges in long-term memory.

The fix is *philosophically meaningful*. Overriding `equals` and `hashCode` to behave consistently is *not* a Java idiom; it's *manually inhabiting value semantics in an identity-default language*. Once students see the fix this way, every subsequent encounter with `equals`/`hashCode` reinforces the duality framework rather than being another rule to memorize.

And the lesson generalizes immediately. *Anywhere your program treats two objects as "the same value," you are imposing value semantics on identity-typed storage, and you need to enforce that discipline by hand.* This applies to set membership, map keys, deduplication, caching, and most database-related code. The discipline is the same discipline; the conflation is the same conflation; the value/identity distinction is the same distinction. One concept, many manifestations.

**A specific teaching artifact you might consider.** The classic exercise is "put a mutable object into a `HashSet`, mutate it, and observe what happens." Show it live. The set *contains* the object — `set.contains(obj)` returns `false`. The object is *in* the set — iterating over the set yields it. The set has *one* element — `set.size()` returns 1. All three observations are simultaneously true. The set is *internally inconsistent* because its invariants depended on a hash that no longer matches the bucket the object lives in.

This demo, done in maybe 5 minutes, surfaces every aspect of the conflation. Students see:
- The contract was violated (because the hash changed).
- The language didn't tell them (silent corruption).
- The collection is in a state that *shouldn't be possible* under its own contract.
- The cause is the mismatch between *what they wanted* (value semantics) and *what they got* (identity-typed storage that the value semantics rode on top of without enforcement).

After the demo, the lesson lands hard: *you cannot use mutable objects as keys, because keys must be values, because hashing requires value semantics, because the language can't enforce value semantics on identity-typed storage*. Every "because" is a step through the conflation. Students who absorb this have internalized the duality framework whether or not they have the vocabulary for it.

**One sharpening of your formulation.** You wrote: *"if you want to use `hashCode()` on a class then you must enforce value semantics — you don't have the choice to use identity-based hashing."* This is *almost* true but worth refining. You *do* have the choice to use identity-based hashing — that's the default. What you don't have the choice to do is *mix* identity-based hashing with value-based equality, or vice versa, or any other combination. The constraint is *consistency*: whatever model of equality you choose, the hash must agree with it. If you use identity-based equality (the default), you must use identity-based hashing (also the default). If you use value-based equality (an override), you must use value-based hashing (another override). The contract enforces internal consistency *within* whatever model you're using.

This refinement matters because it shows that the conflation isn't unique to value semantics; it's a constraint on *any* model. Java requires you to pick one model and stick with it for any given class. The fact that the default is identity-based and the override is value-based is a consequence of Java's overall identity bias, but the structural requirement — that equality and hashing agree — is just *the consistency requirement of any hash-based lookup*. The conflation comes in when you observe that, in practice, *almost all useful overrides are value-based*, because identity-based hashing is rarely what you want when you're putting objects into maps. The contract permits any consistent choice; the world demands value semantics; Java forces you to manually impose them.

Stated this way, the lesson is: *Java's defaults are identity-flavored, but the world is value-flavored, so most real Java programs require you to manually convert identity-typed classes into value-flavored behavior, and the language provides no help in maintaining the conversion correctly.* That's the conflation in one sentence, with `equals`/`hashCode` as the canonical example.

I think you have a genuinely good teaching artifact here. But notice what's happened: the *default* `equals`/`hashCode` behavior treats every object as an *identity*, with identity defined as storage location. The moment you want value semantics — the moment you want two `Customer` instances with the same customer-id to count as equal — you have to *override both methods together*. You have to pull the object out of the identity regime and put it into the value regime by hand. The language doesn't make this easy or safe; it just makes it possible. And if you do it wrong, the bug is silent.

This is what the conflation actually *looks like* in practice. The defaults assume storage-is-identity. The contract is a *value-semantics contract* that you can opt into. The opt-in requires manually overriding two methods that must agree, with no compiler enforcement. The result is a system where doing the right thing requires sustained, error-prone discipline, and doing the wrong thing is silent.

**The contract reveals what `Object` would have looked like in a value-aware language.** Imagine a Java where every class had to declare itself as `value class` or `identity class`. Value classes get structural `equals` and `hashCode` automatically, derived from their fields. Identity classes get the reference-equality defaults. The compiler refuses to put an identity-class instance into a `HashMap` as a key, because identity classes don't have a stable value-hash. You can override the defaults for either kind, but you have to declare what you're doing.

This isn't a fantasy — it's roughly what Java's `record` keyword does, several decades late. A `record` is a class whose `equals` and `hashCode` are auto-derived from its fields, whose fields are final, and whose semantics are explicitly value-flavored. The fact that Java *added* records in 2020 (Java 14) is the language *admitting* that the original design conflated two things that should have been separable, and that programmers need an explicit way to say "I want a value here." Records are the *retroactive separation* of value from identity, built atop a language that originally fused them.

But records are still bolted on. They live alongside the rest of the language, which still defaults to identity. A `HashMap<Customer, Account>` will still happily accept a non-record `Customer` whose `equals` and `hashCode` are inconsistent. The language doesn't enforce the value discipline; it just provides a *convention* (records) that makes opting in cheaper. The fundamental conflation is still there, in every non-record class.

**The pedagogical payoff of this example.** I think `equals`/`hashCode` is the single example that most cleanly *exposes* the conflation to students. It has several properties that make it ideal:

It's a contract students will encounter in their first weeks of using `HashMap`, so it's not hypothetical. They will need to override these methods. They will need to understand why. The motivation is concrete.

The contract is *visible* — `Object`'s Javadoc states it explicitly. Students can read the contract themselves. The tension between the contract (value-semantics) and the language defaults (identity-semantics) is *right there in the documentation*, if you know how to read it.

The bug mode is *catastrophic and silent*. You can show students a working program that breaks the moment you mutate a key. The pain is immediate and dramatic. This is the kind of demonstration that lodges in long-term memory.

The fix is *philosophically meaningful*. Overriding `equals` and `hashCode` to behave consistently is *not* a Java idiom; it's *manually inhabiting value semantics in an identity-default language*. Once students see the fix this way, every subsequent encounter with `equals`/`hashCode` reinforces the duality framework rather than being another rule to memorize.

And the lesson generalizes immediately. *Anywhere your program treats two objects as "the same value," you are imposing value semantics on identity-typed storage, and you need to enforce that discipline by hand.* This applies to set membership, map keys, deduplication, caching, and most database-related code. The discipline is the same discipline; the conflation is the same conflation; the value/identity distinction is the same distinction. One concept, many manifestations.

**A specific teaching artifact you might consider.** The classic exercise is "put a mutable object into a `HashSet`, mutate it, and observe what happens." Show it live. The set *contains* the object — `set.contains(obj)` returns `false`. The object is *in* the set — iterating over the set yields it. The set has *one* element — `set.size()` returns 1. All three observations are simultaneously true. The set is *internally inconsistent* because its invariants depended on a hash that no longer matches the bucket the object lives in.

This demo, done in maybe 5 minutes, surfaces every aspect of the conflation. Students see:
- The contract was violated (because the hash changed).
- The language didn't tell them (silent corruption).
- The collection is in a state that *shouldn't be possible* under its own contract.
- The cause is the mismatch between *what they wanted* (value semantics) and *what they got* (identity-typed storage that the value semantics rode on top of without enforcement).

After the demo, the lesson lands hard: *you cannot use mutable objects as keys, because keys must be values, because hashing requires value semantics, because the language can't enforce value semantics on identity-typed storage*. Every "because" is a step through the conflation. Students who absorb this have internalized the duality framework whether or not they have the vocabulary for it.

You *do* have the choice to use identity-based hashing — that's the default. What you don't have the choice to do is *mix* identity-based hashing with value-based equality, or vice versa, or any other combination. The constraint is *consistency*: whatever model of equality you choose, the hash must agree with it. If you use identity-based equality (the default), you must use identity-based hashing (also the default). If you use value-based equality (an override), you must use value-based hashing (another override). The contract enforces internal consistency *within* whatever model you're using.

This refinement matters because it shows that the conflation isn't unique to value semantics; it's a constraint on *any* model. Java requires you to pick one model and stick with it for any given class. The fact that the default is identity-based and the override is value-based is a consequence of Java's overall identity bias, but the structural requirement — that equality and hashing agree — is just *the consistency requirement of any hash-based lookup*. The conflation comes in when you observe that, in practice, *almost all useful overrides are value-based*, because identity-based hashing is rarely what you want when you're putting objects into maps. The contract permits any consistent choice; the world demands value semantics; Java forces you to manually impose them.

The mutable-key-in-a-hashset demo is concrete enough to do in five minutes, and the conceptual scaffolding behind it is deep enough to anchor an entire framework. That's an interesting move, and I want to think carefully before agreeing or disagreeing — because there's a real structural parallel here, but it's *not quite* a syllogism, and getting the relationship right matters.

**Where the analogy works.** The parallel you're reaching for, I think, is something like:

- Values are *pure* in the sense that they have no hidden context — they are what they are, and that's all. Two `5`s are interchangeable; nothing distinguishes them.
- Functions are pure in the sense that they have no hidden context — they map inputs to outputs deterministically, with no internal state to consult or update.
- Identities have *implicit context* — namely, the question of "which one." Two `Customer`s with the same fields are still two different customers because their identity carries information beyond their value.
- Methods have *implicit context* — namely, the receiver. `customer.getName()` is really `getName(customer)` with the first argument hidden. The method carries an extra argument the call site doesn't write down.

In this framing, both pairs are about *what's explicit versus what's implicit*. Values and functions are minimal — everything is in the surface. Identities and methods add an implicit layer that doesn't appear in the literal expression but is essential to what's happening.

**Why this is suggestive but not a syllogism.** A true analogy of the form A:B::C:D claims that the relationship between A and B is structurally the *same* as the relationship between C and D. Here, both pairs share the *flavor* of "explicit vs. implicit context," but the *content* of that context is different in each pair, and the implications differ.

In value/identity, the implicit context is *which instance we're talking about* — a question about reference, about the place this thing occupies in some space of distinguishable things. Adding identity to a value gives you something that can be *located* and *mutated* and *aliased*.

In function/method, the implicit context is *the receiver* — a specific argument that's been singled out as "the one the dispatch is happening on." Adding method-ness to a function gives you something that can be *dispatched dynamically* and *organized around a particular argument*.

These are related — both are forms of "implicit information attached to an otherwise explicit thing" — but they're not the same kind of implicit information. The first is *referential* (about identity in a space of things), the second is *dispatch-related* (about which argument controls behavior). You can have one without the other, in either direction.

**Cases that break the strict analogy.**

*Methods on values.* Java's `Integer.toString()` is a method on a value. The receiver is being treated as a value (Integer has value semantics for equality, ignoring the cache complications), but the call is method-dispatched. This is "value with a method" — the implicit dispatch context exists, but the implicit identity context doesn't really. The receiver isn't an identity in any meaningful sense; it's a value the method happens to dispatch on.

*Functions on identities.* A C-style `void update_customer(Customer* c, ...)` is a function operating on an identity (the customer pointer references a specific identifiable object). The dispatch is static — the function is determined at compile time, no vtable lookup — but the argument is identity-typed. This is "identity without method dispatch" — the implicit identity context exists, but the function isn't doing method-style dispatch on it.

These cases show that the two pairs are *orthogonal*, not parallel. You can independently have or not have implicit identity, and independently have or not have implicit dispatch. The two dualities live on different axes.

**A more accurate way to state the relationship.**

I think the deeper structural observation is this: *both pairs involve a choice about what to make implicit in a notation.*

Mathematics, by tradition, makes everything explicit at the cost of verbosity. A pure function `f(x, y)` makes both arguments visible; a pure value `5` has no hidden context. This is the *fully explicit* baseline.

Imperative programming traditions have, over decades, accreted layers of implicit context to make code more concise and "natural":
- *Object identity* makes the "which one" question implicit and accessible through reference operations like `==` and aliasing.
- *Method dispatch* makes the "which one" question (specifically about the receiver) implicit in the call syntax, and selects behavior based on it.
- *Implicit `this`* extends this further, making the receiver invisible even inside the method body.
- *Closures* make the *captured environment* implicit in the function value.
- *Exception handling* makes the *control flow context* implicit (where does this throw go?).
- *Garbage collection* makes the *lifecycle context* implicit.
- *Type inference* makes the *type annotations* implicit.

Every one of these "implicit context" choices is a *design decision* with consequences. They make code shorter but harder to reason about, especially when several are combined. They make some operations natural and others impossible. They couple aspects of the program that, in a fully explicit notation, would be separable.

In this larger view, your proposed syllogism is *one instance of a more general pattern*: both pairs are about how a language hides one specific kind of context. Value/identity hides the *reference* question. Function/method hides the *dispatch* question. The pairs are *sister cases*, not strict analogues.

**The mathematical reformulation that makes this precise.**

A function in math, `f: A → B`, takes one explicit argument and returns one result. A multi-argument function `f: A × B → C` takes a tuple. There's nothing implicit.

A method `obj.f(x)` can be modeled mathematically as `f: Self → A → B`, where the receiver is just the first argument, written with special syntax. Nothing fundamental changes by adding the special syntax; what changes is that *the language gives the first argument special status* (for dispatch, for inheritance, for `this`-based access to other members).

A value `5` is just an element of some set, say `ℕ`. It has no internal state; it has no identity beyond being the element it is. Two references to `5` are the same `5`.

An identity is harder to model mathematically. The cleanest version is: an identity is an element of some set `I` (the set of identifiers), paired with a function `state: I × Time → V` that gives the value of that identity at each moment. The identity is *the index*; the value at any given time is *what you'd observe by inspecting it*. Mutation is a change in the `state` function over time.

In this model, the analogy you proposed becomes: *just as a method packages a function with an implicit receiver argument, an identity packages a value with an implicit "which instance" index.* That's actually a real structural parallel, stated precisely. Both involve adding an implicit index to something that would otherwise be context-free.

But here's the wrinkle: methods aren't *really* a new mathematical object — they're just functions with a syntactic convention for the first argument. The implicit-receiver story is *purely about notation and dispatch*. Identities, by contrast, are *genuinely* a new mathematical object compared to values — they involve a separate set (the identifier space), a temporal dimension (state over time), and a notion of equality that depends on identifier rather than content. The two implicit-context stories are *not* equivalent in depth.

So your syllogism captures a *notational* parallel that's real, but it papers over a *semantic* asymmetry: identity is doing more work than methods are. Identity introduces time, location, and aliasing as genuinely new concepts; methods just rearrange how arguments are written and dispatched. The implicit-context framing is true of both, but the implicit context in the identity case is *load-bearing for the whole semantics of mutation and concurrency*, while the implicit context in the method case is *mostly cosmetic and dispatch-related*.

**Where the analogy is most useful pedagogically.**

I don't think the syllogism quite holds as a structural claim, but I do think the *family resemblance* is teachable and worthwhile. The deep point is: *programming language design is full of these "make-the-implicit-explicit-or-vice-versa" choices, and each choice has consequences*. Showing students that this is a recurring pattern — not just one or two isolated tradeoffs — gives them a meta-framework for understanding language design generally.

Concretely, the lesson might be: *Java makes both identity and dispatch implicit by default. C makes both explicit (you pass pointers explicitly, you call functions on those pointers). Functional languages typically make identity explicit (or eliminate it entirely) but keep dispatch implicit (typeclasses, multimethods, pattern matching). Logic programming makes both explicit and uses unification to handle dispatch. Each combination has different teachability, different correctness properties, different concurrency stories.*

Students who absorb this meta-framework gain something more valuable than knowing the specific dualities: they gain *the habit of asking, for any language feature, "what is being made implicit here, and what's the cost?"* That habit transfers to every language they'll ever encounter. They become engineers who can read a new language's spec and immediately ask the right questions, rather than engineers who only know their one or two languages and treat their conventions as the nature of programming.

So: I'd resist promoting your proposed syllogism to a strict structural claim, but I'd absolutely promote the *underlying intuition* — that programming language design involves a family of "what to make implicit" decisions, and that value/identity and function/method are two instances of this family. The framing is generative and teachable, and it gives students a place to file every future language feature they encounter. *"Oh, this language is making X implicit where my familiar language makes it explicit. What does that buy and cost?"* is one of the most powerful questions a working programmer can learn to ask.

There's also a more provocative way to put this, if you want to lean into it: *the history of programming languages is largely a history of debates about what to make implicit*. Assembly makes nothing implicit. High-level languages make the instruction stream implicit (the compiler generates it). OOP makes the receiver implicit. GC makes lifecycle implicit. Type inference makes types implicit. Each move trades verbosity for the possibility of error from things you can no longer see. The wisdom of the field is largely about *which implicits cost more than they save*, and the consensus has shifted over time as systems have gotten larger and reasoning has gotten harder. This is the real story of language design, told as a coherent narrative, and your dualities sit naturally within it.

Would you want to develop this further — perhaps by identifying the full taxonomy of "implicit context" decisions and where various languages sit on them — or come back to the immediate teaching question of how to thread the value/identity and data/codata dualities through week one without losing the students who came in expecting a normal Java review?

No, it's fine, I think maybe value:function::object:method is the better formulation but it's not important.

Or maybe it is? We talked about how the class machinery is intended to be used for encapsulation in defense of an invariant that defines what it means to be a semantically valid instance of the data type. This implies that classes (and encapsulation more generally) are only truly necessary when you cannot "make invalid states unrepresentable" through static analysis. But, and here's the kicker, this *doesn't* mean that any old data type, defined as a plain struct, must be encapsulated in a class just because some of the inhabitants of the product type are semantically invalid.

Let's go back to the `Date` example: if you choose to represent your Date as three integers, then obviously you're going to have invalid combinations. Even if you constrain each of the fields by making it an enum type, you've still got semantically invalid combinations: June 31st, or February 29th 2001. That doesn't mean you need a class to "defend the invariant"; it just means you need a better representation (like a UNIX timestamp) where dates really are just values.

It's unfortunate that Java had no concept of a plain structural type for so long. Maybe the best thing I can do at this point (and it's probably controversial) is to demand that students use `record` for any type that has only value semantics.

The first question to ask is: *can I choose a representation in which every inhabitant is valid?* If yes, no class is needed — the type itself enforces validity, with no runtime checks required. If no, then encapsulation steps in as the workaround, with runtime checks at the boundary.

Encapsulation lets you check at the boundary, but the underlying representation still permits the invalid states — you've just defended against them. With a Unix timestamp, *every* `long` is a valid moment in time. There's nothing to check, nothing to defend, because there's no invalid state to reach.

The implication: *encapsulation is the consolation prize when you can't get a perfect representation*. The better move is always to find a representation that makes invalid states unrepresentable, and reserve classes for the cases where you genuinely can't. Most data types — points, dates, money, durations, colors, units of measure — admit perfect representations. They should be values, full stop, with no class machinery.

It comes from the functional programming tradition where sum types and product types give you fine-grained control over representation, and you can often design types where the type system itself enforces validity. Java got sum types properly only with sealed types in Java 17 and pattern matching in Java 21; before that, "make invalid states unrepresentable" was hard to do cleanly. **Why `record` is the right tool for the value-typed work.** Records do three things that hand-rolled value classes typically get wrong:

1. *They make the value contract structural.* A `record Customer(String name, int id)` has `equals` and `hashCode` auto-derived from the fields, and the derivation is *guaranteed correct* — you can't accidentally violate the contract. This eliminates an entire category of bug that hand-rolled equals/hashCode introduces.

2. *They make immutability the default.* Record fields are final. You can't reassign them. You can't have a record with an internally mutable state that breaks the value contract over time. This eliminates the hash-key bug, the aliasing bug, and the defensive-copy requirement.

3. *They communicate intent.* A `record` in a codebase *announces* that this type is value-flavored. A reader knows immediately that they don't need to worry about mutation, aliasing, or identity. The mental load of working with the type is dramatically lower than for a class, because so many questions are answered by the declaration itself.

public record Date(int year, int month, int day) {

    }
}

*Records of records compose cleanly.* A `record Range(LocalDate start, LocalDate end)` where `LocalDate` is itself a value type gives you a fully value-typed range with derived equality and hashing. *Records can have static factory methods.* You can declare `Date.of(year, month, day)` that does normalization, validation, or caching, and return a `Date` from it. *Records and serialization.* Records serialize naturally — their state is exactly their declared fields, no hidden state to worry about. This is another small win.

- Stateful behavior that changes over its lifetime (a counter, a builder, a stream position, a network connection).
- Identity that's distinct from value (a `Customer` whose two instances with the same fields are still considered different customers — say, because the database row count matters).
- Internal representation that should be hidden from clients (an `ArrayStack` that uses an array internally but exposes only stack operations).
- Subclass-based polymorphism (which your principles mostly disallow anyway, but occasionally is needed).

Students who default to records and only reach for classes when they can articulate a *specific reason* records won't work are doing the right thing, even when they occasionally need to escalate.

**The pedagogical value of this rule.** Mandating records for value types is a *teaching device* as much as a coding discipline. It forces students to:

1. *Explicitly decide* whether each type is value-flavored or identity-flavored. The choice of record vs. class is now a *conscious decision*, made visibly in the code.

2. *Recognize that most domain types are values*. When students start using records reflexively for things like points, dates, sizes, colors, money, units — they're internalizing that *most things students naively model as classes are actually values*. The naive textbook OOP — where Student, Customer, Account, Book are all classes — gets challenged at the type-system level. Many of those should be records. Some are genuine entities with identity. The discipline of having to choose forces the question.

3. *Reserve class machinery for cases that need it*. When students do declare a class, it's because they've considered records and rejected them. The class is doing real work — it has invariants to enforce, state to encapsulate, behavior to manage. This is exactly Stroustrup's "real class with a real invariant" criterion, mechanized through the record/class distinction in the language.

4. *Read other code more critically*. Once students have internalized that records exist, they will see classes-that-should-have-been-records everywhere in legacy code, in tutorials, in their classmates' work. They'll be able to articulate why those classes are bad. This is exactly the critical reading capacity you want them to develop.

The discipline is also *self-reinforcing*. Records are *easier* to use correctly than classes. Once students taste the difference — auto-derived equals/hashCode, no defensive copying, no aliasing worries — they don't want to go back. The discipline becomes preference, then habit, then default.

**A teaching sequence I'd suggest.** This is a natural follow-up to the equals/hashCode discussion. Once students have seen the conflation laid bare by the mutable-key demo, the natural response is "okay, then how do I avoid the conflation when I want value semantics?" Records are the answer. You introduce them as *the solution to the problem you just demonstrated*. The motivation is built-in. The discipline isn't an arbitrary rule; it's the *fix* for a problem they just felt.

The order might be:

1. *Establish the duality framework.* Identity vs. value, data vs. codata.
2. *Demonstrate the conflation through equals/hashCode and mutable keys.* Students feel the pain.
3. *Show records as the language's mechanism for value semantics.* Auto-derived equality, immutability, no conflation hazards.
4. *Mandate records for value-flavored types.* This is now an *easier* discipline than the alternative.
5. *Throughout the rest of the course, default to records for new value-typed code.* Reinforces the habit by repetition.

By the end, students who reach for a class when they meant a record will *feel* the wrongness — and that's the discipline becoming intuition.

**One thing worth saying directly to students about why this is "controversial."** It's controversial only in the sense that *much existing Java code doesn't do this* — because records didn't exist until 2020 and most working programmers learned Java in an era when value semantics required hand-rolling. So legacy codebases are full of classes-that-should-have-been-records, written by people who didn't have the choice. Your students will encounter that code in industry. They should *recognize* it as the legacy of a language without records, not as a model to emulate.

This is, again, the *engineering profession* framing. Civil engineers know that lead pipes were once standard practice and are now recognized as harmful. They don't install lead pipes; they know how to replace them when they encounter them. Java's pre-record classes for value types are an analogous situation. Students should know how to write the modern equivalent, and how to recognize and improve the older versions when they meet them.

So yes — make the rule. *Records for any type that has only value semantics.* It's principled, it's pedagogically clean, it's mechanizable, it's enforceable in code review, and it's exactly the right discipline for students learning Java in 2026. The handful of cases where records aren't quite enough (canonical constructors with validation, factory methods, sealed hierarchies) are *exactly* the cases that teach students the nuances, and records handle them well. The rule has no significant downsides. Make it.

And if you wanted one more layer of justification: this is exactly how the Java community is moving. Brian Goetz and the Project Amber team have been explicit that records are intended to be the *default* for value-flavored data. Effective Java's 3rd edition (which predates records) recommends "favor immutability" as a general principle; records are the language's mechanism for following that recommendation. You're not innovating; you're catching your students up to where the language designers want them to be. The discipline is *consensus*, not idiosyncrasy, even if many practitioners haven't internalized it yet.

Yes — and you've just articulated something that the literature *sort of* dances around but rarely states this directly. Let me work it out, because I think you've put your finger on the precise confusion that makes "ADT" and "OOP" feel like they're describing the same thing when they really aren't.

**The clean separation.** An ADT specifies *a set of values together with operations on them*. That's the whole definition. A stack ADT specifies the set of all possible stack-values (the empty stack, single-element stacks, and so on) along with the operations push, pop, peek. Two stacks containing the same elements in the same order *are the same stack-value*. The representation — whether you implement it with an array or a linked list or a balanced tree — is irrelevant to *which stack-value* you're talking about.

An interface, in the Java sense, is a *signature* — a list of method declarations with types. It says nothing about *what values exist* or *what equality means*. A Java `Stack` interface declares that any class implementing it must have a `push` method and a `pop` method, but it doesn't say that two `Stack` instances with the same elements should be `.equals()` — that's up to the implementation, which might or might not get it right.

So an ADT is *more* than an interface. It's an interface *plus* a specification of the value set *plus* the equational laws the operations must satisfy. The interface alone gives you syntactic conformance; the ADT gives you semantic conformance.

**Where Cook's framing fits.** When Cook says ADTs have a fundamental model based on existential types, he's saying: *the value set is fully specified, but the representation is hidden behind an existential quantifier*. The client can reason about which values exist, what operations do to them, what laws they obey — and the implementer is free to choose any representation that satisfies the specification. The existential isn't hiding *what's there*; it's hiding *how it's stored*.

This is exactly your point: *abstract* in ADT means *abstracted from representation*, not *underspecified*. The value semantics are crisp. The representation is opaque. The two are independent properties of the design.

**Where Java interfaces fall short.** A Java interface gives you the *opaque representation* part — clients work against the interface, implementers choose their classes — but it doesn't give you the *specified value set* part. The interface doesn't say "two stacks with the same elements are the same." It just declares methods. Whether the implementation enforces value semantics is up to the implementer, with the language unable to help.

Worse, the *default* behavior of a Java object — reference equality via `==` and identity-derived `hashCode` — is *anti-ADT*. It explicitly distinguishes two objects with the same content, treating them as different even when the ADT contract says they should be the same. To make a Java class implement an ADT correctly, you have to actively *override* the default behavior to install value semantics on top of identity-typed storage. The language fights you.

This is the conflation you've been circling, now sharpened: *Java interfaces give you the existential abstraction of an ADT, but Java's identity-default semantics give you the wrong value contract*. To get a proper ADT in Java, you need both: the interface to hide the representation, *and* a manual installation of value semantics on whatever implementation you choose.

**Records as the missing piece.** Now your record proposal lands with full force. A record gives you the *value semantics* part automatically — structural equality, structural hashing, immutability — which is exactly the part Java interfaces don't provide. An interface plus a record implementation gets you an ADT, with the interface hiding the representation and the record installing the right equality contract.

```java
public interface Stack<T> {
    Stack<T> push(T item);
    T peek();
    Stack<T> pop();
}

public record ArrayStack<T>(T[] elements) implements Stack<T> {
    // ...
}
```

This is the closest thing to a proper ADT that Java permits. The interface is the existential — clients don't know whether they have an `ArrayStack` or a `LinkedStack`. The record is the witness — for any particular existential, *this* is the value semantics. Clients calling `.equals()` get structural equality. Clients hashing get a hash that respects the equality. The conflation is resolved.

Compare to the conventional Java approach: `class ArrayStack<T> implements Stack<T>` with mutable internal state and identity-default equality. Two stacks with the same contents are unequal. Hashing distinguishes them. The interface gives the appearance of an ADT, but the implementation breaks every property an ADT is supposed to have. The conventional Java approach *isn't an ADT*; it's an object that happens to have stack-like operations.

**Where objects-as-ADT-implementations get interesting.** Your observation that *objects can implement ADTs but carry around more than necessary* is exactly right, and it's worth unpacking the "more than necessary."

When you implement an ADT with an object, the object provides:
1. *The operations* (interface methods) — necessary for ADT.
2. *A hidden representation* (private state) — necessary for ADT.
3. *Identity* (which instance is which) — *not part of the ADT contract*.
4. *Mutation* (state changes over time) — *not part of the ADT contract*.
5. *Reference sharing* (multiple aliases to the same instance) — *consequence of identity*.

Items 1 and 2 are the ADT essence. Items 3-5 are *object machinery* the implementation language is adding for free, whether you want it or not.

For some ADTs, this object machinery is harmless and convenient. A pure functional stack can be implemented as an object with immutable state — the identity is unused, the mutation is forbidden, the reference sharing is fine because the state never changes. The object is an ADT implementation that *happens* to be wrapped in object machinery the ADT doesn't care about.

For other ADTs, the object machinery is *actively harmful*. A stack implemented with mutable state behaves differently from the ADT it nominally implements: `push` doesn't return a new stack; it mutates the existing one. Clients holding multiple references see the mutation through all of them. The ADT specifies one thing; the object does another. The ADT contract is *broken* by the object's identity and mutation, even though the operation signatures match.

This is the deep observation: *objects can faithfully implement ADTs only when the object's identity and mutability features are either unused or carefully aligned with the ADT's value semantics*. In practice, this means using immutable objects (or records). Mutable objects with ADT-style interfaces are *almost always* a category error — they're not really ADTs, they're stateful processes with ADT-shaped operations grafted onto them.

**The reframing of "object."** Cook's paper makes this point in language-theoretic terms: *objects are procedural abstractions, not data abstractions*. The "more than necessary" you're identifying is exactly the procedural part. Identity, mutation, and reference sharing are features of *processes*, not of *values*. An object models a *process* — something with state that responds to messages over time — while an ADT models a *value* — something timeless and structurally defined.

This is why the two notions are often conflated but shouldn't be: they're describing different kinds of computational artifacts. Sometimes the kind of artifact you want is genuinely a process — a network connection, a UI widget, a database cursor. Then objects are the right tool. Sometimes the kind of artifact you want is genuinely a value — a date, a point, an immutable collection. Then objects are wrong, and you should reach for records (or, in other languages, value types and ADTs directly).

The reason this gets confused in Java is that the language uses the *same construct* — `class` — for both kinds. If a value: it has timeless structural identity, its operations either don't mutate it or produce new values, equality is structural, sharing is harmless. Use a record. The ADT is the natural abstraction.

If a process: it has identity across time, its operations may mutate internal state, equality is referential (or some other notion of "same process"), sharing requires coordination. Use a class. The object is the natural abstraction.

If you don't know: ask whether two of these, with the same observable history, are *the same thing* or *two things*. If the same, value. If different, process.

This single question — *value or process?* — operationalizes the entire framework. Students who learn to ask it before reaching for `class` will make different design decisions than students who reflexively reach for `class` because that's what the textbook showed. And the answer cleanly maps to *record or class*, which maps to *ADT or object*, which maps to *value semantics or identity semantics*.

Python has classes with reference semantics by default. You're saying: in Java, records give you data abstraction, classes give you procedural abstraction, and the discipline is to use each for its proper purpose. Records are for values. - The data/codata duality, which separates "what can be observed" into enumerable and protocol-driven.
- The value/identity duality, which separates "what makes two things the same" into structural and referential.
- The manifold view, where storage strategy and other implementation choices are points along axes that follow from these dualities.
- The conflation critique, which explains why Java's defaults make these distinctions hard to maintain and why records were added.
- The ADT-vs-object distinction, which explains what classes are *for* (processes) and what records are *for* (values).
- The discipline rule, which mechanizes the framework: records for values, classes for processes, interfaces for hiding representations of either.

Every design principle you teach can be derived from this framework. Every example you encounter in the course can be characterized within it. Every code review judgment can be motivated by it. The students who leave the course with this framework will be better Java programmers than students who left without it — and they'll be better programmers in any language they encounter later, because the framework is about programming, not about Java.

With the source, they have a common origin and will naturally cohere.

A stack ADT specifies the set of all possible stack-values (the empty stack, single-element stacks, and so on) along with the operations push, pop, peek. Two stacks containing the same elements in the same order *are the same stack-value*. The representation — whether you implement it with an array or a linked list or a balanced tree — is irrelevant to *which stack-value* you're talking about.

So an ADT is *more* than an interface. It's an interface *plus* a specification of the value set *plus* the equational laws the operations must satisfy. The interface alone gives you syntactic conformance; the ADT gives you semantic conformance.

**Where Cook's framing fits.** When Cook says ADTs have a fundamental model based on existential types, he's saying: *the value set is fully specified, but the representation is hidden behind an existential quantifier*. The client can reason about which values exist, what operations do to them, what laws they obey — and the implementer is free to choose any representation that satisfies the specification. The existential isn't hiding *what's there*; it's hiding *how it's stored*.

This is exactly your point: *abstract* in ADT means *abstracted from representation*, not *underspecified*. The value semantics are crisp. The representation is opaque. The two are independent properties of the design.

The interface doesn't say "two stacks with the same elements are the same." It just declares methods. Whether the implementation enforces value semantics is up to the implementer, with the language unable to help.

Worse, the *default* behavior of a Java object — reference equality via `==` and identity-derived `hashCode` — is *anti-ADT*. It explicitly distinguishes two objects with the same content, treating them as different even when the ADT contract says they should be the same.     Stack<T> pop();

    // ...
}
```

Hashing distinguishes them. The interface gives the appearance of an ADT, but the implementation breaks every property an ADT is supposed to have. The conventional Java approach *isn't an ADT*; it's an object that happens to have stack-like operations.

**Where objects-as-ADT-implementations get interesting.** Your observation that *objects can implement ADTs but carry around more than necessary* is exactly right, and it's worth unpacking the "more than necessary."

When you implement an ADT with an object, the object provides:
1. *The operations* (interface methods) — necessary for ADT.
2. *A hidden representation* (private state) — necessary for ADT.
3. *Identity* (which instance is which) — *not part of the ADT contract*.
4. *Mutation* (state changes over time) — *not part of the ADT contract*.
5. *Reference sharing* (multiple aliases to the same instance) — *consequence of identity*.

Items 1 and 2 are the ADT essence. Items 3-5 are *object machinery* the implementation language is adding for free, whether you want it or not.
