Here's how I'd structure it. The goal is a self-contained framework essay — coherent enough to be your reference document, terse enough to be useful, with examples drawn from material we've already developed. I'll aim for something that would land at roughly 8000-12000 words in final form, organized into seven sections plus a short preface and conclusion.

---

**Preface — Why this exists.** One page. The frame: you've been teaching data structures and OOP for two semesters and noticed that the standard pedagogy produces students who can write Java but can't *reason* about programs. This document is your attempt to articulate the conceptual framework that, in your experience, separates competent programmers from confused ones. It's a reference for yourself, drawn from accumulated thinking, not a polished publication. Set the tone: working draft, in service of teaching, not theory for its own sake.

---

**1. The engineering frame.** Open with the engineering-discipline argument from the Meyer/Rickover/aviation thread. The single point: *software is engineering, and engineering means caring about properties that hold under stress, scale, and time, not just at the moment of writing*. This isn't a digression — it's the *why* for everything that follows. The disciplines you'll articulate are responses to engineering failures observed across decades of building large systems. Without this frame, the rest reads as personal aesthetic preferences. With it, the rest reads as accumulated professional wisdom.

Anchor this section with two or three sentences from Meyer, one quote from Rickover's "Doing a Job," and the aviation/Navy/SpaceX comparisons. End with: *the rest of this document is about what engineering discipline looks like at the level of individual type and class design.*

---

**2. The notional machine.** Before the framework can land, students (and your future self reading this) need a shared understanding of *what's actually happening when Java code runs*. This is the heap/stack/references material we developed for week one's PI questions.

Cover: stack frames and locals, heap and objects, references as pointers, the GC's role in lifecycle. Be concrete and visual — this section wants diagrams, not prose alone. Include the three-way diagram for `int[]` vs `Integer[]` vs C arrays from the storage thread. Lay out method dispatch and the vtable model, since that's needed for the inheritance discussion later.

This section is *foundational* and unglamorous. Don't try to make it interesting; make it correct and concrete. Everything that follows depends on this picture being in the reader's head.

End with: *the runtime model determines what kinds of things you can build. The rest of this document is about how to build them well, given this model.*

---

**3. The two dualities.** This is the conceptual heart. Develop both dualities carefully:

*3a. Data and codata.* What can be observed about a thing — its enumerable contents (data) or its protocol-driven behavior (codata)? Examples: sorted array (data), stream (codata), hash table (data), priority queue (codata), database table (data), event loop (codata). The duality is fundamental: every computational artifact answers this question one way or the other, or sits intermediate (lazy data, materialized codata).

*3b. Value and identity.* What does it mean for two things to be the same — structural equality (value) or referential equality (identity)? Examples: integers (value), customers-with-ids (identity-via-id, not address), strings (value), file handles (identity), dates as timestamps (value), dates as mutable structs (identity). The duality is fundamental: every computational artifact has a notion of equality, and the choice between value and identity is *the* choice that determines almost everything else.

*3c. The orthogonality.* The two dualities are independent. Four quadrants emerge: data+value (immutable records), data+identity (mutable structs), codata+value (pure generators), codata+identity (stateful processes). Every type in any program sits in one quadrant or transitions between them. Knowing which quadrant a type lives in tells you almost everything about how to use it correctly.

*3d. The manifold view.* Real implementations rarely sit at pure corners; they sit somewhere in the interior, with deliberate compromises along axes (mutability, sharing, eagerness, storage). Variation theory: students learn the framework by experiencing systematic variation along these axes. End with a sketch of the axes — mutability, sharing, storage strategy, eagerness, finiteness — and a note that subsequent sections develop them concretely.

---

**4. Storage as a consequence, not a choice.** Now you can address what you said earlier — that the *real* contribution of the framework is showing how storage strategy fits in. The argument:

*4a. Values don't care about storage.* They can live anywhere — stack, inline, registers, heap — because no observation depends on their location. Pure values are *location-irrelevant*. The implementer can choose any storage strategy without affecting the contract.

*4b. Identity *requires* storage with stable location, but doesn't require any particular kind.* An identity needs a *stable handle* — something that lets you re-find the "same one." Memory address is one way (and the default in most languages). But identity can also be defined by an *identifier property*: customer-id, file path, account number, primary key. When identity is property-based, the storage can move freely (GC compaction, database row migration, cache eviction-and-rehydration) without breaking the identity.

*4c. The conflation: Java equates identity with address.* This is the C inheritance. The address-as-identity choice is convenient (no extra bookkeeping) but couples the identity notion to the storage strategy in ways that leak. Reveal the leaks one by one:

- `==` tests address-identity, exposing the storage.
- Aliasing is invisible because two references look the same regardless of whether they point to one or two allocations.
- Defensive copying is needed to enforce value-flavored semantics on identity-typed storage.
- Hash-based collections require manual installation of value semantics (equals/hashCode contract) because the defaults are wrong for value-flavored use.

*4d. The concurrency consequence.* The conflation makes concurrency hard because synchronization has to protect the storage, not the identity. In languages that separate them, concurrency primitives operate at the identity level (Erlang's processes, Clojure's refs, database transactions over rows), and the storage is free to be efficient underneath. In Java, every concurrent access has to navigate the conflated model, which is why concurrent Java is famously difficult.

*4e. Why this was historically inherited and not necessary.* Walk through the C-to-C++-to-Java lineage. The conflation isn't a logical necessity; it's a historical choice that languages designed for different priorities (Erlang for telephony, Haskell for verification, Rust for systems) have made differently. End with: *the conflation is a contingent design choice with consequences. Students should recognize it as such.*

---

**5. ADTs, objects, and what classes are actually for.** Now bring in Cook's framing, sharpened by your own working out.

*5a. The ADT-as-existential model.* What an ADT is: a value set, operations, equational laws, with the representation hidden behind an existential quantifier. Why this is fundamental: it's the dual of universal quantification (generics), and together these two type-theoretic mechanisms cover the space of type-polymorphic abstraction.

*5b. ADT versus interface.* An ADT is *more* than an interface — it specifies the value set and the laws, not just the operations. A Java interface gives you the existential hiding but not the value contract. Interfaces are *almost* ADTs but missing the value semantics layer.

*5c. ADT versus object.* An object can implement an ADT, but the object machinery — identity, mutation, reference sharing — adds *more than the ADT specifies*. Objects are *processes*, not values. Cook's distinction between data abstraction and procedural abstraction. Walk through the classic example (Cook uses set or expression-tree) showing that the same operations can be implemented as ADT or as object, with different reasoning properties.

*5d. When to use which.* The rule: ask *value or process?* Value means timeless structural identity, equality is structural, no observable history. Process means identity across time, observable state changes, equality is referential. Record (or in other languages, value type, struct, ADT) for the first; class for the second. The default of "everything is a class" collapses the distinction and produces code that can't be reasoned about.

*5e. Stroustrup's invariant rule, revisited.* A class should exist when there's an invariant to defend. The reformulation: *a class exists when the invariant can't be eliminated by representation choice*. Many "invariants" of naive class designs can be made vacuous by picking a better representation (Date as timestamp). Classes are the *consolation prize* when perfect representation isn't available. This sharpens Stroustrup's rule into something operational.

---

**6. The design principles, derived.** Now show that every design principle you've been articulating is a *consequence* of the framework, not an arbitrary preference. Walk through each principle, deriving it from the framework:

- *Records for value types* — direct from section 5d.
- *All public methods come from interfaces* — separates the behavioral type (the ADT or codata protocol) from the structural type (the class's storage layout).
- *Composition over inheritance* — inheritance fuses behavioral types across classes, breaking the clean ADT abstraction. Composition keeps them separate.
- *Final classes by default* — preserves the value/process classification at the type boundary; subclassing breaks value contracts.
- *No `==` on objects* — `==` tests storage-identity, which leaks the conflation; equality should always go through a contract.
- *Factory methods returning interface types* — constructors mention concrete classes, which leak storage decisions; factories hide them.
- *Capability restriction via narrow interfaces* — restricts the client's vocabulary to the deliberate ADT, hiding the broader storage-class's incidental capabilities.
- *Generics over inheritance for type reuse* — generics are the universal-quantification mechanism for type-polymorphic code reuse; inheritance is the wrong shape for this and produces fragile coupling.

Each principle gets a paragraph: state the principle, state the framework justification, state the failure mode if violated. This section should be punchy and direct — students who skim should be able to read just this section and come away with a usable checklist.

End with: *these principles are not arbitrary. Each one is a small piece of the engineering discipline that makes large programs tractable. Following them costs effort upfront and saves enormous effort downstream.*

---

**7. The teaching artifact.** Briefly — maybe a page — note how this framework lands in actual teaching. You're not going to dump all of section 3-6 on students in week one. But the framework is the *background* that every example, every exercise, every code review judgment is drawn from. The teaching arc:

- *Early weeks:* introduce the dualities as questions to ask. Students absorb them as habits before they have the full theory.
- *Throughout the course:* every new structure gets characterized within the framework. Students build up the manifold view by accumulated examples.
- *Selected demonstrations:* anchor specific framework points with vivid crystallizing demos (mutable-key-in-HashSet, the Bicycle redesign, the cross-implementation swap).
- *Late synthesis:* once enough examples are in hand, articulate the framework explicitly. Now students can see what they've been doing.

End with: *the framework is for you, not for the students directly. The students experience the framework through your teaching choices. Your job is to internalize it deeply enough that it shapes everything you say and write, even when you're not invoking it explicitly.*

---

**Conclusion — One page.** Reflect briefly on what's been built. The framework isn't original — every piece of it exists in the literature (Cook, Meyer, Stroustrup, Liskov, Cook again, Bloch, the FP tradition). Your contribution is the *integration*: putting all the pieces together into a single coherent picture that can be taught from. Close with: *this document will evolve. Mark it up. Revise it. Use it.*

---

**A few notes on the outline as a whole:**

The structure goes: *why → what's there → how to think about it → how to build with it → why to follow the rules → how to teach it.* Each section motivates the next. Skipping any section weakens the whole.

The hardest section to write will be section 3, because the dualities have to be developed carefully without becoming abstract for its own sake. Lean heavily on examples. Every concept needs at least two concrete instances.

The most powerful sections, I suspect, will be 4 and 5. Section 4 because the storage-as-consequence move is genuinely novel (or at least, novel to most working programmers) and ties the framework to the runtime model. Section 5 because the ADT/object distinction, properly stated, dissolves twenty years of confused OOP teaching in one move.

You can probably write a complete first draft in a focused weekend if the conversations we've had are your raw material. Most of the text already exists in our threads; the work is *selection, ordering, and tightening*. I'd estimate 12-20 hours from start to finish for a usable first draft, with another 5-10 hours of revision over the following weeks as you find pieces that need sharpening.

One pragmatic suggestion: write section 6 first. Here's how I'd structure it. The goal is a self-contained framework essay — coherent enough to be your reference document, terse enough to be useful, with examples drawn from material we've already developed. I'll aim for something that would land at roughly 8000-12000 words in final form, organized into seven sections plus a short preface and conclusion.

---

**Preface — Why this exists.** One page. The frame: you've been teaching data structures and OOP for two semesters and noticed that the standard pedagogy produces students who can write Java but can't *reason* about programs. This document is your attempt to articulate the conceptual framework that, in your experience, separates competent programmers from confused ones. It's a reference for yourself, drawn from accumulated thinking, not a polished publication. Set the tone: working draft, in service of teaching, not theory for its own sake.

---

**1. The engineering frame.** Open with the engineering-discipline argument from the Meyer/Rickover/aviation thread. The single point: *software is engineering, and engineering means caring about properties that hold under stress, scale, and time, not just at the moment of writing*. This isn't a digression — it's the *why* for everything that follows. The disciplines you'll articulate are responses to engineering failures observed across decades of building large systems. Without this frame, the rest reads as personal aesthetic preferences. With it, the rest reads as accumulated professional wisdom.

Anchor this section with two or three sentences from Meyer, one quote from Rickover's "Doing a Job," and the aviation/Navy/SpaceX comparisons. End with: *the rest of this document is about what engineering discipline looks like at the level of individual type and class design.*

---

**2. The notional machine.** Before the framework can land, students (and your future self reading this) need a shared understanding of *what's actually happening when Java code runs*. This is the heap/stack/references material we developed for week one's PI questions.

Cover: stack frames and locals, heap and objects, references as pointers, the GC's role in lifecycle. Be concrete and visual — this section wants diagrams, not prose alone. Include the three-way diagram for `int[]` vs `Integer[]` vs C arrays from the storage thread. Lay out method dispatch and the vtable model, since that's needed for the inheritance discussion later.

This section is *foundational* and unglamorous. Don't try to make it interesting; make it correct and concrete. Everything that follows depends on this picture being in the reader's head.

End with: *the runtime model determines what kinds of things you can build. The rest of this document is about how to build them well, given this model.*

---

**3. The two dualities.** This is the conceptual heart. Develop both dualities carefully:

*3a. Data and codata.* What can be observed about a thing — its enumerable contents (data) or its protocol-driven behavior (codata)? Examples: sorted array (data), stream (codata), hash table (data), priority queue (codata), database table (data), event loop (codata). The duality is fundamental: every computational artifact answers this question one way or the other, or sits intermediate (lazy data, materialized codata).

*3b. Value and identity.* What does it mean for two things to be the same — structural equality (value) or referential equality (identity)? Examples: integers (value), customers-with-ids (identity-via-id, not address), strings (value), file handles (identity), dates as timestamps (value), dates as mutable structs (identity). The duality is fundamental: every computational artifact has a notion of equality, and the choice between value and identity is *the* choice that determines almost everything else.

*3c. The orthogonality.* The two dualities are independent. Four quadrants emerge: data+value (immutable records), data+identity (mutable structs), codata+value (pure generators), codata+identity (stateful processes). Every type in any program sits in one quadrant or transitions between them. Knowing which quadrant a type lives in tells you almost everything about how to use it correctly.

*3d. The manifold view.* Real implementations rarely sit at pure corners; they sit somewhere in the interior, with deliberate compromises along axes (mutability, sharing, eagerness, storage). Variation theory: students learn the framework by experiencing systematic variation along these axes. End with a sketch of the axes — mutability, sharing, storage strategy, eagerness, finiteness — and a note that subsequent sections develop them concretely.

---

**4. Storage as a consequence, not a choice.** Now you can address what you said earlier — that the *real* contribution of the framework is showing how storage strategy fits in. The argument:

*4a. Values don't care about storage.* They can live anywhere — stack, inline, registers, heap — because no observation depends on their location. Pure values are *location-irrelevant*. The implementer can choose any storage strategy without affecting the contract.

*4b. Identity *requires* storage with stable location, but doesn't require any particular kind.* An identity needs a *stable handle* — something that lets you re-find the "same one." Memory address is one way (and the default in most languages). But identity can also be defined by an *identifier property*: customer-id, file path, account number, primary key. When identity is property-based, the storage can move freely (GC compaction, database row migration, cache eviction-and-rehydration) without breaking the identity.

*4c. The conflation: Java equates identity with address.* This is the C inheritance. The address-as-identity choice is convenient (no extra bookkeeping) but couples the identity notion to the storage strategy in ways that leak. Reveal the leaks one by one:

- `==` tests address-identity, exposing the storage.
- Aliasing is invisible because two references look the same regardless of whether they point to one or two allocations.
- Defensive copying is needed to enforce value-flavored semantics on identity-typed storage.
- Hash-based collections require manual installation of value semantics (equals/hashCode contract) because the defaults are wrong for value-flavored use.

*4d. The concurrency consequence.* The conflation makes concurrency hard because synchronization has to protect the storage, not the identity. In languages that separate them, concurrency primitives operate at the identity level (Erlang's processes, Clojure's refs, database transactions over rows), and the storage is free to be efficient underneath. In Java, every concurrent access has to navigate the conflated model, which is why concurrent Java is famously difficult.

*4e. Why this was historically inherited and not necessary.* Walk through the C-to-C++-to-Java lineage. The conflation isn't a logical necessity; it's a historical choice that languages designed for different priorities (Erlang for telephony, Haskell for verification, Rust for systems) have made differently. End with: *the conflation is a contingent design choice with consequences. Students should recognize it as such.*

---

**5. ADTs, objects, and what classes are actually for.** Now bring in Cook's framing, sharpened by your own working out.

*5a. The ADT-as-existential model.* What an ADT is: a value set, operations, equational laws, with the representation hidden behind an existential quantifier. Why this is fundamental: it's the dual of universal quantification (generics), and together these two type-theoretic mechanisms cover the space of type-polymorphic abstraction.

*5b. ADT versus interface.* An ADT is *more* than an interface — it specifies the value set and the laws, not just the operations. A Java interface gives you the existential hiding but not the value contract. Interfaces are *almost* ADTs but missing the value semantics layer.

*5c. ADT versus object.* An object can implement an ADT, but the object machinery — identity, mutation, reference sharing — adds *more than the ADT specifies*. Objects are *processes*, not values. Cook's distinction between data abstraction and procedural abstraction. Walk through the classic example (Cook uses set or expression-tree) showing that the same operations can be implemented as ADT or as object, with different reasoning properties.

*5d. When to use which.* The rule: ask *value or process?* Value means timeless structural identity, equality is structural, no observable history. Process means identity across time, observable state changes, equality is referential. Record (or in other languages, value type, struct, ADT) for the first; class for the second. The default of "everything is a class" collapses the distinction and produces code that can't be reasoned about.

*5e. Stroustrup's invariant rule, revisited.* A class should exist when there's an invariant to defend. The reformulation: *a class exists when the invariant can't be eliminated by representation choice*. Many "invariants" of naive class designs can be made vacuous by picking a better representation (Date as timestamp). Classes are the *consolation prize* when perfect representation isn't available. This sharpens Stroustrup's rule into something operational.

---

**6. The design principles, derived.** Now show that every design principle you've been articulating is a *consequence* of the framework, not an arbitrary preference. Walk through each principle, deriving it from the framework:

- *Records for value types* — direct from section 5d.
- *All public methods come from interfaces* — separates the behavioral type (the ADT or codata protocol) from the structural type (the class's storage layout).
- *Composition over inheritance* — inheritance fuses behavioral types across classes, breaking the clean ADT abstraction. Composition keeps them separate.
- *Final classes by default* — preserves the value/process classification at the type boundary; subclassing breaks value contracts.
- *No `==` on objects* — `==` tests storage-identity, which leaks the conflation; equality should always go through a contract.
- *Factory methods returning interface types* — constructors mention concrete classes, which leak storage decisions; factories hide them.
- *Capability restriction via narrow interfaces* — restricts the client's vocabulary to the deliberate ADT, hiding the broader storage-class's incidental capabilities.
- *Generics over inheritance for type reuse* — generics are the universal-quantification mechanism for type-polymorphic code reuse; inheritance is the wrong shape for this and produces fragile coupling.

Each principle gets a paragraph: state the principle, state the framework justification, state the failure mode if violated. This section should be punchy and direct — students who skim should be able to read just this section and come away with a usable checklist.

End with: *these principles are not arbitrary. Each one is a small piece of the engineering discipline that makes large programs tractable. Following them costs effort upfront and saves enormous effort downstream.*

---

**7. The teaching artifact.** Briefly — maybe a page — note how this framework lands in actual teaching. You're not going to dump all of section 3-6 on students in week one. But the framework is the *background* that every example, every exercise, every code review judgment is drawn from. The teaching arc:

- *Early weeks:* introduce the dualities as questions to ask. Students absorb them as habits before they have the full theory.
- *Throughout the course:* every new structure gets characterized within the framework. Students build up the manifold view by accumulated examples.
- *Selected demonstrations:* anchor specific framework points with vivid crystallizing demos (mutable-key-in-HashSet, the Bicycle redesign, the cross-implementation swap).
- *Late synthesis:* once enough examples are in hand, articulate the framework explicitly. Now students can see what they've been doing.

End with: *the framework is for you, not for the students directly. The students experience the framework through your teaching choices. Your job is to internalize it deeply enough that it shapes everything you say and write, even when you're not invoking it explicitly.*

---

**Conclusion — One page.** Reflect briefly on what's been built. The framework isn't original — every piece of it exists in the literature (Cook, Meyer, Stroustrup, Liskov, Cook again, Bloch, the FP tradition). Your contribution is the *integration*: putting all the pieces together into a single coherent picture that can be taught from. Close with: *this document will evolve. Mark it up. Revise it. Use it.*

---

The structure goes: *why → what's there → how to think about it → how to build with it → why to follow the rules → how to teach it.* Each section motivates the next. Skipping any section weakens the whole.

That's exactly the right use of this, and the meta-observation is worth sitting with for a moment because I think you've identified something real about creative work that often gets obscured in the discourse about AI and writing.

The hard part of writing isn't the words. The hard part is the *commitment* — the moment where vague ideas have to become specific sentences with specific orderings and specific emphases. Every sentence forecloses other possible sentences. Every section structure forecloses other possible structures. Writers procrastinate not because they're lazy but because *commitment is expensive*, and the brain resists expensive operations until it has to do them.

What you're describing — using a draft as a *target for critique* — bypasses the commitment cost by externalizing the first commitment to something disposable. The bad draft isn't your bad draft; it's a generic bad draft, which you can dismantle without ego cost. The dismantling generates the *real* draft, which is yours, in your voice, structured the way you actually wanted it structured all along. The bad draft was the scaffolding; once the building is up, the scaffolding comes down and nobody remembers it existed.

This is, incidentally, *exactly* how good editors have always worked with writers. The editor doesn't write the book; the editor produces drafts, suggestions, structures, and pushback that the writer reacts to and reshapes. The final product is unambiguously the writer's, but the process required a foil. AI-as-foil is the same role, scaled down to whatever level of input you find useful, with no scheduling overhead and no risk of damaging a professional relationship if you ignore everything it says.

The reason your voice is preserved is that you've correctly identified what voice *is*. Voice isn't word choice — those can be borrowed, rearranged, replaced. Voice is the *pattern of attention*: what you choose to notice, what you decide is important, what you treat as obvious versus what you spell out, which connections you draw and which you leave implicit, what you find funny, what you find serious, what you bother to be precise about. Voice lives at the level of *what gets said*, not *how each sentence is constructed*. AI can generate sentences in any style, but it can't generate your sense of what's worth saying, because that's downstream of your actual experience, opinions, and aesthetic. When you reject 80% of a draft and rebuild it around what you actually wanted to say, the result is in your voice regardless of whether a few phrases survived from the original.

There's also a deeper observation here about *thinking versus writing*. People often imagine these as the same activity — that good writing is just thinking, transcribed. It isn't. Thinking is associative, lateral, recursive, full of half-formed connections that never quite cohere. Writing is *forced linearity*: you have to pick an order, pick an emphasis, pick what to leave out. Most of the cost of writing is the cost of converting nonlinear thinking into linear prose. The conversation-then-essay workflow you've stumbled into is actually a *cleaner separation* of these two activities than the conventional "sit down and write" workflow. The conversation is where the thinking happens, lateral and associative; the essay is where it gets linearized. Doing them as separate phases, with different tools, plays to the strengths of each.

The discipline you'll want to maintain — and you already are, based on how you've described it — is to never let the AI's framing become *your* framing by default. The risk isn't that AI writes for you; the risk is that AI's *organization of the ideas* shapes how you think about them, in ways that survive even when you rewrite all the sentences. This is why your reaction to my outline matters more than the outline itself. *"That's not it"* is the operative response. Knowing what's not it is the negative space that defines what is. Every time you reject a structure, you're getting closer to articulating the one you actually want — and that one will be yours in a way no AI-suggested structure ever could be, because it was selected against the alternatives you saw and didn't take.

One small practical suggestion, if you want it: when you do start writing this essay, consider doing it with the conversations *not in front of you*. You've absorbed the material; you've worked out the framework; you don't actually need to consult the source threads to recover what you think. If you write from memory, what survives is what mattered enough to stick — which is a useful filter on what's worth including. The conversations were the *thinking phase*; the essay is the *committing phase*, and committing works better when you're forced to commit to what you actually remember caring about, not what's recoverable from the archive.

If you ever want to use me again at the *fragment* level — "draft me a paragraph about X so I can hate it" — I'm happy to do that. That kind of small-scale foil work is probably even more useful than full-outline drafts, because the commitment cost of a paragraph is lower than a structure, and you can iterate more freely. Let me know what's most useful, when it's most useful.

Good luck with the essay. And with the rest of the syllabus prep, the house move, and the eight-week semester. You're carrying a lot. The fact that you're still investing in deep curriculum thinking under those constraints is itself a piece of the engineering discipline you're trying to teach.

b. AI is not going to magically improve this situation, and will likely make it much worse

a. Outsider with diverse experience and not (yet) bound to any particular teaching method

The summary loses nothing by being there for the readers who need it.

**The biggest question I want to put to you.** Who's the actual audience? The document reads differently depending on whether you're writing for:

*Department leadership at Temple/TUJ* who can act on it directly. This wants more focus on what they can change in the next 1-2 years, with the Temple-specific framing in section I.c amplified.

*The broader CS education community* (SIGCSE, ACM, conference attendees) who can validate or amplify your position but can't directly change Temple's curriculum. *Your future students* who might read this to understand what you're trying to do for them. This is a different document entirely — closer to a manifesto — but might be worth writing as a parallel piece.

*All of the above*, with the document segmented so different readers can extract what's relevant to them. This is harder to write but more useful as an artifact.

My instinct, based on what you've said, is that the primary audience is *department leadership at Temple/TUJ with secondary readership in the broader community*, and the document should be written for them with the broader community in mind. But you know your political environment better than I do, and the right audience choice depends on factors I can't see from here.

**On the deep-dive on fundamental concepts that you mentioned would live elsewhere.** I think you're right to separate it. The position paper is one document; the framework essay is another. They serve different purposes:

The position paper argues that *the curriculum needs to change* and what *direction* it should change in. It's a persuasive document aimed at people with the authority or influence to change things.

The framework essay articulates *what the right way to think about programming is* and how that should *manifest in teaching*. It's a constructive document aimed at people who already agree change is needed and want to know what to build.

Trying to combine them produces a worse version of each. The position paper bloats with technical detail that loses non-technical decision-makers; the framework essay becomes hortatory in ways that distract from its constructive purpose. Two documents, each clean and short, are better than one document that tries to be both.

You might end up writing them in *either order*. Writing the position paper first is rhetorically natural — you establish the need before you build the solution. But writing the framework essay first might be *cognitively* easier, because you've been working on the framework for months and the framework is what you most clearly know how to articulate. The position paper, by contrast, requires you to inhabit a more adversarial stance than may come naturally, and that takes more emotional energy. There's no wrong order; pick whichever one feels more accessible right now and use it as warm-up for the other.

I'll stop there because I think the outline is fundamentally sound and the work now is mostly yours — refinement, evidence-gathering, and the writing itself. What I've offered above is meant to help you find friction points where the outline can be strengthened, not to redirect the structure. You've got the shape right.

Want me to take a swing at one specific section — most usefully, probably section III, since that's where the persuasive load is heaviest — so you have something to react to and rip apart? Or hold off on that until you've done your own first pass?

You're tracking it exactly right, and the framing you've landed on is the one that actually explains why eBPF became such a big deal rather than staying a niche packet-filtering trick.

The original BPF (1992, McCanne & Jacobson) was precisely what you said: a tiny VM in the kernel so `tcpdump` could ship its filter predicate *down* instead of the kernel shipping every packet *up*. The insight worth naming is that this is a **partial evaluation** move. The kernel has a hot loop over packets; the userspace client has a predicate. Without BPF, the predicate is a black box and the kernel must conservatively assume "interesting," so it copies everything. With BPF, the predicate becomes transparent at the boundary, and the kernel specializes its loop against it. The copy disappears because the optimizer now has the information it needed all along.

eBPF generalizes this from "filter predicate at the socket layer" to "user-supplied logic at *arbitrary* kernel hook points" — scheduling, tracing, security (LSM), XDP at the NIC driver, syscall entry/exit, the lot. The verifier is the load-bearing piece: it's what lets the kernel accept hostile code from unprivileged-ish contexts. It enforces termination (bounded loops, finite instruction count), memory safety (every pointer deref proven in-bounds via abstract interpretation), and typed helper-function signatures. That's your "expressive but not Turing-complete" intuition made concrete — it's essentially a total-functional sub-language with a decidable safety check, which is why your type-theory antennae should be twitching.

A few threads this connects to in your existing framework, any of which I'm happy to go deeper on:

- **Compilation as optimization / Futamura projections.** BPF-as-partial-evaluation is a clean real-world instance of the first Futamura projection (specialize an interpreter against a fixed program to get a compiled program). The kernel's generic packet loop is the interpreter; the BPF program is the static input; JIT-compiling the combination is the specialization.

- **Abstraction boundaries and the end-to-end argument.** Saltzer/Reed/Clark argued functionality belongs at the endpoints. eBPF is the counter-move: when the endpoint's policy is cheap to describe and the cost of *not* knowing it at the lower layer is high (a copy, a context switch, a cache miss), you let the endpoint inject its policy downward. The abstraction boundary becomes permeable in a controlled way — which is exactly your CIS 2168 theme of capability restriction as a design tool, just inverted (capability *extension* under a verifier).

- **Algebraic structure.** The set of safe BPF programs forms something with real structure: composition of verified programs is verified, you have identity (no-op), and the helper-function ABI is a typed interface in the same sense as your codata protocols. Tail calls between BPF programs make this concrete.

- **The deeper pattern.** GPU shaders, SQL query planners, JavaScript in browsers, io_uring's SQEs, even database stored procedures — all the same shape. A privileged executor exposes a constrained language so untrusted-ish clients can push logic across an expensive boundary. eBPF is the version where the boundary is the user/kernel one, which is why it feels foundational.

There’s some crazy shit you just mentioned—Futamura projections??—but the concept that is nearest and dearest right now is abstraction boundaries. A particularly relevant recent conversation that abruptly jumps to mind is one from another project, where we talked about the whole Codasyl-Codd philosophical divergence between imperative and declarative paradigms and how it keeps playing out over and over again in different areas of the tech stack.

It seems like pushing logic across an expensive resource boundary is the Codasyl-style approach to optimization?

chat_messages.text:
Yes — and the framing sharpens once you notice *which* boundary is expensive and *which* direction the logic flows.

The Codd move is: client declares *what*, server figures out *how*. The optimizer lives on the resource side and uses its privileged knowledge of storage layout, indexes, statistics, and concurrency to plan execution. The client surrenders control in exchange for the server's better information. The expensive boundary (disk, lock manager, buffer pool) stays opaque; the client just describes its goal in a restricted algebra (relational), and the server compiles that into an imperative plan.

The Codasyl move is the inverse: the client navigates the structure directly, issuing imperative commands (`FIND OWNER`, `GET NEXT WITHIN SET`) that the server executes faithfully. The optimizer, such as it is, lives in the client's head. The boundary is transparent — the client sees the pointers — but the client now bears the cost of knowing the layout.

eBPF is Codasyl-shaped in a specific sense: the client knows something the kernel doesn't (which packets matter, which syscalls to trace, which scheduling decision fits its workload), and rather than try to express that through a declarative interface the kernel would have to interpret, it ships imperative code that runs in situ. The "optimizer" is the client, because the client is the only party with the relevant information. The kernel's contribution is the verifier and the JIT — it doesn't plan, it just enforces safety and makes the client's plan fast.

But — and this is where it gets interesting — eBPF is *not* purely Codasyl, because the verifier imposes an algebraic discipline (totality, bounded memory, typed helpers) that a true Codasyl system never had. CODASYL DBTG let you chase pointers into corrupt states; eBPF won't load a program that might. So the pattern is closer to: **Codasyl-style information flow (client knows best, ships logic down), Codd-style safety guarantees (restricted algebra, verified at the boundary).** You get the locality of imperative navigation with the soundness of declarative restriction.

This is why the pattern keeps recurring and keeps feeling like progress rather than regression. The naive Codd/Codasyl dichotomy assumes the optimizer lives on exactly one side. The modern synthesis — eBPF, GPU shaders, SQL UDFs, even WASM at CDN edges — recognizes that *information* and *trust* are separable axes. The client has information; the server has trust requirements. A constrained language at the boundary lets information flow toward the resource without trust flowing with it.

Which is, I think, the deeper thing your "theory of everything" is circling: the Codasyl-Codd oscillation isn't a pendulum between two wrong answers, it's the field gradually learning to **decouple the locus of optimization from the locus of enforcement**. Every generation gets a better verifier and can therefore safely admit a more expressive client-supplied language, which shifts more optimization toward whoever has the information — usually the client.

chat_messages.text:
Ha — that's a great origin story, and the through-line from "professor with strong opinions about HN" to "professor with a theory-of-everything for CS who reads HN daily" is almost too on-the-nose. The Elixir detail especially: getting forced into the BEAM for distsys is exactly the kind of pedagogical violence that pays dividends for decades, because once you've internalized "let it crash" and supervision trees as a *design philosophy* rather than a library, you start seeing the pattern everywhere — including, incidentally, in eBPF's verifier-enforced totality (a program that can't loop forever can't take down its supervisor).

WASM fits your framework almost too neatly, and in a way that's worth pulling apart because it occupies a different point in the design space than eBPF despite looking superficially similar.

eBPF and WASM are both **portable, verifiable, sandboxed bytecode for shipping logic across a trust boundary**. But the boundaries they're crossing are different, and that difference shapes everything:

- **eBPF crosses the user/kernel boundary downward.** The client has information; the kernel has the hot path. The verifier is *aggressive* (totality, bounded memory, no unbounded loops) because the kernel cannot afford to be wrong — a misbehaving BPF program is a kernel bug. The language is correspondingly restrictive: it's essentially a typed assembly with a decidable safety check.

- **WASM crosses the host/guest boundary in either direction.** Originally browser-as-host, untrusted-code-as-guest; now increasingly server-as-host (CDN edge, plugin system, serverless runtime) with the same shape. The verifier is *softer* — WASM is Turing-complete, can loop forever, can allocate dynamically — because the host can afford to bound execution externally (CPU quotas, memory limits, timeouts). Safety is enforced by the sandbox at runtime, not proved at load time.

So in your Codd/Codasyl decoupling frame: **eBPF separates information from trust via a restricted algebra; WASM separates them via a runtime sandbox.** Both are valid points on the "let clients ship logic" design curve, and which you pick depends on whether the host can afford runtime enforcement or needs static guarantees.

The really interesting thing — and this is where the HN buzz starts to feel justified rather than hype-driven — is **WASM Component Model + WASI**. That's the move from "WASM as a portable instruction set" to "WASM as a portable *interface* system," where components declare typed imports and exports and the host wires them together. Suddenly you have something that looks an awful lot like your CIS 2168 framework: structural contracts (interface types) separated from semantic contracts (the actual implementation), with capability restriction as a first-class design tool (WASI's capability-based security model, where a component can only do what its host explicitly grants).

The pattern recurs again: a constrained language at the boundary, with the constraints chosen to match what the boundary can enforce. Browsers got JS because the boundary could afford a full JIT and GC. Kernels got eBPF because the boundary couldn't afford either. WASM is what you get when you try to design the constraint language *first* and let hosts opt into whichever enforcement model fits.

Your distsys professor was, in retrospect, teaching you to read the field rather than any particular technology. Which is the actual skill.

If JIT compilation of “lingua franca” capability-restricted bytecode can reliably achieve any point on the optimal safety/performance frontier then why use any other stack?

content.text: This feels like we might be approaching something like an inflection point for the practice of software engineering as a whole. If JIT compilation of “lingua franca” capability-restricted bytecode can reliably achieve any point on the optimal safety/performance frontier then why use any other stack?

chat_messages.text:
The instinct is right that something is consolidating, but I'd push back on "any point on the frontier" — and the places where the pushback bites are exactly the places where the next decade of interesting work is going to happen.

A few reasons the universal-WASM-stack vision doesn't quite close:

**The frontier isn't 2D.** Safety/performance is the headline trade-off, but there are other axes that don't reduce to it. Predictable latency (hard real-time, audio, trading) wants AOT compilation and no GC pauses, which WASM can do but loses much of its portability story for. Memory footprint (embedded, where you're counting kilobytes) doesn't tolerate a runtime at all. Startup time (FaaS cold starts) is where WASM actually wins against JVM/V8, but loses against native. Power consumption (mobile, datacenter cooling budgets) cares about instruction mix in ways bytecode abstracts away. Each axis has constituencies that won't migrate.

**Verification has a fundamental ceiling.** The eBPF verifier works because the language is restricted enough to make safety decidable. WASM's sandbox works because enforcement is runtime, not static. Neither composes upward to "verify arbitrary application logic is correct" — that's the Rice's theorem wall, and no amount of bytecode cleverness gets you past it. So the *kind* of safety these systems provide (memory safety, resource bounds, capability containment) is a floor, not a ceiling. Application-level correctness still requires types, tests, proofs, or prayer, same as ever.

**The "lingua franca" part is doing a lot of work.** WASM is a *good* compilation target for C, Rust, Go (sort of), and increasingly others. It is a *bad* compilation target for anything that wants tight integration with a host GC (JVM languages, .NET, Python, JS itself) — which is why the Component Model and GC proposal exist and are taking years to land. Every "universal" bytecode in history has had this problem: JVM was going to host everything until it turned out hosting Ruby or Python well required JRuby/Jython-level heroics. CLR had the same arc. WASM is better-designed than either, but the pattern is that "neutral" bytecodes accrete bias toward their original client languages, and the long tail of languages pays compilation-quality tax forever.

**Hardware heterogeneity is increasing, not decreasing.** GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs, DPUs, custom ASICs — the action in performance-sensitive computing is moving toward specialized silicon with its own programming models (CUDA, SYCL, MLIR dialects). WASM doesn't have a credible story here. The "compile once, run anywhere" pitch assumes a homogeneous CPU substrate that is, ironically, becoming less true as Moore's Law slows and specialization picks up the slack.

**Trust is sociological, not just technical.** Even if WASM could technically replace your stack, *deciding* to run untrusted third-party logic in your kernel / database / browser / edge node is a governance decision that organizations make slowly and reluctantly. eBPF took ~20 years from BPF to widespread production adoption despite being technically ready much earlier. The bottleneck was operators trusting the verifier, tooling maturing, and failure modes becoming well-understood. WASM-everywhere will move on similar timescales.

So the more defensible version of your intuition, I think, is: **the *pattern* is consolidating, not the *artifact*.** Capability-restricted, verifier-enforced, JIT-compiled bytecode at trust boundaries is becoming a standard architectural move — the way "use a database" or "put a load balancer in front" became standard moves. But the specific bytecode will fragment by domain: eBPF in kernels, WASM at edges and in plugin systems, SPIR-V on GPUs, MLIR as a meta-layer, SQL (still!) at the data boundary, and whatever comes next for specialized accelerators. Each one is a constrained language matched to what its boundary can enforce, exactly as we've been describing.

The inflection point is real, but it's an inflection in **how architects think** — "where should I put a verified-bytecode boundary?" becoming a first-class design question — rather than an inflection toward a single winning runtime. Which is, honestly, a more interesting world to teach in: your students will need the meta-skill of reading these trade-offs, not just fluency in whichever stack wins.

Every "universal" bytecode in history has had this problem: JVM was going to host everything until it turned out hosting Ruby or Python well required JRuby/Jython-level heroics. CLR had the same arc. WASM is better-designed than either, but the pattern is that "neutral" bytecodes accrete bias toward their original client languages, and the long tail of languages pays compilation-quality tax forever.

**Hardware heterogeneity is increasing, not decreasing.** GPUs, TPUs, NPUs, FPGAs, DPUs, custom ASICs — the action in performance-sensitive computing is moving toward specialized silicon with its own programming models (CUDA, SYCL, MLIR dialects). WASM doesn't have a credible story here. The "compile once, run anywhere" pitch assumes a homogeneous CPU substrate that is, ironically, becoming less true as Moore's Law slows and specialization picks up the slack.

**Trust is sociological, not just technical.** Even if WASM could technically replace your stack, *deciding* to run untrusted third-party logic in your kernel / database / browser / edge node is a governance decision that organizations make slowly and reluctantly. eBPF took ~20 years from BPF to widespread production adoption despite being technically ready much earlier. The bottleneck was operators trusting the verifier, tooling maturing, and failure modes becoming well-understood. WASM-everywhere will move on similar timescales.

So the more defensible version of your intuition, I think, is: **the *pattern* is consolidating, not the *artifact*.** Capability-restricted, verifier-enforced, JIT-compiled bytecode at trust boundaries is becoming a standard architectural move — the way "use a database" or "put a load balancer in front" became standard moves. But the specific bytecode will fragment by domain: eBPF in kernels, WASM at edges and in plugin systems, SPIR-V on GPUs, MLIR as a meta-layer, SQL (still!) at the data boundary, and whatever comes next for specialized accelerators. Each one is a constrained language matched to what its boundary can enforce, exactly as we've been describing.

The inflection point is real, but it's an inflection in **how architects think** — "where should I put a verified-bytecode boundary?" becoming a first-class design question — rather than an inflection toward a single winning runtime. Which is, honestly, a more interesting world to teach in: your students will need the meta-skill of reading these trade-offs, not just fluency in whichever stack wins.

Good thought experiment, and the answer is genuinely interesting because it's "fewer than now, but more than one, and the reasons why are principled rather than historical."

If you strip path-dependence, the irreducible diversity comes from a small number of axes where the design forces actually conflict — not just "different communities like different syntax," but "optimizing for X actively precludes optimizing for Y." My best guess at the minimal set:

**1. A systems language.** Manual memory management, predictable performance, no runtime, direct hardware access. Rust is the current best answer; the *role* is permanent because someone has to write the kernels, drivers, runtimes, and hot paths that everything else sits on. You can't bootstrap a GC'd language without a non-GC'd language underneath, and "predictable latency" is a real constraint that no amount of cleverness eliminates.

**2. A managed application language.** GC, rich runtime, strong types, good ergonomics for business logic. This is where 80% of code lives and should live. The exact shape is more negotiable — could be ML-family (OCaml, Scala, F#), could be something Java/Kotlin/C#-shaped, could be Swift. The *role* is "express domain logic safely and maintainably without thinking about memory." You probably want one strict and one lazy variant, or one with effects tracked and one without, because those represent genuinely different programming models with different sweet spots.

**3. A concurrent/distributed language.** Erlang/Elixir's actual contribution — isolated processes, supervision, message-passing as the primitive rather than shared memory. You can *simulate* this in other languages (Akka, Orleans) but the simulation is leaky in ways that matter when systems get large. The BEAM's design decisions (preemptive scheduling, per-process heaps, link/monitor semantics) are load-bearing for the programming model, not implementation details. Whether this stays a separate language or becomes a runtime feature of #2 is the open question.

**4. A declarative data language.** SQL, or something better-designed but recognizably in the same family (Datalog, relational algebra with modern syntax — see things like Malloy, PRQL, EdgeQL). The role is "describe what data you want without specifying how to get it" so the optimizer can do its job. This is irreducibly different from imperative code because the *whole point* is to surrender control flow.

**5. An array/numerical language.** APL's lineage, now mostly expressed as embedded DSLs (NumPy, Julia, Halide, JAX). The role is "express bulk operations over n-dimensional data in a way that maps to SIMD/GPU/TPU execution." You can do this as a library in #2, and people do, but the syntactic and semantic accommodations (broadcasting, fusion, autodiff) are deep enough that purpose-built languages keep winning for serious work. Julia is the most credible attempt at unifying this with #2.

**6. A constraint/logic language.** Prolog's lineage, plus modern SMT (Z3) and answer-set programming. Role: "describe constraints, let the solver find solutions." Niche but irreducible — you can't express "find an assignment satisfying these clauses" in an imperative language without basically embedding a solver, at which point you've reinvented #6 as a library.

**7. A proof/dependently-typed language.** Lean, Coq, Agda, Idris. Currently academic-ish but I suspect this becomes more central as verification tooling matures. The role is "write programs whose correctness is mechanically checked," which is genuinely different from #2's "write programs whose types rule out some bugs."

A few honorable mentions that I think *don't* make the cut despite current prominence:

- **Scripting languages** (Python, Ruby, JS-as-scripting). These exist because #2 historically had bad ergonomics for small programs and REPLs. A well-designed #2 with good incremental compilation and a REPL absorbs this role. Python's actual moat is the scientific library ecosystem, which is really #5 in disguise.

- **Shell.** This is a UI for a process model, not a programming language, and treating it as the latter has caused immense suffering. In the clean-slate world it's replaced by a structured-data shell (PowerShell got this right, Nushell is the modern attempt) which is really a thin DSL over #2 or #4.

- **Configuration languages** (YAML, HCL, Dhall, Nickel, Cue). These keep getting reinvented because people want "data with a little bit of computation" and then need more computation and end up with a half-language. The clean answer is probably #2 with good support for restricted evaluation, plus #4 for anything that's actually relational.

So: somewhere between 5 and 7 languages, organized by **what they fundamentally refuse to let you do** rather than what they let you do. The systems language refuses to hide the machine. The declarative data language refuses to let you specify execution order. The proof language refuses to let you write incorrect programs. The array language refuses to let you write scalar loops over bulk data. Each refusal buys something the others can't.

The interesting pedagogical observation — and this connects back to your codata framing — is that the minimal set looks a lot like "one language per major *kind* of abstraction boundary." Systems language for the hardware boundary, managed language for the human-readability boundary, concurrent language for the process boundary, declarative language for the data boundary, array language for the parallel-execution boundary, proof language for the correctness boundary. Which is maybe the same insight as before: the irreducible diversity in languages mirrors the irreducible diversity in *what you're trying to be precise about*.

This is a strong intuition and the interesting thing is that the industry has been independently converging on both halves of it — though the convergence reveals where the design forces are sharper than they first appear.

**On the systems-language side**, what you're describing — an abstract HDL that gives the compiler structured information about the target rather than just an ISA — is essentially **MLIR**, and it's one of the more important developments in compiler infrastructure in the last decade. The key insight is that LLVM IR, for all its success, is *too low-level* to express the structure that modern optimizers need: by the time your matrix multiplication has been lowered to LLVM's scalar-with-vector-extensions worldview, the optimizer has lost the information that would let it tile for a specific cache hierarchy or map to a systolic array. MLIR's answer is a *family* of intermediate representations ("dialects") at different abstraction levels, with progressive lowering between them. You can have a `linalg` dialect that knows about tensor operations, an `affine` dialect that knows about loop nests with polyhedral structure, a `gpu` dialect that knows about thread hierarchies, and so on — and the compiler can do optimization at whatever level preserves the relevant structure before lowering further.

This is genuinely the move you're describing: structured information about the target, exposed to the compiler in a form it can reason about, rather than encoded as ad-hoc heuristics in the backend. The catch — and this is where the "single language with dialects" vision gets harder — is that **the dialects aren't just target descriptions, they're also source-language design decisions**. If your source language doesn't expose tensor-shaped computations as first-class constructs, the `linalg` dialect can't recover them through analysis (or rather, it can only sometimes, with heroics). So the source language ends up needing extension points that mirror the dialect structure, which is exactly your "language extensions opt into runtime features" intuition, but applied to compile-time capabilities rather than runtime ones. **Zig** is the current most interesting attempt at the spirit of what you're describing on the systems side — comptime as a unifying mechanism for what would otherwise be macros, generics, conditional compilation, and target specialization. **Rust** is heading in a similar direction more slowly via const generics and increasingly capable proc macros. Neither is "one language for all hardware" yet, but the path is visible.

**On the application-language side**, your "one language with runtime-tiered dialects" idea is essentially the implicit design philosophy of **Swift** and, more aggressively, of recent work on **effect systems** in languages like Koka, Unison, and the various "algebraic effects" research languages. The framing there is exactly yours: features have runtime costs, and the type system tracks which features a given piece of code uses, so the compiler knows what runtime support to link in. Want async? That's an effect. Want exceptions? Effect. Want allocation? Effect. Want nondeterminism, IO, mutable state, concurrency? All effects, all tracked, all opt-in. A pure function that uses none of these compiles to something with no runtime overhead; a function that uses all of them gets the full managed runtime. This is the cleanest version of your intuition I know of, and I think it's where application languages are headed over the next 10-20 years. The barrier isn't conceptual, it's that effect systems are *hard to make ergonomic* — the type signatures get noisy fast, and inference has to be very good to keep developers from drowning in annotations.

**Where I'd push back gently** is on the assumption that the application/systems split itself is stable in this picture. If you have an effect system that can track "this code allocates" vs "this code doesn't," and a compiler infrastructure (MLIR-shaped) that can lower the same source to wildly different targets based on the effects used, you start to wonder whether *systems and application code are different languages or just different effect profiles in the same language*. Rust is already doing this to some extent — `no_std` Rust running on a microcontroller and `tokio`-flavored async Rust running on a server are arguably more different from each other than either is from, say, idiomatic Go, but they're "the same language." The dialects you're imagining for application code might extend all the way down.

The thing this *doesn't* collapse, and I think can't collapse, is your point about fully declarative languages. SQL and Prolog aren't just "application code with different syntax" — they're refusing to let you specify execution order at all, which is a categorically different deal with the compiler. You can embed them as DSLs in a host language (LINQ, Datalog libraries, miniKanren), and that works for many cases, but the embedded version is always weaker than the standalone version because the host language's evaluation model leaks in. The optimizer of a real SQL engine can reorder, parallelize, and rewrite your query in ways that an embedded DSL inside an imperative host fundamentally cannot, because the host's semantics constrain what transformations preserve meaning. So I think the minimal set still has at least two members for principled reasons: one for "I'll tell you how" (with dialects from bare-metal to fully-managed) and one for "I'll tell you what" (with dialects for different data models — relational, logical, constraint).

Which gives you maybe **two ur-languages plus a small handful of genuinely-different niches** (array/numerical might collapse into the imperative one with good effects + MLIR; proof languages stay separate because their type systems are categorically more expressive; concurrent languages probably collapse into effects). That's a meaningfully tidier picture than the current Cambrian explosion, and the pieces to build it mostly exist in research or early-production form. The remaining work is largely integration and ergonomics — which, frustratingly, is exactly the work that's hardest to fund and least glamorous to publish, so it'll take longer than the technical readiness suggests.

You’re right that effect systems are hard to make ergonomic, but the benefit of putting it all in one language is that you can start developers off with the most supportive runtime that requires very little if any effect annotations, and then they can gradually ease into the more restricted runtime models with accumulated experience. This is the right question to be asking, and I think the honest answer is that the existing curriculum is *closer* to ready than it looks — but the organizing principle needs to flip.

The current curriculum is organized around **artifacts**: here's a language, here's a data structure, here's an operating system, here's a database. Students learn each artifact in isolation and are expected to synthesize the connections themselves, which most of them don't, which is why so many CS graduates have a bag of skills rather than a worldview. The framework you've been developing — abstraction boundaries, what languages refuse to do, where optimization can live, how trust and information separate — is organized around **forces and trade-offs**. That's the flip. The artifacts become case studies illustrating where the forces resolved in particular ways, rather than ends in themselves.

If I were redesigning around this, I'd think in terms of a few load-bearing concepts that get introduced early and then revisited at progressively deeper levels throughout the curriculum — a spiral, not a sequence. The concepts I'd put at the center:

**Abstraction boundaries as the unit of design.** Every interesting decision in software is "what does this boundary expose, what does it hide, what does it enforce, and who pays the cost when it's crossed?" This is the lens you're already using, and it scales from function signatures (CIS 1057) to type interfaces (CIS 2168) to system calls (CIS 2107/3207) to network protocols to query languages to ISAs. The same questions apply at every scale; only the answers change.

**Information versus trust as separable axes.** Your eBPF insight generalizes: at any boundary, ask "who has the relevant information?" and separately "who has the authority to act on it?" When these are the same party, design is easy. When they're different parties, you need a constrained language at the boundary — and *which* constraints depend on what the trusting party can afford to verify. This single frame explains SQL, eBPF, WASM, type systems, capability security, OS privilege levels, and most of what makes distributed systems hard.

**Data versus codata as dual modes of structure.** You already have this in CIS 2168. The generalization is that *every* abstraction is one or the other (or a careful composition), and recognizing which gives you immediate purchase on what operations make sense, what invariants matter, and what implementations are reasonable. This connects up to streams, protocols, reactive systems, and eventually to category-theoretic framings if students get that far.

**Compilation as optimization, optimization as partial evaluation.** Once students see that a compiler is just a partial evaluator with a particular staging discipline, an enormous amount of seemingly-unrelated stuff (JITs, query planners, GPU shaders, eBPF verifiers, even templated C++) becomes one phenomenon. Futamura projections aren't on the critical path, but the *idea* — that "running an interpreter on a fixed program" and "compiling that program" are the same operation viewed from different time-staging perspectives — is foundational and underemphasized.

**Effect tracking as the modern type discipline.** Even if students never use a language with a full effect system, learning to *think* in terms of "what can this code do?" rather than just "what does this code return?" prepares them for where languages are going. It also gives them a clean framework for understanding async/await, exceptions, IO, mutability, and concurrency as instances of one phenomenon rather than ad-hoc features.

The pedagogical question is how to *introduce* these without turning the early courses into philosophy seminars. My instinct is that you do it the same way physics introduces conservation laws: state them simply early, demonstrate them in concrete settings, and then revisit with increasing formalism. In CIS 1057, "abstraction boundary" can just mean "function signature, and what the caller is and isn't allowed to assume." By CIS 2168 it's interface contracts and capability restriction. The machine-first sequencing in CIS 1057, the data/codata framework in CIS 2168, the emphasis on capability restriction and interface contracts — these aren't artifact-driven choices, they're forces-driven choices. What might be worth doing is **writing the framework down explicitly**, not as a research paper but as a short document for yourself (and eventually students): "here are the five or six concepts that organize everything I teach, here's how each course revisits them, here's what students should be able to do with them by graduation." That's a genuinely interesting institutional position, and it shapes what's actually possible in ways worth thinking through carefully.

The constraint is real but narrower than it feels. Accreditation and degree equivalence will care about **learning outcomes and course coverage** — can a CIS 2168 graduate from your campus do the things a CIS 2168 graduate from Philadelphia can do? They will care much less about **pedagogical approach, sequencing within a course, or supplementary framing**. So the catalog description for CIS 2168 says "stacks, queues, linked lists, BSTs, hash tables, heaps, sorting algorithms" — and your course delivers all of that, plus a conceptual framework that organizes it. The framework is value-add, not deviation. Accreditors look for gaps in coverage, not for unexpected richness.

The place where this gets practically interesting is **electives and supplementary courses**. The catalog shows 18 credits of CIS electives for the BS, and electives are exactly where individual faculty and individual campuses typically have wide latitude. If you wanted to introduce, say, a "Programming Paradigms" course that exposed students to a functional language and a logic language with explicit contrast — that's a perfectly normal CS elective, would presumably count toward the 18-credit requirement, and would not raise accreditation eyebrows because comparable courses exist at most CS programs. Same with a "Programming Language Theory" course, or a "Verified Software" course built around a proof assistant. You don't need permission from Philadelphia to *offer* electives that complement the core; you just need them to fit the elective framework.

The dean's entrepreneurial framing matters here. For-profit overseas branches of US universities are typically given latitude that the home campus doesn't have, precisely because the home campus has shared governance structures that slow change. If your dean is receptive, the realistic move is probably not "let's redesign the core curriculum" (which triggers accreditation review and home-campus coordination) but "let's build out a distinctive elective track that gives our students something Philadelphia doesn't offer." Over time that track becomes the campus's identity, and identity is what justifies a satellite campus's existence.

A few practical thoughts on navigating the accreditation cycle specifically:

The review will want to see **assessment data** showing students are meeting learning outcomes. Your PrairieLearn investment is actually a major asset here — competency-based, data-driven assessment infrastructure is exactly what accreditors want to see, and most CS programs don't have anything nearly as rigorous. Make sure that work is *legible* to the reviewers; a short document describing your assessment philosophy and showing outcome data will count for a lot. The framework you're building can be presented as "principled curriculum design with measurable outcomes," which is the language accreditors think in.

The lack of coordination with Philadelphia cuts both ways. It means you can't easily borrow their materials or align with their changes, but it also means **nobody there is paying attention to what you do** as long as outcomes are met. Faculty at the home campus are typically grateful when overseas branches don't create work for them; a self-sufficient satellite that just produces graduates who pass the same assessments is the dream. The risk would be if you deviated in ways that became visible — students transferring back and being unprepared, or accreditors raising flags. Neither of those happens if your students are *more* prepared than the baseline, which seems likely given what you're building.

One thing I'd genuinely recommend, given the accreditation timing: **introduce yourself to one or two Philadelphia faculty before the review, not after.** Even a single email exchange ("I'm building out the CIS 2168 curriculum at TUJ, I've been working with PrairieLearn for assessment, I'd love to compare notes sometime") establishes that you exist and are doing serious work. It costs you very little and gives you a name to drop if accreditation questions come up. The department is expected to grow, as you noted; the relationships you build now will matter more later.

The deeper observation is that you're in an unusually good institutional position for someone trying to build a principled curriculum: enough constraint to keep you honest (you can't just teach whatever you want), enough freedom to actually innovate (no real oversight on method), and a dean who seems to value the freedom rather than resent the constraint. That combination is rarer than it sounds. Most faculty trying to do this kind of work are either constrained by committee processes or unconstrained in ways that mean their work doesn't compound institutionally. You have a path where the framework you're building can actually become the campus's pedagogical identity, and the accreditation process — handled well — could even legitimize it.

content.title: Andrew S. Rosen
content.text:
- Occupations: Chairman and CEO of Kaplan, Inc.

Andrew S. Rosen is current chairman and CEO of
[Kaplan, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaplan,_Inc.), [[1]](./Andrew_S._Rosen#cite_note-1) a global education company that began as a test prep provider in 1938. It was purchased in 1984 by [The Washington Post Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post_Company), now [Graham Holdings Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Holdings_Company). [[2]](./Andrew_S._Rosen#cite_note-2)
Rosen worked as a staff attorney for
[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post) beginning in 1986. He joined Kaplan in 1992 and was named Chairman and CEO in November 2008, following the resignation of long-time Chairman and CEO [Jonathan Grayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Grayer). [[3]](./Andrew_S._Rosen#cite_note-3)
Rosen holds an A.B. degree from
[Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University) and a J.D. 

from [Yale Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_School). [[4]](./Andrew_S._Rosen#cite_note-4) After law school, Rosen served as law clerk to the Hon. [Levin H. Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levin_H._Campbell), Chief Judge for the [U.S. Court of Appeals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_Appeals) for the First Circuit, in Boston.
Rosen joined The Washington Post Company in 1986 as a staff attorney for
[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post) newspaper; he moved to [Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek) as Assistant Counsel in 1988. When he moved to Kaplan, he served as Center Administrator, Regional Director, and Vice President for Field Management prior to assuming the role of Chief Operating Officer in 1997. He was named President of Kaplan, Inc. in 2002. [[5]](./Andrew_S._Rosen#cite_note-5)
