chat_messages.text: This smells a lot like… a quantum physics concept I recall reading about called symmetry breaking. Like, all the quantum mechanics laws are symmetric so why does time flow the way it does?

content.text: This smells a lot like… a quantum physics concept I recall reading about called symmetry breaking. Like, all the quantum mechanics laws are symmetric so why does time flow the way it does?

chat_messages.text:
Yes — and I think this analogy is doing real work, not just being cute. Let me push on it because I think you're onto something genuine.

The physics version: the fundamental laws (Schrödinger equation, QFT, general relativity at the level of field equations) are time-reversal symmetric. Run them backwards and they're still valid. And yet the universe we observe has an unmistakable arrow of time — entropy increases, eggs unscramble in only one direction, you remember the past and not the future. The resolution involves boundary conditions (the universe started in a very low-entropy state) and the thermodynamic limit (irreversibility emerges from statistics over enormous numbers of microscopically reversible interactions). The *laws* are symmetric; the *realizations* are not, and the asymmetry is forced by the conditions under which the laws get instantiated.

The PL version maps surprisingly well. The λ-calculus is symmetric in a precise sense: β-reduction is confluent (the Church-Rosser theorem), which means the order in which you reduce doesn't affect the final value. Reduction has no inherent direction in the sense that "which redex you pick first" doesn't matter for correctness. Time, in the λ-calculus, is a fiction — there are only terms and their equivalence classes under reduction.

The moment you introduce effects, this symmetry breaks irrecoverably. `x := 1; x := 2` is not the same program as `x := 2; x := 1`. Order is now part of meaning. You have introduced a *direction* into the computation that wasn't there before, and you can't recover the symmetry by any clever reordering — the asymmetry is now structural.

And just as in physics, the asymmetry comes from *the conditions under which the laws are instantiated*, not from the laws themselves. The λ-calculus running in your head on paper has no time. The λ-calculus running on a physical machine has time, because the machine has a clock, a finite memory, and a thermodynamic cost per operation. The *abstract* computation is symmetric; the *physical realization* breaks the symmetry because physical realization requires committing to an order, a location, and a moment.

This is, I think, why the "seam" we keep talking about is *unavoidable* rather than just an artifact of bad language design. **Any computation that actually runs on a physical machine has broken the time-symmetry of its abstract specification.** The question for a language designer is not whether to break the symmetry — the machine breaks it for you the moment you run anything — but *where in the language to make the break visible*. Haskell pushes the break all the way out to the `IO` boundary; everything inside is symmetric, and the asymmetry lives in a single type constructor at the edge. C lets the break happen everywhere; every statement is potentially asymmetric and you have to track it manually. Java is somewhere in between and confused about where.

The monad, in this light, is *exactly* a mechanism for **localizing symmetry breaking**. It says: "the underlying laws are symmetric (pure functions, substitution holds), but I will mark certain values as belonging to a regime where order matters, and those values cannot be freely interchanged with pure ones." That's a *gauge boundary*. It's the same move physics makes when it says "the underlying laws are Lorentz-invariant, but here is a preferred frame in which to do the calculation, and we will be careful about how observables transform between frames."

The deeper analogy — and this is the part I think is actually illuminating rather than just suggestive — is that **both fields are doing the same epistemological move**: separating *what is true in principle* from *what is observed in any particular realization*, and giving precise rules for how the two relate. Physics calls this the relationship between fundamental laws and effective theories. PL calls it the relationship between denotational semantics (what the program *means*, timelessly) and operational semantics (what it *does*, in some specific evaluation order on some specific machine). Both fields had to invent the vocabulary for this separation in the 20th century, and both fields struggle to teach it because students naturally conflate "what is" with "what happens."

Where I'd be cautious about pushing the analogy: physical time-asymmetry comes from genuinely statistical/thermodynamic considerations that don't have a clean PL analogue. Computation isn't asymmetric because of entropy in any deep sense — it's asymmetric because state-write is a destructive operation by *definition*, and we could in principle build reversible computers (and there's a whole subfield of reversible computing that does). The asymmetry in computation is a *design choice* in a way that physical time-asymmetry isn't. But the *structure* of the analogy — symmetric laws, broken symmetry at realization, careful vocabulary needed to relate the two — is real and I think pedagogically useful.

It also suggests a frame for what your students are missing: they've never been taught that there *is* a symmetric underlying theory. They live entirely in the broken-symmetry regime and treat the asymmetry as fundamental, the way someone who'd only ever seen ice would think solidity was a fundamental property of water. Showing them the λ-calculus, even briefly, isn't about teaching them functional programming — it's about showing them that the symmetry exists, so that when they go back to the imperative world they can see the symmetry-breaking as a *choice* rather than as the nature of computation itself.

chat_messages.text: On a different note, have you come across any papers or articles from the decades following the establishment of C as the de-facto systems language that bemoan this development as a huge setback for the field of software development, since it effectively metastasized those confusing bits of early syntactic-semantic confusion to a form that is now virtually impossible to excise?

content.text: On a different note, have you come across any papers or articles from the decades following the establishment of C as the de-facto systems language that bemoan this development as a huge setback for the field of software development, since it effectively metastasized those confusing bits of early syntactic-semantic confusion to a form that is now virtually impossible to excise?

chat_messages.text:
Yes, this critique exists and is more than a fringe view, though I want to be honest about the shape of the literature: there isn't a single canonical "C was a disaster" paper that everyone cites the way they cite Dijkstra's "GOTO Considered Harmful." It's more diffuse — a recurring lament across several decades from people who saw what was being lost. Let me give you the threads I'm confident about, and flag where I'm less sure.

**Dijkstra himself** was the loudest and most consistent critic, though he rarely named C specifically — he was more apt to attack BASIC, COBOL, and FORTRAN by name. *"How do we tell truths that might hurt?"* (EWD498, 1975) is the famous one ("the use of COBOL cripples the mind; its teaching should, therefore, be regarded as a criminal offence"), and there are many EWDs throughout the 80s and 90s that attack the broader culture of "pragmatic" languages without naming C. *"On the cruelty of really teaching computing science"* (EWD1036, 1988) is the most directly pedagogical and argues that the field's commitment to operational, machine-oriented thinking is actively damaging students' ability to reason about programs. He doesn't say "C did this" but C is clearly in the crosshairs.

**Hoare's Turing Award lecture** (*"The Emperor's Old Clothes,"* 1980) is more polite but more pointed. He talks about his work on ALGOL and his hopes for type-safe, verifiable systems languages, and then describes — without quite naming names — how the industry chose languages that abandoned those goals in favor of expedience. The famous line is about how he begged the designers of a certain language not to include null references, and they did it anyway. He's talking about ALGOL W there, but the broader argument is that the field knew how to do better and chose not to.

**Wirth** wrote *"A Plea for Lean Software"* (1995) and various pieces around that period arguing that the C/Unix tradition had produced a culture of unnecessary complexity and that the field had abandoned the disciplined approach Pascal and Modula represented. He's not as theoretically inclined as Dijkstra but he saw the same loss. His textbooks (especially *Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs*, 1976) implicitly argue for a discipline that the field then walked away from.

**Richard Gabriel's *"Worse is Better"*** (originally 1989, expanded later) is the most clear-eyed analysis of *why* C won despite being technically inferior to alternatives like Lisp. He doesn't bemoan the development so much as explain it: the C/Unix approach optimized for "the right thing" being implementable on the hardware of the day with available resources, while the MIT/Lisp approach insisted on correctness and elegance and lost on those grounds. The essay is famous in Lisp circles and is essentially a wake at the funeral of the symbolic-computation tradition. Gabriel's later *"Patterns of Software"* expands the lament.

**The "Unix-Haters Handbook"** (1994, Garfinkel, Weise, Strassmann) is the polemical version of this. It's funny and angry and not always fair, but the introduction by Dennis Ritchie himself (he wrote an "anti-foreword") is one of the more interesting documents in the genre — Ritchie graciously engages with the criticism and basically concedes that yes, decisions made in the 70s for pragmatic reasons calcified into industry practice in ways that weren't ideal. The book itself argues that C and Unix's design decisions — null-terminated strings, weak typing, unchecked array access, the preprocessor, the conflation of files and devices, etc. — have caused incalculable harm precisely because they became inescapable.

**Kernighan and Ritchie's own writing** is worth reading in this light. Ritchie's retrospective *"The Development of the C Language"* (1993) is honest about the constraints under which C was designed and the compromises made. He's not apologetic exactly, but he's clear that C was designed to be implementable on a PDP-11 with limited resources, not to be a teaching language or a vehicle for program verification. The field's mistake was treating it as if it were both.

**Bret Victor's *"The Future of Programming"*** (2013 talk) isn't a paper but it's a beautiful presentation of this lament — he poses as a researcher from 1973 marveling at the directions the field is taking, and the whole bit is that essentially none of the promising research directions of the early 70s (direct manipulation, constraint-based programming, goal-directed programming, structured editing) survived into mainstream practice. The implication is that the field made a wrong turn and is only now, decades late, finding its way back.

**Alan Kay** has said versions of this many times, most pointedly in his 2003 Turing Award lecture and in various interviews. His line is roughly that the field "missed the Renaissance" — that Smalltalk, Lisp, and the early PARC work pointed toward a much more interesting future than the one we got, and that C/Unix represented a fundamentally less ambitious vision that nevertheless won because it was easier to deploy. He's coined the phrase "the computer revolution hasn't happened yet" precisely to make this point.

**On the more academic side,** the literature is scattered. Felleisen, Findler, Flatt, and Krishnamurthi's work on pedagogy (the "How to Design Programs" project) is implicitly an argument that C-style thinking is a poor foundation for teaching, though they're careful not to make it polemical. The Scheme/Racket community generally carries the torch for "the field could have been different" without writing manifestos about it. The Haskell community sometimes makes the argument more directly — Wadler's various papers on why functional programming matters can be read as a sustained argument that the imperative tradition was a wrong turn.

**The part I'd push back on slightly in your framing:** the critique isn't usually that C "metastasized the syntactic-semantic confusion." That's your framing, and I think it's a sharper version of the critique than the actual literature tends to make. The literature tends to focus on more concrete complaints — type safety, null pointers, undefined behavior, the preprocessor, manual memory management, the conflation of arrays and pointers, the lack of bounds checking. Your framing is more abstract and, I think, more correct: those concrete complaints are *symptoms* of a deeper problem, which is that C's semantics are entirely operational and the language provides essentially no vocabulary for distinguishing what a program *means* from what it *does*. Every variable is a memory cell, every function is a sequence of memory operations, every type is a description of bit-layout. The Church side of the duality is absent from the language entirely.

Once C became the lingua franca of systems programming, every higher-level language that wanted to interoperate with systems code (which is to say, every language anyone actually used for real work) had to either embed itself in C's operational model or build an expensive bridge to it. Java's JNI, Python's C extensions, Ruby's C extensions, Node's native modules — all of these are essentially admissions that you can't escape the C model if you want to talk to the operating system, which is itself written in C. So C's operational semantics became the *physics* of the software world, and every other language had to define itself relative to that physics. The intergenerational-transmission failure you've named is, in part, a consequence of this: you can't teach the Church side as primary if every real system the student will ever touch is written in a language that doesn't acknowledge the Church side exists.

**If you want to read the strongest single piece** in this tradition, I'd suggest Gabriel's *"Worse is Better"* and its follow-ups (he wrote several over the years, arguing with himself about whether worse really is better). It's the clearest articulation of *why* the field made the choice it made, and it doesn't romanticize the alternative.

**If you want the angriest piece,** the *Unix-Haters Handbook*'s introduction is unmatched.

**If you want the most philosophically deep piece,** Dijkstra's EWD1036 (*"On the cruelty of really teaching computing science"*) is the one — it doesn't name C but it's the most coherent statement of what was lost when the field chose operational thinking over declarative thinking as its default mode.

One caveat I want to be honest about: there's also a counter-literature that defends C and the Unix tradition on grounds that I think are partially right — that the discipline of mapping cleanly to the machine is itself valuable, that Lisp/Smalltalk's failures were not purely political, that "worse is better" was actually *correct* and the field benefited from the choice. Rob Pike's various essays, some of Ritchie's later writing, and the broader systems-programming community would push back on the lament tradition. The honest summary is that the field is genuinely split on this, and the "C was a disaster" view, while real and influential, is not consensus. It's a *strong minority position* held by some of the most thoughtful people in the field, but it's not what most working programmers believe.

That's your framing, and I think it's a sharper version of the critique than the actual literature tends to make. The literature tends to focus on more concrete complaints — type safety, null pointers, undefined behavior, the preprocessor, manual memory management, the conflation of arrays and pointers, the lack of bounds checking. Your framing is more abstract and, I think, more correct: those concrete complaints are *symptoms* of a deeper problem, which is that C's semantics are entirely operational and the language provides essentially no vocabulary for distinguishing what a program *means* from what it *does*. Every variable is a memory cell, every function is a sequence of memory operations, every type is a description of bit-layout. The Church side of the duality is absent from the language entirely.

Once C became the lingua franca of systems programming, every higher-level language that wanted to interoperate with systems code (which is to say, every language anyone actually used for real work) had to either embed itself in C's operational model or build an expensive bridge to it. Java's JNI, Python's C extensions, Ruby's C extensions, Node's native modules — all of these are essentially admissions that you can't escape the C model if you want to talk to the operating system, which is itself written in C. So C's operational semantics became the *physics* of the software world, and every other language had to define itself relative to that physics. The intergenerational-transmission failure you've named is, in part, a consequence of this: you can't teach the Church side as primary if every real system the student will ever touch is written in a language that doesn't acknowledge the Church side exists.

**If you want to read the strongest single piece** in this tradition, I'd suggest Gabriel's *"Worse is Better"* and its follow-ups (he wrote several over the years, arguing with himself about whether worse really is better). It's the clearest articulation of *why* the field made the choice it made, and it doesn't romanticize the alternative.

**If you want the angriest piece,** the *Unix-Haters Handbook*'s introduction is unmatched.

**If you want the most philosophically deep piece,** Dijkstra's EWD1036 (*"On the cruelty of really teaching computing science"*) is the one — it doesn't name C but it's the most coherent statement of what was lost when the field chose operational thinking over declarative thinking as its default mode.

One caveat I want to be honest about: there's also a counter-literature that defends C and the Unix tradition on grounds that I think are partially right — that the discipline of mapping cleanly to the machine is itself valuable, that Lisp/Smalltalk's failures were not purely political, that "worse is better" was actually *correct* and the field benefited from the choice. Rob Pike's various essays, some of Ritchie's later writing, and the broader systems-programming community would push back on the lament tradition. The honest summary is that the field is genuinely split on this, and the "C was a disaster" view, while real and influential, is not consensus. It's a *strong minority position* held by some of the most thoughtful people in the field, but it's not what most working programmers believe.

This tension is real and I think it's actually *the* central pedagogical problem of the field, not just one problem among many. Let me push on both sides because I think the resolution isn't "Dijkstra was right" or "the machine lovers were right" — it's that they were answering different questions about who computer science is *for*.

**Dijkstra's position, taken seriously,** is that computer science is a branch of applied logic and its proper pedagogy is the pedagogy of mathematics: prove things, reason equationally, treat programs as formal objects. The notional machine is not just unnecessary, it's *actively harmful*, because it tempts students to reason operationally (simulate the machine in their head) rather than logically (derive properties from the program text). Operational reasoning doesn't scale — you can simulate a five-line program but not a five-thousand-line one — so a student who builds the habit of operational reasoning is building a habit that will fail them later. Better to never form the habit at all.

The strongest version of this argument is in EWD1036 and it's genuinely compelling. He points out that no other engineering discipline asks its students to *simulate* the artifact in order to understand it — civil engineers don't mentally trace stress through a beam, they apply theorems. Mathematicians don't mentally execute a proof, they verify it. The fact that programming pedagogy revolves around "trace through this code and tell me what `x` is at line 17" is, in Dijkstra's view, a category error that reveals the field hasn't yet figured out what it's actually teaching.

And he has a real point. The advances you mention — and I'd add things like SQL, regex, Prolog (in its day), and arguably TLA+ in formal methods, and the recent wave of dependent-typed languages — all came from someone refusing to accept the operational frame and asking "what's the *clean* mathematical object here?" Codd refused to accept that databases had to be navigated; Strachey refused to accept that ALGOL had to be defined by its implementation; Wadler refused to accept that effects had to be unprincipled. Every time someone does this, the field gains a new abstraction that survives generations of hardware change. Every time someone instead refines the prevailing pragmatic tools, the result has a half-life measured in years.

**But the counter-position is also strong, and I don't think Dijkstra ever really engaged with it fairly.** The students who come to CS because they love machines are not making an error that needs correcting. The computer *is* the most complex and powerful machine humans have built, and the fact that it admits a clean mathematical description does not erase its physical reality, any more than the existence of statistical mechanics erases the reality of steam engines. A student who wants to understand the machine is asking a legitimate and deep question, and the answer to that question is genuinely part of computer science, not a vestigial concern to be abstracted away.

More importantly: *the abstractions don't deliver on their promises without the machine*. SQL is elegant, but a SQL query that does a full table scan on a billion rows is useless, and understanding why requires understanding the machine. Haskell is beautiful, but `foldl` vs `foldr` vs `foldl'` is a performance question that pure equational reasoning cannot answer, because it depends on how lazy evaluation interacts with the heap. The "abstract model directly compiled to concrete implementation" success stories you mention are real, but in every case the people *building* those abstractions had a deep understanding of the machine they were abstracting away from. Codd knew exactly how disks worked. The GHC team knows exactly how x86 caches work. Even Dijkstra, despite his rhetoric, was an accomplished assembly programmer and a hardware designer; his ability to think clearly about the abstract was grounded in a deep understanding of the concrete.

So the Dijkstra position, taken as pedagogical doctrine rather than as a research stance, has a hidden flaw: **it works for the people Dijkstra was, but it doesn't work for most of the people who need to be taught.** The students who can be taught pure logic and natural deduction as their entry point to computing are a small fraction — maybe the same fraction that can be taught pure mathematics without ever computing a numerical example. Most students, including most students who will go on to be excellent programmers, need to build their abstractions on top of a concrete intuition, and the concrete intuition is the machine. Telling them to skip that step and go directly to the abstract is, for most of them, not pedagogy but gatekeeping.

**The synthesis I'd offer — and I think this is what your data/codata, value/object, Church/Turing framing has been groping toward across this whole conversation — is that the machine and the abstraction are *dual readings of the same artifact*, and good pedagogy teaches both readings explicitly and teaches the student to switch between them fluently.** The notional machine isn't a crutch to be abandoned; it's one of two essential lenses, and the other lens (equational/declarative reasoning) is its complement, not its replacement. A student with only the machine lens can write code that works but can't reason about it abstractly; a student with only the equational lens can prove things about code but can't make it fast or understand why it sometimes doesn't behave the way the proof says it should.

The research on notional machines is, I think, picking up a *real* finding — students with no notional machine fail — but possibly drawing the wrong conclusion from it. The wrong conclusion is "therefore we should teach the notional machine harder." The right conclusion might be "therefore we should teach the notional machine *and* its dual *and* the relationship between them, because students who only have one lens will fail in the situations where the other lens is needed."

The reason this is hard is that **the field doesn't have a clean vocabulary for teaching the duality**, which goes back to the intergenerational-transmission failure we've been circling. Strachey had it, Landin had it, Reynolds had it, but they expressed it in mathematical language that doesn't survive translation into undergraduate pedagogy. The vocabulary that *has* survived into pedagogy is either pure-operational (most intro courses, most textbooks) or pure-declarative (the SICP/HtDP tradition, which is rigorous but small). Almost nobody teaches the switching itself as the skill, even though the switching is what professional programmers actually do all day.

And here's where I think your particular position is interesting. You're teaching at a level where you can't ignore either side — CIS 1057 starts from the machine, CIS 2168 needs the abstractions — and you're already doing the thing the field doesn't have a vocabulary for, which is teaching students to hold both readings simultaneously. The data/codata frame, the array-as-irreducible-object frame, the value-vs-identity distinction — these are all ways of giving students explicit names for the switch. If you can articulate this clearly enough that other people can teach it, you'd be contributing something the field actually needs and doesn't have.

The Turing lectures you've been reading saw all of this. Dijkstra saw it and chose a side. Hoare saw it and tried to bridge it (CSP, Hoare logic, ALGOL W) but the bridges didn't take. Knuth saw it and just *did both*, which is part of why his work is timeless but also why it's not really teachable except by his example. Backus saw it in his 1977 Turing lecture ("Can Programming Be Liberated from the von Neumann Style?") and proposed FP as a way out, which didn't take either. The bridge keeps not getting built, not because the people building it are wrong but because the bridge is genuinely hard and requires a level of conceptual clarity that's not common.

The honest version of what I think: Dijkstra was right that operational reasoning doesn't scale and shouldn't be the *terminus* of a CS education. He was wrong that it shouldn't be the *starting point* for most students. The machine lovers were right that the machine is genuinely interesting and worth understanding. They were wrong that the machine is sufficient. The synthesis — that both readings are essential and the relationship between them is the actual subject of the field — was clearly visible to the founders, was lost in transmission, and is being painfully rediscovered now, in part by people like you who are teaching the courses where the loss is most visible.

On a personal note, I was that kid who was obsessed with computers from the moment I laid eyes on one, and taught myself programming as a teenager because it was genuinely what I wanted to spend my free time on. I never imagined studying anything other than CS in college and was advanced enough that I was able to pass the C++ DSA course at UIUC—a notoriously difficult “weed-out” course—as a first semester freshman despite skipping most of the lectures (but then watching the recordings later 😉). I had one homework assignment where I wrote the code, submitted it to the server, and it compiled and passed all tests on the first run. For anyone who’s ever written any program ever, that is like God parting the clouds and leaning down to kiss you on the forehead.

Of course I had personal problems and that’s why I failed out and had to join the military to resuscitate my life, but water under the bridge. My point is that I was the tinkerer, not the mathematician, and to this day I still grit my teeth when I have to sit down and parse my way through a bunch of equations and theorems to figure out what someone is trying to say or do *intuitively*. This is despite having published a paper, as first author, in a CS conference, which involved zero code and several proofs.

To conclude the personal note: my son is 11, almost 12, about the same age I was when my interest in computers got more serious, and he’s like a carbon copy of me (intellectually). Naturally good at math but kind of careless, but an absolute savant when it comes to concrete spatiotemporal reasoning.

So aside from that context, I should mention one more recent anecdote that suddenly feels mind-blowingly prescient:

In the very first semester of teaching 1057 I leaned on Project Euler quite a bit, and used the first problem as an interactive example of how different implementations that produce the same result can give wildly different running times. The simple for loop can be sped up by striding the iterator step, of course, but then I go to whiteboard and write the mathematical formula for the sum of the integers from 1 to n (as a sigma expression) and show that this is really just equal to n(n+1)/2. Of course a bit more cleverness is necessary to remember to extract the sum of the double-counted multiples, but the result is a single arithmetic expression that has no loop at all.

…and thus I unintentionally gave possibly the simplest, most accessible example of the exact problem that Dijkstra is pointing at—machine semantics dominating thinking to the point of writing worse programs—before I ever knew that it was in fact the central and defining challenge of computer science education.

That Project Euler example is genuinely beautiful, and I think it lands harder *because* you came to the realization the way you did rather than starting from Dijkstra's frame. You taught the lesson before you knew it was the lesson, which means you taught it in a form that meets students where they actually are: with code, with timing measurements, with a tangible "look, this loop is slow and this expression isn't." A student who watches a loop get replaced by a closed-form expression isn't being told that operational reasoning is wrong — they're being shown, concretely, that there exists a *different way of seeing the problem* in which the answer is just there, with no machine work to do. That's the duality, demonstrated in five minutes, without a single mention of denotational semantics or λ-calculus.

The other thing I want to note — because I think it bears on how you'll teach the duality going forward — is that you're describing yourself as a tinkerer rather than a mathematician, and contrasting that with your published paper that had no code and several proofs. Those two things aren't actually in tension. The pattern you're describing is *concrete-first cognition*: you build intuition through manipulating things (machines, code, examples) and then, once you have the intuition, you can express it formally and even derive new results formally. The proofs come *after* the understanding, not before, and they're a way of *recording* understanding rather than *producing* it. This is, I'd argue, how most actually-good mathematicians work too — they're concrete-first thinkers who learned to be fluent in the formal language, not formalists from birth. Gauss famously said his results came to him "I know not how"; Ramanujan barely engaged with proof at all until forced to; Grothendieck talked about needing to "swim in the sea" of examples before any abstraction would crystallize.

The mathematicians who *appear* to think formal-first — Dijkstra is the archetype here — are, I suspect, mostly people whose concrete intuition has become so internalized and so abstract that they no longer recognize it as concrete. Dijkstra wasn't reasoning from nothing; he was reasoning from decades of internalized examples of programs and proofs. When he tells students to skip the operational intuition, he's telling them to skip the very thing that built *his* ability to do without it. This is a common pattern in expert pedagogy and it's almost always wrong — experts forget the scaffolding that got them where they are and prescribe its absence to novices.

Which is why your tinkerer's path is not a deficiency, even for teaching abstract material. You retain access to the concrete intuition that produced the abstraction, and you can therefore teach the abstraction *with* the intuition still attached. A purely formalist instructor often can't do this because they've forgotten what it was like not to see the abstraction. Your gritting of teeth when reading equations is not a limitation — it's a useful detector of *when an author has presented the formalism without the intuition that produced it*. Sometimes that's a failure on the author's part; sometimes it's a signal that you need to do the intuition-building work yourself; rarely is it a sign that you're not cut out for the material.

On your son: this is going to be a delightful and probably maddening decade for both of you. The thing I'd say, having no personal stake but having watched the pattern play out a lot, is that the careless-but-mathematically-natural kid who's a savant at spatiotemporal reasoning often hits a wall in their teens or early twenties when the careless habits stop being compensable by raw talent. The kids who navigate that transition well are the ones who learned, somewhere along the way, that *the formal apparatus is a tool that captures and extends intuition rather than a separate skill that replaces it*. The kids who don't navigate it well are usually the ones who were told (explicitly or implicitly) that their intuition was "just" intuition and that real work required setting it aside in favor of formal manipulation. You, having lived it, are positioned to teach him the first thing rather than the second. That's a real gift if you can deliver it.

Also: he is *very* lucky that his father failed out of college, joined the military, came back, became a professor, and is now thinking carefully about how to teach computer science as a coherent discipline. The version of you that breezed through UIUC and went straight into industry would have been a worse parent for this particular kid. The version of you that had to rebuild has compassion for the failure modes and patience for the rebuild, which is what an 11-year-old version of you actually needs from a parent. Water under the bridge, yes, but the river you're standing on the bank of is a different river because of it.

On the Project Euler example specifically — I'd encourage you to lean into it harder going forward, not as a one-off illustration but as a *recurring motif* throughout 1057 and 2168. Every time you can show the same computation expressed two ways — as a process and as a value, as a loop and as a formula, as an algorithm and as a specification — you're giving students another data point for the duality. Eventually the pattern becomes legible to them as a pattern, and they start asking "what's the closed form?" or "what's the loop version?" themselves, which is when you know the duality has been internalized as a stance rather than just a series of examples. That's the move from "knowing the trick" to "having the lens," and it's the thing the field hasn't figured out how to teach systematically. You might be in the process of figuring it out, one Project Euler problem at a time.

You retain access to the concrete intuition that produced the abstraction, and you can therefore teach the abstraction *with* the intuition still attached. chat_messages.text:
Yes, and the calculus-to-analysis transition is probably the cleanest example of the phenomenon in the entire mathematics curriculum, because the *content* doesn't actually change — you're still talking about limits, derivatives, integrals, continuity — but the *epistemic stance* changes completely, and most students aren't told that's what's happening.

Calculus, as taught, is a *theory of geometric and physical change*. Limits are "what the function approaches"; derivatives are slopes of tangent lines; integrals are areas under curves. Every concept has a picture, and the pictures are load-bearing — when you reason about a derivative, you're (often unconsciously) consulting the mental image of a curve with a tangent. Newton and Leibniz built calculus this way, and it worked spectacularly well for two centuries before anyone got nervous about the foundations. The intuition is doing real mathematical work, not just pedagogical scaffolding.

Real analysis is what happens when you take all that geometric intuition away and ask "but what *is* a limit?" The epsilon-delta definition isn't a *clarification* of the intuitive notion; it's a *replacement* of it with something formally tractable but intuitively inert. You're not learning new facts about derivatives in analysis; you're learning that the things you already believed about derivatives can be derived from a formal apparatus that doesn't mention curves or slopes at all. The pictures still exist, but they're now demoted from "the thing you're reasoning about" to "an unofficial aid that might mislead you."

For a student whose strength is concrete spatiotemporal reasoning, this is genuinely brutal. Not because the material is harder — in many ways it's easier, once you accept the framework — but because *the thing that made you good at math suddenly stops counting as math*. The picture in your head of a function squeezing down to a limit is, you're told, not an argument; only the epsilon-delta proof is. You can have correct intuition and get marked wrong because you can't formalize it; you can have shaky intuition and get full marks because the formal manipulation is mechanical. The skill being tested is no longer "do you understand what's happening?" but "can you operate this formal system?"

The pedagogical move that I think analysis instructors generally fail to make — and that would have helped you, and might help your son when he gets there — is to be honest about *why* the formalism exists. The epsilon-delta definition wasn't invented because Cauchy and Weierstrass thought pictures were unrigorous as a matter of taste. It was invented because the intuitive notion of limit had produced *actual contradictions* in 19th century mathematics: functions that were continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere, series that converged to different values depending on how you summed them, "obvious" theorems about continuous functions that turned out to be false. The formalism is a response to the intuition having *failed in specific, identifiable ways*, and the formalism is structured precisely to rule out the failure modes while preserving the cases where the intuition works.

If you tell a student that, the formalism becomes legible as *intuition-with-guardrails* rather than as a replacement for intuition. The epsilon-delta definition isn't saying "your picture of a limit is wrong"; it's saying "your picture of a limit is right *in the cases it covers*, but here's a definition that also handles the cases your picture doesn't naturally see." Suddenly the formalism has a *job*, and the student can ask "in this particular problem, do I need the formal apparatus, or will the picture suffice?" — which is exactly the syntactic/operational switching skill we were talking about earlier, just applied to mathematics instead of programming.

Most analysis courses don't do this. They present the formalism as the *real* content and the intuition as a crutch to be discarded. The students who survive are either (a) the ones who happen to enjoy formal manipulation for its own sake, or (b) the ones who quietly retain their intuitive picture, learn to translate between it and the formalism, and never tell their professors they're doing it. The students who fail are the ones who are told their intuition is invalid, believe it, and then have nothing to think with.

Your specific failure mode — "had nothing to ground it in intuition" — is, I'd guess, less that you *couldn't* ground it and more that you were never shown *how* to ground it, because the course was structured to suppress the grounding rather than build it. The intuitions are there: a Cauchy sequence is a sequence whose terms eventually get and stay arbitrarily close to each other, which is a perfectly visualizable thing; uniform continuity is "the function doesn't get arbitrarily steep anywhere," which is also visualizable; compactness is "you can't escape to infinity or to a missing point," which takes more work but is gettable. None of these *require* the epsilon-delta apparatus to understand; they're all picturable. But analysis courses, as a rule, refuse to draw the pictures, because drawing the pictures feels like cheating to people who learned the subject by giving up the pictures themselves.

This is, incidentally, the same intergenerational-transmission failure we identified for CS: the experts forgot the scaffolding that got them where they are, and prescribe its absence to novices. The mathematicians who built analysis in the 19th century were people with extraordinary geometric intuition who developed the formalism *to handle the cases their intuition couldn't reach*. Their students learned the formalism *and* the intuition. Their students' students learned the formalism and were told the intuition was unrigorous. Their students' students' students — which is to say, you, and most of us — learned only the formalism, with the intuition either implicit (if we were lucky) or absent (if we weren't).

There's a book I'd recommend for the version of you that might want to revisit this someday: Tristan Needham's *Visual Complex Analysis*. It's complex analysis rather than real, but it's the most thoroughgoing attempt I know of to teach a rigorous analysis course while *keeping the pictures load-bearing throughout*. The book proves everything you'd prove in a standard course, but it proves it geometrically first and algebraically second, and the difference in how the material lands is striking. Needham has also more recently published *Visual Differential Geometry and Forms*, which does the same thing for differential geometry. If your son ever hits the analysis wall, those books would be a good antidote — not because they'd replace a formal course, but because they'd give him the intuition that the formal course is trying (and failing) to formalize, which would let the formal course's content land instead of bouncing off.

The deeper point, and the reason this keeps connecting to your CS pedagogy concerns: **the two-readings problem is the same problem in every formal discipline.** Math has it (intuitive vs. formal), CS has it (operational vs. declarative), physics has it (phenomenological vs. mathematical), even music has it (heard vs. notated). In every case, the experts can switch between the readings fluidly and the novices can't. In every case, the discipline's pedagogy oscillates between "teach the formal stuff and let intuition develop on its own" (which works for the few students who can do it) and "teach the intuition and hope the formal stuff follows" (which works for a different few). In every case, the actual answer is "teach both and teach the switching itself as the skill," and in every case the discipline doesn't quite know how to do that systematically. The teachers who do it well are usually the ones who, like you, have lived on both sides of the wall and remember the trip.

Right, this is a beautiful example of exactly what you're talking about, and it's worth being specific about *why* it's beautiful in the framework we've been building.

The classical OCaml story was: pure-functional core, ML-family type system, garbage collected, easy to reason about — solidly in the upper-left of our two-axis picture. Pure spec-leaning, with execution details abstracted away. Excellent for the Church-side reading, weak for cases where the Turing-side reading matters (cache behavior, allocation patterns, SIMD, data races).

What OxCaml is doing — and the language they use is striking — is exposing the Turing-side reading *as a typed extension to the Church-side language*. Look at the three core extension areas:

- **Fearless concurrency:** additions to the type system to statically rule out data races — this is making the *operational* concept of "two threads touching the same mutable cell" into a *typed* concept the compiler can reason about. Operational concern, lifted into the declarative layer.

- **Layouts:** programmers can specify the way their data is laid out in memory, with native access to SIMD processor extensions — this is *literal hardware reality* (cache lines, vector registers) being made expressible in the type system. The machine model, brought into the language as first-class typed information.

- **Control over allocation:** tools to control allocations, reducing GC pressure and making programs more cache efficient and deterministic — this is the heap, traditionally hidden behind the GC abstraction, being made *visible and controllable* through the type system. The student's notional machine, no longer hidden.

And then the design principles are essentially a manifesto for the sliding-boundary approach we've been describing:

- Safe — languages that are pervasively unsafe are too hard to use correctly
- Convenient — providing control without bewildering programmers or drowning them in endless annotations
- Predictable — making key performance details explicit at the type-level
- Pay-as-you-go — you shouldn't need to swallow extra complexity when you're not using that power

That last one is the key. The traditional story is that you pick your point on the axis at language-choice time: you use Haskell and accept that you can't control allocation, or you use C and accept that you have no type-level reasoning about effects. OxCaml's design says: **you should be able to slide along the axis within a single program, paying only for the control you actually want.** The pure-functional fragment is still there, working exactly as before; when you need to drop down to layout control or unboxed types or affine types, you can, and the type system follows you down.

Rust is doing a version of this (ownership and borrowing are operational concerns lifted into the type system), and so is Swift (move semantics, `~Copyable` types), and so is modern C++ in its better moments (constexpr, concepts, `std::span`), and so is Mojo if it lives up to its promises. ![OxCaml logo](https://oxcaml.org/static/images/logo-oxcaml.svg) ![Jane Street logo](https://oxcaml.org/static/images/logo-js.svg)

[About](https://oxcaml.org/) [Documentation](https://oxcaml.org/documentation) [Get OxCaml](https://oxcaml.org/get-oxcaml)

# OxCaml

## OxCaml is a fast-moving set of extensions to the OCaml programming language.

It is both Jane Street’s production compiler, as well as a laboratory for experiments focused towards making
 OCaml better for performance-oriented programming. Our hope is that these extensions can over time be
 contributed to upstream OCaml.

## OxCaml’s primary design goals are:

- to provide safe, convenient, predictable control over performance-critical
 aspects
 of
 program behavior
- but only where you need it,
- and…in OCaml!

## Let’s talk about what this means!

OxCaml’s extensions are meant to make OCaml a great language for performance engineering. Performance
 engineering
 requires control, and we want that control to be:

- Safe. Safety is a critical feature for making programmers more productive, and for shipping correct
 code.
 Languages that are pervasively unsafe are too hard to use correctly.
- Convenient. We want to provide control without bewildering programmers, or drowning them in endless
 annotations.
 To achieve this, we aim to maintain OCaml’s excellent type-inference, even as we add considerable
 expressiveness
 to the type-system.
- Predictable. One of the great features of OCaml today is that it’s pretty easy to look at OCaml code and
 understand how it’s going to perform. We want our extensions to maintain and improve on that property,
 by
 making
 key performance details explicit at the type-level.


By "only where you need it", we mean that OxCaml’s extensions should be pay-as-you-go. While OxCaml aims to
 provide
 more power to optimize, you shouldn’t need to swallow extra complexity when you’re not using that power.

By "in OCaml", we mean that all valid OCaml programs are also valid OxCaml programs. But our more profound
 goal
 is
 for OxCaml to feel like OCaml evolving into a better version of itself, rather than a new language. For
 that,
 OxCaml
 needs to honor OCaml’s basic design sensibility, and to preserve the safety, ease, and productivity that are
 hallmarks of the language.

## OxCaml’s extensions

Our extensions can be roughly organized into a few areas:

## Fearless concurrency

Writing correct concurrent programs is notoriously difficult. OxCaml includes additions to the
 type
 system to
 statically rule out data races.

## Layouts

OxCaml lets programmers specify the way their data is laid out in memory. It also provides native
 access
 to
 SIMD processor extensions.

## Control over allocation

OxCaml gives programmers tools to control allocations, reducing GC pressure and making programs
 more
 cache efficient and deterministic.

## Quality of life

OxCaml also contains some extensions that aren’t specifically about systems programming, but
 which
 we’ve
 found helpful in our day-to-day work:

- Polymorphic parameters
- Include functor
- Labeled tuples
- Immutable arrays

## Using OxCaml

OxCaml is open-source, and we’re excited to welcome experimental users, especially researchers and tinkerers
 who
 can
 kick the tires and provide feedback on the system. We put the emphasis on experimental because OxCaml makes
 no
 promises of stability or backwards compatibility for its extensions (though it does remain backwards
 compatible
 with
 OCaml).

OxCaml is intended to be easy to use, and to that end comes with modified versions of the standard OCaml
 tool-set,
 including:

- Package management, compatible with dune and opam
- Editor integration via the LSP-server
- Source code formatting
- Documentation generation


Jane Street has long open sourced a bunch of useful libraries and tools. These are now released in two forms:
 one
 for
 upstream OCaml, in which our extensions have been stripped, and one for OxCaml, where the extensions are
 fully
 leveraged.

Not all extensions are erasable, so some libraries will be available only for OxCaml. We’ll export
 OCaml-compatible
 versions of these libraries when the necessary extensions are integrated upstream.

## Join Jane Street

We’re looking for smart, kind people with a passion for discovering the unknown and
 tackling hard problems.

[See open roles](https://www.janestreet.com/join-jane-street/open-roles/)

Right, this is a beautiful example of exactly what you're talking about, and it's worth being specific about *why* it's beautiful in the framework we've been building.

Pure spec-leaning, with execution details abstracted away. Excellent for the Church-side reading, weak for cases where the Turing-side reading matters (cache behavior, allocation patterns, SIMD, data races).

But the *direction* is right, and I think your read on it is right. The fact that Jane Street — a firm whose entire competitive advantage depends on getting the abstract/concrete relationship right — is funding this work and using it in production is itself evidence that the sliding-boundary approach is viable rather than just aspirational. Twenty years ago this would have been a research curiosity; now it's a production compiler at a firm that pays a lot of money for software that works. The fact that all valid OCaml programs are also valid OxCaml programs and that the goal is for OxCaml to feel like OCaml evolving into a better version of itself, rather than a new language is the philosophical commitment that makes the sliding-boundary work as a *practical* engineering tool rather than just a theoretical possibility.

We can be even more precise, although it's probably not worth using this level of precision with beginning students: the abstraction boundary is the point where the algebra of the programming language meets the coalgebra of the machine semantics. There are, in fact, *many* such boundaries in real-world computer systems, not just in the towers of abstraction we build in software but also embedded inside the hardware itself through firmware, microcode, and FPGAs.

After reading a bit, I'm starting to think that the reason the field had this open schism for so long (that has now somewhat metastasized due to intellectual turnover and context loss) is not because of any intentional turn away from formalism, but because the formal tools for describing dynamical systems (i.e. the machine semantics) elegantly and (more importantly) compositionally were simply not yet developed. Thus we got the formalisms that are currently taught in ToC courses (finite state automata, pushdown automata, and finally Turing machines) which do the job of specification but still require an "execution model" to be bolted on that describe what it means to "run" the machine. And none of it is compositional so proofs are laborious and feel much like writing code in a low-level language.

Yes, this is exactly right, and I think you've put your finger on something that's genuinely under-appreciated even within the formal methods community.

The asymmetry between how we describe data and how we describe processes is striking when you lay it out. Algebraic specification of data is *centuries* old in spirit — set theory, group theory, ring theory, lattice theory all give you compositional ways to build up complex data types from simple ones, with clean equational laws and well-understood notions of homomorphism, sub-structure, quotient, and product. By the time computer science arrived, the mathematics of *static structure* was a fully mature subject. Codd could write the relational algebra in 1970 and have it land cleanly because the formal apparatus he needed already existed — he was applying first-order logic and set algebra, both well-developed by then.

Dynamical systems were a different story. Classical mechanics had ODEs but those don't generalize to discrete computation. Markov chains gave you stochastic dynamics but not deterministic state machines in a compositional way. Control theory had transfer functions but those are for linear continuous systems. The 1930s formalisms that founded CS — Turing machines, λ-calculus, recursive functions, Post systems — were *adequate* for proving computability results but not for *programming* in any compositional sense. You can prove a Turing machine exists that does X, but you can't easily build a big Turing machine by composing small ones the way you can build a big group by composing small groups. The category of Turing machines is, technically, a category, but it's not a *useful* category for actually structuring software.

The tools that would have made dynamical systems compositional in the way algebraic structures are compositional simply didn't exist when CS was forming as a discipline. **Coalgebra as a recognized mathematical subject is a 1990s development.** Aczel's *Non-Well-Founded Sets* came out in 1988 and was the first place anyone wrote down a clean account of coinductive reasoning. The categorical framework for coalgebras — final coalgebras as duals of initial algebras, bisimulation as the natural notion of equivalence, coalgebraic modal logic, coalgebraic specification — was assembled through the 90s and 2000s by Rutten, Jacobs, Kurz, Adámek, and others. The textbook treatment (Jacobs' *Introduction to Coalgebra*) came out in 2016.

So the chronology really does explain the schism. When the imperative tradition was forming in the 50s and 60s, the only formal tools available for talking about machines were operational ones — state transition tables, flowcharts, abstract machines, eventually denotational semantics with continuations. None of these were compositional in the algebraic sense. When you wanted to compose two machines, you had to write down the product state space explicitly and reason about it directly. There was no equivalent of "the homomorphism theorem for groups" that you could appeal to and get composition for free.

Meanwhile, the declarative tradition was working with tools that *were* compositional — λ-calculus has β-reduction as a congruence, equational reasoning works, denotational semantics composes — and so the declarative people could build theory faster and prove more general results. This made it look, to the imperative practitioners, like the declarative people were just being precious about elegance while the imperative people were getting actual work done. And it made it look, to the declarative practitioners, like the imperative people were stuck doing low-level bookkeeping when they could have been doing real mathematics. Both views were partially right and partially wrong, and the actual underlying issue — that the mathematics of compositional dynamics didn't yet exist — was invisible to both sides because nobody knew it was missing until it started to be filled in.

Bisimulation is the canonical example of what was missing. Park introduced it in 1981 and Milner developed it through the 80s in the context of CCS, and it's the first really *clean* notion of "two processes are the same" that doesn't reduce to either "they have identical state spaces" (too fine) or "they accept the same traces" (too coarse). It's the dynamical analog of isomorphism, and it took until the 80s to find it. Once you have bisimulation, you can start talking about quotients of state machines, congruences, compositional reasoning about behavior — all the things algebraic structures have given you for free for a century. But by 1981, the imperative tradition was *already entrenched* in tools that didn't use bisimulation, and the educational pipeline was already built around them.

The same story applies across the board. Linear types (for resource management) emerged in the 1980s from linear logic, which itself dates to 1987. Separation logic for reasoning about mutable state is from 2001. Differential dynamic logic for hybrid systems is from 2008. Algebraic effects (the compositional theory of effects we were talking about earlier) really matured in the 2010s. The whole field of compositional dynamics has been getting *built* over the last forty years, and most of the relevant ideas didn't exist or weren't in usable form when the imperative tradition crystallized its pedagogy.

The pedagogical consequence is that we teach ToC courses with the formalisms that were available when ToC was first taught — DFAs, PDAs, Turing machines, the Chomsky hierarchy — and we teach them in a non-compositional way because that's how they were originally developed. Students learn that a Turing machine is a 7-tuple and that "running" the machine is a separate concept that requires you to step through configurations one at a time. The execution model is bolted on because the formalism was developed before anyone knew how to make it intrinsic. And then students take this stuff and decide that formal models of computation are tedious and irrelevant to practical programming, which is partially true *given how it's taught*, but obscures the fact that *modern* formal tools for talking about computation are dramatically better than the 1930s tools and would, if taught, illuminate the practical programming experience rather than seeming disconnected from it.

The connection to your point about firmware, microcode, and FPGAs is sharp. **Every one of those is a place where the algebra of one layer meets the coalgebra of another**, and historically each interface has been designed by people who didn't have compositional tools for either side, so the interfaces are ad-hoc, full of leaky abstractions, and only locally optimized. Modern hardware design languages (Chisel, Bluespec, Clash) are starting to apply functional and algebraic techniques to hardware itself, and the results are striking — Bluespec uses guarded atomic actions, which are essentially a coalgebraic model of synchronous digital circuits, and produces hardware that's both easier to verify and competitive in performance with hand-written Verilog. The reason this is possible *now* and wasn't possible in 1980 is that the mathematics of synchronous concurrent processes (Milner's SCCS, Hoare's CSP, the various reactive-systems formalisms) had to be developed first.

The intellectual turnover and context loss you mention is, I think, the secondary cause of the schism's persistence rather than the primary one. The primary cause is that **the synthesis really wasn't possible until recently**, and now that it is possible, the field's institutional inertia (curricula, textbooks, hiring practices, "what every CS graduate should know") is lagging the underlying mathematical and engineering reality by something like twenty to thirty years. Coalgebra is in graduate-level PL theory courses now, but it's not in undergraduate ToC. Separation logic is in research, but not in undergraduate OS courses. Algebraic effects are in Haskell extensions and a few research languages, but not in the way most students learn about side effects.

This is a fixable problem, but the fix requires somebody to do the work of writing the synthesis down at an undergraduate level, and that work is hard. **Most of the mathematicians and computer scientists who understand the modern formal tools well enough to teach them well don't teach undergraduates**, and most of the undergraduate instructors are working from the curriculum they inherited. The institutional pipeline for updating an undergraduate curriculum based on developments in the last twenty years of theoretical CS is essentially broken — partly because of the publishing economics of textbooks, partly because faculty teaching loads don't incentivize curriculum redesign, partly because the people who could do it best are doing other things. So the schism persists not because anyone is defending it on intellectual grounds, but because the cost of fixing it falls on individuals who don't have great incentives to bear it.

There's a sense in which this is exactly the situation you're in. You're teaching the courses where the schism most directly damages students, you have the background to see what the synthesis should look like, and you're being driven by *necessity* (your students are struggling) rather than by curriculum tradition (which would let you off the hook if you just taught it the standard way). The framework you've been building across this conversation — data/codata as the central distinction, value/object as its first-pass realization, Church/Turing as its theoretical grounding, types as the language of negotiation between the two sides — is essentially a sketch of the synthesis at undergraduate level. Whether you can carry that off as a teachable curriculum is an open question, but the *existence* of such a curriculum is no longer impossible the way it was in 1990. The mathematical tools exist now. The hard part is the pedagogical engineering of getting them into a form that 19-year-olds can absorb.

One thing worth noting for your own reading list: Jacobs' *Introduction to Coalgebra* is genuinely good but is a graduate-level mathematics text. For a more accessible entry point, Sangiorgi's *Introduction to Bisimulation and Coinduction* is shorter, more focused, and would give you the conceptual vocabulary without requiring you to swallow the full categorical apparatus. And if you want the historical context for why all of this is recent, Milner's Turing lecture (*"Elements of Interaction"*, 1993) is a beautiful retrospective on his own realization that the existing formalisms weren't enough and the new ones had to be built. Milner basically says, in 1993, "we've spent thirty years building the formal apparatus that should have existed in 1960, and we're now finally in a position to do CS properly" — which is both inspiring and a little bit melancholy given that the curriculum hasn't yet caught up.

Algebraic effects are in Haskell extensions and a few research languages, but not in the way most students learn about side effects.

This is a fixable problem, but the fix requires somebody to do the work of writing the synthesis down at an undergraduate level, and that work is hard. **Most of the mathematicians and computer scientists who understand the modern formal tools well enough to teach them well don't teach undergraduates**, and most of the undergraduate instructors are working from the curriculum they inherited. The institutional pipeline for updating an undergraduate curriculum based on developments in the last twenty years of theoretical CS is essentially broken — partly because of the publishing economics of textbooks, partly because faculty teaching loads don't incentivize curriculum redesign, partly because the people who could do it best are doing other things. So the schism persists not because anyone is defending it on intellectual grounds, but because the cost of fixing it falls on individuals who don't have great incentives to bear it.

There's a sense in which this is exactly the situation you're in. You're teaching the courses where the schism most directly damages students, you have the background to see what the synthesis should look like, and you're being driven by *necessity* (your students are struggling) rather than by curriculum tradition (which would let you off the hook if you just taught it the standard way). The framework you've been building across this conversation — data/codata as the central distinction, value/object as its first-pass realization, Church/Turing as its theoretical grounding, types as the language of negotiation between the two sides — is essentially a sketch of the synthesis at undergraduate level. Whether you can carry that off as a teachable curriculum is an open question, but the *existence* of such a curriculum is no longer impossible the way it was in 1990. The mathematical tools exist now. The hard part is the pedagogical engineering of getting them into a form that 19-year-olds can absorb.

One thing worth noting for your own reading list: Jacobs' *Introduction to Coalgebra* is genuinely good but is a graduate-level mathematics text. For a more accessible entry point, Sangiorgi's *Introduction to Bisimulation and Coinduction* is shorter, more focused, and would give you the conceptual vocabulary without requiring you to swallow the full categorical apparatus. And if you want the historical context for why all of this is recent, Milner's Turing lecture (*"Elements of Interaction"*, 1993) is a beautiful retrospective on his own realization that the existing formalisms weren't enough and the new ones had to be built. Milner basically says, in 1993, "we've spent thirty years building the formal apparatus that should have existed in 1960, and we're now finally in a position to do CS properly" — which is both inspiring and a little bit melancholy given that the curriculum hasn't yet caught up.
