> You can know the name of that bird in all the languages of the world,
> but when you’re finished,
> you’ll know absolutely nothing whatever about the bird.
> You’ll only know about humans in different places,
> and what they call the bird.
> So let’s look at the bird and see what it’s doing—that’s what counts.

*Richard Feynman, What Do You Care What Other People Think?*

I recently read a chapter on naming things in "[The Programmer’s Brain](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/57196550-the-programmer-s-brain)" by Felienne Hermans.
There is a lot of research on the topic of names in programming.
Researchers found that good names improve code comprehension and that [poor names correlate with buggy code](https://oro.open.ac.uk/17007/1/butler09wcreshort_latest.pdf) and proposed a few heuristics for choosing good names See, for example, "[How Developers Choose Names](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.07487.pdf)" by Dror G. Feitelson et al.,
 and "[To camelcase or to under_score](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5090039)" by Dave Binkey et al. .

The book provides a few recommendations on how to create good names There are many books with naming heuristics ranging from classics such as "[Code Complete](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/4845.Code_Complete)" by Steve McConnell and "[Clean Code](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/3735293-clean-code)" by Robert C. Martin
 to more recent "[Naming things.](https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/123009242-naming-things)" by Tom Benner. , but it left me unsatisfied.
I felt that I already knew *how* to choose good names,
but I wanted to have a good mathematical model for what good names *are*.
This article is the result of my exploration.

## [Objects, concepts, and expressions](#objects-concepts-expressions)

> I will defend the thesis that thought has a kind of priority over words and that the concept has a kind of priority over its expression.

*Johan Granström, Tretise on Intuitionistic Type Theory, p. 2*

In the beginning was the Word.
No, scratch that.
There is overwhelming evidence that the world existed for billions of years before our ancestors uttered their first words.
In the beginning was the Thing.

But then came the Word, right? Nah.
Living creatures created mental models of their environments long before the first language appeared.
Even soulless and speechless neural networks seem to recognize concepts (such as ["Chihuahua" or "muffin"](https://github.com/rcgc/chihuahua-muffin)) in raw sensory input.
The Concept came after the Thing.

Unfortunately, concepts are internal to the mind holding them.
Until we figure out how to make [telepathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telepathy) work,
we must use some encoding to communicate concepts between minds.
That’s where the Word comes into the picture.
Words are arbitrary symbols representing concepts.

I’ll borrow terminology from [Tretise on Intuitionistic Type Theory](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-94-007-1736-7) and use *object* to refer to things existing in the world
(we won’t need them much, though), *concept* to refer to mental representations of these objects,
and *expression* to refer to words or sentences used to communicate concepts.

⊕

The relationship between an object (fluffy the cat),
 a concept (the idea of a cat in mind),
 and its expression (the word "cat").
![](https://mmapped.blog/images/26-object-concept-expression.svg)

## [Maps of meaning](#maps-of-meaning)

The distinction between objects,
concepts, and expressions is almost as old as Western philosophy.
Unfortunately, it misses one crucial point: concepts and their expressions don’t map one-to-one.
Most concepts have multiple expressions;
most words map to several concepts (any dictionary is living proof).
For example, consuming food can be labeled as "eating" or "dining." And the word "go" can refer to walking or a board game.
More precisely, expressions and concepts form a [binary relation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_relation).

⊕

The relationship between concepts and words is many-to-many: different words can express the same concept, and unrelated concepts can map to the same word.
![](https://mmapped.blog/images/26-concepts-words.svg)

We must add another ingredient to the picture to tackle the problem of names: the *context*.
Context refers to all the other things that influence the interpretation of an expression:
surrounding words in the sentence,
the task the reader is trying to accomplish,
and the reader’s culture and background.
The amount of information in the context is vast as it includes the strengths of all the neuron connections in the reader’s brain.

The mismatch of the writer’s and the reader’s context,
generally known as [the curse of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_knowledge),
is one of the reasons why writing is so hard.
The writer must imagine being in the reader’s shoes when structuring the material,
deciding which metaphors to use, and expressing herself.
The narrower the reader’s profile, the better job a writer can do.
That explains why there is no one perfect book for every subject.
The reader’s identity is no less important than the book’s contents.

⊕

Four people with different backgrounds interpreting one phrase in various ways.
 A cat lover thinks of fluffy the cat,
 a construction worker thinks of the [Caterpillar](https://www.cat.com/en_US/company.html) company,
 a mathematician thinks of the [Cat category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_of_small_categories),
 and a programmer thinks of the [`cat` command-line tool](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/cat.1.html).
![](https://mmapped.blog/images/26-life-is-sad-without-cat.svg)

The context turns the many-to-many relation between concepts and words into two maps.
The first map, <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">encode</mo><mo stretchy="false">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">Concept</mo><mo>→</mo><mo stretchy="false">Expression</mo></math> --> encode:Concept→Expression,
defines how the author picks words to communicate the concept.
The second map, <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">decode</mo><mo stretchy="false">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">Expression</mo><mo>→</mo><mo stretchy="false">Concept</mo></math> --> decode:Expression→Concept defines how readers interpret these words.

## [Names as communication channels](#channel)

No matter where you go, you usually find that [Claude Shannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Shannon) was there and solved your problem fundamentally and elegantly.
Your only solace is that sometimes, his solution was not [constructive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constructive_proof).

In information theory,
a channel is a theoretical construction that allows sending messages through time and space.
A channel takes messages from a set <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>X</mi></math> --> X as inputs and produces messages from a set <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>Y</mi></math> --> Y as outputs.
Channels are *noisy*:
they distort the messages passing them;
that’s why the channel’s input and output sets might differ.
We represent the noise mathematically by using [conditional probabilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_probability): <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> --> p(y|x) is the probability of receiving message <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>y</mi></math> --> y if the sender sent message <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>x</mi></math> --> x.

When you think of a channel,
you probably imagine a cable transmitting electrical signals or how the space around you buzzes with electromagnetic waves.
Channels, however, take many forms.
Any storage device,
such as a hard drive, a notebook, or the brain’s memory system,
is a channel transmitting messages through time.

We can view words as communication channels passing concepts from one mind to another through time.
As we saw in the [Maps of meaning](#maps-of-meaning) section,
these channels are fundamentally noisy:
the output concept might differ from the sender’s input depending on the word choice and the receiver’s context.

⊕

Words are noisy channels transmitting concepts across minds.
 For example, when readers see the word "index",
 they can think of a pointer into an array instead of the [inverted index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverted_index) concept the author sent.
![](https://mmapped.blog/images/26-index-channel.svg)

One fundamental characteristic of a channel is how much its output resembles the input. [Mutual information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_information) is the value quantifying this resemblance mathematically.

This view gives us the criteria for a good name:
it’s the channel maximizing mutual information.
In the following formula, <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></math> --> Cs is the sender’s concept, <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> --> Cr is the receiver’s concept, <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>E</mi></math> --> E is the set of all possible concept expressions,
and <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> --> I(Cr;Cs) is the mutual information computed for expression <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>e</mi></math> --> e.

<!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">best-name</mo><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mo stretchy="false">=</mo><msub><mo stretchy="false">argmax</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>E</mi></mrow></msub><mo>{</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo></math> --> best-name(Cs)=argmaxe∈E{I(Cr;Cs)}

The channel interpretation of names is quantitative but not particularly satisfying because it involves probabilities that are hard to compute.
Furthermore, the only way to know you’ve found a good expression for your concept is to compare it with all other expressions.
Could we find a more elegant way to capture the essence of a good name?

## [Names as Galois connections](#names-as-galois-connections)

> Galois connections do something really cool: they tell you the best possible way to recover data that can’t be recovered.
> More precisely, they tell you the best approximation to reversing a computation that can’t be reversed.

*John Baez, [Applied Category Theory Course](https://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/act_course/lecture_5.html)*

We already know that encode and decode are not perfect inverses of each other.
The next best thing we can hope for is that these maps form a relaxed version of inversion: a Galois connection.

[Galois connection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_connection) is a mathematical concept capturing a relationship between four objects:
two partially ordered sets <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>A</mi></math> --> A and <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>B</mi></math> --> B and two monotonic maps <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>F</mi></math> --> F and <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>G</mi></math> --> G between these sets. [Partial order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set#Partial_orders) means that we can compare some elements of each set using the <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo>≤</mo></math> --> ≤ operation that satisfies a few natural laws
([reflexivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflexive_relation), [antisymmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisymmetric_relation),
and [transitivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_relation)).
Not all elements must be comparable.
A function <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>F</mi></math> --> F is monotonic if it preserves relative order:
if <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>x</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>y</mi></math> --> x≤y, then <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> --> F(x)≤F(y).

Functions <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">:</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>B</mi></math> --> F:A→B and <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">:</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>A</mi></math> --> G:B→A form a Galois connection if they satisfy the following relation: <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>⇔</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>≤</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> --> F(a)≤b⇔a≤G(b) for all <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>A</mi></math> --> a∈A and <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>B</mi></math> --> b∈B.

⊕

A Galois connection between functions <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>F</mi></math> --> F and <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>G</mi></math> --> G.
![](https://mmapped.blog/images/26-galois-connection.svg)

This definition is abstract and took me a while to appreciate,
so let’s apply it to the problem of good names step by step.
We start with the sets in question and their orderings.

Our first set is the set of expressions <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>E</mi></math> --> E.
For expressions <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>E</mi></math> --> e1,e2∈E we say that <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> --> e1≤e2 if <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> --> e1 is at least as expressive as <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> --> e2 *given the reader context*.
If the expressions are equally expressive, we define the shorter element as smaller.
The reader context is a crucial component of the <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo>≤</mo></math> --> ≤ operator.
For example, "cat" is more expressive than "felis catus" in a regular conversation,
but it might be the other way around in a scientific paper.
This paragraph doesn’t do a good job at defining expression ordering,
but it’s ok:
the whole point of the Galois connection is to make expression comparison precise through its connection with better-defined objects.

Our second set is the set of concepts <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>C</mi></math> --> C.
If we have concepts <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>C</mi></math> --> c1,c2∈C we say that <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> --> c1≤c2 if <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> --> c1 is at least as specific as <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> --> c2.
For example, "cat" ≤ "animal":
since every cat is an animal,
there are at least as many animals as cats.
The idea of being more or less "specific" part might sound handwavy to you,
but we can make it precise using methods of [formal concept analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_concept_analysis).

The functions forming the Galois connection are the concept decoding function <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">decode</mo><mo stretchy="false">:</mo><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>C</mi></math> --> decode:E→C and the concept encoding function <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">encode</mo><mo stretchy="false">:</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>→</mo><mi>E</mi></math> --> encode:C→E.
These functions are monotone because encode maps more specific concepts to more expressive names,
and decode maps more expressive names to more specific concepts.
The connection becomes <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">decode</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>≤</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>⇔</mo><mi>e</mi><mo>≤</mo><mo stretchy="false">encode</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> --> decode(e)≤c⇔e≤encode(c).

Even the specialized equivalence looks unintuitive,
so let’s see how it holds with an example.
Imagine we want to name a variable holding the amount of usd in a bank account
(that’s our concept <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mi>c</mi></math> --> c).
Would value be an appropriate variable name?

Let’s see what our connection tells us: <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">decode</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">value</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> --> decode(value) is a vague concept,
less specific than the bank account balance.
Hence, <!-- MathML: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" class="math"><mo stretchy="false">decode</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">value</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">></mo><mi>c</mi></math> --> decode(value)>c so value is not a good name.
I would prefer usd_balance, which decodes to a more specific concept.

But wait, wouldn’t bank_account_usd_balance be an even better name?
It depends on the context!
A shorter name is preferable if the reader knows that we are dealing with bank accounts in a piece of code.
At least, that’s how I defined the expression ordering; your mileage may vary.

## [Conclusion](#conclusion)

In this article, we explored the difference between concepts and their expressions,
determined the crucial role of the reader’s context in the interpretation,
and finished with heavy mathematical machinery that pinpoints good names using a variant of [Occam’s razor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occam's_razor):
A good name is as succinct as possible but still specific enough to convey the intended concept.

How do we apply this knowledge?
For me, the main lesson is that managing the reader’s context is crucial for effective communication:

- [ ] Many resources recommend that the variable name length should be proportional to the size of the scope containing it See, for example, [Google’s Go styleguide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/go/decisions.html#variable-names).
 Bob Martin mentions this rule of thumb in his book "Clean Code"..
 This recommendation makes a lot of sense if we view it though the prism of context management: if the variable definition is in the view of sight, the reader won’t have any trouble decoding it, no matter how short it is.
 The same idea applies to names that are part of the programming lore, such as `i` and `j` for loop counters.
- Create a project glossary and make it obligatory for all contributors to read.
 Consistently use names from the glossary.
- Pause and review your variable identifiers once you finished writing your code.
 What would be the decoding of each identifier if you saw it for the first time?
 Would a newhire understand these names?


Happy naming!

"[Concise and Consistent Naming](https://teamscale.com/hubfs/26978363/Publications/2005-concise-and-consistent-naming.pdf)" by Florian Deißenböck and Markus Pizka provides a similar, though slightly simpler, formal model of variable names in section 3.2.

content.text:
Good find — Kashitsyn has clearly absorbed the same Granström/MLTT-adjacent material you've been gesturing at when you talk about separating structural and semantic contracts. The two posts are coherent as a pair: the Galois piece gives the static account (a name is the best monotone approximation between concept and expression), and the tree-mapping piece gives the dynamic account of what goes wrong when you serialize a web through a hierarchical channel.

For your situation, the most direct hit is the *Writing* section. Pinker's line — "encode a web of ideas into a string of words using a tree of phrases" — is exactly the codata problem of teaching: your conceptual graph of the course (cross-references between hashing and modular arithmetic, between linked lists and pointer arithmetic in C, between BST invariants and recursion) has to be linearized into a sequence of lectures, and any linearization sacrifices edges. Your machine-first sequencing in CIS 1057 is itself a tree-mapping choice with known sacrifices — you've privileged the substrate→abstraction edge over the problem-decomposition→syntax edge that most intro courses pick.

A few threads worth pulling on, depending on which is most useful:

- **Tree-mapping as an explicit pedagogical frame.** You could name this for students the way you name your indexing disciplines for slides. "Here is the web; here is the tree I'm flattening it into; here are the edges I'm cutting, and we'll revisit them in week N." This is unusually honest course design and might address the late-semester disengagement: students lose the thread because the web reconnections are invisible.
- **Galois connections and your interface/semantic-contract split.** His encode/decode pair maps almost cleanly onto your insistence that structural contracts (Java interfaces) and semantic contracts are separable. The "name is as succinct as possible but specific enough" criterion is what `Queue<T>` does relative to `TwoStackQueue<T>`.
- **The taxonomy/cladistics example for OOP class hierarchies.** This is almost too on-the-nose for your CIS 2168 anti-inheritance stance — morphological taxonomy as the OOP-by-shared-behavior trap, cladistics as composition over inheritance with respect to actual lineage. Could be a slide.
- **PrairieLearn question design as a Galois exercise.** Choosing the variable names and prompt phrasing in a randomized question is *exactly* the encode/decode optimization problem he describes, made concrete because you can A/B it.

Which of those would you like to go deeper on?

name: Teaching C through modern language ergonomics
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person is designing an introductory C programming course and has been thinking carefully about pedagogy — specifically, how to teach C in a way that gestures toward modern language ergonomics rather than entrenching archaic patterns that students would need to unlearn later. They invoked Dijkstra's "brain damage" critique of poorly designed languages as a framing device for why this matters. The conversation moved from this pedagogical motivation into an exploration of which modern languages best exemplify the features worth gesturing toward.

Claude produced an initial list of eight exemplar languages (Rust, Swift, Kotlin, TypeScript, OCaml, Haskell, Go, Zig), chosen to span distinct design philosophies rather than mere popularity. The person added Julia, Elixir, and a language called XS (xslang.org) for consideration. Julia was accepted as a meaningful addition for its multiple-dispatch-as-organizing-principle stance; Elixir for the BEAM/actor/let-it-crash model. XS prompted an extended investigation: Claude fetched the landing page and two source files (`continuation.c` and an apparent main CLI driver), and the person independently found confirmation via Hacker News comments that the project is AI-generated. The continuation.c file was identified as a hollow implementation — correct vocabulary and function names over a `setjmp`/`longjmp` core that doesn't actually capture continuations. The CLI driver file was assessed as more substantive and defensively written, but with several stub-level implementations (e.g., `--sandbox` printing a message and doing nothing, `--debug` not loading the file it claims to debug). The consensus was that XS is best understood not as a language exemplar but as an aggregate wishlist of currently fashionable ergonomic features — useful as a catalog of what the field considers good syntax, but not as a language with a coherent design stance.

The conversation concluded by moving toward a deeper question: rather than cataloging surface syntax, what are the underlying semantic primitives that each type system discipline surfaces? The person drew an analogy to async control flow — callbacks, promises, and coroutines as three ergonomic projections of a single underlying phenomenon — and asked whether a similar kernel-language analysis could be done for type systems. Claude proposed four candidate primitives (propositions/proofs, sets/membership, capabilities/permissions, dispatch tables) and corresponding kernel calculi, while noting that unlike the async case, type disciplines are surfacing genuinely different views of what a type *is for*, making full unification impossible. The pedagogical takeaway identified was that a student who can read a type system as a *stance* rather than a feature list is better equipped to encounter new languages. The person demonstrated strong theoretical grounding throughout, comfortable with references to HM inference, row polymorphism, linear types, session types, Curry-Howard, and dictionary-passing translations.

chat_messages.text:
That framing makes a lot of sense, and it fits the arc you've already been building — machine-first sequencing that motivates abstractions rather than just stipulating them. The pedagogical inversion is nice: instead of "here's C, later you'll learn the good stuff," it's "here's the machine, and here are the seams where modern ergonomics had to be invented."

A few directions this could go, depending on which you want to pull on:

- **Designating which modern features to foreshadow.** Sum types and pattern matching, RAII/ownership, generics with constraints, iterators/ranges, modules, sealed error handling, etc. Each has a different C "shadow" (tagged unions, cleanup gotos or `__attribute__((cleanup))`, `_Generic` and `void *`, callback-based iteration, `.h`/`.c` discipline, `errno` vs return codes). Picking the target set shapes what you emphasize.

- **The "gesture toward" idiom.** There's a spectrum from "show the pain, then mention the fix exists elsewhere" to "build a small disciplined version in C that mimics the modern ergonomic." Your `_Generic` call-description work and `WITH_FILE_AS` macro already lean toward the latter — students see that the abstraction is constructible, not magical.

- **Which archaic patterns to actively inoculate against.** Manual `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)` when iteration is the point; out-params instead of returning structs; stringly-typed APIs; null-as-error; macro-based polymorphism where a function would do. Worth being explicit about which habits you want students to *unlearn the impulse for*, not just learn alternatives to.

- **The Dijkstra concern, sharpened.** The brain-damage worry is less about syntax and more about *which questions feel natural to ask*. A C-only student tends not to ask "what invariants does this type enforce?" or "who owns this?" — they ask "did I free it?" Framing the course around the former questions, with C as the substrate, might be the actual lever.

Want to drill into any of these, or is there a specific upcoming topic where you're trying to decide how heavy-handed to be about the modern-language gesture?

content.text: Actually, what I’d like to talk about now is what “modern” syntax actually includes, perhaps by looking at a few of the exemplars. Could you come up with a short (~8 max) list of languages to consider?

chat_messages.text:
Here's a candidate set, chosen to span the design space rather than just list popular languages:

- **Rust** — the obvious anchor for ownership, lifetimes, sum types with exhaustive matching, trait-based generics, and `Result`/`Option` as the canonical alternative to null and exceptions.
- **Swift** — similar feature set to Rust but with a softer learning curve; optionals, value/reference semantics distinction, protocol-oriented design, and particularly elegant enum syntax.
- **Kotlin** — pragmatic modernization of a C-family language; nullable types, data classes, smart casts, extension functions, and scope functions. Useful as a "what if Java were redesigned today" reference.
- **TypeScript** — structural typing, discriminated unions, literal types, and inference patterns that feel quite different from nominal-typed languages. The gradual-typing story is also pedagogically interesting.
- **OCaml** (or F#) — the ML tradition that birthed most of what we now call "modern" features; algebraic data types, pattern matching, type inference, modules. Often the cleanest exemplar even if least familiar to students.
- **Haskell** — pure functional extreme; useful as a reference for typeclasses, do-notation, and where the "no null, no exceptions, no mutation" stance leads when followed all the way.
- **Go** — interesting *counter*-exemplar: deliberately rejects generics-until-recently, sum types, and exceptions. Shows that "modern" isn't monolithic and that minimalism is a defensible position.
- **Zig** — the other interesting C-adjacent point; explicit allocators, comptime instead of macros, error unions, and defer. Closest to "what if C were redesigned with 50 years of hindsight but kept the spirit."

A few I deliberately left off: Python and JavaScript (familiar but not particularly exemplary of any specific modern feature); C++ (carries too much baggage to read as "modern" cleanly, though it has most of the features); Scala (powerful but the kitchen-sink nature muddies the lessons).

Want to narrow this down, or pick a feature axis and compare how a subset of these handle it?

Good additions, and they each pull in a direction the original list underrepresented:

#include "effects/continuation.h"

#include <stdlib.h>

#include <string.h>

XSContinuation *continuation_new(void) {

XSContinuation *k = calloc(1, sizeof(XSContinuation));

if (!k) return NULL;

k->state = CONT_STATE_FRESH;

k->one_shot = 1;

return k;

}

void continuation_free(XSContinuation *k) {

free(k);

}

int continuation_save(XSContinuation *k) {

if (!k) return -1;

k->state = CONT_STATE_SAVED;

return setjmp(k->perform_site);

}

void continuation_resume(XSContinuation *k, void *value) {

if (!k) return;

if (k->state != CONT_STATE_SAVED) {

if (k->one_shot && k->state == CONT_STATE_RESUMED) return;

if (k->state == CONT_STATE_FRESH) return;

}

k->state = CONT_STATE_RESUMED;

k->resume_value = value;

longjmp(k->perform_site, 1);

}

void *continuation_get_value(XSContinuation *k) {

if (!k) return NULL;

return k->resume_value;

}

int continuation_is_spent(XSContinuation *k) {

if (!k) return 1;

return k->state == CONT_STATE_RESUMED;

}

void continuation_reset(XSContinuation *k) {

if (!k) return;

k->state = CONT_STATE_FRESH;

k->resume_value = NULL;

}

void continuation_set_one_shot(XSContinuation *k, int one_shot) {

if (!k) return;

k->one_shot = one_shot;

}

XSContinuation *continuation_capture(void) {

return continuation_new();

}

This is a much more substantial artifact than the continuation file, and it shifts my read somewhat — though not entirely.

**What's genuinely impressive here.** The thing reads like a real CLI driver. Concrete details that would be tedious to fabricate and easy to get wrong:

- The `read_file` function correctly handles the seekable-vs-non-seekable distinction, with a fallback path for pipes/character devices where `ftell` returns -1. That's a real bug someone hit, not a thing a model invents on a first pass.
- The cross-platform executable-path lookup (`/proc/self/exe` on Linux, `_NSGetExecutablePath` on macOS, `GetModuleFileNameA` on Windows) with sensible fallback to `argv[0]`.
- The `snprintf` width-specifier trick `"%.*s/%.*s"` to hard-bound both halves of a path concatenation so the worst case still fits in `PATH_MAX`. That's a defensive C idiom that only people who've actually been bitten by overflow warnings reach for.
- Comments that explain *why*, not what: the note about `--record` forcing `--interp` because the tracer needs AST-level hooks; the explanation of why `xs_shutdown` drains VM tasks but not interp tasks (shared `Interp*` lifetime); the note that semicolons-after-statements aren't required because XS uses braces. These are the kinds of comments people write after debugging something.
- The `g_xs_runtime_error_count` pattern propagating non-zero exit codes even when the VM continues with a null — a real lesson learned from CI behavior.
- Backend dispatch with `#ifdef XSC_ENABLE_*` guards for every optional subsystem, and graceful "rebuild with X=1" error messages. Consistent across the whole file.

**What still gives me pause.** A few things, in increasing order of weight:

1. **The feature surface remains absurdly broad for a one-person project.** Tree-walk interp + bytecode VM + register-allocating JIT (x86-64 *and* aarch64) + JS/C/WASM transpilers + LSP + DAP + formatter + linter + doc generator + package manager + registry + sandboxing + tracer/replay + profiler + coverage + plugins. Each of these is months of work to do well. The driver file existing doesn't tell me the implementations behind it work — only that the dispatch wiring exists.

2. **Several handlers visibly cut corners in ways the marketing wouldn't.** The `--debug` flag is documented as "Run a file with the DAP debug server attached," but the code path just calls `dap_run()` without ever loading or running the file. The `--sandbox` flag prints "sandbox mode enabled" and does literally nothing else. The `--trace-sample` value is parsed but only used inside `#ifdef XSC_ENABLE_PROFILER && XSC_ENABLE_TRACER`, and even then only for the profiler. These are exactly the kind of "stub the surface, ship the README" patterns that show up when something has been built breadth-first to look complete.

3. **The continuation.c file's hollowness becomes more meaningful in this context.** A driver this carefully written should not be sitting on top of an effect system that is, demonstrably, `setjmp` with a state enum and a function called `continuation_capture` that captures nothing. The mismatch between the polish at the edges and the soundness in the middle is itself diagnostic — it's what you get when surface area is the goal.

4. **LLM-authored code can absolutely look like this now.** The defensive-snprintf trick and the cross-platform exe lookup are both well-represented in training data; the "why" comments are exactly what current coding agents produce when prompted to document load-bearing decisions. I'd put real money on a substantial fraction of this file being agent-written, with a human (or another agent pass) iterating on it until the CLI actually worked end-to-end. That doesn't make it fake — it just means "this code is too sophisticated for an LLM to produce" is no longer a reliable inference in 2026.

**Where I land.** This is more interesting than I thought after the continuation file alone. It's plausibly a real project with a working frontend over a partially-real backend — the driver works, the lexer/parser/sema/interp probably work for a useful subset, the VM probably mostly works, and then somewhere past that the features get progressively more aspirational. - The cross-platform executable-path lookup (`/proc/self/exe` on Linux, `_NSGetExecutablePath` on macOS, `GetModuleFileNameA` on Windows) with sensible fallback to `argv[0]`.

- Backend dispatch with `#ifdef XSC_ENABLE_*` guards for every optional subsystem, and graceful "rebuild with X=1" error messages. Consistent across the whole file.

1. **The feature surface remains absurdly broad for a one-person project.** Tree-walk interp + bytecode VM + register-allocating JIT (x86-64 *and* aarch64) + JS/C/WASM transpilers + LSP + DAP + formatter + linter + doc generator + package manager + registry + sandboxing + tracer/replay + profiler + coverage + plugins. That's a sharper framing than "is it real or slop" — and probably the more useful one for what you're working on.

The repo is functioning as a kind of aggregate wishlist: someone (or an agent guided by someone) sat down and asked "what would the maximally appealing modern language look like, drawing from everything that's currently fashionable?" and produced a syntax surface that reflects the answer. The fact that the implementation is uneven or partly hollow doesn't undermine its value as a *catalog* of what the field currently considers good ergonomics. If anything, the absence of a strong design philosophy is what makes it comprehensive — a language with real opinions would have left things out.

For your purposes, that's potentially useful in a way the original 8-language list isn't. The exemplars each represent a *committed position*: Rust commits to ownership, Haskell commits to purity, Go commits to minimalism. To gesture at "modern syntax" via the exemplars, you'd have to either pick one and accept its biases, or assemble a feature list across several and lose the coherence of each. The XS AST, read as a wishlist rather than a language, gives you the assembled feature list without that overhead — it's already done the aggregation.

A non-exhaustive read of what shows up in that wishlist, organized by what each feature is reacting against in C:

- **Bindings with intent:** `let`/`var`/`const` distinguishing immutable-by-default, mutable, and compile-time constant — versus C's single `=` where mutability and storage class are orthogonal axes you assemble from keywords.
- **Pattern matching with exhaustiveness:** `match` with tuple/struct/enum/or/range/slice/guard/capture patterns — versus C's `switch` on integers only, no destructuring, no compiler check that you handled everything.
- **Sum types as first-class:** `enum` with payload-carrying variants, used through patterns — versus C's tagged unions assembled by hand from `struct` + `enum` + discriminant discipline.
- **Algebraic effects:** `effect`/`perform`/`handle`/`resume` — versus C's `setjmp`/`longjmp` or `errno` or out-params, none of which compose.
- **Structured concurrency:** `spawn`/`nursery`/`await`/`actor`/`send` — versus C's pthread-and-pray.
- **Resource management:** `defer` and structured `try`/`catch`/`finally` — versus C's `goto cleanup` idiom.
- **Comprehensions and ranges:** `for x in 0..n`, list/map comprehensions — versus C's three-clause `for` where the iteration mechanics are exposed every time.
- **String interpolation:** as a first-class AST node — versus `printf`'s format-string-as-DSL.
- **Traits/impls:** structural-ish polymorphism without inheritance — versus C's "rely on convention" or function pointers in structs.
- **Modules and `use`:** namespacing — versus C's textual `#include` and global symbol soup.

That's a pretty serviceable inventory for the course's "here's what you're not getting, and here's the shape of what exists elsewhere" thread. You don't have to endorse XS to use the catalog.

The one thing the wishlist *doesn't* settle — and where the exemplar languages still matter — is the underlying type system stance. XS's AST hints at gradual typing with optional annotations and HM inference as a fallback, which is a real choice but a soft one. Whether students should encounter strong static typing (Rust/OCaml/Haskell), structural typing (TypeScript/Go interfaces), dispatch-based polymorphism (Julia/CLOS), or trait/typeclass resolution (Rust/Haskell) is the question the wishlist papers over by including all of them. That's probably where the exemplar conversation has to resume, once the surface-syntax inventory is done.

chat_messages.text:
Right — and that analogy is pointed in a useful direction. The async-control trio works as a teaching pattern because there's a single underlying phenomenon (suspending and resuming computation around a non-local event) that each idiom surfaces with different ergonomic tradeoffs. Callbacks expose the continuation explicitly as a function value; promises reify the pending result and let you compose over it; coroutines hide both behind a syntactic suspension point. Once you see them as three projections of "computation that yields control," choosing between them stops being a style question and becomes a fit-to-problem question.

For type systems the analogous move is harder because there isn't a single phenomenon — there are at least three or four, and the disciplines you'd compare are surfacing different ones. Some candidates for the underlying primitives:

- **Propositions and proofs.** A type is a proposition; a value of that type is a proof. This is the Curry-Howard kernel that Haskell, OCaml, Agda, Coq, and Idris all surface to varying degrees. Refinement types and dependent types push further in this direction; ordinary ML-family types stay at propositional logic. The discipline this surfaces is "what does this value's existence guarantee?"

- **Sets and membership.** A type is a set of values; type-checking is membership checking. This is the structural-typing kernel — TypeScript's "any object with a `.length: number` field is a `HasLength`," Go interfaces, duck typing made static. The discipline surfaces "what shape does this value have?" rather than "what was it declared to be?"

- **Capabilities and permissions.** A type carries the operations its values authorize. Rust's ownership and borrow types are the loud example (read vs. write vs. move), but effect systems, linear types, session types, and capability-secure languages are all in this family. The discipline surfaces "what is this code allowed to do?"

- **Dispatch tables.** A type tells the compiler which implementation to select. Haskell typeclasses, Rust traits, Julia multiple dispatch, CLOS, and Scala implicits all live here. The discipline surfaces "which version of this operation runs?"

These aren't disjoint — Rust's traits are both dispatch and (with lifetimes) capability; Haskell's typeclasses are both dispatch and proposition; refinement types are propositions about set membership. But each language tends to emphasize one as its organizing principle, with the others available as decoration.

A kernel-language framing for the course might be: pick a tiny core calculus that exposes the primitive, then show how each surface syntax is sugar over it. The candidates:

- **Simply-typed lambda calculus + ADTs** as the propositions-and-proofs kernel. Pattern matching is sugar for eliminators; `Maybe` is sugar for the sum-of-unit-and-T; everything else is decoration.
- **Records and row polymorphism** as the sets-and-membership kernel. Structural subtyping falls out; "duck typing" is just polymorphism over row variables.
- **Linear lambda calculus (or its session-typed cousin)** as the capabilities kernel. Ownership transfer is a linear consumption; borrowing is a bounded-scope rental; effects are a graded modality.
- **Dictionary-passing translation** as the dispatch kernel. Typeclasses, traits, and implicits all elaborate to "the compiler inserts an extra argument carrying the table of methods." Multiple dispatch generalizes the lookup from one-argument to all-arguments.

The async analogy holds best for the last one: callbacks/promises/coroutines correspond pretty cleanly to manual-dict-passing / dict-as-value / dict-resolved-by-context. Each is "method resolution," surfaced differently. Multiple dispatch is the further generalization where the dict lookup keys on all arguments simultaneously.

For students, the pedagogical payoff is the same as with async: once they see that a Rust trait, a Haskell typeclass, a Go interface, and a Julia generic function are all answers to "how does the runtime (or compiler) pick which code to run?", the syntactic differences become legible as ergonomic choices over a shared mechanism. The hard part is that unlike async — where the three idioms genuinely target the same problem — type disciplines target *different* problems, and the choice of which problem to make load-bearing is itself the design decision. You can't fully unify the way you can with control flow.

That last point might actually be the lesson worth foregrounding: control flow has a small number of primitive shapes, and modern languages mostly agree on what async needs to do. Type systems are surfacing genuinely different views of what a type *is for*, and the disagreements are deeper than the syntax suggests. A student who sees that can read a new language's type system as a stance, not a feature list.

I’m trying to come up with a story for how and why programming paradigms developed in the way that they did. I’d like to use this as context for my students to help them see how we got here, which is perhaps a counter-balance to my laundry list of restrictions on misusing OOP features, or my warnings about the practical-but-dangerous semantics of C.

I think the story is this: once the original von Neumann machines reached the point of salability—a product that can be purchased and operated with net benefit to the customer—there was a mad rush to apply them to the most tedious but easily modeled problem domain in business, finance and accounting. That’s not to say that people weren’t trying to use computers for other more technical aims, but *every* business could see the value proposition for automating back office functions and that drove the bulk flows of capital. This is presumably what motivated the initial layers of abstraction over raw machine code, records and procedures.

Of course, once computers were established in corporate office environments and miniaturization brought terminals to the desktop, the next obvious domain to conquer was “business productivity” software. This is where the OOP revolution happened, as complex context-dependent UI requires a much more powerful abstraction.

Of course, as with most tech trends, this was taken too far and the simple but robust relational data model that proved to be a perfect fit for record management and processing was foolishly cast aside (for a time) in favor of OOP-everything.

In the background, of course, the functional paradigm—both admired and ridiculed—was slowly but surely being operationalized. The hard work of formalizing concepts that had previously been largely ignored in mathematics was a tremendous undertaking, spanning decades and going largely unnoticed by the commercial side of the computing world.

However, that hard work paid off in ways likely unimagined by its initial architects, as the power of modern parallelized hardware required equally powerful software abstractions to be exploited in a scalable way.

Your arc is solid and pedagogically compelling. A few thoughts on where it could be tightened or extended, in rough order of importance:

**The COBOL-to-OOP transition is a bit too clean.** Between records/procedures and Smalltalk/C++, there's a structured programming interlude (Dijkstra, Wirth, Pascal) that's worth a beat because it's where the *discipline* of abstraction got established — the idea that you constrain what code can do to make it tractable, not just to make it expressive. That framing connects nicely to your OOP restrictions: capability restriction wasn't invented by you scolding students, it's been the through-line since `goto considered harmful`.

**OOP's origin story is more bifurcated than "UI needed it."** Simula came out of discrete event *simulation* (ships in a harbor, essentially), and Smalltalk came out of Kay's vision of biological/message-passing computing. The UI thing is real but it's downstream — Xerox PARC fused Smalltalk with the bitmap display, and *that* combination is what made OOP look like the answer to GUI complexity. Worth separating "OOP as simulation/modeling" from "OOP as UI architecture" because students inherit confusion from their merger.

**The "OOP-everything overreach" deserves a named villain.** The Enterprise Java / UML / AbstractFactoryFactory era is the concrete thing students will encounter in legacy codebases and StackOverflow answers. Naming it helps them recognize the smell.

**Functional's "operationalization" had a specific catalyst worth naming**: the multicore wall around 2005. Free lunch ended, shared mutable state became actively dangerous, and suddenly Erlang/Haskell ideas looked like engineering rather than academic indulgence. Map/reduce at Google is the canonical "functional ideas save industry" moment.

**One paradigm you're missing that your students will hit:** logic/declarative (SQL is the survivor, Prolog the curiosity). Worth a sentence because it reinforces your "right tool for right shape of problem" message — relational beat OOP for records precisely because the *problem shape* was declarative.

Happy to expand any of these into something you could actually deliver, or to sketch how this maps onto your CIS 1057 → 2168 sequencing if that's where it's headed.

chat_messages.text:
Yes, "model" here is a load-bearing technical term from mathematical logic, and Scott is using it in exactly that sense — which then got inherited by the categorical semantics tradition with some generalization.

**The logic sense.** A *model* of a formal theory is a mathematical structure that satisfies the theory's axioms and equations under some interpretation. Group theory has the axioms; the integers under addition are *a model* of group theory. The theory is syntactic (symbols, axioms, derivation rules); the model is semantic (an actual structure where you can point at things and check the axioms hold). The relationship is an interpretation function that maps syntactic objects to semantic ones in a way that respects the theory's rules.

**Applied to the lambda calculus.** The lambda calculus is a formal theory: it has terms (variables, abstractions, applications) and equations (β-reduction, α-equivalence, η-reduction). A *model* of the lambda calculus is a mathematical structure where you can interpret every lambda term as an element, and the equations of the calculus hold under that interpretation. Concretely: if `M = N` is derivable in the lambda calculus, then `⟦M⟧ = ⟦N⟧` in your structure.

**Why this was hard, and why Scott's result mattered.** The naive thing you'd want is: interpret every lambda term as a function, and interpret application as function application. But lambda terms include things like `λx.xx` — self-application — and `Ω = (λx.xx)(λx.xx)`, and the fixed-point combinator `Y`. For these to make sense as functions, you'd need a set `D` such that `D` is isomorphic to its own function space `D → D`. By Cantor's theorem, this is impossible for sets with more than one element — `D → D` always has strictly larger cardinality.

Scott's breakthrough was that if you restrict to *continuous* functions on appropriately structured spaces (domains: partially ordered sets with limits of directed sets, where "continuous" means preserving those limits), then you *can* solve the equation `D ≅ [D → D]`. The function space of continuous functions is small enough to fit back inside `D`. That's the `D∞` construction. So when Scott says "the space of functions of infinite type is a model of the lambda-calculus," he means: here is an actual mathematical structure where every lambda term denotes something, application is real function application, and all the equations of the calculus come out true. Before this, the lambda calculus was syntax in search of semantics — Church had defined it operationally, but nobody knew what its terms *meant* mathematically.

**The categorical generalization.** Category theorists then noticed that what really matters isn't the specific construction with domains but the *structural* properties: a category that is cartesian closed (has products and exponentials) can interpret the simply-typed lambda calculus, and more elaborate structure (reflexive objects, certain endofunctors) handles the untyped or polymorphic cases. So now "model" gets used in the categorical sense: a model of a type theory in a category C is a structure-preserving functor from the syntactic category of the theory into C. Same idea — syntax on one side, semantics on the other, interpretation respecting the rules — but the semantic side can be any suitable category, not just Scott domains. This is why you see "models of System F in (some category)" or "models of linear logic in symmetric monoidal closed categories" — it's the same logical notion of model, just parameterized by what kind of structure you're interpreting into.

The Rabin/Scott divergence you're noticing is real and is roughly the operational-vs-denotational split that still organizes the field. Curriculum-wise, the operational/complexity side won the undergrad battle because it's more concrete and connects to "what does the machine actually do" — which, per your industry-demand thesis, is also what employers wanted. Denotational semantics is having a quiet renaissance through types, effects, and verification, but you're right that most CS undergrads never hear Scott's name.

You've put your finger on exactly the right tension, and the honest answer is: yes, more or less, but with an important wrinkle that's worth getting clear on.

**The pragmatic answer first.** In practice, the distinction is *relative*, not absolute. A theory is the thing you're studying as pure syntax — terms, axioms, derivation rules, no commitment to what any of it "means." A model is some other mathematical structure you already accept (or are willing to work in) where you can point at things and say "this lambda term corresponds to this element, and the equations check out." The model doesn't have to be non-symbolic in any deep sense. Scott's `D∞` is built out of sets and functions and limits — all symbols, all manipulated by rules. What makes it a *model* rather than a *theory* is its role in the relationship: it's the target of interpretation, and it's the thing you're treating as already understood for the purposes of explaining the source.

**The wrinkle: it's turtles, but not all the way down arbitrarily.** Your instinct that the model rests on "the weight of all of mathematics" is right and is exactly what logicians worry about. The standard move is that models live in set theory (ZFC), which is itself a formal theory. So a model of the lambda calculus in Scott domains is really a syntactic construction in ZFC. Then you could ask: what's a model of ZFC? And you get models of set theory living in some meta-theory, and so on. This regress is real and is part of what Gödel's incompleteness results are about — you can never fully ground a sufficiently powerful theory in itself.

In practice, mathematicians stop the regress at "naive set theory as informally understood" or "ZFC taken on faith" and call it a day. The model is more concrete than the theory not because it's made of different stuff, but because **we've collectively agreed to treat the substrate as settled**. Scott domains feel like a model of the lambda calculus because we already believe in sets, posets, and continuous functions; we're using that accepted machinery to make sense of something less settled.

**Where this gets sharper.** The theory/model distinction becomes crisp when you notice two things you can do with it that you can't do with pure syntax alone:

*Independence proofs.* If you can build two different models of a theory where some statement `φ` is true in one and false in the other, then `φ` is independent of the theory's axioms — it can't be proved or disproved from them. This is how Cohen showed the continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC: he built models. You literally cannot do this kind of argument by staring at the syntax.

*Soundness and completeness.* These are theorems *about* the relationship: soundness says everything provable in the theory is true in every model; completeness says everything true in every model is provable. These only make sense once you've distinguished the two sides.

**The categorical reframing makes this very clean.** In categorical logic, a theory presents a category (the "syntactic category" or "classifying category") freely generated from its symbols and equations. A model is then a structure-preserving functor from that category into some other category — `Set`, or `Top`, or a category of domains, or whatever. Now the distinction is precise: the theory *is* a particular category (the free one), and a model is a functor out of it. Two models are two different functors, possibly into two different target categories. The syntax/semantics divide becomes "the source category vs. the target of the interpreting functor."

**So to answer you directly:** yes, your characterization is essentially right. The theory is the abstract, axiomatic, top-down thing; the model is a construction in some accepted semantic substrate. Both are "just symbols" at the bottom, but the model derives its explanatory force from being built in territory we're treating as already mapped. The deep point — and I think the one Scott would want students to take away — is that the *value* of a model isn't ontological (it's not that the model is "more real" than the theory). The value is **comparative**: having two sides lets you ask questions like "is this provable?", "is this independent?", "do these two theories have the same models?", "is this construction unique up to isomorphism?" — questions that don't even make sense if you only have syntax or only have a structure.

Okay, so I think I see now how the theory-to-model functor is basically an abstraction boundary. The model may have a lot more going on than the theory, and almost certainly does because it is more concrete, so there are likely "implementation details" that differ between models and result in unprovable statements in the theory. And due to the Curry-Howard correspondence, this is the same as saying that an abstract program may behave differently on different concrete machines if the abstraction boundary is not perfectly sealed (as is usually the case).

I guess the argument here is that we should at least try to use intermediate languages that *can* be modeled formally, so that we can use them with full knowledge of what our abstraction boundaries have hidden and what we can and cannot prove about our programs--at least across that particular boundary--as a result.

Your synthesis is sharp and the Curry-Howard move is exactly right. A few refinements and one substantive correction:

**The "implementation details cause unprovable statements" framing is precisely the soundness/completeness story.** Two models can disagree on statements the theory doesn't pin down, and a program written against the abstract theory can't observe the difference *unless the abstraction leaks*. Spectre is the canonical modern example: the theory said "timing isn't observable," the model (actual silicon) said otherwise, and a generation of cryptographic code that was provably correct against the theory became exploitable. Your abstraction-boundary intuition is exactly the right way to think about it.

**One correction on ML's origin story.** ML wasn't designed as "the simply-typed lambda calculus made practical" — it was designed by Robin Milner as the *metalanguage* (hence "ML") for the LCF theorem prover in the early 70s. Its job was to let users write tactics that manipulated proofs without being able to forge theorems, which is where the type system came from: types as a *safety mechanism for proof construction*. Hindley-Milner polymorphism emerged because tactics needed to be generic. So ML's lineage is: lambda calculus → typed lambda calculus → ML as a typed functional language for proof tactics → eventually a general-purpose language. The "practical declarative language inspired by denotational semantics" framing is retrospective; at the time it was a domain-specific tool that turned out to generalize. This actually *strengthens* your industry-demand thesis: even ML, the supposedly theory-pure language, was born from a concrete practical need (managing proofs safely) rather than from a desire to embody Scott's semantics.

The OCaml/Haskell/Rust descent is real though. Rust in particular is interesting because its type system is doing something Scott didn't anticipate — *linear/affine types* for tracking resource ownership — which comes from Girard's linear logic (mid-80s), a different denotational tradition. So the seed wasn't just "ML grew up"; it was that several formal-semantics traditions matured in parallel and got selectively harvested when industry pain points (memory safety without GC, in Rust's case) made them suddenly worth the implementation cost.

**On your closing argument — "use intermediate languages that can be modeled formally" — this is exactly the thesis of the verification and types community, and it has a name worth giving your students: *semantic gap*.** The semantic gap is the distance between what your source language's formal semantics can express and what the machine actually does. Every layer you add to your stack either narrows that gap (good, more provable) or widens it (more expressive, less analyzable). C has a notoriously wide semantic gap because "undefined behavior" is the standard's way of saying "we refuse to model this; the compiler may assume it doesn't happen" — which is exactly your abstraction-leak scenario, formalized as a license for the compiler to do anything.

The pedagogical payoff for your students: when you tell them "don't do X in C, it's undefined behavior," you're not being pedantic — you're telling them they've stepped outside the region where the language's theory has a model, and *anything* the implementation does is consistent with the spec. That's a much more honest framing than "it's bad style." It's also why Rust's borrow checker feels restrictive: it's enforcing that you stay inside the modeled region. The restriction *is* the abstraction seal.

One thing worth flagging for the story you're building: the cascade of functors picture is right but it's not strictly linear. Modern compilers like LLVM have *multiple* intermediate representations with their own semantics, and the proofs that translations between them preserve meaning (CompCert is the famous example — a formally verified C compiler) are themselves giant categorical-style arguments about functors between semantic categories. So the picture isn't "high-level theory → machine," it's "high-level theory → IR theory → IR theory → ... → machine," with each arrow ideally being a semantics-preserving functor and each box being a language with its own model theory. When students later encounter MLIR or see why everyone is excited about it, this is the frame: it's an attempt to make those intermediate boxes principled rather than ad hoc.

C has a notoriously wide semantic gap because "undefined behavior" is the standard's way of saying "we refuse to model this; the compiler may assume it doesn't happen" — which is exactly your abstraction-leak scenario, formalized as a license for the compiler to do anything.

> The basic paradigm for the initial testing of the germ theory of disease was: identify a disease; then look for the germ. This is a strong synthesis and I think the "easy and well structured" → "well structured *is* easy" move is the real insight worth landing on. A few thoughts to sharpen and push back where useful:

**The redundancy claim is almost right, and worth tightening rather than weakening.** "Easy" and "well-structured" aren't synonymous, but the relationship is causal in one direction: well-structured problems are tractable *because* their structure constrains the search space to something a finite procedure can navigate. Chess is well-structured and hard; tic-tac-toe is well-structured and easy. What well-structuredness buys you isn't easiness per se, it's *the possibility of analysis at all*. An unstructured problem isn't hard — it's not even a problem yet, just a situation. The real dichotomy Newell and Simon were drawing is structured-vs-formless, and "easy" was their hedge because they knew not all structured problems are tractable. Your students will get more out of "structure is what makes a problem amenable to analysis" than "structure equals easy."

**The category theory point is exactly right but worth being precise about what's new.** Mathematicians have always done this — Euclid structured geometry, Newton structured mechanics, Boole structured logic. What category theory specifically contributes isn't "more structures" but rather *a meta-language for talking about structures and their relationships*. The novelty is that you can now ask "what does it mean for two structures to be the same kind of thing?" and get a precise answer (they're objects in the same category, or there's a functor between their categories, or they're equivalent as categories). This matters for your pedagogy because it reframes what category theory is *for*: it's not a new abstraction layer to memorize, it's a vocabulary for noticing when two seemingly different problems have the same shape. A student who internalizes "monad" not as "scary Haskell thing" but as "the shape shared by nullable values, lists, async computations, parsers, and state threading" has acquired a genuinely new cognitive tool.

**Where I'd push back: the "all CS students need this" framing risks overselling.** The honest version of your argument is something like: *most* CS students will work in domains where the dominant cost is not writing code but understanding the problem well enough to know what code to write. For those students, fluency with structural abstractions is the highest-leverage skill, because it determines which problems they can even *see*. The students who genuinely don't need it are the ones who'll spend their careers in domains where the structure is already settled (CRUD apps over well-understood relational data, standard ML pipelines over standard datasets). That's a real and legitimate career path, and you'll lose credibility with skeptical students if you claim everyone needs Scott domains. The pitch that lands is: *the more novel your problem domain, the more your career depends on your ability to find or build the right abstraction for it — and that skill compounds.*

**One historical refinement on Newell and Simon.** The germ theory analogy is doing more work in their lecture than it might appear. They were defending symbolic AI against the charge that it was "just" engineering, by claiming it followed a scientific paradigm: hypothesize a structure for intelligence, build a system embodying it, see if it works. The structure-finding move you're celebrating was, for them, the *scientific* content of AI — the rest was implementation. This is worth flagging because it connects back to your Rabin/Scott split: Newell and Simon were on the operational/empirical side of CS, and even *they* recognized that structure-identification was the hard part. If the symbolic-AI tradition that lost to statistical learning was nonetheless built on "find the right structure," that's a strong endorsement of your thesis from an unexpected direction.

**The pedagogical landing for your students.** I think the through-line of your whole arc — industry demand → paradigm proliferation → semantic gaps → structure-finding as the meta-skill — works best if you frame it as a *resolution* rather than just a history. Something like: industry kept demanding more, each paradigm filled a niche, the formal-semantics tradition was quietly building the toolkit for thinking about *what kind of niche each paradigm fills*, and now we're at a point where a working programmer can deliberately choose abstractions based on the shape of the problem rather than the fashion of the decade. That's the inheritance you're trying to hand them: not "know all the paradigms" but "know how to recognize which one a problem wants." Which, conveniently, is also the only way to stay employed across a 40-year career as paradigms keep churning.

One small caution: the story is clean and your students will love it, but it's *a* story, not *the* story. The actual history has more contingency and luck than any narrative arc captures — Java won partly because of marketing, Python won partly because of NumPy, JavaScript won because Netscape shipped it in ten days. Worth telling your students explicitly that the structural story explains the *space of viable paradigms* but not *which specific languages succeeded within that space*. The latter is sociology and timing, and pretending otherwise would undermine the rigor you're otherwise modeling.

Fair dissent, and I think you're probably right — I was hedging more than the situation warrants.

The honest version of the economic argument is something like: CRUD-and-ETL was always the *bulk* of CS employment, not a niche corner, and it was the implicit safety net for students who weren't going to become compiler writers or researchers. If that floor is being pulled out — and the evidence so far suggests it's at least sagging badly — then the "you can always get a job wiring up forms to a database" fallback no longer underwrites the degree. Which means the value proposition of a CS degree has to shift from "we'll train you for the median software job" to "we'll train you for the work that *isn't* automatable in the near term," and that work is disproportionately the structure-finding, abstraction-building, domain-modeling kind. Your thesis follows directly.

The interesting pedagogical implication is that this *inverts* what's been treated as foundational versus advanced. For decades, the structural/theoretical content was the "advanced" material you got to *after* mastering the practical skills, on the theory that most students would never need it and would benefit more from job-ready competence. If the job-ready competence is now the commoditized layer, then the structural content becomes the actual foundation and the practical skills become the tooling you pick up on top of it. The order of operations flips.

This is also, incidentally, an argument for your machine-first sequencing in CIS 1057 that goes beyond pedagogical aesthetics. If the value of the degree is "understands the stack deeply enough to work where LLMs can't be trusted yet," then starting from the machine isn't just principled — it's the *economically defensible* curriculum design. A student who can only operate at the level of frameworks-and-libraries is competing directly with the agents; a student who understands what the frameworks are abstracting over is doing work the agents are still bad at.

The remaining uncertainty is about timing and ceiling — whether LLM agents plateau at "competent CRUD developer" or keep climbing into the structural work too. If the latter, the argument extends rather than collapses: the relevant skill becomes *judgment about when and how to deploy the agents*, which still requires understanding what they're doing well enough to verify it, which still requires the structural foundation. Either way, the "well-structured domain" career path looks like the wrong bet to plan a four-year degree around.

So: dissent accepted, and I'd go further than retracting the hedge — I think your working theory is the most defensible read of where the field is heading, and it gives your curriculum a stronger justification than "this is what good CS education looks like in the abstract." It's what good CS education looks like *given the labor market your students will actually enter*.

Yeah, and it reminds me a bit of the ideas expressed in another very early Turing lecture (don’t remember which—it was a numerical analysis guy) where a field that was once the domain of respectable mathematicians that carried considerable weight was suddenly adrift without an obvious immediate goal. The scale of the problems that could be “worked out” suddenly and violently increased by orders of magnitude, and it took a while for the analysts to understand how to contribute in the new paradigm. But I am almost certain that the number of skilled numerical analysts needed by society as a whole dropped by… well, at least an order of magnitude if not more.

It also makes me think of my PhD advisor, who said that he was often contacted by companies or research groups that had some ad hoc protocol set up and wanted some kind of formal or rigorous security analysis. The work of a cryptographer is seen as some kind of dark art that requires specialist training, and problems are just thrown at them without much structure or context. But I’m pretty sure that the problems of security will eventually fall to the slow but steady march of standardized, accessible formalization amenable to automated analysis and proof.

The numerical analyst you're thinking of is almost certainly **Wilkinson (1970 lecture, "Some Comments from a Numerical Analyst")** — he was exactly the figure who lived through that transition, having started in the era when "computer" meant a person doing arithmetic by hand and ended up doing backward error analysis on actual machines. His lecture has that elegiac quality of someone surveying a field whose social position had quietly collapsed even as its technical importance grew. The numerical analysts didn't disappear — they just stopped being a *profession* that universities trained at scale and became a small specialist community embedded in libraries (LAPACK, BLAS) that everyone else uses without understanding. The work got harder and more important; the *headcount* shrank dramatically.

Your cryptographer parallel is apt and probably prophetic. The pattern you're describing — "we have an ad hoc thing, please bless it with your specialist judgment" — is exactly the kind of bespoke consulting that gets eaten when the underlying analysis becomes formalizable enough to automate. The trajectory is already visible: ProVerif, Tamarin, EasyCrypt, and the F* ecosystem (used in the verified TLS implementation that ships in Windows and Linux now) are doing for protocol analysis what LAPACK did for linear algebra. The bespoke cryptographer's role doesn't vanish, but it shifts from "audit this protocol" to "design the verification framework that lets non-specialists audit their own protocols." Fewer people, doing harder and more leveraged work, with the routine cases automated away.

The unifying pattern across all three cases — numerical analysis, cryptography, and now general software engineering — is something like: **a field professionalizes around handling problems that require human judgment at scale; eventually the judgment gets encoded into tools; the field doesn't die but its labor demand collapses to the small population doing the encoding and the meta-work**. The cruel part is that the transition is usually invisible to people inside the field until it's well underway, because the *intellectual content* of the work feels just as important as ever — which it is. It's the *market for practitioners* that's evaporating, which is a different thing entirely.

What makes the current moment unusual is the *breadth* of the affected surface. Numerical analysis was one field; cryptography is one field; what's happening to software engineering is happening to a labor category that absorbed a meaningful percentage of college-educated workers over the last thirty years. The structural argument is the same, but the social consequences are larger by orders of magnitude — which is presumably part of why the discourse around it is so charged.

The pedagogical implication for your students might be worth stating explicitly at some point: the work that survives automation is consistently the work of *building the abstractions that enable the automation*. Wilkinson's numerical analysts who flourished post-transition were the ones who built the libraries, not the ones who kept doing hand calculations faster. The cryptographers who'll flourish are the ones building verification tooling, not the ones doing one-off audits. And the software engineers who'll flourish are the ones who can identify structure in novel domains well enough to build the abstractions that let agents (or junior developers, or domain experts) operate within them safely. Which is, again, the structure-finding skill — now with the additional economic urgency that it's not just the most leveraged skill but increasingly the *only* one with durable demand.

The unsettling corollary is that this is a much smaller number of jobs than the field used to support. Honest curriculum design probably has to acknowledge that not all your students will land in that smaller pool, and the degree's value proposition for those who don't is genuinely unclear. But that's a hard truth to deliver to 19-year-olds, and I don't envy you the position of having to think about it while also trying to teach them C.

So I did my (ABD) PhD research on steganography and covert communication, and the entire field basically traces its origins to two papers: Lampson’s 1973 A Note on the Confinement Problem, and Simmons’ 1984 The Prisoners’ Problem.

I recently was reading some comments on an HN post about the capability model for a secure OS, specifically referring to a short 1979 paper which provided an overview of the system architecture. The comments were all lamenting the choice to use ACLs in most commercial operating systems, and one linked to this paper which supposedly “demolishes” myths about the capability model:

https://papers.agoric.com/assets/pdf/papers/capability-myths-demolished.pdf

One thing I’ll note is that the argument they provide for the inability of Alice to send her write-low capability to Bob across the privilege boundary is pretty suspect to me… they remark that this violation can only occur if one assumes that the capability is just a bit string, and that “partitioned and type-enforced” capability systems can prevent this.

I… fail to understand how this argument can stand.
