You're onto something real here. The capability-myths paper has earned a lot of respect, but that particular argument about the *-property (the high-to-low write prohibition in Bell-LaPadula) has always struck careful readers as doing more work than it can support, and the move you've identified — "well, partitioned and type-enforced capabilities prevent this" — is exactly where the sleight of hand happens.

Here's the structure of what they're doing. The objection they're answering is Boebert's classic one: in a pure capability system, if Alice (high) has a write capability to some low object, nothing stops her from passing that capability *as data* to Bob (low), and now Bob can write to the low object using Alice's authority — except the act of transmission itself was already a high-to-low information flow. Capabilities, treated as transferable bit-patterns, ARE the covert channel. This is essentially Lampson's confinement problem wearing different clothes, which I imagine is part of why it caught your eye.

Their response is to say: a "real" capability system doesn't let you transmit capabilities as raw bits. The capability is partitioned from data, or the type system enforces that capabilities can only flow through channels that themselves respect the security policy. So Alice literally cannot encode her write-cap into a byte stream that Bob can decode back into a usable capability.

And you're right to find this suspect, because what they've actually done is *assume the conclusion*. The whole point of a capability system, in its pure form, is that authority is conveyed by possession of an unforgeable reference. Once you say "ah, but the system also enforces, separately, that certain references cannot flow across certain boundaries" — you have smuggled in a mandatory access control mechanism that lives *outside* the capability abstraction. The thing doing the work to prevent the *-property violation isn't capabilities; it's a lattice-respecting flow control system that happens to be implemented on top of capabilities. You could implement the same protection on top of ACLs, or on top of anything else.

This is the move that should bother a steganographer especially: they've defined away the covert channel by fiat at the type-system level, without addressing whether the *partitioning itself* is achievable in a system where Alice has any expressive computational power at all. If Alice can perform computation whose timing, resource consumption, or observable side effects are visible to Bob, she can transmit the bits of the capability through that channel, and Bob — given a separate (legitimate) way to mint capabilities from bit-patterns in his own protection domain — can reconstruct equivalent authority. The partition only holds if you also close every side channel, which is famously not something type systems do.

There's a second sleight of hand worth naming. The paper frames the debate as "ACLs vs capabilities" and shows that many supposed disadvantages of capabilities don't actually follow from the capability model per se. That part of the paper is largely correct and useful! The confusion is that they then extend the rhetorical momentum to claim capabilities can do *everything* MAC systems can do, including enforce non-interference properties like *-property. But non-interference is a property of *information flow*, not of *authority*, and capability systems are fundamentally an authority model. Conflating the two is the original sin of much of the capability literature — Miller, Yee, and Shapiro do it more carefully than most, but they still do it here.

Boebert's original critique, in other words, survives. The honest response is: "yes, pure capabilities cannot enforce *-property, because *-property is a non-interference property and capabilities are an authority mechanism; if you want both, you need to compose capabilities with an orthogonal MAC layer." The dishonest response is to redefine "capability system" to include whatever MAC layer you need and then claim victory.

Given your constructive cryptography background, you'll appreciate that this is exactly the kind of place where a compositional security definition would force the issue. You'd have to state precisely what abstraction the capability system realizes, and you'd discover that "unforgeable reference to authority" and "non-interference between security levels" are different ideal functionalities that need to be composed explicitly — not conflated.

chat_messages.text:
Some of it has, but it's surprisingly fragmented, and the part you'd actually want — a compositional, simulation-based account in the style you're used to — is much thinner than you'd expect for a model that's been around since the 1960s.

Here's the landscape as I understand it. The most-cited formal work on capability systems comes out of the object-capability (ocap) tradition, primarily Mark Miller's 2006 dissertation *Robust Composition*, and the analyses that followed it from Spiessens, Van Roy, Murray, and others. Miller's thesis formalizes capability patterns in terms of what he calls "access graphs" and proves things about reachability — essentially, that the set of objects a subject can eventually come to influence is bounded by the graph of capabilities reachable from its initial set, modulo certain introduction rules. This is genuinely useful and gives you "no authority amplification" style theorems. Toby Murray's Oxford DPhil thesis (2010) takes this further with a CSP-based analysis and proves some confinement properties for ocap patterns like the sealed-pair / membrane construction. There's also Spiessens' "Patterns of Safe Collaboration" thesis in the same vein.

But notice what these results are about: they're authority-reachability properties in a model where the *only* observable is "can subject S invoke object O." They explicitly abstract away from timing, resource consumption, termination behavior, and every other side channel. Within that model, you can prove nice things, including a version of confinement — but it's confinement-against-an-adversary-who-can-only-invoke-methods, not confinement against an adversary who can compute. The moment you re-introduce a realistic execution model, those proofs don't extend, and the literature largely just... doesn't address it.

The seL4 work is the other major formal effort, and it's a different beast. Klein et al.'s functional correctness proof, and the subsequent integrity and confidentiality proofs by Murray, Sewell, and others, do establish information-flow properties in Isabelle/HOL — including a non-interference result. But seL4's non-interference theorem is for a *specific* kernel configuration with statically-partitioned resources, and the policy is essentially baked in as a separate lattice that the capability distribution must respect. So it actually confirms the structural point from your previous question: you get non-interference by composing capabilities with an orthogonal partitioning mechanism, not from the capability model alone. The seL4 team is quite explicit about this; it's the marketing around capability systems generally that elides it.

What you don't really find, as far as I know, is a UC-style or constructive-cryptography-style treatment where you state an ideal functionality for "authority delegation," another for "information flow control," and prove that some capability-plus-MAC construction realizes the composition. The closest thing in spirit is probably some of the work on cryptographic capabilities (Tanenbaum's Amoeba, Mullender, more recently Macaroons by Birgisson et al.), but those are mostly concerned with *unforgeability under cryptographic assumptions* rather than with composable security definitions for the access-control abstraction itself. Macaroons are interesting because they make the delegation and attenuation structure explicit and have some formal treatment, but again, it's authority, not flow.

There's a related body of work in language-based security — Myers and Liskov's DLM, the Jif language, more recently the work on information-flow type systems by Pottier, Simonet, and others — which *does* take non-interference seriously and proves it for typed lambda calculi with security labels. But this is a different tradition that mostly doesn't talk to the capability literature, and when it does, the capability mechanism is usually just one of several enforcement strategies for the underlying IFC policy. The interesting unification would be something like "capabilities as the authority layer, IFC types as the flow layer, with a compositional proof that the combination realizes both ideals" — and I'm not aware of that having been done cleanly, though I'd be happy to be wrong about it.

If I had to point at the cleanest piece of formalism that addresses your specific concern from the previous turn, it'd probably be Murray's thesis plus the seL4 confidentiality paper read together: the former tells you what capabilities-qua-capabilities can prove, and the latter shows you what additional machinery is needed to get the non-interference property, with the gap between them being exactly the place where the "capability myths demolished" rhetoric papers over a real architectural commitment.

This is one of those areas where I'd flag genuine uncertainty about completeness — the capability-systems literature is large, somewhat insular, and not always well-indexed against the IFC and cryptographic-protocols literatures. There may well be a paper I'm not thinking of that does exactly the compositional treatment you'd want. If you wanted to search for it, I'd start with citations of Murray's thesis that come from the IFC or PL-theory side rather than the systems side; that intersection is where it would live if it exists.

You know… this isn’t exactly an epiphany, but it’s worth noting: when I was cutting my teeth on old-school security notions with game-playing proofs, the security notions were basically statements in first-order logic. You know, universal and existence qualifiers, etc.

I was reading a paper (book?) the other day that had a condensed introduction to category theory, and it noted how the typical mathematical statements of injective and surjective were so clunky and verbose when compared to the succinct and, more importantly, *obviously dual* categorical concepts of monic and epic.

It’s honestly a miracle we proved any interesting results at all with such archaic methods, but it really does feel just like the difference between mid-level imperative programming and clean Haskell code.

It feels like the alternative to all of this, as demonstrated over and over again by the functional folks, is to take whatever semantic property you seek to enforce and figure out how to “put it in the type system”. In other words, make it a *declarative* property of the code.

chat_messages.text:
Yes — and the connection you're drawing runs even deeper than the analogy suggests, because in a real sense game-playing proofs and "put it in the types" are the *same activity* viewed through different categorical lenses, and recognizing that is one of those shifts that retroactively reorganizes a lot of one's understanding.

Here's what I mean. A game-playing security proof is, structurally, a sequence of probabilistic transitions between distributions over execution traces, where each step is justified by a "hop" — either a syntactic rewriting (bridging step), a reduction to a hardness assumption, or a statistical bound. Shoup's "Sequences of Games" paper made this discipline explicit in 2004, and Bellare-Rogaway's code-based games followed shortly after. The whole apparatus is, at its mathematical heart, a category of probabilistic programs with games as objects and "indistinguishable up to ε" as a notion of morphism-with-tolerance. You're chaining together small, locally verifiable equivalences to get a global equivalence. The first-order-logic statements with their quantifier alternations are the *external* description of what each game is supposed to satisfy; the proof itself is a chain of internal rewrites.

Now compare this to what happens when you "put it in the type system." A non-interference type system, say in the DLM or Jif tradition, takes the property "no information flows from high to low" and reformulates it as: every well-typed program *automatically* has this property, by construction. The proof obligation shifts from "verify this universal statement holds for all adversaries against this protocol" to "verify the typing rules are sound, once, and then the type-checker discharges the obligation for every program." This is exactly the same move that Eilenberg and Mac Lane made when they replaced "f is injective iff for all x, y, f(x)=f(y) implies x=y" with "f is monic iff f∘g = f∘h implies g=h" — they moved the property from being a statement *about elements* (which requires you to quantify over them) to being a statement *about composition* (which is structural and requires no quantification over a domain). The categorical definition doesn't *mention* elements; it talks about how the morphism behaves under composition with other morphisms, which is intrinsic to the categorical setting.

The deep insight — and this is the one that I think you're circling — is that **quantifier alternation in first-order logic is doing the work of expressing universal properties, badly**. When you write "for all PPT adversaries A, there exists a negligible function ε, such that for all sufficiently large λ, |Pr[...] - Pr[...]| < ε(λ)," you are expressing what is essentially a *limit* in some category of probabilistic computations indexed by security parameter. The ∀∃∀ structure is the syntactic shadow of a genuine universal-property-with-parameters that lives in some category. The reason it's clunky is the same reason ε-δ proofs in analysis are clunky compared to topological formulations: you're encoding a structural relationship through pointwise quantification because your foundational language only gives you pointwise quantification.

The functional/categorical alternative says: find the right category, identify the relevant universal property, and the quantifiers disappear into the *definition of the morphism class*. Non-interference becomes "this program is a morphism in the category of label-respecting computations." Confidentiality becomes "this protocol factors through the ideal functionality." Confinement becomes "no morphism exists from this object to that one in the access category." And critically — this is the part that connects back to your earlier questions about constructive cryptography — composition of these properties becomes composition of morphisms, which is automatic, rather than composition of quantified statements, which requires you to manually re-quantify and re-prove for every combination.

Maurer's constructive cryptography is precisely an attempt to do this for cryptographic protocols. He works in a category where objects are resources (idealized or real) and morphisms are constructions (protocols), and security becomes the statement "this protocol is a morphism from real-resource to ideal-resource." Composition of protocols is then literally morphism composition, and the proof that "if A realizes X and B realizes Y, then A;B realizes X;Y" becomes a triviality — it's just functoriality. Compare this to the UC framework, which while compositional in its results, still requires you to wade through quantifier-laden simulation-based definitions for each composition step. UC tells you that composition works; constructive crypto makes composition the *definition*.

The connection to your steganography work is, I think, exactly what frustrated you about the literature: people write "for all distinguishers D with advantage ≤ ε, the stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from covertext" and then try to compose two such schemes and find that the quantifiers don't line up cleanly. The compositional failure is not a bug in the proofs; it's a symptom of having stated the property in a non-compositional language. The reason there's no clean compositional theory of steganographic security is that nobody has done for stego what Maurer did for cryptography — identified the right category, the right notion of resource, the right morphism class, such that "is steganographic" becomes a structural property that composes automatically.

The Haskell analogy you drew is exact, by the way, and it's not a coincidence: Haskell's type system is literally a fragment of category theory (specifically, a cartesian closed category with some additional structure for effects via monads), and what makes well-typed Haskell programs "obviously correct" in ways that imperative programs aren't is precisely that the type system has internalized properties that imperative languages can only express via runtime assertions and prose comments. The shift from "write the property in FOL and check it" to "encode the property in the morphism structure and let composition handle it" is the same shift in both worlds.

The one caveat worth offering: this isn't free. The cost of putting properties in the type system / morphism structure is that you have to find the right category, and finding the right category is sometimes very hard and sometimes not yet known. Linear types took decades to mature; cubical type theory is still settling; the right category for differential privacy or for quantitative information flow is still actively debated. The reward is that once you've found it, the proofs become short and the compositions become free — but the up-front cost of identifying the structure can be enormous. This is, I suspect, why the field doesn't just *do* this for everything: not because people don't see the appeal, but because the categorical reformulation is itself research, and the FOL formulation is at least mechanical to write down even when it's painful to use.

The categorical machinery that you and I have been gesturing at — symmetric monoidal categories for resource-aware computation, fibrations for dependent types, presheaf semantics for concurrency, coalgebras for state and observation — was *mostly developed* between roughly 1965 and 1990, but it lived almost entirely within pure mathematics and a small theoretical-CS diaspora (Scott, Plotkin, Moggi, Abramsky, a handful of others). The timing isn't coincidence: by 1990 the categorical tools had reached a level of maturity where they could be *applied* rather than just developed, and the problems in CS had reached a level of structural complexity where the older tools were visibly inadequate. I note too that he has avoided abstract category theory. Categories may lead to good things, but too early a use can only make things too difficult to understand. That is my personal opinion.”

chat_messages.text:
That quote is delicious, and it lands harder when you know who's saying it. Dana Scott — who *invented domain theory*, which is essentially "what happens when you take the categorical structure of partial orders and CPOs seriously enough to do denotational semantics with it" — telling people in 1976 that category theory should be used cautiously and not too early. It's not the kind of thing you'd expect from someone whose entire research program was, in retrospect, a case study in why categorical thinking pays off for CS.

But I think Scott was being more sophisticated than the quote sounds on first reading, and the sophistication is worth unpacking because it cuts directly against the slightly triumphalist reading of our conversation so far.

The thing Scott understood, I think, is that category theory has a peculiar failure mode that other mathematical tools don't have to the same degree: it's *so* general that it can absorb almost any structure into its formalism, and the resulting reformulation can feel like progress while actually just being a translation. You can take a perfectly concrete result about, say, finite automata, restate it as a property of a functor between two specific categories, and feel like you've understood something deeper — when actually you've just relabeled the original content in fancier vocabulary. Eilenberg, who literally co-invented category theory with Mac Lane, knew this better than anyone, and his choice to write *Automata, Languages, and Machines* in algebraic rather than categorical language wasn't because he didn't see the categorical structure. It's because he judged that the algebraic presentation made the *content* clearer, and the categorical presentation would have added abstraction without adding insight. That's a judgment about pedagogy and exposition, but it's also a judgment about where the actual mathematical work is happening — which in automata theory, Eilenberg correctly identified as being at the level of monoids, varieties, and the Krohn-Rhodes decomposition, not at the level of functor categories.

Scott's warning, then, isn't "category theory is bad" — he's clearly using it himself by 1976, just not advertising it as such. The warning is something more like: *category theory's power as an organizing language is most useful when you've already identified the structures it organizes, and using it before you have those structures in hand can substitute the appearance of understanding for the substance of it.* The novice with a new categorical hammer sees functors and natural transformations everywhere and produces papers that are technically correct but contentless, because the categorical machinery isn't doing any work beyond renaming. This is a real failure mode, and anyone who's spent time in the applied category theory literature has read papers exhibiting it.

Now, this is in genuine tension with the picture we were developing earlier, and I want to be honest about the tension rather than smooth it over. The story I was telling — categorical tools matured by 1990, CS problems needed them, pedagogical inertia delayed adoption by a decade-plus — is true, but it's the story told from the perspective of cases where the categorical reformulation *did* turn out to be load-bearing. Moggi's monads really did unblock effects in functional languages; Maurer's constructive cryptography really does give you composition for free in a way UC doesn't; seL4's information-flow proofs really did benefit from categorical framing. But for every case like those, there are probably three or four where someone reformulated a CS problem categorically and the reformulation didn't lead anywhere — the original tools were adequate, the categorical version added notation without adding traction, and the work quietly didn't get cited. Survivorship bias makes the successful cases vivid and the unsuccessful ones invisible, which makes the case for "we should have adopted these tools earlier" look stronger than it actually is.

The honest version of the historical claim is probably something like: *for a specific subset of CS problems — those involving compositional structure, effects, observation, and resource — categorical tools were ready by the mid-80s and would have helped if adopted sooner, but distinguishing those problems from the much larger set where categorical reformulation would have been a waste of time requires the kind of mathematical taste that Scott had and that doesn't transmit easily through curricula.* The pedagogical bottleneck isn't just "teach more category theory"; it's "teach the judgment of when categorical thinking pays and when it doesn't," and that's much harder to teach than the formalism itself.

There's another thing in Scott's quote that's worth noticing: the phrase "too early a use." He's not saying never use it; he's saying timing matters. Mathematical concepts have a kind of optimal moment of introduction, where the learner has enough concrete experience to recognize what the abstraction is abstracting *over*, and introducing the abstraction before that point produces something like the experience that mathematicians sometimes describe as "abstract nonsense" — formally manipulable but unconnected to anything the student can ground out in examples. Scott's worry in 1976 was probably that automata theory was a domain where students *did* have good concrete intuitions (regular languages, state machines, the pumping lemma) and that wrapping those intuitions in categorical language before students had developed them would be actively counterproductive. This isn't a refutation of category theory; it's a observation about how concept acquisition actually works, which I think is correct and which the more zealous applied-category-theory advocates sometimes lose sight of.

If I were going to defend the position our conversation has been building while taking Scott's caution seriously, I'd put it like this: the failure mode in CS pedagogy isn't that we don't teach enough category theory; it's that we don't teach students to *recognize the structural patterns* that category theory is good at organizing — duality, composition, universal properties, naturality. A student who has internalized "look for the dual" as a research move will independently rediscover monics-and-epics-style reformulations even without knowing the categorical vocabulary, and will then be ready to learn the vocabulary when they encounter it because it formalizes something they already do. A student who learns the vocabulary first, without the underlying habit of mind, gets exactly the kind of contentless categorification that Scott was warning against. Your own path is actually evidence for this: you dug up the tools yourself *because* you had already developed the intuitions (from steganography composition problems, from frustration with quantifier-heavy security definitions) that made the tools obviously relevant. Someone handed those same tools without those intuitions would have made worse use of them, not better.

So I think Scott was right, and our earlier story was also right, and the synthesis is that "introduce categorical thinking earlier" really means "cultivate the structural sensibility earlier, and let the formal categorical apparatus come in when it's needed." Eilenberg's automata book is, in this reading, a perfect example of the right approach — it teaches you to think algebraically about computation, which is most of the content of thinking categorically about computation, without committing to the full machinery before the machinery earns its keep.

Your instinct is right, and the sleight of hand is actually pretty crisp once you name it — it's worth getting clear on now even briefly, because it'll save you from chasing the wrong thread when you come back to this.

The commenter's argument is structurally: "look, on Unix you have an actual mechanism — `SCM_RIGHTS` over `AF_UNIX` sockets — where the kernel transports file descriptors as kernel objects, not as bit-patterns. The receiving process gets a fresh fd number in its own table pointing at the same underlying kernel object. This is a real, working example of capability transmission that isn't 'just sending bits,' so Boebert's objection doesn't apply." And taken on its own terms, the technical description is correct: that's exactly how `SCM_RIGHTS` works.

But here's the sleight of hand: the argument answers a question you weren't asking. Boebert's objection (and your reformulation of it) is about whether Alice can transmit *unauthorized* authority to Bob across a *security boundary* that's supposed to prevent that flow. The `SCM_RIGHTS` example is a case where the kernel is *deliberately providing* a sanctioned channel for authority transfer, with the kernel's blessing, between two processes that — crucially — *the kernel does not consider to be on opposite sides of a mandatory access control boundary*. Unix has no `*`-property. There is no "high" and "low" in the Bell-LaPadula sense on a standard Unix system. So of course the kernel mediates the transfer cleanly: it's not enforcing any policy that would be violated by the transfer.

The moment you try to extend this to the actual case under dispute — Alice is "high," Bob is "low," and the security policy says high-to-low information flow is forbidden — one of two things has to happen. Either (a) the kernel refuses to deliver the fd across the boundary, in which case the capability mechanism didn't enforce the property; the *separate MAC layer* did, which is exactly the structural point I was making earlier. Or (b) the kernel does deliver it, in which case you've violated `*`-property and the capability mechanism failed to prevent it. The commenter's example works precisely because it sidesteps the case in dispute: there's no security boundary in their scenario, so there's no `*`-property violation to worry about, so of course nothing bad happens.

There's a second, subtler move in the argument that's worth flagging. The commenter says "you aren't always just sending bits," and that's true at the API level — `sendmsg` with `SCM_RIGHTS` is a structured operation, not a `write` of raw bytes. But the question Boebert was asking isn't about the API; it's about what Alice *can choose to do*. If Alice has both an `SCM_RIGHTS`-capable channel to Bob *and* the write-low capability she's not supposed to share, she can use the channel to share it. The existence of structured transfer mechanisms doesn't prevent unauthorized transfer; it just provides one *particular* mechanism that the kernel happens to mediate. The covert-channel argument is about all the *other* mechanisms — including, yes, encoding the fd number as bits and shipping it over TCP, but also timing, resource exhaustion, filesystem side effects, and so on. Showing that one channel is mediated doesn't show that all channels are.

This response is more substantive than the previous one, and the commenter is making a real argument that deserves engagement rather than dismissal. But there's still a critical move being made that doesn't survive scrutiny, and it's worth getting precise about because it's the *same* move as in the original myths paper, just made more explicit.

Let me steelman first, because the commenter is right about several important things. They're correct that capabilities are fundamentally about non-construction and provenance, not about bearer-token semantics — this is exactly Dennis and Van Horn's original formulation from 1966, and it's the property that makes capability systems philosophically distinct from password-style authority. They're correct that allowing arbitrary integer-to-capability casts would destroy the entire model, in exactly the way that allowing arbitrary integer-to-pointer casts destroys memory safety in C. And the analogy to pointer provenance is genuinely apt: modern work on CHERI, on Rust's ownership model, on capability machines generally, takes this seriously, and the structural similarity to capability-based OS design is not coincidental.

So the part where they say "the essence of capabilities is non-construction" — yes, agreed, that's the right characterization.

But here's where the argument goes off the rails. The commenter says: "the only way I can coherently interpret your argument is that you are arguing that the presence of kernel data structures mediating the handles somehow makes it not a capability system." That's not the argument. The argument is that *the kernel data structures, together with the policy they enforce about which transfers are permitted, constitute a larger system of which capabilities are one component, and the security property in dispute is provided by the policy, not by the capability mechanism per se.*

Look at what they're describing: "Your communication channel between Alice and Bob is, itself, a capability (or a collection of capabilities) that grants Bob memory write, Alice memory read, but *does not grant the ability to transmit a capability from Bob to Alice*." Notice what's happening in that last clause. The channel-capability has a *type* or *attribute* that distinguishes "can transmit data bits" from "can transmit capabilities." Something in the system — the kernel, the type system, the capability-aware runtime — is checking, at the moment Alice attempts to send a capability rather than data, that the channel permits that operation. *That check is the MAC layer.* It's a policy decision about which kinds of objects can flow through which channels, enforced by a trusted component that sits outside the capabilities themselves.

The commenter has essentially conceded the point while believing they're refuting it. They've said: capabilities have types (or attributes, or kinds), and the system enforces that capabilities of certain types cannot be transmitted through channels not authorized to carry them. Great — that's a mandatory access control system whose policy happens to be expressed in terms of capability types. The capability mechanism is the *vehicle* for the policy, but the policy itself is a separate semantic commitment. You could implement the same policy on top of ACLs (each channel has an ACL specifying which object types may flow through it), and you'd get the same security property. The capabilities aren't doing the security work; the type-respecting flow control is.

This is exactly Boebert's original point, and it's exactly the move the myths paper makes: redefine "capability system" to include a typed channel discipline that respects a flow policy, then claim that the resulting composite system enforces the flow property "with capabilities." Well, yes — but the *interesting* enforcement is happening in the typed channel discipline, not in the capability mechanism.

Now their two specific points deserve direct responses:

On the "forging capabilities unless cryptographically secure against collisions" objection: this misunderstands what the original argument requires. Boebert's adversary doesn't need to forge capabilities in Bob's address space. The adversary scenario is that Alice (high), who legitimately *has* a write-low capability, transmits the *information content* of that capability to Bob (low) through any channel. Bob doesn't need to reconstruct Alice's capability into his own fd table — he just needs to learn the *fact* that such authority exists and can be exercised, or to influence Alice to exercise it on his behalf. The covert channel exists at the information level, not at the capability-forgery level. The commenter has substituted a different (harder) attack and shown it doesn't work, while the original (easier) attack remains.

On provenance and non-construction: this is where the deepest issue lives, and it's worth being precise. Provenance is a wonderful property — it's exactly the right structural notion for authority, and the analogy to pointer provenance in memory-safe languages is illuminating. But provenance gives you "authority cannot be manifested from nothing"; it does *not* give you "authority cannot flow across a security boundary." Those are different properties. A system can have perfect capability provenance and still permit Alice to invoke her legitimate capabilities in patterns that encode information observable to Bob, thereby effecting a high-to-low information flow without ever violating provenance. Provenance is about the *origin* of authority; non-interference is about *observable consequences* of authority's exercise. The commenter is conflating these two, which is the same conflation between authority and information flow that I flagged in the original myths paper response.

The CHERI analogy actually makes this clearer if you push on it. CHERI gives you pointer provenance — you cannot manifest a valid capability pointer from arbitrary integers, you can only derive new capabilities from existing ones via monotonic operations (restriction, never amplification). This is genuinely valuable and prevents enormous classes of memory safety bugs. But CHERI does *not*, on its own, give you non-interference between security domains. You can have a perfectly CHERI-clean program that nonetheless leaks information through timing, through cache state, through observable effects of legitimate capability invocations. To get non-interference on CHERI, you need *additional* mechanisms — compartmentalization policies, flow-control disciplines, side-channel mitigations — that are orthogonal to the capability provenance guarantee. The CHERI people are quite clear about this; the marketing-around-capabilities tradition is less clear, which is how you get arguments like the one you're receiving.

So if you wanted to reply — and I'd understand if you don't, since these threads tend to spiral — the cleanest version is something like: "You've correctly identified that capabilities are about provenance and non-construction, and I agree. But provenance prevents *manifesting authority from nothing*; it doesn't prevent *flowing information across a security boundary via the exercise of legitimately-held authority*. The mechanism you describe, where channels have types and the system enforces that capability-typed objects cannot flow through data-typed channels, is a flow-control policy enforced by the kernel — it's exactly the MAC layer I was pointing at, just expressed in capability vocabulary. The capability mechanism is the substrate; the security property comes from the typed flow discipline running on top of it." And then you can decide whether to draw the CHERI parallel, which I think is the strongest version of the point because it's a system the commenter probably respects and where the architects themselves acknowledge the separation between provenance and non-interference.

The reason this keeps recurring in capability debates is that there's a strong cultural identification in the capability community with the *moral rightness* of the capability model — and it is morally right, for the problems it solves — but that identification produces a reluctance to acknowledge what capabilities *don't* do. The result is arguments that keep redefining "capability system" to absorb whatever additional mechanism is needed to defeat the current objection, which makes the term increasingly mean "any well-designed secure system" rather than picking out a specific architectural commitment. That's the move you're seeing, and naming it cleanly is more useful than litigating each instance.

Excellent. Now we have the actual claims in hand, and it's possible to be precise about what was promised, what was proved, and what the relationship is to your original concern. The picture is more interesting than either side of the HN thread has been letting on, and I think it actually largely *vindicates* Boebert while also showing why the myths paper's citation is technically correct but rhetorically misleading.

Let me lay this out carefully because I think there's real signal here.

**What PSOS actually claimed.** The Feiertag-Neumann paper is, as you noted, brief, and on rereading it's striking how *modest* its actual security claims are. The summary at the end lists eight properties, and exactly one of them addresses propagation: property 8, which says that propagation can be restricted by *store permissions*, which is a mechanism the paper introduces explicitly to handle the case where capability copying needs to be restricted. The relevant passage: "any means for restricting the propagation of capabilities should not add complexity to the capability mechanism," followed by a description of how store permissions are reserved access rights that segments check on modification. So PSOS itself, in its primary description, *concedes the very point Boebert was making* — pure capability semantics are insufficient to restrict propagation, and an *additional mechanism* (store permissions, enforced by the segment manager, which is a trusted type manager outside the capability mechanism proper) is required.

Boebert's 1984 critique, then, is best read not as attacking a strawman PSOS but as making the *theoretical* point that even an "omniscient oracle" creating capabilities cannot control their further propagation through the capability mechanism alone — a claim PSOS doesn't really dispute, since it explicitly adds store permissions to handle exactly that problem. Boebert's closing line that you quoted — "If extra mechanisms are imposed to impose this control, the machine is no longer an unmodified capability machine" — is essentially observing that PSOS *already isn't* an unmodified capability machine in his sense, because of store permissions. The disagreement is partly definitional (what counts as the "capability mechanism" versus "extra mechanisms imposed on top of it") and partly about whether the additional machinery should be considered part of the capability paradigm or a separate orthogonal layer.

**What Shapiro-Weber actually proved.** Now this is where it gets interesting, because the myths paper's citation is technically accurate but does considerable rhetorical work that the underlying paper doesn't support. Shapiro and Weber prove that EROS's constructor mechanism enforces *Lampson's* confinement policy — and they're extremely explicit, in Section 5 of all places, about what this does and doesn't mean. The relevant passage, which is worth quoting carefully:

> Karger has also shown that unmodified capability systems cannot enforce the confinement policy. The apparent discrepancy results from differences in term definition. Karger's confinement policy is a mandatory access control policy: "this piece of information must not be disclosed to that set of unauthorized parties." That is, it is a policy concerning the flow of information to subjects. Lampson's confinement problem imposes a weaker constraint: information can flow out of the subsystem only through authorized channels.

And earlier:

> Boebert and Karger show that pure capability systems cannot enforce the \*-property. While their conclusion is correct, capability systems do provide sufficient strength to construct mandatory policies at a higher level of abstraction with reasonable performance, as has been done in KeySafe.

And:

> We believe that the KeySafe architecture can enforce both the \*-property and Karger's confinement policy, but this does not directly contradict their claims. KeySafe is a reference monitor built on top of a more primitive capability mechanism; *such a reference monitor constitutes a modified capability system in the sense of Karger's discussion.*

That last sentence is the smoking gun. Shapiro and Weber explicitly *concede* Boebert's and Karger's structural point: enforcing \*-property requires a reference monitor (KeySafe) layered on top of the capability mechanism, and that reference monitor is, in the relevant sense, the "modification" that Boebert was talking about. They're not refuting Boebert; they're saying "yes, you need a reference monitor, and here's how to architect one elegantly using capabilities as the substrate." This is a substantively important contribution — KeySafe really is a clever design and the proof really does work — but it doesn't contradict the original critique.

Also worth noting: the paper is extremely upfront about what it's *not* doing. From the introduction:

> This paper does not address the issue of covert channel suppression. While important, reducing such channels is largely orthogonal to restricting explicit information flow, and is of interest only when it has first been shown that overt channels have been closed.

So the entire side-channel / covert-channel dimension we were discussing earlier — which is where the deepest version of the steganographic objection lives — is explicitly out of scope. They're proving something about overt information flow under their formal model, and they're clear that this is a partial result.

**What the myths paper does with this.** Now reread the citation from the myths paper: "it has been formally verified that any capability system enforcing independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer can enforce both confinement and the *-Property." The phrase doing all the work is "enforcing independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer." That clause is precisely the additional mechanism — store permissions in PSOS, the weak attribute plus constructor checks plus KeySafe in EROS — that Boebert was pointing at when he said "if extra mechanisms are imposed to impose this control, the machine is no longer an unmodified capability machine." The myths paper has restated Boebert's conclusion as a premise of the theorem and then claimed the theorem refutes Boebert. *Of course* you can enforce \*-property if you assume mechanisms enforcing independent controls on capability transfer; that's substantively what \*-property *means* applied to capabilities. The interesting question, which Boebert raised and which the myths paper doesn't engage on its own terms, is whether those independent controls are properly understood as part of the "capability system" or as a separate MAC layer.

**Where this leaves your original concern.** I think your instinct that the original myths-paper argument was suspect is now demonstrably correct, and you can be quite precise about why:

1. PSOS itself, in 1979, already conceded that pure capability semantics are insufficient for propagation control and added store permissions. So the version of "capability system" being defended by the myths paper was never actually proposed by PSOS in unmodified form.

2. Boebert's 1984 objection correctly identified that the addition of such mechanisms takes you outside the "pure" capability model — a claim that's structurally true regardless of whether one considers it pejorative.

3. Shapiro-Weber's 2000 proof, far from refuting Boebert, explicitly affirms his structural point ("KeySafe... constitutes a modified capability system in the sense of Karger's discussion") while showing that one *particular* such modification (the EROS constructor mechanism with weak capabilities, plus KeySafe as a reference monitor) elegantly enforces Lampson-style confinement under a model that excludes covert channels.

4. The myths paper's citation of Shapiro-Weber is technically accurate — the theorem does say what it says — but its rhetorical deployment elides the fact that the theorem's antecedent ("independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer") is essentially the modification Boebert was talking about.

The honest version of the capability community's position, which Shapiro-Weber actually articulates and the myths paper obscures, is something like: "Pure capability systems cannot enforce \*-property or MAC-style confinement; but capability systems are an excellent *substrate* on which to build reference monitors that do enforce these properties, and the resulting composite systems have better modularity, smaller TCBs, and clearer security arguments than ACL-based alternatives." That's a defensible and probably correct position. It's not the same position as "the myths about capabilities are demolished and Boebert was wrong," which is the position the myths paper rhetorically advances.

**On the commenter specifically.** I think you now have a fairly devastating response available if you choose to deploy it, which is: point them at Section 5 of Shapiro-Weber. The paper they're implicitly relying on (because it's the proof that EROS works, and EROS is the cleanest realization of the ocap vision they're defending) *explicitly concedes* that Boebert and Karger were correct about pure capability systems, *explicitly identifies* the reference monitor as the modification, and *explicitly disclaims* covert channels. The commenter's argument — that capability-typed channels prevent unauthorized transfer — is exactly the kind of reference-monitor-built-on-capabilities architecture that Shapiro-Weber acknowledges is necessary and that Boebert was pointing to as the structural concession. There's no actual disagreement at the level of the formal results; the disagreement is entirely about how to label them.

This is, I think, a clean instance of the general pattern we were discussing earlier about quantifier-laden FOL definitions and categorical reformulations: the field developed a security property (\*-property) in one vocabulary, a mechanism (capabilities) in another, proved results about how to compose them, and then — partly through rhetorical accretion in survey-style papers and advocacy literature — collapsed the distinction between "capabilities are a useful substrate for enforcing this property" and "capabilities enforce this property." A compositional treatment in the Maurer style would make the distinction crisp: there's an ideal functionality for authority, there's an ideal functionality for information flow, capabilities realize the former, KeySafe-style reference monitors compose with capabilities to realize the latter, and the composition is what gives you the full security guarantee. None of that is in tension with the technical results; it just resists the rhetorical move of treating the composite system as definitionally what "capability system" means.

content.text: Good instinct on going to primary sources. Let me pull the PSOS paper and the Shapiro-Weber paper so we can ground this in what was actually claimed and what was actually proven, rather than the secondary literature's gloss on either.

1
The foundations of a provably secure operating system (PSOS)
By Richard J. Feiertag and Peter G. Neumann
SRI International
Menlo Park, California
Proceedings of the National Computer Conference
AFIPS Press, 1979, pages 329-334.
INTRODUCTION
PSOS has been designed according to a set of formal techniques embodying the SRI Hierarchical Development
Methodology (HDM). HDM has been described elsewhere, 1-3 and thus is only summarized here. The influence of
HDM on the security of PSOS is also discussed elsewhere.
4
 In addition, Linden5 gives a general discussion of the
impact of structured design techniques on the security of operating systems (including capability systems).
HDM employs formally stated requirements, formal specifications defining the design of each module in a
hierarchical collection of modules, and formal statements of the module interconnections. In the case of PSOS,
there is a formal model describing the requirements of the basic protection mechanism and additional formal models
of the requirements of various applications (e.g., Reference 6). HDM provides the formalism and the structure that
make the formal verification of the system design and implementation possible and conceptually straightforward.
This formal verification consists of formal proofs that specifications satisfy the desired requirements.6 and
subsequently that the actual programs for the system and its applications are consistent with those specifications.2
The design of PSOS has been formally specified using a SPECIfication and Assertion Language called
SPECIAL.7 These specifications 1 define PSOS as a collection of about 20 hierarchically-organized modules. Each
module typically is responsible for objects of a particular type defined by that module. From the user point of view,
the most important modules are those for capabilities, for virtual memory segments, directories, user processes, and
for creating user defined abstract objects. Some modules are to be implemented in software, some in firmware, and
some in hardware—as dictated by the efficiency required.
Capabilities provide the protection mechanism for all such objects in PSOS, and are discussed in the next
section. The subsequent sections of this paper summarize the development methodology used in PSOS, present the
protection mechanism provided by PSOS capabilities, exhibit its properties, show its applicability in developing data
and procedure abstractions, and contrast the PSOS approach with the kernel approach to achieving secure systems.
There are many important issues relating to the use of capabilities in PSOS (and other computer systems) that are
not presented in this paper. Many of these issues are discussed in the references cited here.
PSOS CAPABILITIES
The concept of the capability has appeared in several other operating systems (e.g., References 8-13).
Although capabilities are a fundamental part of the design of each of these systems, they all differ in the way they
use and interpret capabilities. PSOS differs from its predecessors in its uniform use of capabilities throughout the
system and in the simplicity and primitive nature of the basic capability mechanism.
Each object in PSOS can be accessed only upon presentation of an appropriate capability to a module
responsible for that object. Capabilities can be neither forged nor altered. As a consequence, capabilities provide a
controllable basis for implementing the operating system and its applications, as there is no other way of accessing
an object other than by presenting an appropriate capability designating that object.
Each PSOS capability consists of two parts; a unique identifier (uid) and a set of access rights (represented
as a Boolean array). By definition neither part is modifiable, once a capability is created.
2
• Unique Identifiers—PSOS generates only one original capability for each uid. Any number of copies
can be made of a given capability for which a copy is to be made. 
Therefore, a procedure or task that creates a
new capability with some uid knows that the only capabilities that can have that uid must have been
copied either directly or indirectly from the original. In other words, the creator of a capability with a
given uid is able to retain control over the distribution of capabilities with that uid.
• Access Rights—The set of access rights in a capability for an object is interpreted by the module
responsible for that object to define what operations may be performed by using that capability. The
interpretation of the access rights is constrained by a monotonicity rule, namely that the presence of a
right is always more powerful than its absence. The interpretation of the access rights may differ for
different objects, but the monotonicity rule must always apply.
The access rights for a segment capability (as interpreted by the segment manager) indicate whether that
capability may be used to write information into the designated segment, to read that information, to call that
segment as a procedure, and to delete that segment. In PSOS, a directory contains entries, each of which is a
mapping from a symbolic object name to a capability. Each directory is accessed via a capability for that directory.
For directories, the interpretation of access rights is done by the directory manager. The access rights for a directory
capability indicate whether that capability may be used to add entries to the designated directory, to remove entries,
and to use the capability contained in that entry.
A copy of a capability may be made, but the resulting capability cannot have any access rights that the
original capability did not—as is seen from the following list of possible operations upon capabilities. (There are
other access rights, meaningful to capabilities of all types, to be discussed under storage permissions.)
THE PSOS PROTECTION MECHANISM
Capabilities provide the basis for a flexible protection mechanism, as follows:
Tagging of capabilities
In PSOS, capabilities can be distinguished from other data because they are tagged throughout the system
(i.e., in the processor, and in both primary and secondary memory) by means of a tag bit inaccessible to programs.
Consequently, the hardware can enforce the nonforgeability and unalterability of capabilities.
Operations upon capabilities
There are only two basic operations that involve actions upon capabilities (as opposed to actions based on
capabilities, which is the normal mode of accessing objects), as follows.
c = create_capability (i.e., with a previously unused uid) having all access rights.
cl = restrict_acess(c, mask) creates a capability with the same uid as the given capability c and with access rights
that are the intersection of those of the given capability c and the given maximum (mask); i.e., it creates a possibly
restricted copy.
Store permissions
The second capability operation described above appears to permit unrestricted copying of capabilities. For
certain types of security policies this unrestricted copying is too liberal. For example, one may wish to give the
ability to access some object to a particular user but not permit that user to pass that ability on to other users. Because
simplicity of the basic capability mechanism is extremely important to achieve the goals of PSOS, any means for
restricting the propagation of capabilities should not add complexity to the capability mechanism.
A few access rights (only one is currently used by PSOS itself) are reserved as store permissions. This is
the only burden placed on the capability mechanism. The interpretation of the store permissions is performed by the
basic storage object manager of PSOS, namely the segment manager. Each segment in the system is designated as
to whether or not it is capability store limited for each store permission. If a segment is capability store limited for a
3
particular store permission, then it can contain only capabilities that have that store permission. This restriction can
be enforced by a simple check on all segment-modifying operations.
By properly choosing the segments that are capability store limited, some very useful restrictions on the
propagation of capabilities can be achieved. The restriction used in PSOS is not allowing a process to pass certain
capabilities to other processes or to place these capabilities in storage locations (e.g., a directory or interprocess
communication channel) accessible to other processes. (Other restrictions are also possible using store permissions,
such as restricting a capability to a subsystem or a particular invocation of a subsystem. For example, see Reference
1, page II-25.) More general means for restricting propagation of capabilities and for revoking the privilege granted
by a capability can be implemented as subsystems of PSOS. The store permission mechanism has been selected as
primitive in the system because it achieves the desired result with negligible additional complexity or cost.
DATA AND PROCEDURE ABSTRACTIONS
PSOS consists of a collection of data and procedure abstractions constructed in a hierarchical fashion as
shown in Table I. Each level in the hierarchy represents a collection of abstractions introduced at that level.
Abstractions at higher (numbered) levels are implemented using abstract objects introduced at lower levels in the
design. It is unimportant whether an abstraction is implemented in hardware, firmware, or software. It is reasonable
that abstractions introduced at lower levels be implemented largely in hardware or firmware and that abstractions
introduced at higher levels be implemented largely in software. However the demarcation between hardware and
software is not established by the design, and it is quite possible that abstractions occurring throughout the system be
implemented as hybrids, i.e., partially in hardware and partially in software.
Level Abstractions
16 user request interpretation
15 user environments and name spaces
14 user input-output
13 procedure records
12 user processes and visible input-output
11 creation and deletion of user objects
10 directories
9 abstract object manager
8 segments and windows
7 pages
6 system processes and system input-output
5 primitive input-output
4 arithmetic and other basic procedures
3 clocks
2 interrupts
1 registers and other storage
0 capabilities
TABLE I--PSOS Abstraction Hierarchy
It is convenient to group the levels of Table I into generic categories as shown in Table II. The generic
categories collect abstractions satisfying similar goals. At the base of the hierarchy is the capability mechanism,
from which all other abstractions in the system are constructed. Above the basic capability mechanisms are all the
physical resources of the system, e.g., primary and secondary storage, processors and input/output devices. From
the physical resources are constructed the virtual resources. These virtual resources present a more convenient
interface to the programmer than the physical resources, permit multiplexing of the physical resources in a manner
largely invisible to the user, and allow the system to allocate the physical resources so as to maximize their efficient
use. Next in the PSOS hierarchy comes the abstract object manager, providing the mechanism by which higher-level
abstractions may be created. As will be discussed in detail, it is possible to construct higher-level abstractions based
solely on the capability mechanism; however, the abstract object manager provides services that make construction
of such abstractions easier. The top two categories in the generic hierarchy include community abstractions and
4
user-created abstractions. The community abstractions are intended to be used by a large group of users, e.g., by all
the users at a particular site. Such abstractions may be simple utility routines such as a compiler, or may actually
create and control access to new virtual resources such as directories. The user abstractions are those intended for
use by a limited group of individuals.
5
Level Abstractions PSOS Levels
F User abstractions 14-16
E Community abstractions 10-13
D Abstract object manager 9
C Virtual resources 6-8
B Physical resources 1-5
A Capabilities 0
TABLE II-- PSOS Generic Hierarchy
Of the properties stated previously, there are two important ones that make PSOS capability particularly
useful in the construction of abstract objects.
1. The capability serves as a unique name for an abstract object.
2. The capability is unforgeable.
This means that a capability can be used as a name (guaranteed to be unique) by which an abstract object can be
referenced, and access to the object can be controlled by limiting the distribution of the capability.
In addition, there are several important pragmatic reasons why PSOS capabilities are useful as a naming
and protection mechanism for supporting abstract objects.
1. The capability mechanism has a very simple implementation. This allows capabilities to be built into
the system at the lowest level of abstraction, thus making capabilities available for the most primitive
objects.
2. Capabilities are uniform in size, making them easy to manage.
3. The inclusion of access rights in capabilities permits efficient fine-grained control of access to objects.
4. Capabilities can be written into storage (including secondary storage) and retrieved from storage in the
same manner as other data, and therefore have many of the properties of other data.
Capabilities serve as names or tokens for all objects of PSOS. It is because the basic capability mechanism is so
simple in concept and in implementation that construction of the most primitive objects (e.g., input/output channels,
processors, and primary memory) as well as the most complex system objects (e.g., directories and user processes)
and user application objects (e.g., a data management system) is possible using capabilities. This promotes a high
degree of uniformity throughout the system and eliminates the need for many special-purpose facilities.
Objects that have many properties and operations in common and are managed by a single program are said
to have a common type; that program is called a type manager. The type manager implements operations on an
abstract object in terms of operations on the more primitive objects used to represent the abstract object. The type
manager must be able to determine which objects are part of the representation used to implement an abstract object
denoted by a given capability. In other words, a type manager must be able to map the unique identifier of a given
capability into capabilities for its representation objects. The capability mechanism of PSOS does not predispose a
type manager to any particular implementation of this mapping. Different type managers will require diverse
mapping algorithms, depending upon the number of abstract objects and representation objects they must manage,
the desired efficiency of operations on the abstract object, the desired simplicity of the mapping algorithm, and
numerous other factors. For example, the segment type manager uses a mapping algorithm that is in almost all cases
extremely fast; however, the algorithm is quite complex, requiring implementation in both hardware and software.
Extreme speed is essential to the operations of the segment type manager because the segment operations are useful
very frequently (at least once on everyinstruction). The directory type manager uses a less speedy algorithm because
fast access is less essential.
Although the capability mechanism of PSOS does not prescribe a particular mapping algorithm, the system
does provide some assistance in managing abstract objects. The abstract object manager provides a set of operations
by which type managers can associate capabilities for abstract object with the capabilities for their representation
objects. The type manager can then retrieve the representation capabilities by presenting to the abstract object
manager the abstract object capability. This is done in such a way that only the type manager program itself can
6
obtain the representation capabilities, and then only upon presentation of the abstract object capability. The abstract
object manager performs the mapping from abstract object capabilities to representation object capabilities, some of
the bookkeeping functions necessary to implement abstract objects, and some storage allocation. Although the
abstract object manager is intended to be useful and appropriate for a wide variety of type managers and does make
the programming of a type manager much easier, it is only a service and is not essential to the construction of type
managers.
The capability mechanism itself could have been constructed with many of the facilities of the abstract
object manager included. This would have resulted in a capability mechanism that would be more elaborate and—
for some applications—more efficient and easier to use. This is the approach taken by other capability systems cited
above. On the other hand, such a capability mechanism would have required a more complex implementation.
More significantly, the capability mechanism could then not have been placed at the lowest level of abstraction in
the system design, and some of the physical and virtual resources of the system could not have been implemented
using capabilities—requiring a different means for reference. Although having several different naming schemes is
possible (and common in most systems), it destroys the uniformity, conceptual simplicity, elegance, ease of use, and
possibly the efficiency of the system. It is for this reason that PSOS has a very simple, but fully general, capability
mechanism, and that programs enhancing the use of the capability mechanism can be introduced as extensions at
higher levels of the design.
As noted above, there is no clearly delineated system boundary in PSOS. One would normally draw the
system boundary at the interface to the community abstractions. However, all the programs that implement the
community abstractions (such as directories or user processes) could be provided by users as user programs. The
community programs have no special privilege other than claiming resources at initialization by taking possession of
certain capabilities. For example, the user-process type manager takes possession of the capabilities for certain
system processes, which it then multiplexes to create many user processes. If the system’s user-process type
manager did not claim all the available system processes, then it would be possible for a user to provide a different
user-process type manager with the same or different facilities. Similarly, the abstract object manager has no special
privilege at all. A user might program his own abstract object manager if he so desired.
The abstractions at or below any level in the design of Table I form a consistent and useful system.
Clearly, the lower the level chosen as the “top level” of the system, the more primitive that system will be. If all of
the physical resources (levels 1 through 5) are present, then the full PSOS could be reconstructed on the restricted
system, but more likely, one would construct a somewhat different system. Thus, the PSOS design represents a
family of systems. One can choose the level that provides the best set of resources to fulfill the needs of the desired
system without having to include unnecessary facilities. Then one can augment this level with the new type
managers to create abstract objects appropriate to the desired applications. Writing such “system” type managers
requires no additional skill or privilege other than that required to write ordinary user programs. The distinction
between a “system” program and a “user” program is thus indeed blurred.
PSOS RELATIONSHIP TO KERNELS
Several recent operating systems have been constructed using a “kernel” architecture. Such systems
include the Kernelized Secure Operating System (KSOS) 14,15 and two precursor systems developed at MITRE 16, 17
and UCLA.18 The term kernel is used loosely in the literature, but for the purpose of this discussion a kernel is that
part of the operating system that is both necessary and sufficient to satisfy certain requirements of the system. For
example, if the essential requirement of a system is that it enforces a certain security policy, then that part of the
system that enforces the security policy constitutes the kernel. By this definition, a kernel is meaningful only with
respect to some requirement or some set of requirements. The kernel must contain all those parts of the system that
pertain to meeting the requirements, i.e., there is no part of the system outside the kernel that can cause the system
not to meet its requirements. Also, the kernel can contain only those parts of the system that are necessary to meet
the requirements, i.e., the kernel should not contain anything that does not pertain to the meeting of the
requirements. The reasoning behind kernel-based architectures is that since a kernel contains only that part of the
system essential to meeting requirements, it can be small, compared to the system as a whole, and therefore has a
better chance of being correct. One of the main advantages of the kernel approach is the clear statement of purpose
of the system. Since a kernel is meaningful only with respect to some explicit requirements, these requirements
serve as the statement of purpose of the system. The other main advantage is the enhanced probability of correct
operation. Since the programs that are critical to the correct operation of the system are isolated in the kernel, a
great deal of attention can be paid to getting this code right, and less attention can be paid to other system code that
7
may be important but is not critical. The relatively small size of the kernel significantly improves the chances of
applying formal verification techniques to the programs in the kernel in a cost-effective manner, where applying
these techniques to the entire system would be unwieldy.
There are, as one might expect, some disadvantages to the use of kernels. Kernels cannot be casually
modified because, by definition, all the code in the kernel is essential to meeting the requirements of the system, and
any modification is likely to cause the system to deviate from that which is required. One must take extreme care to
be sure that a change in the kernel will not compromise its correct operation.
In order to be able to construct a small kernel, the requirements limit the applications for which the kernel
is useful. For, example, if the requirement of a kernel is to enforce a particular security policy, then only
applications requiring that policy can be reasonably implemented using that kernel. It is not possible to implement
another security policy that is inconsistent with the given security policy.
Yet another of the major problems with the kernel approach is the difficulty of designing a system in such a
way that those programs essential to meeting the requirements are isolated from the nonessential programs. Finally,
experience with the systems mentioned above indicates that kernels are still quite large. Clearly the size of a kernel
depends upon the requirements it is supposed to meet, but reasonable requirements tend to require a large part of the
system to be part of the kernel. Large kernels do not enhance one’s confidence in the correct operation of the
system.
Consider, for example, the kernels of KSOS and of the MITRE system. The requirement of these kernels is
that they enforce a multilevel security policy. Upon close examination of these systems, it is seen that what is
labeled the “kernel” is not really the kernel at all, but is only part of the kernel. These systems have so-called
trusted processes, namely programs that are internally able to violate the requirements, but whose external interface
is consistent with the requirements. These trusted processes include programs for file system backup and retrieval,
I/O spooling, and network interfaces. These programs are not labeled as part of the kernel because their function is
in some sense peripheral to the main task of the system. However, their correct operation is as essential to meeting
the requirements as any kernel program. If the system is to be proven correct, the programs that are used by the
trusted processes must be formally verified. Inclusion of the code for the trusted processes into the kernel makes the
resulting kernel much larger. This illustrates a difficulty in designing a small kernel.
It is a matter of judgment as to whether the advantages of the kernel approach outweigh the disadvantages.
For the situation in which one has clearly defined, specific-overriding requirements for which a small kernel can be
constructed, then the kernel approach is ideal.
PSOS is well suited to situations in which one wants to support many applications with different or
conflicting requirements. Because PSOS is highly extensible and easily supports different type managers with
strong control over access to objects and type managers, it makes possible the support of many different sets of
requirements on one PSOS implementation. For example, several subsystems have been designed for PSOS that
enforce different security constraints. A particular task could be constrained to have access to only one of these
subsystems, but several tasks may be executing different subsystems simultaneously. In a sense, each of these
subsystems can be viewed as a “kernel” for the tasks having access to them, but PSOS can support any number of
such subsystems. Of course, one still has the problem of assuring the correctness of these subsystems and those
parts of PSOS which the subsystems use. However, assuring the correctness of these subsystems on PSOS should
be significantly easier than assuring the correctness of a stand-alone kernel, because each subsystem will be much
smaller and simpler than it would be if it had to be implemented as a stand-alone system. The UCLA system 18 is an
interesting case in that its requirements for security are very broad and general. The UCLA kernel attempts to be
like PSOS in its ability to support a wide range of security policies simultaneously. However, the resulting
requirement does not permit as wide a range of policies to be implemented, and the system design is not as uniform
or elegant as the PSOS design.
SUMMARY
The capabilities of PSOS provide a flexible naming and protection mechanism that can be used to
implement arbitrarily complex subsystems efficiently fulfilling a wide variety of requirements. The properties of
PSOS that make this possible are summarized as follows.
1. The capability mechanism is extremely simple, with only two operations involving the creation of
capabilities and none permitting the alteration of capabilities. There is no policy embedded in the
mechanism.
8
2. The operations on capabilities can be completely controlled at the most primitive conceptual level of
the system design and implemented in hardware. Capabilities are tagged and nonforgeable, and the
protection they provide is not bypassable.
3. Capabilities and other PSOS facilities encourage strong modularity via the creation of data and
procedure abstractions. Such abstractions are the basis of the design of the PSOS system itself and can
be used equally well in application programming.
4. The capability mechanism can be used equally well for user programs. There are no special protection
mechanisms necessary to protect system programs.
5. The capability mechanism is fully general and can simultaneously support subsystems that implement
arbitrary policies. Mechanisms for initialization, backup and recovery, and auditing for both PSOS
and its subsystems can be constructed without subverting the protection mechanism.
6. The operations that can be performed on an object of a particular type are precisely those defined by
the type manager for that object. The operations permitted upon the particular object designated by a
given capability are limited by the access rights of the given capability.
7. If a user is in possession of only one capability for an object, and he wishes to confer some or all of the
access rights to another user (or to another program), he may create and pass a new capability whose
access rights are a subset of those of the original capability. There is no way in which an additional
access right can be introduced. (Note, however, that type managers must consistently enforce the
monotonicity of access rights. That is, the presence of the right must be more powerful than the
absence of that right. This is guaranteed for system-defined object types, and must be assured by the
type managers for other types.)
8. Propagation of capabilities can be restricted by use of capability store permissions. The passage of a
capability to other users can be prevented by not including process store permission in that capability's
access rights.
Although no single commercially available computer has the facilities necessary to implement PSOS
efficiently, each of the required facilities does exist on some computer. Therefore, the proper hardware support for
PSOS can be implemented using established techniques. The formal techniques used to design PSOS make
implementation straightforward 19 and make formal verification of correct operation possible. All of the advantages
summarized here can make PSOS and subsystems implemented on PSOS far more secure and reliable than
contemporary operating systems.
ACKNOWLEDGMENTS
The design of PSOS was accomplished by the close cooperation of several people. Outstanding among
these are Larry Robinson who is primarily responsible for the development of HDM and who played a major role in
the early design of the system, Karl Levitt who designed security related subsystems, and Bob Boyer who is
responsible for the formal mathematical theory.
