Verifying the EROS Confinement Mechanism
Jonathan S. Shapiro Sam Weber
IBM T.J. Watson Research Center
shapj,samweber@us.ibm.com
Abstract
Capability systems can be used to implement higher-level security policies including the
*-property if a mechanism exists to ensure confinement. The implementation can be efficient if the “weak”
access restriction described in this paper is introduced.
In the course of developing EROS, a pure capability
system, it became clear that verifying the correctness of the
confinement mechanism was necessary in establishing the
security of the operating system.
This paper presents a verification of the EROS confinement mechanism with respect to a broad class of capability
architectures (including EROS). We give a formal statement
of the requirements, construct a model of the architecture’s
security policy and operational semantics, and show that
architectures covered by this model enforce the confinement
requirements if a small number of initial static checks on
the confined subsystem are satisfied. The method used generalizes to any capability system.
Keywords: operating systems, capability systems, proof of
correctness, confinement, verification, formal specification.
1. Introduction
EROS [20] is a pure capability system that provides a
mechanism for creating and instantiating confined subsystems: the constructor. This mechanism is part of the system’s trusted computing base. EROS is a clean-room reimplementation of the KeyKOS architecture [2, 6] (originally
called GNOSIS [3]). It builds on the KeySafe [14] design
as the basis for mandatory security policy enforcement. The
security enforcement provided by KeySafe is predicated on
the correctness of the constructor. 
This work is a continuation of work started at the University of Pennsylvania. Portions of this were supported by DARPA under Contracts
#N66001-96-C-852, #MDA972-95-1-0013, and #DABT63-95-C-0073.
Additional support was provided by the AT&T Foundation, and the
Hewlett-Packard and Intel Corporations.
Boebert [1] and Karger [9] have argued that unmodified capability systems cannot enforce even basic mandatory access controls such as the *-property. Both have proposed solutions in the form of hybrid protection architectures. Karger has also argued that unmodified capability
systems cannot enforce confinement [8]. Given that EROS
is a pure capability system, and that its security design rests
on its ability to enforce confinement, a rigorous verification
of the EROS confinement mechanism is necessary.
As described by Lampson [10], the confinement problem is to establish a runtime compartment satisfying two
requirements. First, entities inside the compartment may
transmit information to entities outside the compartment
only via authorized channels of communication. Mutations
inside the compartment therefore may not be observed outside the compartment unless explicitly authorized by the
client. Second, entities outside the compartment may not inspect entities inside the compartment without their consent.
We define a confinement policy that ensures these requirements by testing whether a set of initial static preconditions
is satisfied:
1. All capabilities initially held by the confined subsystem either (a) convey no mutate authority, (b) are authorized channels, or (c) are capabilities to constructor that (recursively) instantiate confined subsystems.
Since no unauthorized mutations are possible, no external observations of unauthorized mutations are possible.
2. No entity outside the confinement boundary holds read
authority to any entity within the newly instantiated
confined subsystem.
We will show that this policy can be enforced in capability
systems, and can be enforced efficiently if a new primitive
access right is introduced.
This paper does not address the issue of covert channel
suppression. While important, reducing such channels is
largely orthogonal to restricting explicit information flow,
and is of interest only when it has first been shown that
overt channels have been closed. Similarly, this paper does

KeySafe enforces mandatory security policies across
confined compartments. Communication between compartments is mediated by a user-level reference monitor, which
relies on knowledge of the semantics of the “primitive” objects to decide what operations and authority transfers are
authorized. To allow later revocation, the reference monitor
inserts transparent forwarding objects in front of all capabilities that are allowed to pass from one compartment to
another. Implementing the reference monitor outside the
kernel allows policies to be updated as new primitive object
types are introduced, and facilitates adaptation of mandatory policies to the needs of particular applications.
In this paper we show that the confinement test used by
the EROS constructor mechanism is correct. That is, we
model a broad class of capability systems, and show that
given a correct implementation of any capability system satisfying our model, the checks performed by the constructor
certify that the newly instantiated service is properly sandboxed, and that (unless permitted by the service) the client
cannot inspect the service. To verify that EROS can enforce
confinement, we have developed a formal statement of requirements and a simplified model, SW, that is both strictly
more powerful and more general than the EROS architecture. SW treats the OS-provided primitive operations as a
serializably concurrent language whose operations are the
kernel calls. We have modeled EROS’s security policy, access control mechanisms, and operational semantics, and
have shown that the EROS semantics satisfies the requirements of confinement.
The balance of this paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 presents a brief summary of EROS and the constructor mechanism, and provides an informal intuition for why
the constructor mechanism results in confinement. Having
described the architecture and mechanism, we describe and
justify key parts of our modeling and proof methodology
(Section 3). Section 4 presents the model itself, the formal
statement of requirements, and the key pieces of the correctness proof (an unabridged proof may be found in [18, 21]).
Some related work is discussed in Section 5. Finally, we
discuss the implications of this work and its effect on the
original system architecture and design.
2. EROS and the Constructor
EROS [20] is a pure capability system. The architecture incorporates what has come to be the conventional nonbuffering interprocess communication primitives [12, 19],
with a novel twist providing for “at most one” reply. Metadata such as mapping structures that are typically considered part of the operating system are exported by EROS
via capability-controlled structures. Both address translation and process state structures are stored in nodes (the
EROS term for c-lists). Data and capabilities are partitioned
to prevent forgery.
For purposes of verification, the essential EROS resource types are processes, data pages, capability pages, and
nodes.1 A process names an address space and executes the
program in that address space in the usual way. Load and
store operations require that data go to data pages and capabilities to capability pages and nodes. Address spaces are
constructed as a tree of nodes whose leaves are data pages.

The EROS object and protection model are extended to
secondary storage by transparent persistence [11]. This ensures that the security model does not change at the secondary storage boundary. Periodically, the system performs
an efficient checkpoint operation, recording the state of
all objects changed since the last snapshot, including processes. There is no kernel-implemented file system; if filelike behavior is required by an application, a process is constructed that implements file behavior.

the resource it designates, it permits the holder to fetch any
read-write capabilities that may reside in that resource. The

2.2. Constructors
The constructor is a trusted EROS application that
builds new program (or subsystem) instances and certifies
whether these instances are confined. The developer (or
installer) of an application obtains a constructor that initially holds no capabilities, and installs those capabilities
that an instance of the application should hold when it is
first started. As each capability is added to the constructor,
the constructor examines it to see if it conveys any authority
to mutate objects. A capability is “safe” if:  It trivially conveys no mutate authority, or  It is a read-only, weak capability, or  It is a capability to a constructor that (recursively) generates confined products.
If the capability is not safe, the constructor records it in a
set of known holes. When all desired capabilities have been
installed, the builder then “freezes” the constructor, after
which it will accept no further capabilities. Once frozen,
all holes are known to the constructor, and the constructor
can therefore determine whether the program instances it
creates are confined.
When a client wishes to create a new instance of a subsystem, such as a file or a sort utility, it presents a set of authorized capabilities to the constructor and asks if the constructor output (the “yield”) is confined modulo those capabilities. If holes  authorized, the product is confined.
The intuition is this: there is no way to cause damage via
safe capabilities, and the user has authorized all of the others. Because capabilities to safe constructors are safe, the
constructor mechanism permits relatively complex subsystems to be built behind a confinement boundary.
Weak capabilities allow a capability pointing to a complex structure to be added safely without requiring that the
structure be traversed. Safety might also be accomplished
using a “deep copy” of the structure, but the weak access restriction makes the copy unnecessary, and thereby allows a
dominating compartment to be granted weak access to content in a lesser compartment without the need for further
mediation. It also allows multiple readers to have consistent
read-only access to a data structure that is being updated.
3. Verification Requirements and Modeling
Method
To verify the constructor mechanism, we must construct
SW, a model of the EROS system, specify the requirements
of confinement in terms independent of both the access control model and the operational semantics, and describe the
access control model. Finally, we must show that the system’s security policies implement its requirements.
System Model Because EROS is persistent, a natural
level of analysis is to examine operations on nodes and
pages. The only additional state saved by the EROS checkpoint mechanism is the list of currently running processes
at the time of the checkpoint. All operations performed by
the kernel consist of modifications to nodes and pages.
SW may safely deviate from the actual system provided
that SW is at least as powerful as EROS. Any behavior that
could occur in EROS must be possible in SW. If this is so,
and if no information can flow out of a confined subsystem
in SW, then the same will hold true in EROS. For modeling
purposes, we have made several departures from the actual
system:
1. The model uses permissions rather than restrictions.
This is merely a switch from subtractive to additive
logic. While the model is richer than the system, every
capability permission existing in the real system can
be captured using the permissions of the model.
2. In the model, no distinction is made between nodes,
pages, and processes. Note that processes are strictly
more powerful than either nodes or pages, and that SW
is therefore more powerful than EROS as a result of
this simplification.
3. The real system uses objects of bounded size. The
model uses sets, both to avoid dependency on any particular object size and to generalize the model to cover
similar systems.
4. EROS keeps capabilities and data in objects of distinct
type. SW allows objects to contain both, but the operational semantics has no operations that allow them
to be interconverted. One may imagine the model objects to consist of a data part and a capability part. The
EROS system represents the subcase in which either
the data or the capability part of each object is required
to be empty.
5. EROS has process states, three invocation operations,
and a special capability type supporting return-once
semantics. In this paper, we have simplified this to
a single, more general invocation type and omitted the

special capability type. Earlier versions of the operational semantics and proof have included both [18, 21].
Their omission here is for brevity and clarity.
6. Reading a page in EROS produces the value that was
last written. SW does not keep track of the contents of
pages. Ignoring page state results in a more powerful
model: processes are maximally hostile. Finally, we
demonstrate that the security of EROS does not rely
upon values computed by applications.
7. The EROS storage allocator is implemented by trusted
user-level software. In SW, its behavior is represented
by the create() and destroy() operations. A complication potentially arises from the fact that the real system reallocates objects. When an object is destroyed,
the allocator reinitializes the object and invalidates all
capabilities to that object by incrementing its version
number. Since there is a finite bound on version numbers, and each version is allocated at most once, we
consider each version of an EROS object to be a distinct SW object for modeling purposes.
8. Real applications obey sequential programs, and their
behavior is highly predictable. SW instead assumes
that the behavior of a program is completely nondeterministic. If it is possible for a program to perform a
particular operation, SW assumes that it does so. This
means that the verification’s correctness does not rely
on peculiarities of instruction sequencing.
Each of these changes makes SW more powerful than
EROS.

it is desirable for the corresponding security policy to be

Excellent. Now we have the actual claims in hand, and it's possible to be precise about what was promised, what was proved, and what the relationship is to your original concern. The picture is more interesting than either side of the HN thread has been letting on, and I think it actually largely *vindicates* Boebert while also showing why the myths paper's citation is technically correct but rhetorically misleading.

Let me lay this out carefully because I think there's real signal here.

**What PSOS actually claimed.** The Feiertag-Neumann paper is, as you noted, brief, and on rereading it's striking how *modest* its actual security claims are. The summary at the end lists eight properties, and exactly one of them addresses propagation: property 8, which says that propagation can be restricted by *store permissions*, which is a mechanism the paper introduces explicitly to handle the case where capability copying needs to be restricted. The relevant passage: "any means for restricting the propagation of capabilities should not add complexity to the capability mechanism," followed by a description of how store permissions are reserved access rights that segments check on modification. So PSOS itself, in its primary description, *concedes the very point Boebert was making* — pure capability semantics are insufficient to restrict propagation, and an *additional mechanism* (store permissions, enforced by the segment manager, which is a trusted type manager outside the capability mechanism proper) is required.

Boebert's 1984 critique, then, is best read not as attacking a strawman PSOS but as making the *theoretical* point that even an "omniscient oracle" creating capabilities cannot control their further propagation through the capability mechanism alone — a claim PSOS doesn't really dispute, since it explicitly adds store permissions to handle exactly that problem. Boebert's closing line that you quoted — "If extra mechanisms are imposed to impose this control, the machine is no longer an unmodified capability machine" — is essentially observing that PSOS *already isn't* an unmodified capability machine in his sense, because of store permissions. The disagreement is partly definitional (what counts as the "capability mechanism" versus "extra mechanisms imposed on top of it") and partly about whether the additional machinery should be considered part of the capability paradigm or a separate orthogonal layer.

**What Shapiro-Weber actually proved.** Now this is where it gets interesting, because the myths paper's citation is technically accurate but does considerable rhetorical work that the underlying paper doesn't support. Shapiro and Weber prove that EROS's constructor mechanism enforces *Lampson's* confinement policy — and they're extremely explicit, in Section 5 of all places, about what this does and doesn't mean. The relevant passage, which is worth quoting carefully:

> Karger has also shown that unmodified capability systems cannot enforce the confinement policy. The apparent discrepancy results from differences in term definition. Karger's confinement policy is a mandatory access control policy: "this piece of information must not be disclosed to that set of unauthorized parties." That is, it is a policy concerning the flow of information to subjects. Lampson's confinement problem imposes a weaker constraint: information can flow out of the subsystem only through authorized channels.

And earlier:

> Boebert and Karger show that pure capability systems cannot enforce the \*-property. While their conclusion is correct, capability systems do provide sufficient strength to construct mandatory policies at a higher level of abstraction with reasonable performance, as has been done in KeySafe.

And:

> We believe that the KeySafe architecture can enforce both the \*-property and Karger's confinement policy, but this does not directly contradict their claims. KeySafe is a reference monitor built on top of a more primitive capability mechanism; *such a reference monitor constitutes a modified capability system in the sense of Karger's discussion.*

That last sentence is the smoking gun. Shapiro and Weber explicitly *concede* Boebert's and Karger's structural point: enforcing \*-property requires a reference monitor (KeySafe) layered on top of the capability mechanism, and that reference monitor is, in the relevant sense, the "modification" that Boebert was talking about. They're not refuting Boebert; they're saying "yes, you need a reference monitor, and here's how to architect one elegantly using capabilities as the substrate." This is a substantively important contribution — KeySafe really is a clever design and the proof really does work — but it doesn't contradict the original critique.

Also worth noting: the paper is extremely upfront about what it's *not* doing. From the introduction:

> This paper does not address the issue of covert channel suppression. While important, reducing such channels is largely orthogonal to restricting explicit information flow, and is of interest only when it has first been shown that overt channels have been closed.

So the entire side-channel / covert-channel dimension we were discussing earlier — which is where the deepest version of the steganographic objection lives — is explicitly out of scope. They're proving something about overt information flow under their formal model, and they're clear that this is a partial result.

**What the myths paper does with this.** Now reread the citation from the myths paper: "it has been formally verified that any capability system enforcing independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer can enforce both confinement and the *-Property." The phrase doing all the work is "enforcing independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer." That clause is precisely the additional mechanism — store permissions in PSOS, the weak attribute plus constructor checks plus KeySafe in EROS — that Boebert was pointing at when he said "if extra mechanisms are imposed to impose this control, the machine is no longer an unmodified capability machine." The myths paper has restated Boebert's conclusion as a premise of the theorem and then claimed the theorem refutes Boebert. *Of course* you can enforce \*-property if you assume mechanisms enforcing independent controls on capability transfer; that's substantively what \*-property *means* applied to capabilities. The interesting question, which Boebert raised and which the myths paper doesn't engage on its own terms, is whether those independent controls are properly understood as part of the "capability system" or as a separate MAC layer.

**Where this leaves your original concern.** I think your instinct that the original myths-paper argument was suspect is now demonstrably correct, and you can be quite precise about why:

1. PSOS itself, in 1979, already conceded that pure capability semantics are insufficient for propagation control and added store permissions. So the version of "capability system" being defended by the myths paper was never actually proposed by PSOS in unmodified form.

2. Boebert's 1984 objection correctly identified that the addition of such mechanisms takes you outside the "pure" capability model — a claim that's structurally true regardless of whether one considers it pejorative.

3. Shapiro-Weber's 2000 proof, far from refuting Boebert, explicitly affirms his structural point ("KeySafe... constitutes a modified capability system in the sense of Karger's discussion") while showing that one *particular* such modification (the EROS constructor mechanism with weak capabilities, plus KeySafe as a reference monitor) elegantly enforces Lampson-style confinement under a model that excludes covert channels.

4. The myths paper's citation of Shapiro-Weber is technically accurate — the theorem does say what it says — but its rhetorical deployment elides the fact that the theorem's antecedent ("independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer") is essentially the modification Boebert was talking about.

The honest version of the capability community's position, which Shapiro-Weber actually articulates and the myths paper obscures, is something like: "Pure capability systems cannot enforce \*-property or MAC-style confinement; but capability systems are an excellent *substrate* on which to build reference monitors that do enforce these properties, and the resulting composite systems have better modularity, smaller TCBs, and clearer security arguments than ACL-based alternatives." That's a defensible and probably correct position. It's not the same position as "the myths about capabilities are demolished and Boebert was wrong," which is the position the myths paper rhetorically advances.

**On the commenter specifically.** I think you now have a fairly devastating response available if you choose to deploy it, which is: point them at Section 5 of Shapiro-Weber. The paper they're implicitly relying on (because it's the proof that EROS works, and EROS is the cleanest realization of the ocap vision they're defending) *explicitly concedes* that Boebert and Karger were correct about pure capability systems, *explicitly identifies* the reference monitor as the modification, and *explicitly disclaims* covert channels. The commenter's argument — that capability-typed channels prevent unauthorized transfer — is exactly the kind of reference-monitor-built-on-capabilities architecture that Shapiro-Weber acknowledges is necessary and that Boebert was pointing to as the structural concession. There's no actual disagreement at the level of the formal results; the disagreement is entirely about how to label them.

This is, I think, a clean instance of the general pattern we were discussing earlier about quantifier-laden FOL definitions and categorical reformulations: the field developed a security property (\*-property) in one vocabulary, a mechanism (capabilities) in another, proved results about how to compose them, and then — partly through rhetorical accretion in survey-style papers and advocacy literature — collapsed the distinction between "capabilities are a useful substrate for enforcing this property" and "capabilities enforce this property." A compositional treatment in the Maurer style would make the distinction crisp: there's an ideal functionality for authority, there's an ideal functionality for information flow, capabilities realize the former, KeySafe-style reference monitors compose with capabilities to realize the latter, and the composition is what gives you the full security guarantee. None of that is in tension with the technical results; it just resists the rhetorical move of treating the composite system as definitionally what "capability system" means.

Yes, I think you've put your finger on it exactly, and I'd actually push your reading a little further: this isn't just a presentational matter where PSOS happened to bury the lede. There's a deeper rhetorical/conceptual structure to what's happening, and once you see it, the whole shape of the historical debate becomes legible.

The tension you've identified between those two passages is the tension at the heart of the entire capability tradition's self-presentation, and it's been there since the beginning. On the one hand, capabilities are valorized precisely because they unify naming and authority into a single uniform mechanism — "Capabilities can be written into storage... and therefore have many of the properties of other data." This uniformity is the thing that makes capabilities ergonomically and architecturally elegant: you don't need separate machinery for naming versus protection, references propagate through normal data-flow channels, and the system has a clean compositional structure where every object is reached through a capability and nothing else. This is genuinely beautiful and it's what attracts good designers to the model. On the other hand, the moment you want to enforce any *policy* about which subjects should have which authorities, you run into the fact that "treats like data" means "propagates like data," and you have to introduce some mechanism — store permissions, weak attributes, constructors, reference monitors — that *restricts* the data-like behavior. And every such restriction is, in a precise sense, a step away from the very uniformity that motivated the model in the first place.

So you have two visions of what a capability system is for, in tension:

**Vision A (ergonomic/architectural):** Capabilities are a clean, uniform mechanism for naming and authority that makes the *positive* part of authority management — granting, delegating, attenuating, composing — natural and compositional. The system's claim to security rests on (a) unforgeability, which prevents authority manifestation from nothing, and (b) the fact that authority can only flow along paths that the architecture makes visible, which makes the *analysis* of authority flow tractable. This vision is fundamentally about making security *auditable* and *compositional*, not about enforcing specific MAC policies.

**Vision B (mandatory-policy enforcement):** Capabilities are a substrate on which one can enforce traditional security policies like \*-property and confinement, doing so more cleanly than ACL-based systems because the unforgeability and provenance properties give you better starting axioms for proofs. This vision is fundamentally about *replacing* ACL-based MAC systems with capability-based ones that do the same job better.

These are different visions. Vision A is defensible on its own terms and doesn't require Vision B; you can perfectly well prefer ocap-style design for its architectural cleanliness without committing to the claim that it solves the MAC enforcement problem. Vision B is the contested one, and it's where Boebert and Karger correctly identified that you have to add machinery beyond pure capabilities to get there. The historical problem is that the capability tradition has consistently presented itself as offering both, and has used the genuine appeal of Vision A to underwrite contested claims about Vision B.

Reread the PSOS paper with this lens and the passage you quoted reveals itself as exactly the rhetorical move that creates the tension. The "Capabilities can be written into storage... and therefore have many of the properties of other data" line is a Vision A claim — it's celebrating the uniformity that makes ocap design elegant. The "store permissions" discussion is a grudging concession to Vision B realities — they need *some* mechanism to restrict propagation, but they want to minimize its conceptual footprint because it's in tension with the Vision A story. Hence the framing: "any means for restricting the propagation of capabilities should *not add complexity to the capability mechanism*." Store permissions are introduced as a kind of minimal additional access right, almost an afterthought, deliberately positioned as a small adjustment rather than a fundamental architectural concession. But as you correctly observe, what they're calling a minor "burden" *is in fact the entire load-bearing structure* for any non-trivial security policy. Every interesting MAC property in PSOS lives in the store permission mechanism and the type managers that interpret it, not in the capability mechanism proper.

Boebert's critique, read in this light, is essentially: "you've buried the load-bearing security mechanism inside a footnote about 'store permissions' and pretended the architectural story is about the elegant capability layer. The capability tradition has a recurring pattern where, when pressed on a specific limitation, advocates either (a) introduce an additional mechanism and treat it as a natural extension of the capability model, or (b) redefine "capability system" to include whatever's needed to defeat the current objection. The cleaner presentation would have been more intellectually honest, would have made the field's actual contribution clearer, and would have avoided forty-plus years of recurring HN-style arguments where one side overclaims, the other side correctly objects, and the resulting debate generates more heat than light because the participants are talking past each other about what "capability system" even means. The cleaner presentation would also have positioned ocap design for what it's actually good for — building modular, auditable, compositional systems where authority flow is visible and analyzable — which is genuinely valuable and doesn't need the inflated claims about MAC enforcement to justify itself.

There's a meta-observation here that connects back to our earlier thread about category theory and structural sensibility: one of the things a categorical/compositional framing forces on you is *honesty about layers*. If you have to state your ideal functionalities precisely and prove that your construction realizes their composition, you can't fudge the question of which layer does which work. You have to say "this construction realizes the authority functionality" and "this construction realizes the flow-control functionality" and "their composition realizes the combined functionality." I'm going to first apologize for engaging in rhetorical sleight of hand myself, since I indulged in a bit of the hand-wavy argumentation that happens so often in these nit-picky debates. I'm going to respond cleanly here mostly to sharpen my own argumentative saw.

The original PSOS paper makes a few claims that are in tension with one another, and then buries the lede about how that tension can be addressed. Here's a few passages, directly quoted from the paper:

> [...] there are several important pragmatic reasons why PSOS capabilities are useful as a naming and protection mechanism for supporting abstract objects.
> 1. The capability mechanism has a very simple implementation. This allows capabilities to be built into the system at the lowest level of abstraction, thus making capabilities available for the most primitive objects.
> 2. Capabilities are uniform in size, making them easy to manage.
> 3. The inclusion of access rights in capabilities permits efficient fine-grained control of access to objects.
> 4. Capabilities can be written into storage (including secondary storage) and retrieved from storage in the same manner as other data, and therefore have many of the properties of other data.

Item 4 above is the one that should draw the most attention. I don't think anyone would contest the claim that PSOS has wonderful ergonomics for managing access to resources, *but* the moment you want to impose a system-wide access control policy then you must add another security mechanism, completely outside the capability abstraction, that adds some friction. This is fully acknowledged by the PSOS authors, although frankly they buried the lede since this is the only thing that the secure systems folks really cared about at the time. From the section on *Store permissions":

> Because simplicity of the basic capability mechanism is extremely important to achieve the goals of PSOS, any means for restricting the propagation of capabilities should not add complexity to the capability mechanism. [...] A few access rights (only one is currently used by PSOS itself) are reserved as *store permissions*. This is the only burden placed on the capability mechanism.

> By properly choosing the segments that are capability store limited, some very useful restrictions on the propagation of capabilities can be achieved. The restriction used in PSOS is not allowing a process to pass certain capabilities to other processes or to place these capabilities in storage locations (e.g., a directory or interprocess communication channel) accessible to other processes. [...] The store permission mechanism has been selected as primitive in the system because it achieves the desired result with negligible additional complexity or cost.

This appears as claim 8 in the summary section of the paper near the end:

> Propagation of capabilities can be restricted by use of capability store permissions. The passage of a capability to other users can be prevented by not including process store permission in that capability's access rights.

Ok, so that's the PSOS paper and it's claims. Boebert's paper--if it can be called that, since it is a mere 3 pages--states its argument in fairly direct terms:

> The attack is made possible by an inherent attribute of pure capability machines: the right to exercise access carries with it the right to propagate that access. Thus even if an omniscient oracle correctly creates capabilities, it cannot control their further propagation. If extra mechanisms are imposed to impose this control, the machine is no longer an unmodified capability machine.

The only issue here is, perhaps, semantic: Boebert (correctly) states that an *unmodified* capability machine cannot provide what is considered a very basic mandatory security policy, but the PSOS folks already acknowledged this by stating that the system needs a capability store permission manager for mandatory security policy enforcement. The phrasing that they used--"the store permission mechanism has been selected as primitive in the system"--is the bait-and-switch where they treat it like part of the capability model rather than making it clear that it is an entirely distinct mechanism that must be *composed* with pure capabilities to achieve the (genuinely difficult) security properties that systems designers were seeking.

I suspect the horse is already dead it's worth double-tapping to make sure, so let's continue. The *Myths* paper muddies the waters further by making this claim after supposedly debunking Boebert:

> Boebert’s result is valid in any capability system that cannot distinguish between data transfer and capability transfer. But partitioned and type-enforced capability systems do not have this problem, and password capability systems have been engineered to avoid this problem [1, 11].
> Moreover, it has been formally verified that any capability system enforcing independent controls on data transfer and capability transfer can enforce both confinement and the \*-Property [22].

We'll focus on reference [22] since that is the stronger claim here. That paper is Shapiro & Weber (2000) "Verifying the EROS Confinement Mechanism": https://flint.cs.yale.edu/cs428/doc/eros-verify.pdf

This is the motivation for their paper, which is stated unambiguously:

> Boebert [1] and Karger [9] have argued that unmodified capability systems cannot enforce even basic mandatory access controls such as the \*-property. Both have proposed solutions in the form of hybrid protection architectures. Karger has also argued that unmodified capability systems cannot enforce confinement [8]. Given that EROS is a pure capability system, and that its security design rests on its ability to enforce confinement, a rigorous verification of the EROS confinement mechanism is necessary.

For some reason, they decide to respond to these claims in the *Related work* section, just before their conclusion, although they do address them head-on:

> Boebert [1] and Karger [9] show that pure capability systems cannot enforce the \*-property. While their conclusion is correct, capability systems do provide sufficient strength to construct mandatory policies at a higher level of abstraction with reasonable performance, as has been done in KeySafe [14].
> Karger has also shown that unmodified capability systems cannot enforce the confinement policy [8]. The apparent discrepancy results from differences in term definition. Karger’s confinement policy is a mandatory access control policy: "this piece of information must not be disclosed
to that set of unauthorized parties." That is, it is a policy concerning the flow of information to subjects. Lampson’s confinement problem [10] imposes a weaker constraint: information can flow out of the subsystem only through authorized channels. That is, in the Lampson definition the channels define an encapsulation boundary to be enforced.
> We believe that the KeySafe architecture can enforce both the \*-property and Karger’s confinement policy, but this does not directly contradict their claims. KeySafe is a reference monitor built on top of a more primitive capability mechanism; such a reference monitor constitutes a modified capability system in the sense of Karger’s discussion.

I think it's pretty clear that once you pin down a precise definition of the terms used in the discussion, there is little disagreement among any of these authors. However, in casual arguments this precision is lost and you end up with a situation where two things are true at the same time but people choose to talk about only one at a time and think they're winning arguments:

1. An unmodified capability machine cannot enforce the \*-property or mandatory access control confinement policies.

2. Modifying a capability machine to enforce such policies (and provide proof of enforcement) is straightforward because there is a single clearly-defined interface through which the systems may be composed.

My stance is that the PSOS folks screwed up their marketing. They really do have a superior product, so to speak, but they tried to downplay the fact that it did not provide a solution to the genuinely difficult problem of enforcing MAC policies (which was really all about crypto, not capabilities or ACLs). The right pitch for ocap design is "we offer a cleaner, more compositional, more auditable substrate for authority management--which is itself a substantial contribution and worth caring about--and on top of that substrate you can build the same MAC policies you'd build on any other substrate, but with better starting axioms and clearer proof structures." That's a contribution that doesn't need to be defended against Boebert because it doesn't claim (or appear to claim) what Boebert showed couldn't be claimed.

At least, I *think* that's what is happening.

Your intuition here is exactly right, and the connection is even tighter than you're sketching — once you see it, a lot of Pony's design becomes obviously coherent in a way that the documentation doesn't always make clear. Let me try to make the connection precise, because I think it ties together the whole arc of this conversation in a way that's worth seeing.

Start with what's actually happening with Pony's object capabilities, since you're approximately right but it's worth being careful. Pony has *two* capability systems that are easy to conflate but are doing different work:

**Reference capabilities** (`iso`, `trn`, `ref`, `val`, `box`, `tag`) are Pony's substructural type system. They're a refinement of linear/affine types that encodes, in the type, the sharing and mutability discipline of a reference. `iso` is "isolated" — at most one writable alias exists in the entire program; `val` is "value" — globally immutable, so unbounded sharing is safe; `tag` is "opaque identity" — you can hold the reference and pass it around but cannot read or write through it. The full lattice manages the data-race-freedom proof: the compiler statically verifies that no two actors can simultaneously hold aliases that would permit a race. This is descended from work on uniqueness types (Clean), linear types (Wadler and the linear-logic tradition), and ownership types (the Cyclone/Rust lineage), with the specific contribution being a particularly clean lattice that handles the actor model's needs.

**Object capabilities** in Pony are the ocap tradition you're already familiar with, lifted into the type system. The standard examples are things like `AmbientAuth` and the various authority tokens for filesystem, network, environment access. To open a TCP socket you need a `TCPConnectionAuth`, which you can only get from a `NetAuth`, which you can only get from `AmbientAuth`, which is only available in `Main.create()`. The chain of constructors is the provenance chain; the type system enforces non-construction (you cannot just write `recover NetAuth end` from nowhere; the constructor is private and only accepts the parent authority).

Now your insight — and this is the part I want to validate and sharpen — is that *these two systems are deeply related, and the relation is the thing that makes Pony's design coherent*. You said "the runtime never needs to store an actual token value, because the mere presence of a value is equivalent to a provenance proof generated by the static typing discipline." That's exactly right, and it's worth dwelling on because it's a genuinely beautiful piece of design.

In a traditional capability OS like EROS or KeyKOS, capabilities are *runtime* objects. The kernel maintains c-lists, the unforgeability is enforced by hardware tag bits or by the kernel mediating all references, and the provenance discipline (you can only get a new capability by deriving it from an existing one) is enforced by runtime checks in the kernel's capability invocation paths. In Pony, all of that runtime machinery disappears, because the compiler does it at compile time. An `AmbientAuth` value is, at runtime, just... a pointer to nothing in particular, or maybe even nothing at all (the compiler might be able to optimize it away entirely if all uses are erased). The *type* `AmbientAuth` is what carries the authority; the value is just a witness that you have a value of that type. Since the type system enforces that you can only construct values of that type through the legitimate constructor chain, having a value of that type *is* a static proof that you obtained it through a legitimate provenance path. The capability has been compiled away into the type discipline.

This is the same move that makes phantom types in Haskell so powerful — types that have no runtime representation but encode invariants that the compiler enforces. `STRef s a` works exactly this way: the `s` parameter is a phantom that prevents references from escaping their `runST` scope, even though `s` is never instantiated to anything that exists at runtime. Pony's ocap system is doing this at the system-design level: authority is a static, type-level concept that the runtime never needs to know about, because the compiler has already verified that every use site has a legitimate provenance.

Now here's where the connection to the entire historical thread you've been investigating becomes deep. Recall the move I described earlier — from "express the property in first-order logic and verify it" to "encode the property in the morphism structure and let composition handle it." Pony's ocap system *is that move applied to capabilities*. The traditional capability tradition expressed the property "this subject has legitimate authority over that object" as a runtime predicate, checked by the kernel on every invocation. Pony expresses the same property as a *typing rule*: this term has type `T`, and `T` is constructed in such a way that having a value of `T` is equivalent to having traversed a legitimate authority chain. The runtime checks vanish because the proof is in the typing derivation, and the typing derivation has already been verified by the time the program runs.

This is *exactly* the categorical-reformulation pattern we've been talking about throughout this conversation. Authority becomes a property of morphisms in the category of well-typed Pony programs, rather than a property of values manipulated by an external reference monitor. Composition of authority becomes composition of typed terms. Attenuation becomes a typing rule. The whole ocap discipline, instead of being implemented by a kernel that intercepts every invocation, is implemented by the structure of the type system itself.

And this is where your historical speculation about the seed connection becomes really interesting. The connection between capabilities and linear types isn't coincidental, and it isn't a recent discovery; it goes back at least to the late 80s and early 90s, when people like Henry Baker were writing about "use-once variables" and linear logic was being recognized as the right substructural framework for reasoning about resource use. The intellectual lineage runs roughly: Dennis and Van Horn's capabilities (1966) establish authority as an unforgeable reference with a provenance discipline; Girard's linear logic (1987) provides a logical framework for reasoning about resources that can be used exactly once; Wadler and others (late 80s, early 90s) connect linear logic to programming language type systems; Clean's uniqueness types and the various ownership-type proposals (90s and 2000s) work out how to make this practical for systems programming; Rust (2010s) demonstrates it can be done at production scale; Pony recognizes that the *same machinery* that enforces uniqueness for data-race-freedom can be reused, almost without modification, to enforce capability provenance for security.

The reason it can be reused is that the underlying mathematical structure is the same. Linear types and capabilities are both expressions of *substructural reasoning about resources*: they're both saying "this thing is not freely duplicable; its use is constrained by where it came from." Linear types use this to prevent data races (a resource that can only be held by one party at a time cannot be raced on); capabilities use it to prevent unauthorized access (a resource that can only be derived from a legitimate parent cannot be manifested from nothing). The substructural discipline is the same; the interpretation of what counts as the "resource" is what differs. Pony's `iso` is, structurally, a linear type for memory safety; Pony's `AmbientAuth` is, structurally, a linear-ish type (it's actually `val`-like for distribution but the provenance chain is what matters) for authority management. They share machinery because they're doing the same kind of work.

This connects back to your steganography and constructive cryptography background in a way I think you'll find pleasing. Linear types and ocap authority are both, at root, *compositional* security mechanisms — they have the property that the security guarantee of a composite system follows from the security guarantees of its parts, by virtue of how the parts compose. That's the Maurer-style property we were discussing earlier. The categorical structure that makes Pony work is the same structure that makes constructive cryptography work: identify the right notion of resource, the right notion of construction, and prove that constructions compose. The fact that Pony can give you both data-race-freedom and capability security from essentially the same type machinery is evidence that you've found the right underlying category — one where the morphisms naturally respect both properties.

There's a further point worth making about your "Elixir for systems programming" framing, because I think it's structurally apt in a way that goes beyond the actor model surface similarity. Elixir gets its safety properties largely from the absence of shared mutable state — actors communicate via immutable messages, and the BEAM runtime guarantees that no actor can corrupt another's state because there *is* no shared state to corrupt. This is a runtime discipline; the cost is that everything is immutable and you pay for copies. Pony gets the same safety properties by using the type system to permit *controlled* sharing of mutable state, where the type system proves that no two actors can simultaneously hold writable aliases. The actor model is the same; the difference is that Elixir achieves safety by forbidding the dangerous patterns at runtime, while Pony achieves safety by *typing* the dangerous patterns so that only safe instances of them are compilable. This is again the pattern of moving a property from runtime check to static guarantee, and again it's the same move that makes Pony's ocap system work without runtime capability machinery.

If I were going to push your insight one step further, I'd say this: the fact that Pony quietly implements its ocap system through the type discipline, almost as a side effect of the reference capability work, is actually evidence that the capability tradition had identified the right underlying structural property all along but lacked the type-theoretic vocabulary to express it cleanly. Dennis and Van Horn in 1966 were reaching for "unforgeable, provenance-respecting references," but they expressed it in terms of kernel-mediated runtime objects because that was the only vocabulary available. Pony in the 2010s expresses the same property in terms of types because that vocabulary now exists. The transition from runtime-mediated capabilities to type-level capabilities is the same kind of transition as the transition from runtime bounds-checking to dependently-typed array indexing, or from runtime null checks to `Maybe`/`Option` types: the property moves from being enforced by execution to being enforced by the structure of the program, with all the compositional and verification benefits that move brings.

So yes, the connection is real, it's deep, and it's exactly the kind of thing that retroactively makes the entire historical capability project legible as having been pointing at something true even when its proponents couldn't quite articulate what. The frustration of forty years of arguments about whether capabilities can or can't enforce \*-property looks different when you can see that the *actual* contribution of the capability tradition was identifying a structural property — substructural authority with provenance — that turned out to have a clean type-theoretic realization once the type theory was ready. The capability folks were right that there was something there; they were just trying to express it in an architectural vocabulary that wasn't quite the right level of abstraction, which is why the debates kept getting bogged down in questions about whether the kernel mechanism could enforce this or that property. The right level of abstraction was the type system all along; nobody had it in 1966, and by the time we did the capability tradition had already calcified around the OS-architecture framing.

Pony, in this reading, is one of the first systems that gets to *cash in* on the capability tradition's underlying insight without inheriting the architectural baggage. That's a substantial achievement, and your intuition that it's connected to the whole arc of capability research is exactly correct — it's the same project, with a forty-year detour through OS design before someone figured out that the right place to put it was the compiler.

chat_messages.text:
This is a genuinely interesting architectural sketch, and I want to engage with it seriously rather than just enthusiastically, because I think there are real opportunities here but also some non-obvious tensions that matter for whether the design actually works. Let me try to lay out what I think it would look like at each layer, what gets harder than it sounds, and where the eBPF-style cross-boundary verification would and wouldn't help.

The basic shape is appealing: seL4 gives you a verified kernel with capability-based authority enforcement at the hardware-mediation level; Pony gives you a type-checked language whose substructural discipline encodes both data-race-freedom and capability provenance; the layered abstractions in between progressively elaborate the seL4 primitives into useful services while *preserving* the compositional guarantees. The eBPF analogy says that at certain boundaries, instead of paying the cost of crossing a protection domain on every operation, you push a verified piece of logic *across* the boundary and let it execute in the trusted domain on behalf of the less-trusted one. Done right, this gives you the verification properties of separation with something approaching the performance of in-process calls.

The first thing worth getting clear is that seL4 and Pony are talking about capabilities at *radically different scales*, and bridging them is one of the design's harder problems. seL4 capabilities are kernel objects — they live in cnodes, they're invoked via syscalls that cross the user/kernel boundary, and the protection they provide is enforced by the hardware (page tables, etc.) under the kernel's discipline. Pony capabilities are type-level — they're erased at runtime and the compiler discharges the proof obligations statically. When you build the service-abstraction layer, you have to decide how seL4 capabilities are *represented* in the Pony type system and what relationship the type-level discipline bears to the kernel-level discipline.

The cleanest design — and I think this is what you'd want to aim for — is that each seL4 capability the process holds is *witnessed* by a Pony value of a type that is constructed only at the entry point where the seL4 cap is received, and whose provenance discipline in the Pony type system mirrors the seL4 derivation discipline. So if your process is granted, at startup, a capability to some endpoint, you get a Pony value of type `EndpointCap` whose constructor is unreachable except from the runtime initialization that received the seL4 cap. Subsequent derivations (minting attenuated caps, transferring caps via IPC) happen at both levels in lockstep: the Pony program calls a service that, internally, performs the seL4 derivation and returns a Pony value of the appropriately attenuated type, with the constructor again hidden behind the derivation interface. The Pony type system enforces that you cannot manifest a capability witness from nothing; seL4 enforces that you cannot manifest a kernel capability from nothing; the two enforcements run in parallel and the layered abstractions are responsible for keeping them synchronized.

The thing that makes this work — and the thing that's often missed in casual sketches of "Pony on seL4" — is that the Pony layer adds something seL4 doesn't have, which is *intra-process* capability discipline. seL4 enforces capabilities between processes (cnodes are per-process, invocation crosses the kernel), but inside a process, once you hold a capability, the kernel doesn't care what you do with it. Pony's type system can enforce that within a process, an `EndpointCap` is held by exactly one component, can only be attenuated downward, and cannot be copied to a component that shouldn't have it — all without runtime checks. This is genuinely additive: you're getting authority discipline at the intra-process granularity that seL4 doesn't provide and that's hard to provide any other way without significant runtime overhead. It's the right composition: seL4 for inter-process, Pony for intra-process, both using substructural capability discipline as the underlying model.

Now the layered service abstractions. I'd think about this as a tower where each layer adds expressiveness while preserving the capability discipline:

**Layer 0** is the seL4 kernel itself, which you don't touch. You're consuming its primitives: cnodes, endpoints, notifications, frames, VSpaces, IRQ caps, scheduling contexts. The seL4 user-level libraries (libsel4, sel4utils, etc.) wrap the raw syscalls.

**Layer 1** is the Pony binding to libsel4: types like `EndpointCap`, `NotificationCap`, `FrameCap`, etc., with constructors that are private and only reachable from the runtime bootstrap that imports the initial cspace. Derivation operations (mint, copy, move) are typed such that they consume input capabilities and produce output capabilities with the appropriate attenuation reflected in the type. This layer is mostly about getting the type-level representation right and ensuring the witnessing discipline I described above. The verification obligation here is "the Pony type system's provenance discipline correctly mirrors the seL4 derivation discipline," which is non-trivial but tractable.

**Layer 2** is service abstractions over seL4 primitives: a memory allocator that hands out typed frame capabilities, a thread/process manager that creates new VSpaces and cspaces with controlled initial endowments, a clock service, an interrupt dispatcher. Each of these is structured as a Pony actor (or set of actors) that holds the relevant seL4 capabilities and exposes a typed interface. The capability discipline propagates: requesting memory from the allocator returns an `OwnedFrame` (analogous to `Box<T>` in Rust, an `iso` thing); requesting a new thread returns a `ThreadHandle` that lets the caller pause/resume/destroy but cannot peek at the thread's state. This is the layer where Pony's `iso`/`val`/`tag` distinctions start really earning their keep, because you want to express things like "this frame is exclusively owned by this component" or "this notification cap is held by anyone but only the holder of the matching endpoint cap can signal it."

**Layer 3** is "POSIX-ish" services: a filesystem, a network stack, a process model that looks more like Unix to programs that want that. The interesting design question here is which services are implemented as separate seL4 processes (with all IPC crossing the kernel) versus as Pony libraries linked into client processes (with the type system providing the discipline that would otherwise come from process separation). The right answer depends on the trust model: if the filesystem must protect against malicious clients, it needs to be a separate process; if it only needs to protect against accidental misuse by trusted clients, it can be a Pony library and you save the IPC cost. The fact that Pony's type system can enforce capability discipline within a process means you have a *finer-grained choice* than the seL4-only design: instead of every service being either fully co-located or fully separated, you can pick the threat model per service.

**Layer 4** is application-level service abstractions: object stores, databases, web frameworks, whatever. By this point you're mostly in normal Pony territory, with the layers underneath providing a substrate that gives you both authority discipline and data-race-freedom by construction.

Now the eBPF-analog idea, which is where I want to push back a little because I think it's where the design gets harder than it sounds, but also where the most interesting possibilities live.

The eBPF model works because BPF programs are written in a constrained language, verified by an in-kernel verifier (no unbounded loops, bounded memory access, type-checked helpers), and then JIT-compiled to run in kernel context with performance comparable to native kernel code. The verification is tractable because the BPF language is *deliberately* limited: no unbounded recursion, no arbitrary pointer arithmetic, a small set of helper functions, a verifier that's been hardened over years against escape attacks. The key insight is that you accept significant expressiveness restrictions in exchange for being able to push code across a trust boundary with strong static guarantees.

Translating this to a Pony-on-seL4 setting, the natural analog is: you have a service running in one process, and clients running in other processes. Normally, every client request crosses the seL4 IPC boundary, with all the cost that entails. The eBPF-style optimization is to let the client *upload* a verified fragment of logic — written in some constrained subset of Pony, or in a separate restricted language compiled to a verified IR — that runs *in the service's address space* on the client's behalf, batching operations or doing local computation that would otherwise require multiple IPC round-trips.

The thing that makes this potentially work better in Pony than in BPF is that *Pony's type system is already doing verification*. The reference capability discipline already proves data-race-freedom; the ocap discipline already proves authority. So in principle, a "Pony BPF" subset doesn't need a separate verifier the way BPF does — the type system *is* the verifier, you just need to characterize the subset of Pony programs that can be safely cross-loaded.

But here's where it gets hard: the safety property you need for cross-loading isn't just "this code is well-typed Pony." It's something like "this code, when executed in the service's address space with access to a restricted set of the service's capabilities, cannot violate the service's invariants." That's a much stronger property, and it requires:

First, a *capability discipline for the uploaded code* that's stricter than normal Pony. The uploaded fragment can only see capabilities it's explicitly granted, and it can't construct new ones except through allowed derivations. This is approximately what Pony already gives you, but you have to make sure the uploaded code can't access ambient authority by, e.g., importing a module that exports access to something it shouldn't have.

Second, *termination/resource bounds*. Pony doesn't, in general, enforce termination — actors can loop forever, allocate unboundedly, etc. For an eBPF-style use case you need some way to bound resource consumption of the uploaded code. This probably means restricting to a subset without unbounded recursion (or with structural recursion only), with bounded loops, with explicit resource limits enforced by the runtime. None of this is hard in principle but it requires designing a subset language and a verifier for that subset, which is real work.

Third, and this is the deep one, *information flow control between the uploaded code and the host service*. The uploaded code is running in the service's address space, where the service has access to all sorts of state that the client shouldn't observe. Pony's type system gives you authority discipline but doesn't, out of the box, give you information flow control — the discipline that says "the value of this variable cannot influence the value of that one." For eBPF-style cross-loading to be safe, you need *some* discipline preventing the uploaded code from leaking the service's secrets back to the client. The simplest version is structural: the uploaded code's only output is its return value, and the return value's type is restricted to things the client is allowed to learn. This is genuinely additional verification machinery that Pony doesn't provide; you'd be adding an IFC layer on top of the capability layer.

The good news is that this addition fits cleanly into the architectural story we were developing earlier in this conversation. The capability discipline (substructural, authority-focused) and the information-flow discipline (lattice-respecting, non-interference-focused) are *orthogonal*, which is exactly what Shapiro-Weber and the rest of the capability tradition acknowledged when pressed. The cross-boundary verification story makes the orthogonality concrete: capabilities handle "what can this code access," IFC handles "what can this code reveal about what it accessed," and the composition gives you the full property you need. If you were going to build the system, you'd want the IFC layer to be a separate piece, both because the disciplines compose cleanly and because IFC is genuinely harder to design well and you don't want to entangle it with the capability layer.

Where the eBPF analogy gets really interesting is in the *progressive specialization* you mentioned. You could imagine a tower where:

At the most restrictive level, cross-loaded code is essentially a sequence of capability invocations with structural data dependencies — basically a batched RPC, statically verified to be well-typed and bounded. This is the safest case and probably handles 80% of the actual performance wins (eliminating round-trips for common batched operations).

At the next level, cross-loaded code can do limited computation: structural recursion, bounded loops, pure functions on capability invocation results. Now you can push down predicates, filters, aggregations — the kind of thing you'd do with map/filter/reduce on collection-like service responses.

At the most expressive level, cross-loaded code can be arbitrary well-typed Pony (within the relevant subset), with IFC labels constraining what can flow to the output. Now you can express custom service-side logic, with the verification cost being correspondingly higher.

Each level corresponds to a stronger set of guarantees and a more restrictive language; the client picks the level appropriate to what it's trying to do. This is a much richer design space than BPF currently inhabits, because BPF is essentially "one level: heavily restricted, lots of helpers," whereas the Pony version could have a real tower of expressiveness/verification trade-offs.

Now the harder questions I want to flag, because I think they're where this kind of design actually founders if it's not handled carefully.

**Compilation and trust.** Pony's safety properties depend on the compiler's correctness. seL4 has been formally verified; the Pony compiler has not. For the cross-loading case, you'd be trusting the Pony compiler to verify code that runs in trusted address spaces, which means the compiler is now in your TCB. This is a real problem: you'd want either a verified compiler (à la CompCert, which is a multi-year project for any non-trivial language), or a verification step on the compiled output (carrying the type derivation alongside the binary and re-checking, in some Proof-Carrying Code style). Neither is impossible but both are significant work, and "we'll just use the Pony compiler" understates the trust requirement.

**Runtime in the TCB.** Pony has a runtime — actor scheduler, garbage collector, message queues. For a system where Pony is the user-level lingua franca, the runtime is in every process; for cross-loaded code, the runtime is shared between trust domains. Pony's runtime is more complex than seL4's verified kernel, and it's not verified. Reducing the runtime to a minimum, or verifying it, becomes important. There's some work on this in the Pony community but it's not at production scale.

**Capability revocation.** seL4 handles revocation through the CDT (capability derivation tree); when a capability is revoked, all derived capabilities are also revoked, atomically, from the kernel's perspective. Pony's type-level capability discipline has no concept of revocation — once you've type-checked a program, the witness is "valid" forever from the type system's perspective. For services that need to revoke authority (e.g., closing a file handle, terminating a session), you need a runtime mechanism — typically a level of indirection through a token that can be invalidated — that lives alongside the type-level discipline. This is solvable (it's basically the membrane pattern from ocap, or the sealer/unsealer trick) but it adds runtime cost and design complexity, and it means that "type system encodes authority" is not the whole story — there's a runtime layer for the dynamic parts.

**Inter-language interop.** A real system has C libraries, drivers, hardware abstractions written in unsafe languages. The Pony FFI lets you call C, but every FFI call is a hole in the type discipline. For a Pony-on-seL4 system to actually be deployable, you need a discipline for FFI that preserves the capability guarantees, which probably means structured wrappers around C libraries that re-impose the type-level discipline at the FFI boundary. This is doable but it's a lot of work and it's where the real engineering effort would go.

What I think is genuinely promising about the overall direction is that it's the first design I can think of that could *unify* the hardware-mediated capability discipline (seL4) with the language-mediated capability discipline (Pony) into a single coherent architecture where the discipline is enforced at the appropriate granularity at each level. seL4-only designs end up with everything being a process boundary, which has performance costs; Pony-only designs (running on Linux or whatever) end up with the type system protecting against accidental misuse but not against malicious code outside the type system's reach. The combination potentially gets you both: hardware enforcement where you need it for adversarial separation, language enforcement where you need it for fine-grained intra-process discipline, with explicit cross-boundary mechanisms (the eBPF-style cross-loading) for performance optimization where the language guarantees are strong enough to substitute for hardware enforcement.

The honest assessment is that no one has built this, the engineering would be substantial (multi-year, multi-person), and several of the harder pieces (verified Pony compiler, runtime minimization, IFC layer, FFI discipline) are themselves significant research problems rather than just engineering. But the architectural story is coherent in a way that most "secure microkernel + safe language" sketches aren't, because it's grounded in the recognition that both seL4 and Pony are doing the *same kind of thing* at different scales, and the composition leverages that rather than fighting it. That's a thesis-worth-of-work observation, and if you ever wanted to pick up the unfinished PhD with a new direction, this is a research program that has genuine intellectual depth and would produce real artifacts.
